# Where is the Copilot Prompt Gallery? Prompt length, system prompts and prompt engineers
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/copilot-prompt-gallery-and-prompt-length/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

The Copilot Prompt Gallery is Microsoft's collection of ready-made prompts for Microsoft 365 Copilot, organised by app, task and role, which you can open from the Copilot app or on the web, try and save. This page explains where to find it and why prompting matters so much for Copilot, then answers practical questions about length: how long a prompt, a system prompt, Claude's own system prompt and a creative writing prompt should be. It ends with how long it takes to learn prompt engineering and what prompt engineers do, including in India. Where is the Copilot Prompt Gallery? The Copilot Prompt Gallery is available in the Microsoft 365 Copilot app and on the web, and you can also open it from Copilot inside apps such as Word, Teams and Outlook, often through a "view prompts" option. It was previously called Copilot Lab. Also asked as: where copilot prompt gallery In the gallery you can filter prompts by app, such as Excel or Teams, by task, such as summarise or create, and by role. You can save your favourite prompts and, in many organisations, share prompts with colleagues. Using it is a fast way to learn what Copilot can do: try a prompt as written, then adapt it with your own files and goals. Availability depends on your licence and organisation settings. Why is prompt engineering important for Copilot? Copilot answers from your organisation's content, so a good prompt tells it what you want, which content to use and what form the answer should take. Vague prompts make Copilot search broadly and guess. Microsoft's guidance on Copilot prompts centres on four elements: the goal, the context, the source to use, and your expectations for the answer. For example, "Summarise the decisions from yesterday's project sync meeting and the follow-up email from the client, as five bullet points with owners" works far better than "what happened yesterday?". Referencing specific files, people or meetings directly improves grounding. Good prompts also reduce errors, because Copilot has less room to fill gaps with assumptions. How long should a prompt be? As long as needed to be clear, and no longer. A simple question can be one line; a complex task may need a few paragraphs with context, constraints, examples and the output format. Clarity matters more than length. Rules of thumb: Include the goal, audience, constraints and format. Add the material to work on, such as a document or data, which can be long. Use examples when format matters. Remove repeated or contradictory instructions. Put the most important instruction clearly, not buried in the middle. Models accept very long inputs, but a long prompt full of loosely related text can dilute what matters. If a prompt keeps growing, split the task into steps. How long is too long for a system prompt? There is no fixed limit, since modern models accept long system prompts, but a system prompt is too long when instructions start contradicting each other, important rules get lost among details, or performance on your test cases stops improving as you add more. Signs to trim: the model ignores some rules, behaviour changes unpredictably when you add instructions, or most lines cover rare edge cases. Better structure helps: clear sections for role, rules, tools and output format; examples only where they change behaviour; and moving reference material into retrieval or attached documents rather than the system prompt. Measure with an evaluation set when you add or remove instructions, rather than guessing. How long is Claude's system prompt? Anthropic publishes the system prompts used in its Claude apps in its documentation's release notes. They are long, detailed documents covering behaviour, formatting, tool use and safety, and they change as new models and features are released. These published prompts apply to Claude's own apps, such as claude.ai and the mobile apps, not to the Claude API, where developers write their own system prompts. Reading them is a useful lesson in how a production assistant is specified: clear sections, explicit guidance on edge cases, and descriptions of available tools. They also explain why the same model can behave somewhat differently in the app and through the API. How long is a writing prompt? A creative writing prompt is usually short, a sentence or two, sometimes a single line or image, designed to spark ideas rather than specify the piece. Prompts for school or exams may add requirements such as word count, form or audience. When you give a writing task to an AI model, a longer brief usually works better than a short spark: describe the genre, audience, tone, length, point of view and anything to avoid, and include an example of the style you like. For your own practice, short prompts are best, because they leave room for your ideas. If you are learning to write, use AI for feedback on your drafts rather than for producing the piece. How long is a prompt engineering course? Short courses take one to a few hours, such as free courses on prompting for developers. Broader courses that include building applications with LLMs, retrieval and evaluation take several weeks part-time. Also asked as: how long is prompt engineering course Course length matters less than practice. A practical path: a few hours on an official prompting guide and a short course, then two to four weeks building one small application, such as a document Q&amp;A bot or an extraction tool, with a test set to measure improvements. Look for recently updated courses, because techniques change as models improve, and prefer ones that include structured outputs and evaluation, not just prompt templates. How long does it take to master prompt engineering? The basics take days. Being genuinely skilled, able to design prompts for real applications, measure them, and handle edge cases, takes months of building and evaluating, and it keeps evolving as models change. What mastery looks like in practice: you can write clear specifications, choose between prompting, retrieval and fine-tuning, design structured outputs, write tool descriptions for agents, build evaluation sets, and diagnose failures from logs. Those skills come from shipping projects. Keep a log of prompts, results and changes for each project; reviewing what worked and why builds judgement faster than reading prompt lists. What are prompt engineers? Prompt engineers design, test and refine the instructions, examples and context that make AI models produce reliable results for specific tasks, often inside products. Today the work is usually part of broader roles such as AI engineer, GenAI developer or conversation designer. Day to day, they write system prompts and tool descriptions, build test sets, run evaluations, analyse failures, and collaborate with domain experts and engineers. In companies building AI products, the skill matters, but standalone "prompt engineer" titles are less common than at first, because the work blends into AI engineering. Students should pair prompting skills with programming, retrieval and evaluation to be employable. How many prompt engineers are there in India? There is no reliable public count, because prompt engineering is rarely a separate job title and is usually part of roles such as AI engineer, data scientist or GenAI developer. Job platforms show many listings mentioning prompt engineering as a skill. What is clear is that demand for people who can build with generative AI is growing in India across startups, IT services firms and product companies. For students, the useful question is not how many prompt engineers exist, but which skills employers ask for: Python, LLM APIs, retrieval-augmented generation, evaluation, deployment and communication. Build a project that demonstrates those, and you will match far more roles than a "prompt engineer" title alone.

# Copilot vs GitHub Copilot: the difference, model updates and limits
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/copilot-vs-github-copilot/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

Microsoft Copilot and GitHub Copilot share a name but do different jobs. Microsoft Copilot is a general AI assistant for questions, writing and Office work; GitHub Copilot is a coding assistant inside VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains IDEs and GitHub itself. This page explains the difference, how new models such as Anthropic's Claude Fable reach Copilot, why Copilot is sometimes wrong, what to do when it seems broken, its usage limits and history, where Copilot Studio agents live, and how GitHub Copilot compares with Cursor, Windsurf and Antigravity. Copilot vs GitHub Copilot: what is the difference? Microsoft Copilot is a general assistant for questions, writing, images and Microsoft 365 work. GitHub Copilot is a coding assistant: completions as you type, chat about your code, and agents that edit files and open pull requests. Also asked as: vs copilot github They use different accounts and plans. Microsoft Copilot signs in with a Microsoft account or a work account; GitHub Copilot signs in with a GitHub account, and GitHub offers a free tier plus paid individual and organisation plans. Their context is different too. Microsoft Copilot sees the web and, for work accounts, your Microsoft 365 files. GitHub Copilot sees your open files, your repository and, on GitHub, issues and pull requests. If your question is about code, use GitHub Copilot or another coding tool, because a general assistant does not see your project. Will Copilot get Fable? Possibly, but only GitHub can say. GitHub Copilot already offers a model picker with models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, and new models are added through announcements on the GitHub changelog. Claude Fable is Anthropic's newest and most capable generally available model tier, above Opus. Whether and when a model appears in Copilot depends on agreements between GitHub and the model provider, and new models often arrive first for some plans or in preview. The reliable way to know is to watch the GitHub changelog and open the model picker in Copilot Chat in your editor. Organisation admins may also have to enable a new model in Copilot policies before members can select it. Microsoft Copilot, the consumer assistant, does not let you pick a model in the same way. Will Copilot get better? Yes, in the sense that the models and features improve with each update, as they have since launch. It will not stop needing review: better models make fewer mistakes, not zero. Most improvements come from three places: stronger underlying models, better retrieval of the right context, such as indexing your whole repository, and agent features that let Copilot check its own work by running tests or builds. You can improve results today without waiting. Keep files and functions small and clearly named, add a .github/copilot-instructions.md file with your project's conventions, give precise requests, and include the error message or failing test when you ask for a fix. Is Copilot ever wrong? Yes. Copilot can state wrong facts confidently, cite sources that do not say what it claims, and suggest code that compiles but has bugs or security problems. That is a property of language models, not a fault in your setup. Habits that catch most errors: Open the citations behind any factual claim you plan to reuse. Run the code and its tests; never merge a suggestion you have not executed. Ask "what could be wrong with this?" for an independent check. Be extra careful with dates, numbers, API names and library versions, which models often get wrong. In my own RAG work the fix for confident errors was a confidence gate that refuses to answer on weak evidence. As a user, your version of that gate is checking before you trust. What is wrong with Copilot today? If Copilot stops responding or gives errors suddenly, check the service status first: GitHub Status for GitHub Copilot and the Microsoft 365 service health or status page for Microsoft Copilot. If the status pages are green, work through the usual causes. Sign out and in again, because expired sessions are common. Update the editor extension, since old versions break when the service changes. Check whether you hit a usage limit for the month or for a premium model. On a work or college network, a proxy or firewall may block the Copilot endpoints; try another network to confirm. In an organisation, an admin policy may have disabled a feature or model. Finally, check the extension's output log in VS Code, which usually names the real error. How many Copilot responses do I get? It depends on the product and plan. Free tiers include a monthly allowance of completions and chat requests, paid plans raise it, and the most capable models count against a separate allowance of premium requests. GitHub publishes the current allowances for each plan in its documentation, and your usage is visible in your GitHub settings. Microsoft Copilot has its own limits per conversation and per day that vary by account type and have changed several times. Quoting numbers here would date quickly, so check the plan page for the current figures. If you keep hitting limits, use a smaller model for routine edits and save the premium model for hard problems, and keep conversations focused, because one long rambling chat burns requests faster. Do Copilot conversations get deleted? Not automatically in most cases. Consumer Copilot keeps your conversation history until you delete it, and work accounts store Copilot interactions under the organisation's retention policies, which admins control. In the consumer Copilot app you can delete individual conversations or clear your history in settings. In Microsoft 365, Copilot interactions are kept in the organisation's own environment and can be retained or deleted by compliance policies, so deleting a chat from view may not remove the record your employer keeps. GitHub Copilot Chat in an editor keeps session history locally in the editor, and GitHub documents what prompt and suggestion data it retains for each plan. Never paste passwords or private keys into any assistant. Where do Copilot Studio agents get stored? Copilot Studio agents are stored in a Microsoft Power Platform environment, inside that environment's Dataverse database, together with their topics, knowledge settings and connections. That has practical effects. You choose the environment when you create the agent, and its region decides where the agent's data lives. Agents move between development, test and production environments as solutions, the same way as other Power Platform components, which is how teams version and deploy them. Knowledge files you upload are stored with the agent, while connected sources such as SharePoint sites stay where they are and are searched at question time. Access to the agent follows the environment's security roles, so plan who can edit it before you build. Can you vibe code with GitHub Copilot? Yes. Agent mode in VS Code and other editors lets you describe a feature in plain language while Copilot plans the change, edits several files, runs commands and fixes its own errors, which is vibe coding in practice. It works best for prototypes, hackathon builds and internal tools. To keep the result maintainable, start each task with a short spec, ask for tests alongside the feature, review every diff before accepting it and commit after each working step. Keep secrets in environment variables, not in prompts or code. If a session goes in circles, stop, revert to the last good commit and restate the task in smaller pieces. You should be able to explain every file in the project, because judges and interviewers will ask. GitHub Copilot vs Cursor vs Windsurf vs Antigravity: which should you use? All four are AI coding environments with chat, multi-file edits and agents. GitHub Copilot plugs into existing editors and GitHub; Cursor and Windsurf are AI-first editors built on VS Code; Antigravity is Google's agent-first development environment. How they differ in practice: GitHub Copilot: best if your team lives on GitHub and wants enterprise controls, issue-to-pull-request agents and support for VS Code, Visual Studio and JetBrains. Cursor: a polished AI-native editor with strong codebase-wide context and fast multi-file edits. Windsurf: an AI-native editor with an agent called Cascade; now owned by Cognition. Antigravity: built around agents that plan and run tasks across the editor, terminal and browser, with Gemini models. Pick by trying one real task, such as adding an endpoint with tests, in each.

# Data analyst vs machine learning engineer vs AI engineer: what each job actually does, the skill overlap, and which path fits you
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/data-analyst-vs-ai-ml-engineer-career-path/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is the difference between a data analyst, an ML engineer, and an AI engineer?

**A data analyst answers business questions using data that already exists: what happened, why, and what it suggests, delivered as a dashboard, a report, or a recommendation. A machine learning engineer builds, trains and ships predictive models: forecasting, classification, recommendation, and takes ownership of getting a model into production and monitored. An AI engineer, increasingly synonymous with GenAI engineer, builds products on top of models, often via API rather than training from scratch, RAG systems, agents, AI features inside a larger application. The tools overlap heavily; the deliverable at the end of the day is what actually differs.**


I get this question constantly from BCA and B.Tech students choosing a direction, because all three paths are taught with overlapping tools in the same few semesters, and the job titles in the market are inconsistent enough to add to the confusion [4].

> Three different jobs can share the same first two years of learning and diverge completely in year three. Know which deliverable you actually want to own before you specialise.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What does a data analyst actually do day to day?

**Pulls data with SQL, cleans and shapes it in Python or a spreadsheet tool, builds dashboards in something like Power BI or Tableau, and answers specific business questions, why did signups drop last month, which channel drives the most retained users. The core skill is turning a vague business question into a precise data question and a clear answer a non-technical stakeholder can act on. Little to no model training; the value is in analysis and communication, not in building systems.**


## What does a machine learning engineer actually do day to day?

**Prepares and validates training data, trains and evaluates models, builds the pipeline that retrains and serves a model in production, and monitors it for drift once it is live. Deep Python, a real understanding of the modelling techniques being used, and increasingly MLOps skills, versioning, deployment, monitoring, because a model that works once in a notebook and a model that keeps working in production under changing data are different achievements entirely.**




## What does an AI or GenAI engineer actually do day to day?

**Builds features on top of existing models rather than training them from scratch in most cases: RAG systems, agents, document extraction pipelines, evaluation suites, and the production code, APIs, validation, logging, that turns a model call into a reliable product feature [5]. The skill that separates this role from a hobbyist prompt-writer is the same discipline an ML engineer applies to a trained model, applied instead to a system built around calls to someone else's model: measured evaluation, validated outputs, monitored production behaviour.**


## Where do the skills overlap, and where do they diverge?

**SQL and Python are near-universal across all three. Statistics and basic modelling concepts show up everywhere, though depth differs sharply. The divergence starts at "what happens with the result": a data analyst's output is a decision someone else acts on; an ML engineer's output is a model running in a pipeline they own; an AI engineer's output is a feature end users touch directly, often without ever training a model themselves. Knowing which of those three endings you actually want to be responsible for is the real decision, more than any specific tool choice.**



## How do I get my first role in each path?

**For a data analyst role: two or three real analyses of public or personal datasets, written up as a decision a stakeholder could act on, not just a chart. For an ML engineer role: one model you trained, evaluated honestly, and deployed, with monitoring, not just a notebook with a good accuracy number. For an AI engineer role: one shipped product using a model, RAG, an agent, an extraction pipeline, with measured evaluation and real users or a realistic test set [6][7]. Each portfolio proves the specific deliverable that role actually owns.**



## Can I move between these paths later?

**Yes, and it is common. A data analyst who learns to train and deploy models moves toward ML engineering. An ML engineer who starts building API-driven product features moves toward AI engineering. The underlying skills, data handling, statistics, evaluation discipline, Python, compound across all three rather than being wasted if you switch. Pick the path that matches what you want to build right now, and treat the switch as a realistic option later rather than a wall.**



## Interview questions across these three paths

**Every one of these roles gets asked "walk me through a project", and the strongest answer matches the role: a data analyst should describe the decision their analysis drove; an ML engineer should describe how they evaluated and monitored their model; an AI engineer should describe how they measured whether their shipped feature actually worked. Confusing which deliverable you are being asked about is the most common way a strong candidate gives a weak answer.**



## Where should I start?

**Write one sentence for each path: the decision, the model, or the feature you would want to be responsible for. Whichever sentence excites you most is the direction to build your next project toward.** For a career session that helps students choose between data, ML and AI engineering paths honestly, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# Dev.to vs Hashnode vs Medium vs your own blog: where should a developer actually write in 2026?
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/dev-to-vs-hashnode-vs-medium-for-developers/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## Where should a developer write in 2026: Dev.to, Hashnode or Medium?

**Your own domain first, for ownership and search equity; Dev.to second, for the fastest path to an engaged developer reader and a free posting API; Hashnode third, if you want a free custom-domain blog, though its API now sits behind a paid plan; Medium last, or not at all, because its paywall and algorithm work against an unknown technical writer. Publish on your own site, then syndicate to Dev.to with a canonical link back. That single habit captures most of the benefit of all four platforms.**


I publish across all of these plus my own site, and the pattern below is what actually moved readers and search rankings, not what each platform promises in its marketing [8][9].

> A platform can promote your post for a week. A domain you own compounds for years.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What is Dev.to, and who is it for?

**A community-run publishing platform for developers, built on the open-source Forem software, with tags, reactions, comments and a genuinely active audience of working developers [1]. Its posting API is free, which makes it the natural platform to auto-publish to alongside your own site. Discovery happens through tags and the community feed rather than search, so a Dev.to post's first burst of readers comes from people who follow the tag, not from Google, though good posts do get indexed and found later [2].**


## What is Hashnode, and what changed with its API?

**A blogging platform built specifically for developers, with a free custom domain from day one, clean themes, and good default SEO, which made it a favourite for a personal tech blog without hosting to manage [3]. As of 2026 its programmatic posting API sits behind a paid plan, which matters if your workflow is automated publishing rather than writing by hand in its editor; manual posting through the dashboard remains free. If you write by hand and want a free-domain blog, it is still a solid choice; if you automate, check current pricing before building on it.**



## What is Medium, and should I bother with it?

**A general publishing platform with a metered paywall, a recommendation algorithm, and the Partner Program for earning from reads [4]. For an unknown technical writer, both work against you: the paywall costs some readers a click, and the algorithm favours engagement patterns that generic, punchy writing produces more than technical depth. Medium can still work if you already have an audience elsewhere, or if you want a specific piece to reach non-developer readers a technical platform would not. As a default home for developer writing, it is not the strongest choice in 2026.**


## Why does my own domain matter more than any platform?

**Because search rankings, backlinks and reader trust accumulate on the domain the content lives on, and that domain is the one thing a platform cannot take from you, change the rules on, or shut down. A post on your own site under your name builds your search presence for years; the same words on a platform mostly build the platform's. Google's canonical URL system exists precisely so the same content can appear in several places while search credit flows to one chosen original [5]. Choose your own site as that original.**



## What is syndication, and how do I do it properly?

**Publish the full post on your own site first. Then post the same content, or a shortened version with a link, on Dev.to and Hashnode, setting the canonical URL field to your original where the platform supports it, which tells search engines your site is the source [5]. Wait a day or two before syndicating so your own site gets indexed first. This way each platform brings you readers who click through, while your domain keeps the search credit.**



## Which should I pick if I can only maintain one?

**Your own site if you can spare an afternoon to set it up on a free host, because everything else follows from having a home. If you genuinely cannot maintain a personal site yet, Dev.to alone, for the free API and the community, is the single best substitute, and you can add your own domain later without losing the posts, since they stay live on Dev.to regardless.**




## What mistakes do developers make with technical writing platforms?

**Writing only on Medium and wondering why nobody in the developer community sees it. Cross-posting without a canonical link and accidentally competing with your own original for search rankings. Building an automated pipeline around an API that then moves behind a paywall, without a fallback. Spreading across five platforms and maintaining none well. Never writing on a domain you control, so years of writing build someone else's audience instead of yours.**



## Where should I start?

**If you do not have a personal site yet, start there this week; if you do, publish your next post on it first and syndicate to Dev.to the same day.** For a session on building a writing habit that compounds into a career, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# Do you actually need a GPU for AI? A plain VRAM and hardware guide for students: what runs on a laptop, what needs to be rented, and what needs neither
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/do-you-need-a-gpu-for-ai-vram-and-hardware-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## Do I actually need a GPU for AI work?

**Usually not, for most of what a student does. Calling a model through an API, ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, needs no GPU at all; the provider's hardware does the generation, and your laptop only sends and receives text. The case that genuinely needs a GPU with real VRAM is running or fine-tuning an open-weight model locally, and even then, free cloud notebooks or an hourly rented GPU usually cover it without buying anything.**


Most of the production systems I run are API-first specifically to avoid this question entirely for the majority of the workload; the GPU question only comes up for the specific slice that touches an open model directly.

> Buy a GPU for the project that actually needs one, not for the fear that every AI project might.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What actually needs GPU memory, and what doesn't?

**Using a hosted model API: no GPU needed. Running a small open model locally for inference, chatting with a 7 to 8 billion parameter model through Ollama: modest VRAM, often fits on a good consumer GPU or even a strong CPU with patience. Fine-tuning a small to medium open model with LoRA or QLoRA: meaningful VRAM, but far less than full fine-tuning thanks to quantization [5]. Training a model from scratch: serious VRAM and usually multiple GPUs, essentially never a student's first project.**



## How much VRAM does a given model actually need?

**Roughly, for inference, a model needs about the number of parameters times the bytes per parameter: a 7 billion parameter model at 16-bit precision needs roughly 14 GB just to hold the weights, before accounting for the activation memory a request also uses. Quantizing to 8-bit roughly halves that, and to 4-bit roughly quarters it, which is why a model that needs 14 GB at full precision can often run in under 5 GB quantized [1][7]. Fine-tuning needs more on top of the base weights for gradients and optimiser state, which is exactly the memory pressure QLoRA was built to reduce [5].**



## What free options exist before I rent or buy anything?

**Google Colab's free tier gives a shared GPU with real, if variable, availability, enough for learning, small experiments, and light fine-tuning runs [2]. Kaggle offers free GPU and TPU hours on notebooks tied to your account, with a generous weekly quota [3]. Both are enough to complete most course exercises, small fine-tuning projects, and learning experiments without spending anything; the free tiers only become the bottleneck once a project needs sustained, guaranteed access or more memory than the free tier's GPU offers.**



## When should I rent a cloud GPU instead of using a free tier?

**When a task needs more VRAM or more sustained, guaranteed time than a free tier reliably offers, a bigger fine-tuning run, a longer training job, or repeated runs where waiting on shared free-tier availability costs more time than the rental costs money. Services that rent GPUs by the hour make this cheap for occasional use: a few hours of a mid-range GPU for a real fine-tuning experiment typically costs less than a two-week wait on an oversubscribed free tier [6].**



## When does buying a personal GPU actually make sense?

**When you run GPU-heavy work often enough that the cumulative cost of renting exceeds a GPU's price within a reasonable time, or when you specifically need a persistent local setup for reasons free and rented options do not cover, offline work, specific hardware experiments, or teaching others hands-on. For most students, this point arrives much later than the anxiety about needing a GPU does; do not buy hardware to solve a problem a free tier or an hour of rental already solves.**



## What mistakes do students make about GPU hardware?

**Assuming every AI project needs a GPU, when most API-based work needs none. Buying hardware before hitting an actual limit on free tiers. Ignoring quantization and assuming a model needs its full-precision memory footprint. Renting a much larger GPU than a quantized, LoRA-adapted fine-tuning run actually requires, paying for headroom nobody used. Never checking a model's actual memory footprint before assuming a task is impossible on the hardware already available.**


## GPU and hardware interview questions

**Explain what determines a model's memory footprint at inference time. Explain how quantization changes that footprint and its trade-offs. Describe when you would use an API instead of running a model locally. Explain the difference in memory needs between inference and fine-tuning. Describe how you would size a GPU rental for a specific fine-tuning job. The strongest answer includes a specific memory calculation you did for a real project.**



## Where should I start?

**Before assuming a project needs a GPU, check whether an API already covers it. If it genuinely needs a local model, try a quantized version on Colab's free tier first, and only look at renting once you hit a real limit.** For a hands-on session on right-sizing AI infrastructure for student budgets, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# Does OCR use AI? OCR and neural networks, ChatGPT, and OCR in Word
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/does-ocr-use-ai/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

Yes, modern OCR uses AI. Today's optical character recognition relies on neural networks to find text in images and recognise it, and often on language models to fix likely errors; older OCR used hand-written rules and templates. OCR is part of computer vision, a branch of AI. This page explains OCR's relationship to AI and neural networks, why people sometimes do not count it as AI, how ChatGPT reads text in images, when to use OCR, and how to OCR images and scanned PDFs with Word and free tools. Does OCR use AI? Yes. Modern OCR engines use machine learning: neural networks detect text regions and recognise characters and words, trained on large sets of text images. Many also use language models to choose the most likely words when characters are unclear. Examples: Tesseract, the widely used open-source engine, uses an LSTM neural network for recognition; cloud OCR services from Google, Microsoft and Amazon use deep learning for layout and text; and newer document models and vision-language models read whole pages directly. This is why OCR now handles varied fonts, photos and some handwriting. AI also means errors can look plausible, so validation remains important for documents that matter. Is OCR part of AI? Yes. OCR belongs to computer vision, the area of AI that interprets images, and to document AI, which extracts structured information from documents. Recognising text from pixels is a classic pattern-recognition problem that AI research worked on for decades. OCR was one of the earliest practical successes of AI and machine learning, used in postal sorting and bank cheque processing long before today's chatbots. Modern document AI goes further than reading text: it understands layout, classifies document types and extracts fields such as dates and totals. DocuLens AI, for example, extracts fields from invoices and contracts with an LLM and validates them against a schema before scoring compliance. Does OCR use neural networks? Modern OCR does. Typical systems use convolutional networks to extract visual features, recurrent or transformer layers to read sequences of characters, and a decoding method such as CTC to turn predictions into text. Detection networks find where text lines are. Older OCR, before deep learning, used feature engineering and template matching, which worked for clean printed fonts but struggled with photos and handwriting. Neural networks learn from examples instead of hand-made rules, which is why accuracy improved sharply. The newest approach, vision-language models, uses a single large transformer that sees the page image and generates text or structured output. Why is OCR sometimes not seen as a good example of AI? Because of the "AI effect": once a technology works reliably and becomes ordinary, people stop calling it intelligence. OCR is everywhere, in scanners, phones and banking, so it feels like a utility rather than AI, even though it is a machine learning application. Also asked as: why can&#x27;t ocr be perceived as a good example of ai There is also a fair technical point: classic OCR performs a narrow perception task, recognising characters, without understanding what the text means. Many people reserve "AI" for systems that reason or generate. Modern document AI blurs that line, since vision-language models both read and understand documents. For exam answers, a balanced view is that OCR is a mature example of narrow AI, specifically pattern recognition, rather than general intelligence. Which OCR does ChatGPT use? ChatGPT reads text in images with its vision-capable models, which process images directly and generate text about them, including transcriptions. OpenAI does not present a separate OCR engine for this, and it does not publish the internal details. In practice, ChatGPT reads clear printed text well, handles many layouts and some handwriting, and can turn tables into Markdown. It may misread small, blurry or unusual text, and like any generative model it can occasionally produce plausible but wrong characters, especially numbers. For long documents or precise extraction, dedicated OCR or document AI services with page references are more reliable, and you should check important values against the original. When should I use OCR? Use OCR whenever text exists only as an image and you need to search, copy, edit, translate, analyse or feed it to software: scanned documents, photos of notes, screenshots, image-only PDFs, receipts and forms. Common uses: Making scanned archives and old PDFs searchable. Turning printed or handwritten notes into editable text. Extracting data from invoices, receipts and forms into spreadsheets. Preparing documents for RAG chatbots, which need text. Accessibility: making images of text readable by screen readers. You do not need OCR for documents that already contain selectable text, such as most digitally created PDFs; extracting their text directly is faster and more accurate. How do I OCR in Word? Word does not run OCR on pictures inside a document. To get text from an image, use OneNote's copy-text-from-picture feature, the Windows Snipping Tool's text actions, or Google Lens, then paste into Word. For scanned PDFs, open the PDF in Word, which converts it into an editable document. Also asked as: how to ocr in word For a single picture, OneNote is the quickest: insert the image into a page, right-click it and choose the option to copy text from the picture, then paste into Word. Word's PDF conversion works best on clear, simple layouts; complex tables and multi-column pages often need fixing afterwards. For many documents, a dedicated OCR tool and then pasting into Word is faster than repairing a messy conversion. How do I OCR an image into Word? Extract the text first, then paste it into Word: use OneNote's copy text from picture, the Snipping Tool's text actions on Windows, Live Text on a Mac or iPhone, or Google Lens on Android or in the browser. Also asked as: how to ocr image in word Steps with the Snipping Tool on Windows: Open the image and take a snip of the text area, or open the image in the Snipping Tool. Use the text actions button to detect text. Copy all text and paste it into Word. Fix formatting and check names and numbers. For a whole page with structure, an AI assistant can transcribe it into headings and lists, which you then paste into Word. Keep the original image in case you need to check a word later. Can OCR convert a scanned PDF to an editable Word document? Yes. Word can open a scanned PDF and convert it to an editable document, Adobe Acrobat exports scanned PDFs to Word with OCR, and Google Docs runs OCR when you open a PDF or image from Google Drive. Also asked as: can ocr convert scanned pdf to editable word Quality depends on scan quality and layout. Plain text pages convert well; tables, columns, stamps and handwriting need checking. For best results, rescan at good resolution if possible, straighten pages and choose the correct language. If you only need searchable text rather than an editable layout, make a searchable PDF instead, for example with OCRmyPDF, and keep the original appearance. Can you convert a PDF to Word for free with OCR? Yes. Free options include opening the PDF in Microsoft Word if you have it, uploading it to Google Drive and opening it with Google Docs, and free tools such as OCRmyPDF to make the PDF searchable before converting. Also asked as: can you convert pdf to word free with ocr With Google Drive: upload the PDF, right-click, choose Open with Google Docs, and Drive runs OCR and creates an editable document, which you can download as a Word file. It works best for text-heavy pages and keeps limited formatting. Avoid uploading confidential documents to unknown free converter websites; prefer tools from Microsoft, Google, Adobe or offline open-source software for anything personal or sensitive.

# What is engineering in college? Admission, difficulty and how to do well
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/engineering-in-college-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

Engineering in college means a degree programme, usually a four-year BTech or BE in India, where you learn mathematics, science and the design of systems in a branch such as computer science, electronics, mechanical or civil engineering. The first year covers shared foundations, later years go deep into your branch with labs, electives, internships and a final project. This page explains how engineering colleges are organised, how admission works, when classes start, how hard it is, how to do well, what NSS is, and how to write your first resume. What is engineering in college? Engineering in college is a professional degree, typically a four-year BTech or BE, that teaches you to apply maths and science to design, build and maintain systems, from software and circuits to machines and buildings. The structure is similar across most colleges. The first year has common subjects such as mathematics, physics or chemistry, basic programming, engineering drawing and workshops. From the second year you focus on your branch: for computer science that means data structures, algorithms, databases, operating systems, networks and electives such as AI. Each semester mixes theory classes, lab sessions and internal assessments, ending with university exams. Summer internships and a final-year project complete the degree. Clubs, hackathons and technical festivals run alongside and often teach the most practical skills. Can you study engineering in college? Yes. Engineering is studied at engineering colleges, institutes of technology and universities. In India you need class 12 with physics, chemistry and maths, and you usually enter through an entrance exam and counselling. You can study engineering at IITs, NITs, IIITs, government and private engineering colleges, and private and deemed universities. Diploma holders can often join a BTech in the second year through lateral entry. If you did not take maths in class 12, a BTech is generally not open to you, but software careers still are through a BCA or BSc in computer science. I took the BCA route and still went on to ship production AI applications, so the door to tech is wider than the BTech alone. Is an engineering college a college or a university? Usually a college. Most engineering colleges in India are affiliated to a university, which sets the syllabus, conducts exams and awards the degree. Some institutions, such as IITs, NITs and deemed universities, award their own degrees. Also asked as: is engineering college or university The difference affects you in practical ways. In an affiliated college, the university fixes the syllabus and exam schedule, so the college has less freedom to update courses. Autonomous colleges set their own syllabus and exams while the university still awards the degree. Institutes of national importance and universities design everything themselves. Check that a college is approved by AICTE for technical programmes and that its university is recognised by the UGC before you join. How do I get admission to an engineering college? Take the entrance exams for the colleges you want, register for counselling, and choose colleges and branches in order of preference. Seats are allotted by rank, category and your choices. Also asked as: how to get admission in engineering college The main routes in India: JEE Main: for NITs, IIITs and many other colleges, and the qualifier for JEE Advanced. JEE Advanced: for the IITs. JoSAA counselling: allots seats at IITs, NITs, IIITs and other centrally funded institutes. State entrance exams and counselling: for state government and private colleges. Institute exams: some private universities, such as BITS, run their own. Keep documents ready: class 10 and 12 mark sheets, category certificates if applicable, and ID proof. Read the official brochure for each exam, because eligibility and dates change. When does engineering college start? First-year engineering classes in India usually start between July and September, after entrance results and counselling rounds finish. Senior batches typically resume earlier in July or August. The exact date depends on the counselling schedule. IITs and NITs start once JoSAA rounds end; state colleges follow their own counselling calendars, which can run later. Many colleges hold an induction programme in the first week or two, covering orientation, clubs, mentoring and basics such as programming. Use the gap between class 12 results and the start of college well: learn basic Python, set up a GitHub account and build one tiny project. You will start ahead of most of your batch. Is engineering in college hard? Engineering is demanding: there is a lot of maths, many subjects each semester, labs, assignments and exams. It is manageable with steady work, and most difficulty comes from falling behind rather than from the material itself. The first year is often the hardest adjustment because study habits from school do not transfer: classes move faster and you are expected to practise on your own. Subjects such as engineering mathematics, data structures and circuits need regular problem solving, not last-minute reading. Study in groups, solve previous years' papers, ask teachers and seniors early, and keep up with labs every week. Balance matters too: students who join one club and one project usually do better than those who only study or only do events. How do I excel in engineering college? Keep your marks steady, but put your extra time into skills that compound: programming, projects, internships, hackathons and people. Those decide your options at graduation more than a small difference in grades. Also asked as: how to excel in engineering college A four-year plan that works: Year 1: fundamentals, one programming language, GitHub, a small project. Year 2: data structures and algorithms, a club or community, your first hackathon. Year 3: one serious project in the area you want to work in, and an internship. Year 4: placement preparation, a polished portfolio, or a startup if you have a real problem to solve. This is the roadmap I share with first-year students: foundations and AI tools first, then hackathons and internships, then placements or a startup. Does the engineering college matter? It matters for the first opportunities: top colleges attract more recruiters, stronger peers and better alumni networks. After your first job or two, skills and work history matter far more than the college name. Also asked as: does engineering college matter For software roles in particular, a student from a lesser-known college with deployed projects, an internship and hackathon results can compete with students from well-known colleges. What the college gives you is environment, so if yours is weaker, build your own: join online communities, contribute to open source, travel to hackathons and find mentors. Choose a college with good faculty, active clubs and real placement data for your branch, and then make the most of whatever you join. What is NSS in engineering college? NSS is the National Service Scheme, a programme of the Government of India's Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports in which college students volunteer for community service. Most engineering colleges have an NSS unit. NSS volunteers take part in activities such as blood donation camps, cleanliness drives, literacy programmes, health awareness and special camps in villages. It builds teamwork, leadership and communication, and certificates for completed service hours are recognised by many universities. For an engineering student it is also a source of real problems: many good hackathon projects start from something seen in community work, such as a farmer's information gap or a hospital queue. Joining is voluntary and usually happens at the start of the year. What should an engineering student's resume look like? A one-page resume with your education, two or three projects with links and results, skills grouped by type, and any internships, hackathons or leadership roles. Projects carry the most weight for students. Also asked as: engineering college student resume examples A simple structure: Header: name, email, phone, GitHub, LinkedIn, portfolio link. Education: degree, college, years, CGPA if it helps. Projects: name, one line on the problem, the tech stack, what you built, a result such as users, accuracy or speed, and a live link. Experience: internships and freelance work with outcomes. Skills: languages, frameworks, tools, databases, cloud. Achievements: hackathon results, competitive programming ranks, certifications that matter. Use action verbs and real numbers. Every line should be something you can explain in an interview.

# FastAPI for AI applications: async endpoints for LLM calls, dependency injection, streaming responses, and the patterns that hold up in production
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/fastapi-for-ai-applications/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## Why is FastAPI the default choice for serving AI applications?

**Because an AI application spends most of its request time waiting on slow network calls, a model API, an embedding call, a vector database query, and FastAPI's async support means the server can handle other requests during that wait instead of blocking a whole worker thread on it [1][6]. Combined with automatic request validation from type hints, a built-in docs UI, and dependency injection for clean wiring of providers and settings, it removes most of the boilerplate a Flask-based service would need to hand-build for the same job.**


Both production systems I run day to day, a RAG platform and a document extraction service, are FastAPI applications underneath, and the async layer is not a nice-to-have, it is the difference between a server that serves five concurrent users and one that serves fifty on the same hardware [11][12].

> A synchronous web server serving LLM calls is a waiter who stands at one table until the kitchen finishes a dish, ignoring everyone else in the restaurant. Async is the waiter who takes the next order while the first dish cooks.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## How does async actually help when the model call is still slow?

**The model call itself is not made faster by async; a five-second generation still takes five seconds. What async changes is what the server does during that five seconds: instead of one worker thread sitting idle waiting for the response, `await`ing an async HTTP call to the model API frees that worker to handle other incoming requests, and resumes this one when the model's response arrives [6]. One process can then hold many concurrent slow requests in flight, which is exactly the shape of load an LLM-backed API sees.**



## What is the single most common FastAPI mistake in AI apps?

**Calling a synchronous client inside an `async def` route. If your model provider's SDK, or your database driver, does not itself support async and you call it directly inside an async route without offloading it, that call blocks the event loop exactly the way a fully synchronous server would, silently cancelling the whole benefit of using FastAPI. The fix is to use the provider's async client if one exists, or run the blocking call in a thread pool with `run_in_threadpool` so it does not block the event loop while it waits.**



## How does dependency injection fit into an AI application?

**FastAPI's dependency injection system is where the clean project structure of settings, providers, and database sessions actually gets wired into each incoming request [2]. A `get_settings()` dependency provides typed configuration; a `get_llm_client()` dependency provides the model provider instance; a `get_db_session()` dependency provides a database session scoped to the request and closed automatically afterward. Routes declare what they need as parameters, and FastAPI resolves and injects them, which keeps route functions thin and makes swapping a provider or a database a change in one place, not a search-and-replace across the codebase.**




## How do I stream LLM responses token by token?

**Return a `StreamingResponse` whose body is an async generator that yields chunks as they arrive from the model provider's streaming API, rather than collecting the full response before returning anything [4]. Most model providers expose a streaming mode over server-sent events specifically for this [5]. The user sees the answer appear progressively, which cuts perceived latency dramatically even though total generation time is unchanged, because the wait for the first token is far shorter than the wait for the whole answer.**



## When do I need background tasks versus a real task queue?

**FastAPI's built-in `BackgroundTasks` is for quick, fire-and-forget work tied to a single request's lifecycle, sending a notification email after a response is returned, with no need to track its status or retry it [3]. A real task queue, Celery or an equivalent, is for anything that needs retries, scheduling, monitoring, or to survive the web server restarting, a long document-processing job, a nightly re-embedding run, a batch of API calls that must complete even if the request that triggered them is long gone [8]. Reaching for background tasks when you actually need a queue is how "fire and forget" jobs quietly disappear when the server restarts mid-job.**



## What does a clean FastAPI layer for an AI app look like?

**Routes stay thin: parse the request, resolve dependencies, call into the application's core logic, return a response, ideally streamed. All the actual work, retrieval, generation, validation, sits in the modules described in a proper project structure, not inline in the route function [10]. Settings come from dependency injection, never read directly from the environment inside a route. Errors from the model provider are caught and translated into clean HTTP error responses, not leaked as raw provider exceptions.**



## FastAPI interview questions for AI roles

**Explain why async matters specifically for LLM-backed APIs. Describe how dependency injection would wire a swappable model provider. Explain how you would stream a model's response to a frontend. Compare BackgroundTasks with a real task queue and say when each applies. Describe the most common way a FastAPI app silently loses its async benefits. The strongest answer includes a concurrency bug you found and fixed, not just the theory.**



## Where should I start?

**Take an existing script that calls a model API and wrap it in a FastAPI route with a streaming response and one dependency for the client. An evening turns a script into a real, concurrent-capable service.** For a hands-on session on serving AI applications with FastAPI, from a script to production, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# Why is FastAPI so popular? Install, docs, ORM choices and production use
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/fastapi-guide-orm-production/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

FastAPI is a modern Python web framework for building APIs, popular because it is fast to write and fast to run: you declare inputs with Python type hints, and FastAPI validates requests, converts data and generates interactive documentation automatically. It is the backend I used across my NextUpgrad applications, including RAG.NextUpgrad and FaceVision's embeddings service. This page covers its popularity and history, installation, the docs, how it achieves performance, ORM choices, production use, how it compares with Node.js, and FastAPI Cloud. Why is FastAPI so popular? FastAPI is popular because it combines very quick development with strong correctness: type hints drive request validation, editor autocompletion and documentation, while async support gives good performance. Developers write less code and catch errors earlier. Other reasons: automatic OpenAPI documentation with interactive Swagger UI, clear error messages for invalid requests, dependency injection for things like database sessions and authentication, and excellent documentation. It also fits the AI era well: most machine learning and LLM work happens in Python, so FastAPI is the natural way to wrap models, RAG pipelines and agents in a web API. For students, its tutorial is one of the best introductions to building APIs properly. When was FastAPI invented? FastAPI was created by Sebastián Ramírez and first released in December 2018. It builds on Starlette for web handling and Pydantic for data validation. Also asked as: when fastapi invented It grew quickly over the following years as teams adopted it for machine learning services and microservices, and it became one of the most used Python web frameworks alongside Django and Flask. Its design reflected newer Python features, such as type hints and async, that older frameworks predated. The project is open source under the MIT licence and maintained on GitHub with a large community. How do I install FastAPI? Create a virtual environment, install FastAPI with its standard extras, write a small app and run it with the FastAPI CLI. Also asked as: how to install fastapi · fastapi vs nodejs pip install &quot;fastapi[standard]&quot; # main.py from fastapi import FastAPI app = FastAPI() @app.get(&quot;/health&quot;) def health(): return {&quot;status&quot;: &quot;ok&quot;} fastapi dev main.py # development server with auto-reload Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs to see the interactive documentation. For production, use fastapi run or a server setup such as Uvicorn with multiple workers behind a reverse proxy. Pin versions in a requirements.txt file, keep the virtual environment out of Git, and read settings such as database URLs from environment variables, so the same code runs on your laptop and in deployment. What are FastAPI's docs? FastAPI automatically generates an OpenAPI schema for your API and serves interactive documentation at /docs, using Swagger UI, and alternative documentation at /redoc. They update as you change your code. Also asked as: what does fastapi docs The docs list every endpoint, its parameters, request bodies and response models, derived from your type hints and Pydantic models, and let you send test requests from the browser. Add descriptions, examples and tags in your code to make them clearer. For public APIs you can disable them or protect them in production. The underlying OpenAPI schema, at /openapi.json, can generate client libraries for front ends and other services. How does FastAPI achieve high performance? FastAPI runs on ASGI, an asynchronous server interface, using Starlette and servers such as Uvicorn, so it can handle many concurrent requests efficiently when endpoints use async and non-blocking I/O. Pydantic's fast validation core adds to this. Performance in practice depends on your code: blocking calls, such as a synchronous database driver or heavy CPU work inside an async endpoint, slow everything down. Use async database drivers or define those endpoints with plain def, which FastAPI runs in a thread pool. For CPU-heavy tasks, such as running a large model, use background workers or separate model servers. Most real bottlenecks are databases and external API calls, not the framework. Does FastAPI have an ORM? No. FastAPI does not include an ORM; it leaves data access to you. Most projects use SQLModel or SQLAlchemy for SQL databases, or an ODM such as Beanie for MongoDB. Also asked as: does fastapi has orm This keeps FastAPI focused and flexible: you choose the database layer that suits your project and can use raw SQL when needed. A common pattern is a dependency that provides a database session to each request and closes it afterwards, plus Alembic for schema migrations. Keep database models separate from API schemas when they differ, so you never accidentally expose fields like password hashes in responses. What is the best ORM for FastAPI? SQLModel is the most natural choice for many projects because it is made by FastAPI's author and combines SQLAlchemy and Pydantic, so one class can serve as both the database table and the API schema. SQLAlchemy 2.0 is the most powerful and flexible option for complex applications. Choose by need: SQLModel: simple CRUD apps and learning; less boilerplate. SQLAlchemy 2.0: complex queries, large codebases, full control; async support available. Tortoise ORM: an async-first, Django-like ORM. Beanie: MongoDB with Pydantic models. Whatever you pick, use migrations with Alembic for SQL databases, connection pooling, and tests against a real database, not only mocks. Can FastAPI be used in production? Yes. FastAPI is used in production by many companies and startups for APIs and machine learning services. Production readiness depends on how you deploy and operate it, not on the framework. A production checklist: Run with fastapi run or Uvicorn workers behind a reverse proxy, or in containers. Use environment variables for configuration and secrets. Add structured logging, metrics and health checks. Validate inputs strictly and set request size and timeout limits. Handle authentication and rate limiting. Run database migrations and keep backups. Write tests with FastAPI's TestClient and run them in CI. RAG.NextUpgrad and my other NextUpgrad apps shipped this way, with Docker, CI/CD, structured logging and metrics. FastAPI vs Node.js: which should I use? Use FastAPI when your backend is close to Python's ecosystem, such as machine learning, data processing, RAG and AI agents. Use Node.js when your team works in JavaScript or TypeScript across front end and back end, or you rely on its large web ecosystem. Both handle high concurrency well with async I/O. Node.js frameworks such as Express, Fastify and NestJS are mature and widely used; TypeScript gives strong typing comparable to FastAPI's type hints. FastAPI's automatic validation and docs are excellent out of the box. Many teams use both: a Next.js front end with its own server routes, and a FastAPI service for AI features, communicating over a clean API. Is FastAPI Cloud free? FastAPI Cloud is a deployment platform from the team behind FastAPI, introduced to make deploying FastAPI apps simple. Its availability, plans and any free tier depend on its current offering, so check its official website. FastAPI itself is free and open source, and you can deploy it on many platforms with free tiers for small projects, such as container hosts and serverless platforms that support Python. For student projects, a free tier on a platform such as Render, Railway or a cloud provider's free allowance is usually enough. Watch for cold starts on free tiers, keep secrets in environment variables, and add a health endpoint so the platform can check your app.

# How to get your first tech job, and what FIRST Tech Challenge is
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/first-tech-job-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

"First tech" usually means one of three things: your first job in the tech industry, FIRST Tech Challenge, a school robotics competition, or First Tech Federal Credit Union, a US bank. This page is about the first two. Most of it covers how to get your first tech job, write the CV, why it feels so hard, how to survive the first months, how long to stay and how to recover if it goes wrong. The last two sections explain FIRST Tech Challenge for students interested in robotics. What is First Tech? "First Tech" most often refers to someone's first job in tech, to FIRST Tech Challenge, a robotics competition for school students run by the non-profit FIRST, or to First Tech Federal Credit Union, a credit union in the United States. If you came here about banking, First Tech Federal Credit Union's own website and support line are the right places for opening hours and account details. This page focuses on careers and robotics. For students and freshers in India, the career question is the one that matters most: how to get from a degree to a first role as a developer, data analyst, AI engineer or similar, and how to do well once you are there. FIRST Tech Challenge is relevant if you are in school and want hands-on engineering experience. How do I get my first tech job? Build proof of skill, make it visible, and apply in a targeted way: two or three deployed projects, an internship or freelance work, an active GitHub and LinkedIn, and referrals to the companies you want. Also asked as: how to get first tech job A plan that works: Pick a lane: backend, frontend, data, mobile or AI. Depth beats a long skills list. Build projects that solve a real problem, deploy them, and write clear READMEs. Get experience: internships, freelance work for local businesses, open source or hackathons. Network: message engineers at target companies with a short note and your best project. Apply consistently: five to ten tailored applications a week, tracked in a sheet. Practise interviews: coding problems and explaining your projects aloud. Expect it to take months, not weeks. How do I write a CV for my first tech job? Keep it to one page, put projects near the top with links and results, list skills grouped by type, and tailor the wording to each job description. Recruiters skim, so every line must earn its place. Also asked as: how to write a cv for your first tech job Structure for a fresher: Header: name, email, phone, GitHub, LinkedIn, portfolio. Projects: name, problem, stack, what you built, a measurable result, live link. Experience: internships and freelance work, with outcomes. Skills: languages, frameworks, databases, tools, cloud. Education: degree, college, years, CGPA if strong. Achievements: hackathons, competitive programming, relevant certifications. Avoid skill bars, photos and objective statements. Use the same words as the job description where they are true, because many companies screen CVs automatically before a person reads them. Why is landing your first tech job harder than expected? Because entry-level roles attract very large numbers of applicants, many companies prefer people with some experience, and AI tools have raised the bar for juniors. Generic CVs and certificate lists no longer stand out. Also asked as: why landing your first tech job is way harder than you expected There is also a mismatch between what college teaches and what jobs need: deploying, debugging, working with Git, writing tests and explaining trade-offs. Many applicants apply through the same portals at the same time, so cold applications have low reply rates. What changes the odds is specificity: a project that matches the role, a referral, a hackathon result, or a short message that shows you understand the company's product. Rejections are normal and rarely personal; track them, adjust one thing at a time, and keep building. How can Gen Z land their first tech jobs? Gen Z candidates have an advantage in using AI tools and building in public; use both. Ship projects with AI help that you fully understand, document them publicly, and use communities and hackathons to meet people who hire. Also asked as: how generation z can land its first tech jobs What works for this generation of graduates: Post short build logs on LinkedIn or X while you work on a project. Join developer communities and contribute: answer questions, run a session, help organise an event. Enter hackathons; they compress learning, teamwork and networking into a weekend. Learn to use AI coding tools well, and be ready to explain every line they wrote. Look beyond big brands: startups and small companies often hire on proof of skill. I founded TechVerse Enclave, a community of 500+ developers, because communities are where students find mentors, teammates and openings. How do I survive my first tech job? Focus on learning the codebase, asking good questions, delivering small things reliably, and communicating clearly. Nobody expects a fresher to know everything; they expect you to learn fast and be dependable. Also asked as: how to survive your first tech job Habits that help in the first months: Write down how to set up, build, test and deploy the project as you learn it. Ask questions after trying for a reasonable time, and show what you tried. Take small tickets first and finish them properly, with tests. Read code reviews carefully and apply feedback the next time. Give short, regular updates so your lead never has to chase you. Keep a "brag document" of what you shipped, for appraisals and your next move. Protect your health; late nights every week are a warning sign, not a badge. How long should I stay at my first tech job? Long enough to finish meaningful projects and learn deeply, which usually means around eighteen months to two years. Leave earlier if the job is harming your health, stopped your learning completely, or you have a clearly better opportunity. Also asked as: how long to stay at first tech job Staying a reasonable time lets you see projects through, from building to running in production, which is where much of the learning is. It also gives you stories for your next interviews. Leaving very quickly is fine once; a pattern of short stints raises questions. Before switching, make sure you are moving towards something: a bigger scope, a better team or a field you care about, not only away from a bad week. How do you recover after getting fired from your first tech job? Take a short pause, understand honestly what went wrong, fix the gap, and start applying again with a calm, factual explanation. Being let go early in a career is more common than people admit, and it is recoverable. Also asked as: how i recovered after getting fired from my first job in tech Steps that help: Ask your former manager or HR for specific feedback if you can. Separate causes you control, such as skills or communication, from ones you do not, such as layoffs or team changes. Spend a few weeks closing the main skill gap and ship a small project that shows it. Prepare a short, honest answer: what happened, what you learned, what you do differently now. Lean on mentors and peers for referrals. Keep your finances and health steady during the search; panic decisions rarely help. What is FIRST Tech Challenge? FIRST Tech Challenge is an international robotics competition for students roughly aged 12 to 18, run by the non-profit FIRST. Teams design, build and program robots to play a new game released at the start of each season. Teams usually have up to fifteen students with adult mentors. They learn mechanical design, electronics, programming, project management and outreach, and they keep an engineering portfolio of their work. Awards recognise not only match results but also design, innovation, outreach and teamwork. For a school student interested in engineering or computer science, it is one of the best hands-on experiences available, and it gives material for college applications and later interviews. Check FIRST's website for teams and events near you. How does FIRST Tech Challenge work? Each season FIRST announces a game. Teams then build a robot from a kit of reusable parts, program it in Java or a block-based tool, and compete in matches where alliances of teams score points in autonomous and driver-controlled periods. A match starts with a short autonomous period in which the robot runs code with no human control, followed by a driver-controlled period. Teams form alliances, so collaboration matters as much as competition. Events progress from local qualifiers to regional or national championships and an international championship. Judging also looks at the team's engineering portfolio and interviews. The programming side is real software engineering: sensors, control loops, computer vision for detecting game elements, and testing under time pressure.
