# Top GenAI and LLM interview questions, plus how to answer coding rounds
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/genai-llm-interview-questions/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

The top GenAI interview questions test three things: whether you understand how large language models work (tokens, embeddings, attention), whether you can design a real system with them (retrieval-augmented generation, fine-tuning, evaluation, cost), and whether you can explain a project you built in depth. Coding rounds still test data structures and algorithms in Python or Java. This page lists the questions that come up most and how to answer them, the types of interview rounds, the coding problems to practise, and how to perform in a live coding round. What are the top GenAI interview questions? Expect questions on how LLMs work, how RAG and fine-tuning differ, how to evaluate outputs, how to reduce hallucinations, and how to control cost and latency. Then expect a deep dive into your own project. Also asked as: top gen ai interview questions · what is genai interview questions · top 50 llm interview questions Questions that come up again and again: What is a transformer, and what does attention do? What are embeddings, and how is semantic search built on them? RAG or fine-tuning: when would you use each? How do you chunk documents, and how do you choose chunk size? How do you evaluate a RAG system? Separate retrieval recall from answer faithfulness. How do you reduce hallucinations? Grounding, citations, refusal on weak evidence. What is LoRA, and why does it make fine-tuning cheaper? How do you handle prompt injection in an app with tools? Answer each with a concept, a trade-off and an example from something you built. What do GenAI interviews actually test? They test whether you can ship, not just define terms. Interviewers check fundamentals, judgement about trade-offs, and evidence that you have built and debugged a real GenAI feature. A typical GenAI role interview has a screening call, a coding round, a machine learning or GenAI concepts round, a system design round such as "design a document question-answering system for a company", and a project deep dive. The deep dive decides many offers. Prepare a two-minute walkthrough: the problem, the architecture, one hard bug, and how you measured quality. When I describe RAG.NextUpgrad, the parts that make the conversation are the specific choices: hybrid dense plus BM25 retrieval with reciprocal-rank fusion, re-ranking, and a confidence gate that refuses to answer on weak evidence. Specifics show you built it. What are the most asked LLM interview questions? The most asked LLM questions cover architecture, training, inference and safety. A focused list beats memorising fifty answers you cannot explain. Prepare short, clear answers to these: What is tokenisation, and why do token counts matter for cost? Self-attention and multi-head attention, in plain words. Encoder, decoder and encoder-decoder models: examples of each. Pretraining versus instruction tuning versus RLHF. What does temperature do? What is top-p sampling? What is a context window, and what happens when you exceed it? KV cache: why it speeds up generation. Quantisation: what 4-bit loading trades away. LoRA and QLoRA: what is trained and what is frozen. Why do models hallucinate, and how do you measure it? For each, have one sentence of definition and one practical consequence. What do LLM interview questions test? They test whether you understand why models behave as they do, so you can make engineering decisions: which model to use, how to prompt it, when to retrieve, when to fine-tune, and how to keep cost and latency under control. Also asked as: what is llm interview questions Interviewers rarely want maths for its own sake. A question about temperature is really asking whether you know to use low temperature for extraction and higher for brainstorming. A question about context windows is asking whether you know that stuffing more text can make answers worse, and that retrieval of the right passages beats long prompts. A question about fine-tuning is asking whether you know it changes behaviour and format, while RAG supplies facts. Link every answer to a decision you would make in a product. What types of questions are asked in an interview? Most tech interviews mix four types: technical concept questions, coding problems, design questions, and behavioural questions about how you work with people and handle problems. Also asked as: which type of questions asked in interview What each type looks for: Concept questions check fundamentals in your area, such as Python, databases, networks or LLMs. Coding problems check problem solving and clean code under time pressure. Design questions check how you structure a system and reason about trade-offs. Behavioural questions, such as "tell me about a conflict in your team", check ownership and communication. For behavioural answers use the STAR structure: situation, task, action, result. Prepare five stories from projects, hackathons or college work that you can adapt to most questions. What are the top Python coding interview questions? Common Python coding questions are classic problems on arrays, strings and hash maps, plus Python-specific checks on lists, dictionaries, generators and complexity. Also asked as: top coding interview questions python Practise these until you can solve them cleanly: Two Sum with a dictionary in one pass. Valid parentheses with a stack. Longest substring without repeating characters with a sliding window. Group anagrams with a dictionary of sorted keys. Merge intervals after sorting. Top K frequent elements with collections.Counter or a heap. Binary search on a sorted array, and its variants. Level-order traversal of a binary tree with collections.deque. Also expect Python questions: list versus tuple, how dictionaries work, mutable default arguments, generators and yield, and the time complexity of common operations. What are the top coding interview questions in Java? Java coding rounds use the same core problems as any language, with extra questions on collections, object-oriented design and Java specifics such as HashMap internals and immutability. Also asked as: top interview coding questions in java The problem list overlaps with Python: Two Sum, reverse a linked list, detect a cycle, merge two sorted lists, valid parentheses, binary tree traversals, lowest common ancestor, number of islands with BFS or DFS, and simple dynamic programming such as climbing stairs and coin change. Java-specific topics to revise: HashMap versus TreeMap versus LinkedHashMap, and how hashing and collisions work. String immutability, StringBuilder, and equals versus ==. Interfaces versus abstract classes. Checked versus unchecked exceptions. Basic concurrency: threads, synchronized and ExecutorService. Write clean method signatures and name variables well; it shows. How do I answer coding interview questions? Talk through a clear process: clarify the problem, give a simple solution, improve it, write clean code, then test it with edge cases. Interviewers grade your reasoning as much as the final answer. Also asked as: how to answer coding interview questions · where to practice coding interview questions A structure that works in every round: Restate the problem and ask about input size, edge cases and constraints. Describe a brute-force solution and its complexity in one sentence. Find the bottleneck and improve it, usually with a hash map, two pointers, sorting or a heap. Write the code while explaining each part. Walk through a small example and edge cases: empty input, one element, duplicates. State the final time and space complexity. If you get stuck, say what you are trying. Silence is the worst signal in a coding round. How should I code during an interview? Write readable code first and clever code never. Use clear names, small helper functions and simple control flow, and test as you go rather than at the end. Also asked as: how to code interview questions Practical habits: Choose the language you are fastest in, usually Python, unless the role requires another. Write the function signature and a few test calls before the body. Prefer standard library tools such as collections and heapq in Python. Avoid premature optimisation; get a correct solution, then improve it. Handle edge cases explicitly instead of hoping they work. In online assessments, read all the problems first and start with the one you can finish. Partial but correct solutions often score better than ambitious unfinished ones. Where can I practise coding interview questions? LeetCode is the standard practice platform, and NeetCode organises the most useful LeetCode problems by pattern with video explanations. HackerRank and Codeforces are also widely used for assessments and contests. Practise by pattern, not at random: arrays and hashing, two pointers, sliding window, stack, binary search, linked lists, trees, graphs, heaps, backtracking and dynamic programming. Solve a few problems per pattern until you can recognise it in a new problem. Track problems you could not solve and redo them a week later. Add timed mock interviews with a friend, a mentor or an AI interviewer that asks you to explain aloud. For GenAI roles, also build and deploy one small RAG project, because a working project answers many interview questions at once.

# Does your GitHub profile matter? How to make, design and update a great one
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/github-profile-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

Yes, your GitHub profile matters if you want a job, internship or freelance work in software: it is public evidence of what you can build. Recruiters, hackathon judges and clients look at pinned projects, READMEs and how you write code. A strong profile does not need hundreds of repositories; it needs a clear introduction and a few well-presented projects. This page covers whether it matters, how to make and design one, README generators and widgets, profile pictures, views, privacy, updating and finding your profile. Does a GitHub profile matter? Yes, especially for students and freshers with little work experience. A GitHub profile lets employers see real code, how you structure projects, how you document them and how consistently you build, which a resume cannot show. Also asked as: does github profile matter What matters is quality, not activity streaks. A profile with three well-documented, deployed projects that match the roles you want is far stronger than hundreds of tutorial clones or a green contribution graph full of trivial commits. Recruiters often spend a minute or two: they read your bio, open a pinned project, read its README and maybe skim the code. Make that minute count. For non-developer roles, GitHub matters less, but a portfolio of some kind still helps. How do I make a GitHub profile? Sign up at github.com with an email you check, choose a professional username, then fill in your profile: name, photo, bio, location, links, a profile README, and pinned repositories. Also asked as: how to make github profile Steps: Choose a username close to your name, since it appears in your profile URL. Add a clear photo and a one-line bio stating your focus, such as "GenAI and backend developer". Link your portfolio, LinkedIn and email. Create a repository named exactly like your username to add a profile README. Pin your best three to six repositories. Enable two-factor authentication. Students can also apply for the GitHub Student Developer Pack, which includes free tools and services. How do I design a great GitHub profile? Keep it clean and focused: a short profile README that says who you are, what you build and what you are looking for, followed by pinned projects with clear names, descriptions and live links. Design comes second to clarity. Also asked as: how to design github profile A profile README structure: One or two lines about you and your focus. Three to five highlights: projects shipped, hackathon results, roles. Your main stack as plain text or a few icons. Links: portfolio, LinkedIn, email. Optional: one small stats card, if it adds information. Each pinned repository needs a README with what it does, a screenshot or demo GIF, how to run it, the tech stack and a live link. Avoid walls of badges, animations and widgets that slow the page and distract from your work. What is the best GitHub profile README generator? Generators that offer form-based builders for profile READMEs can give you a quick starting layout with sections, icons and stats cards. Use one for structure, then rewrite the content in your own words and remove anything unnecessary. Popular tools in the community let you pick sections, add tech-stack icons, social links and stats widgets, and copy the generated Markdown into your profile repository. The risk is a generic profile that looks like thousands of others. Recruiters notice specifics: "built a RAG app used by my department, with citations" is more memorable than a grid of 40 technology logos. Keep the generated layout, write a real introduction, and link to real work. What is the best GitHub profile generator for stats and widgets? Community stats cards and widgets can show language breakdowns, contribution streaks and repository stats inside your profile README by embedding images from third-party services. Use at most one or two. Before adding widgets, ask what each tells a reader. A top-languages card can show your focus; a streak counter mostly signals activity, not skill. Third-party image services can be slow or stop working, leaving broken images on your profile, so check them occasionally. If you enjoy automation, you can generate your own stats images with a scheduled GitHub Actions workflow, which is itself a small project worth showing. What should my GitHub profile picture be? Use a clear, friendly photo of your face with a plain background, the same or similar to your LinkedIn photo, so recruiters recognise you across platforms. A professional illustration or avatar is acceptable but less personal. Also asked as: what should github profile picture be Tips: good lighting, face filling most of the frame, no group photos, no heavy filters, and a square crop that looks good small, because GitHub shows it at small sizes in many places. Consistency across GitHub, LinkedIn and your portfolio builds a recognisable personal brand. Avoid default identicons, which make a profile look abandoned. Can GitHub see who viewed my profile? No. GitHub does not show you who visited your profile. Third-party profile view counters, added as images in your README, can show a total number of views, but not who viewed it. Also asked as: can github see profile views Repository owners can see traffic data for their repositories, such as views, unique visitors and referring sites over recent weeks, in the repository's Insights tab, but not individual identities. So you can learn whether a project gets attention and where it comes from, for example from LinkedIn posts, but not which recruiter looked. Focus on making the profile worth viewing rather than tracking views. Can I hide my GitHub profile? Your profile page is public by default and cannot be fully hidden like a private social account, but you can control what appears: make repositories private, hide private contribution details, remove pinned items and limit personal information. Check GitHub's profile settings for current privacy options. Practical privacy steps: make repositories private when they contain personal or client work, keep your email private in settings, and remove location or other details you do not want public. Never commit secrets such as API keys or passwords; if you do, rotate them immediately, because public history keeps them even after deletion. If you want a completely separate identity for experiments, use a separate account, following GitHub's terms. How do I update my GitHub profile? Click "Edit profile" on your profile page to change name, bio, links and photo; edit the README in your username repository to update the introduction; and use "Customise your pins" to change pinned repositories. Also asked as: how to update github profile A simple routine: after each meaningful project or achievement, update the pinned repositories, refresh the README highlights and make sure the project's own README and live link work. Every few months, archive or unpin old tutorial repositories and check that links and badges still load. An up-to-date profile signals that you are actively building. Where do I find my GitHub profile? Your GitHub profile is at github.com/your-username. When signed in, click your profile picture at the top right and choose "Your profile". The URL in the address bar is the link to share on your resume and LinkedIn. Also asked as: where to find github profile Add the link to your resume header, LinkedIn contact info, portfolio and email signature. For a specific project, link directly to its repository, or better, to its live demo with the repository linked from there. If you have changed your username, update old links everywhere, because the old URL may stop redirecting if someone else claims that name.

# What is Google AI certification? Essentials, cloud certs, cost of time, value
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/google-ai-certification-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

"Google AI certification" covers several credentials. Google AI Essentials, offered through Grow with Google and Coursera, is a short beginner certificate on using generative AI tools at work. Google Cloud's professional certifications, such as Professional Machine Learning Engineer, test whether you can build, deploy and run ML systems on Google Cloud, and newer certifications cover generative AI for leaders. This page explains each, how long they take, free routes, their real value for jobs, and how they compare with AWS and Microsoft certifications. What is Google AI certification? Google AI certification refers to credentials from Google that show AI knowledge or skills. The main ones are Google AI Essentials, a beginner certificate, and Google Cloud certifications for machine learning engineers and for leaders of generative AI projects. Also asked as: what is google ai essentials certification · ai course certification google They serve different audiences. AI Essentials suits anyone, from students to office workers, who wants to use tools such as Gemini responsibly and productively. Google Cloud certifications suit engineers and technical decision-makers working on Google Cloud, and include a proctored exam. Before choosing, decide your goal: using AI in your current work, or building AI systems as an engineer. What is the Google AI Essentials certificate? Google AI Essentials is a short, self-paced course with a certificate that teaches how to use generative AI tools at work: writing effective prompts, using AI for tasks such as drafting and analysis, and using AI responsibly, including bias and privacy. It needs no technical background or coding. It is useful for students in any field and for professionals who want a structured introduction. It does not teach you to build AI applications, train models or write code with AI APIs, so it is not a substitute for technical learning if you want an AI engineering role. Think of it as AI literacy: a sensible first step, after which engineers should move to hands-on building. What is the Google AI professional certification? For technical professionals, Google's main AI credential is the Google Cloud Professional Machine Learning Engineer certification, which tests designing, building, deploying and monitoring ML solutions on Google Cloud. Google Cloud also offers a Generative AI Leader certification aimed at business and technical leaders. Also asked as: what is google ai professional certification The ML Engineer exam covers framing ML problems, data preparation, model development with Vertex AI, MLOps pipelines, serving and monitoring, and responsible AI. It expects real experience with Google Cloud services. Google also offers professional certificates through Coursera in areas such as data analytics and AI-related skills. Check Google Cloud's certification page for the current list, exam guides and recommended experience before booking. Which Google AI course should I take for a certificate? If you are new to AI, start with Google AI Essentials. If you want to build on Google Cloud, use Google Cloud Skills Boost learning paths that prepare for the Professional Machine Learning Engineer exam. If you lead AI projects, look at the Generative AI Leader path. For students aiming at AI engineering, a strong sequence is: a beginner course for vocabulary, then free technical learning such as Google's Machine Learning Crash Course, then a hands-on project using the Gemini API or Vertex AI, and only then a cloud certification if your target employers use Google Cloud. Certificates make the most sense as a checkpoint on skills you are already building, not as the starting point. How long does Google AI certification take? Google AI Essentials takes roughly a day or two of focused study, or a few weeks part-time. Google Cloud professional certifications typically take two to six months of preparation, depending on your experience. Professional certification preparation includes learning paths, hands-on labs and practice questions, and Google recommends prior industry experience with its cloud. The exam itself is a timed proctored test, taken online or at a test centre. Certifications expire after a set period and need renewal, which keeps them current but means ongoing effort. Plan study around a project: preparing while building something on Google Cloud makes both the exam and interviews easier. Can I get Google AI certification for free? Sometimes. The learning material for many Google courses is free or low cost, Coursera offers financial aid for its certificates, Google Cloud Skills Boost has free labs and periodic free credit programmes, and Google has run scholarships for students in India. Also asked as: can i get the google ai certification for free The exams for professional cloud certifications usually have a fee, and vouchers are sometimes offered through events, training programmes or student initiatives. Free learning paths, the Machine Learning Crash Course and Google's AI documentation give you the knowledge without the certificate. Be careful with third-party sites offering "free Google certification"; get certificates only from Google, Coursera or Google Cloud directly. Is Google AI certification worth it? AI Essentials is worth it for AI literacy and a quick CV line, especially for non-technical roles. Google Cloud's ML Engineer certification is worth it for engineers targeting roles on Google Cloud. For most technical hiring, projects and experience count more than any certificate. Value depends on the job market you target. Some employers, especially IT services firms and cloud partners, value certifications because they help them meet partner requirements. Product companies and startups care more about what you have built. The best combination is a certification that matches your target stack plus a deployed project using that stack, so the certificate is backed by evidence. Can you get a job with a Google AI certification? A certification alone rarely gets you a job, but it can help you pass resume screening and show initiative, especially combined with projects. For engineering roles, interviews will test whether you can actually build and explain systems. Also asked as: can you get a job with google ai certification What gets jobs: deployed projects, internships, problem-solving skills and the ability to explain trade-offs. Use the certification to structure your learning and to signal familiarity with a cloud platform. Then build something with it, for example a document Q&amp;A system on Vertex AI or the Gemini API, with a README, a demo video and evaluation results. That combination is far stronger than the certificate alone, and it gives you real stories for interviews. AWS vs Google AI certification: which is better? Neither is better in general; choose the cloud your target employers use. AWS has the largest overall cloud market share, so AWS certifications appear in more job listings, while Google Cloud is strong in data and AI and its certifications suit companies on its platform. AWS offers certifications such as AI Practitioner and Machine Learning Engineer Associate, plus specialty and professional levels; Google offers Professional Machine Learning Engineer and Generative AI Leader. Check job descriptions in the roles and cities you want and count which cloud appears more. Concepts such as data pipelines, model deployment, monitoring and cost control transfer between clouds, so learning one deeply makes the second much easier. Microsoft vs Google AI certification: which should I choose? Choose Microsoft if you target companies built on Azure and Microsoft 365, which includes many enterprises and IT services firms in India. Choose Google if your targets use Google Cloud or you are already building with Gemini and Vertex AI. Microsoft's AI credentials include Azure AI Fundamentals for beginners and role-based certifications for Azure AI engineers, with free learning on Microsoft Learn. Students can also use Azure for Students credits to practise. Google's equivalents are AI Essentials for beginners and the cloud certifications for engineers. If unsure, start with the free fundamentals courses from both, build one small project on each platform, and let job listings decide which certification to pay for.

# What is Google Developer Groups? Joining GDG, GDG on Campus and more
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/google-developer-groups-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

Google Developer Groups (GDG) are local communities of developers interested in Google technologies such as Android, Flutter, Firebase, Google Cloud and Gemini. They are independent, run by volunteer organisers, and host meetups, workshops, study jams and the yearly DevFest conferences. On campuses, the student version, formerly Google Developer Student Clubs, is now called Google Developer Groups on Campus. This page explains each programme, how to join, how campus organisers are selected, how to start a group, whether it is worth it, and how to grow as a developer in Google's ecosystem. What is Google Developer? "Google Developer" usually refers to Google for Developers, Google's hub of documentation, tools and programmes for people building with its technologies, or to a developer who builds on Google platforms such as Android, Firebase, Google Cloud or the Gemini API. Google for Developers includes documentation for every Google API and SDK, codelabs with step-by-step tutorials, and community programmes: Google Developer Groups for local meetups, Google Developer Groups on Campus for students, Women Techmakers, and Google Developer Experts for recognised specialists. There is also the Google Developer Program, a profile with learning badges and benefits. For a student, the useful entry points are codelabs to learn, a local GDG to meet people, and a campus chapter to lead. What is a Google Developer Group? A Google Developer Group is a local community of developers who meet to learn and share knowledge about Google technologies. Each chapter is independent, run by volunteer organisers, and supported by Google with resources and event programmes. Typical activities are talks by local engineers, hands-on workshops, study jams that follow a learning path together, hackathons, and DevFest, an annual community-run developer conference held by chapters around the world. Events are usually free and open to anyone, from students to senior engineers. GDGs exist in many cities across India and worldwide, listed on the GDG community website. They are a good place to meet people working in industry, find teammates for hackathons and practise public speaking in a friendly room. What is Google Developer Groups on Campus? Google Developer Groups on Campus are university-based communities for students interested in developer technologies. They were called Google Developer Student Clubs until Google renamed and folded them into the GDG programme in 2024. Also asked as: how i got selected for google developer groups on campus Each campus chapter has a student organiser, selected through an application process, and often a core team of volunteers. Chapters run workshops, study jams, solution challenges where students build projects for real problems, and events with GDG and industry speakers. Membership is open to students at the college, regardless of branch or year. For students, it is a structured way to learn technologies like Flutter, Firebase, Google Cloud and Gemini with peers, and to build leadership experience that shows on a CV. What is Google Developer Student Clubs? Google Developer Student Clubs, or GDSC, was Google's programme of university clubs for students interested in developer technologies. In 2024 it was renamed Google Developer Groups on Campus and brought under the wider Google Developer Groups programme. The purpose stayed the same: peer-to-peer learning, hands-on workshops and building solutions for local problems, led by a student organiser. If you see "GDSC" on an older CV, event poster or LinkedIn profile, it refers to the same kind of campus club. The rename connects campus chapters more closely with local city GDGs, which gives students easier access to industry speakers, DevFests and mentors after they graduate. How do I join a Google Developer Group? Go to the GDG community website, find the chapter for your city or campus, and join it with your Google account. Then register for an upcoming event; showing up is how membership becomes real. Also asked as: how to join google developer group Steps that make it worthwhile: Join your city's GDG and your campus chapter if your college has one. Attend two or three events and talk to the organisers and speakers afterwards. Volunteer: registration desks, social media, logistics. Organisers notice helpers. Offer a short talk or workshop on something you built. Join the chapter's chat group and help answer questions. There is no fee and no test to join. The people who gain most are the ones who contribute, not the ones who only collect event badges. How do you get selected as a GDG on Campus organiser? Students apply when Google opens applications for the new academic year, then go through a review and usually an interview. Selection looks for a clear plan for the community, the ability to organise events, technical curiosity and commitment for the full year. To strengthen an application: Show you have already built community: a club role, events you ran, a study group you led. Show technical work: projects on GitHub, hackathons, a deployed app. Write a concrete plan: who your members are, three events you will run, how you will reach first-years and non-CS students. Get support from a faculty member. In the interview, be specific and honest about what you have done. Applications, timelines and eligibility change each year, so watch the official GDG on Campus page. How do I start a Google Developer Group? For a city chapter, check that no GDG already covers your area, then apply through Google's GDG programme to become an organiser. For a campus chapter, apply when the GDG on Campus organiser applications open. Also asked as: how to start a google developer group Before applying, test the demand: run two or three meetups informally, gather a small core team and keep a list of attendees. Google looks for organisers who will run regular, inclusive, non-commercial events and follow the programme's guidelines. When I founded TechVerse Enclave, now a community of 500+ developers, the lesson was that consistency beats size: a small, regular event where people build things grows faster than an occasional big one. Plan the first quarter's events before you launch, and recruit co-organisers early so the group does not depend on one person. Is a Google Developer Group worth it? Yes, if you participate. GDGs give you free learning, access to engineers who work on real products, speaking practice, teammates for hackathons and sometimes job leads. If you only attend occasionally and leave, the value is small. Also asked as: is google developer group worth it The benefits compound with involvement: volunteers and speakers get to know organisers, speakers get invited to more events, and organisers build leadership experience and a network that helps for years. For students, a campus chapter is also a low-risk place to practise running projects and teams. The limits are worth knowing: content focuses on Google technologies, event quality varies by chapter, and a GDG badge on a CV means little without projects. Treat it as a community to contribute to, not a certificate. How do I become a Google developer? Learn a Google platform deeply and build with it: Android with Kotlin, Flutter for cross-platform apps, Firebase for backends, Google Cloud for infrastructure, or the Gemini API for AI features. Use the official codelabs and documentation. Also asked as: how to become a google developer A practical path: Pick one platform that matches the work you want. Complete its official learning path or codelabs. Build and publish two projects, for example an app on the Play Store or a deployed Gemini-powered tool. Earn a relevant certification, such as Associate Android Developer or a Google Cloud certification, if it helps your goals. Share what you learn at your GDG. Years later, the Google Developer Experts programme recognises people with deep expertise and community contributions; it works by nomination and a review process. What is the Google Developer Program? The Google Developer Program is a free membership for developers that gives you a Google Developer profile, learning badges, access to some tools and community features, with an optional paid tier for extra benefits. Also asked as: what is google developer program Your developer profile collects badges you earn from codelabs, events and learning pathways, and can be shared like a learning portfolio. It also connects you to community events and developer newsletters. The premium tier has offered extras such as cloud credits and additional learning resources; the exact benefits change, so check the program page. It complements, rather than replaces, real projects: a profile full of badges helps less than one deployed app you can demonstrate and explain.

# Hackathon judging criteria and a rubric organisers can copy: how judges score, how to brief a panel, how to break ties, and how to judge fairly in 15 minutes per team
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/hackathon-judging-criteria-and-rubric/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What are the judging criteria for a hackathon?

**Four things, whatever the rubric calls them: feasibility, does it work and could it exist; innovation, is there a real insight, not a new coat of paint; practicality, would the stated user actually adopt it; and problem solving, did the team understand the problem before building. Presentation and teamwork are usually smaller weights. Organisers dress these up with different names; judges who have sat on panels recognise the same four underneath.**


These four are the ones I put on the screen when I brief a judging room, because I learned them from the other side: three first prizes, one loss, and then panels of my own [1][2]. The full rubric with score anchors is on the portfolio and free to copy.

> Judges do not score the idea. They score the evidence: what ran, what the team understood, what they cut. Write the rubric so it can only be filled in from evidence.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## A rubric you can copy

**Five criteria, weights that sum to one hundred, and score anchors at 2, 5 and 8 out of 10 so every judge means the same thing by a 7.**



Weights are a choice; my reasoning for putting feasibility and problem solving above innovation is that innovation is the easiest criterion to fake with words and the hardest to verify in three minutes [4]. For an AI hackathon, add one line under feasibility: is the model doing real work on real inputs, or is the AI a label on a rules engine?

## How should a judge spend the time per team?

**Fifteen minutes: three for the pitch, two for the demo if it was not live, five for questions, two to score alone, three to confer if the panel scores together. Judge the demo and the answers, not the deck. Ask at least one question that tests understanding rather than the project. Score independently before discussing, then discuss only where scores differ by more than two points.**



## What questions should judges ask?

**Who is this for, and have you spoken to them? What happens when it fails? What did you build yourselves versus take from a library? Why did you cut what you cut? What would you do with a month? How is this different from the existing solution? What did you learn that surprised you? The first and last reveal problem understanding; the middle ones reveal feasibility and judgement.**



## How do I brief a judging panel?

**Fifteen minutes before the first pitch, all judges in one room. Cover: the four criteria and their weights, the score anchors with one example each, the time protocol and who keeps time, the rule of independent scoring before discussion, conflicts of interest and how to declare them, tie-breaking, and how feedback is delivered. Hand each judge a one-page sheet per team. Ask them to score the demo they saw, not the potential they imagine.**


My briefing outline, which takes exactly fifteen minutes, is written up separately [3]. The two things new judges most need to hear: score independently first, and a working small thing beats a described big thing.


## How do you break ties and handle conflicts of interest?

**Decide both before the event and write them down. Tie-break by a pre-declared criterion, usually feasibility, then problem solving, then a short re-demo if still tied; never by adding a new criterion in the room. Conflicts: any judge who has mentored a team, knows a member personally, or works for a sponsor whose product the team used declares it and abstains from scoring that team; the remaining judges' scores are normalised. Publish both rules to teams with the criteria.**


Both processes, with the edge cases I have met, are written up in detail [5][6]. The commonest conflict at college hackathons is a mentor judging their own mentees, and the fix is simply to separate the two roles before the event.

## How should judges give feedback?

**One specific, actionable sentence per team, delivered privately or in writing, that names what would have moved the score: "the demo depended on Wi-Fi; seed the data next time", "you never named the user; start there". Not a ranking, not a critique of the idea, not encouragement without content. Teams remember one clear sentence for years, and it is the only part of judging that improves the next hackathon.**


My notes on feedback that actually helped teams, and the kind that did not, are on the portfolio [7].

## How do the criteria differ for Smart India Hackathon or corporate hackathons?

**The four criteria hold; the weights and a fifth item shift. Smart India Hackathon panels include the problem statement's owners, so fit with existing systems and policy carries extra weight, and the current year's official rubric governs [10]. Corporate hackathons weight practicality toward the sponsor's platform or data. Community events such as those run under Major League Hacking publish organiser guidance that leans toward learning and inclusion [9]. Read the event's own rubric, then map it onto the four.**



## How do I become a hackathon judge?

**Build and ship something first, then attend, then mentor, then ask the organiser for a panel seat. Organisers want judges who have shipped, can follow a rubric, show up on time and write feedback. After the first panel, invitations arrive with speaking invitations. Publish your rubric; organisers copy it and remember where it came from, which is how this one travels.**


My own path from participant to judge, and what organisers told me they look for, is written up separately [8].



## Need a judge, or a briefing for your panel?

**I judge and mentor at college hackathons and internal Smart India Hackathon rounds, on-site across India or remote, and I brief panels using the rubric above. Free for student communities.** Send the date, format and problem statements to pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# Hackathon pitch deck template: the seven slides, the three-minute script, demo rules and what judges score, from three first prizes and the judging table
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/hackathon-pitch-deck-template/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What should a hackathon pitch deck contain?

**Seven slides in this order: the problem in the user's words; the user and what the problem costs them; the live demo, which is not a slide but a switch to your app; how it works, one diagram; what you cut and why; what is next and what you need; the team with roles and contact details. Three minutes total, with about ninety seconds on the demo. Anything else, a market size, a competitor grid, a technology logo wall, comes out.**


I have pitched from the floor three times for a first prize and once for a loss I still learn from, and I have sat on the other side scoring decks with a timer running [7][8]. The structure below is what wins from both seats. The downloadable version and the reasoning behind each slide are on the portfolio [1].

> The judges have seen twenty decks today. They will remember one demo and one sentence. Build the deck to deliver exactly those two things.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What goes on each slide?

**One idea per slide, readable from the back of the room, with the words you will say, not paragraphs you will read. Here is each slide with its job and its time.**



The "what we cut" slide surprises teams, and it is the slide that has most often earned a nod from judges I have sat beside. It says: we understood the problem well enough to know what was not the problem.

## How do I structure a three-minute hackathon pitch?

**Thirty seconds of setup, ninety of demo, sixty of close. Setup: the user, the pain, and the one-line solution. Demo: the happy path, narrated in the user's terms, "Priya uploads her invoice, and here is the total, validated". Close: how it works, what you cut, what is next, the ask. Rehearse with a timer three times. If you run over in rehearsal, cut the setup, never the demo.**



### What is a good opening line for a hackathon pitch?

**The user's name and their problem, in ten words. "Ramesh grows wheat two hours from the nearest town and cannot read the advisory SMS." Not "Hi, we are Team Innovators and we built an AI-powered platform." The first sentence decides whether the judge listens to the second. My two-minute pitch notes cover the opening in detail [2][5].**


## How do I demo without it crashing?

**Freeze the code two hours before. Seed the data so no step depends on a live third-party call or the venue Wi-Fi. Rehearse the exact click path three times on the machine and browser you will present from. Record a full-path video and keep it open in a tab. Assign one person to drive and one to talk. If it breaks anyway, switch to the video without apology and keep narrating; judges score recovery too.**



Our loss at STROT came from a live API call over venue Wi-Fi [8]. My technical checklist for demos that survive is written up separately [3], and every team I mentor gets it before the event.


## What do judges score, and how does the deck serve it?

**Four things: feasibility, innovation, practicality and problem solving, with presentation as a smaller weight. The demo proves feasibility. The problem and user slides prove problem solving and practicality. The how-it-works slide and the "what we cut" slide show innovation and judgement. The close shows you know what a next step is. If a slide does not serve one of those four, remove it.**



## How do I handle Q&A after the pitch?

**Repeat the question aloud, answer the fair part in two sentences, and stop. Expect: who is this for and have you spoken to them; what happens when it fails; how is this different from the existing tool; what did you build versus borrow; what would you do with a month. Say "we did not get to that" when true. Judges test whether you understand your own project, and a short honest answer beats a long confident one every time.**


The full list of questions I have heard and asked, with the answers that landed, is on the portfolio [4].

## How do I adapt the deck for Smart India Hackathon?

**Use the template the portal prescribes for that year exactly, because reviewers check for it [6]. Inside it, keep the same order: the department's problem in its vocabulary, the demo or a video of it, one diagram, feasibility and the constraints you honoured, impact for the department and the citizen, and a pilot plan. Replace "the ask" with "how this runs inside the department next month". Ministry judges reward fit with existing systems more than novelty.**


## What mistakes lose pitches?

**Opening with the team and the stack. A slide of technology logos. Reading paragraphs off the screen. Explaining the architecture before showing the product. A demo that depends on Wi-Fi. Running over time so the demo gets cut. Ending with "thank you" instead of an ask. Five people speaking in turn with no handoff. Every one of these is on the checklists above, and every one I have watched sink a good build.**



## Do I need a video, a one-pager or a repository too?

**Yes to all three, and they take an hour. A two-minute screen recording of the demo for organisers and for your LinkedIn post. A one-page PDF with the problem, the solution, the diagram and the team, for judges who want to remember you. A repository with a README that states the problem, how to run it, and what you would do next. These outlast the event; the deck does not.**



## Can you review our deck before the hackathon?

**If your college or club is preparing teams for a hackathon, I run pitch clinics: each team presents for three minutes, gets scored on the rubric, and revises on the spot.** On-site across India or remote, free for student communities. Email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# Hackathon project ideas that win: 40 AI and software ideas for students, with the hard part of each, from three first prizes
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/hackathon-project-ideas/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What makes a hackathon project idea good?

**A good hackathon idea has four properties: a named user with a real friction, a before-and-after a judge can see in one demo, a hard technical part your team can finish in the time available, and a plausible next step after the event. Ambition is not one of the four. Every first prize I have won came from a smaller idea than the teams we beat, executed completely.**


KrishGyan won Changethon at IIT Roorkee because the demo was a farmer's voice note going in and spoken advice coming out, in the farmer's language, on WhatsApp, with no reading required [1]. Annapurna won BYTEBATTLE because a judge could watch one meal move from a hotel kitchen to a shelter through four clear roles [2]. BrandHive won Product Genesis because we showed the whole loop for a small business, not a features slide [3]. None of those ideas was novel. All of them were complete.

> Judges do not remember the idea. They remember the moment the demo worked and they understood who it was for.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## How do I generate hackathon ideas fast?

**Use a three-column frame: an audience, a friction, and what technology removes it. Audiences: farmers, first-year students, small shopkeepers, clinic staff, college offices, delivery workers, parents. Frictions: a form, a queue, a language barrier, a lost document, a phone call nobody answers, a spreadsheet updated by hand. Technology: voice in and out, document extraction, a RAG assistant over one set of documents, a vision check, an agent that finishes one repetitive task. Combine any row from each column and you have a candidate in thirty seconds.**



## 40 hackathon project ideas, with the hard part named

**Each idea below states the user, the demo and the hard part. Change the audience to match your problem statement; the shape carries over.**


### AI and generative AI

1. **Voice-first advisory over WhatsApp** for farmers or shopkeepers: voice note in, spoken answer out, in a regional language. Hard part: speech recognition quality on real audio. KrishGyan is this idea [1].
2. **RAG assistant over one college's documents**, syllabus, notices, previous-year papers, with page citations. Hard part: chunking messy PDFs so retrieval works.
3. **Invoice or receipt extraction to a spreadsheet** with validation that totals add up. Hard part: deterministic validation after the model extracts.
4. **Prescription reader** that turns a photo into a medication schedule with reminders. Hard part: handwriting and drug-name normalisation; keep a human confirm step.
5. **Lecture recording to notes**: transcribe, segment by topic, produce a summary and a quiz. Hard part: speaker diarisation and long-audio chunking.
6. **Resume to job-fit report** for a specific posting, with the gaps and one project suggestion per gap. Hard part: avoiding generic output; ground it in the posting text.
7. **Government scheme eligibility checker** by conversation: answer five questions, get the schemes you qualify for with the documents needed. Hard part: keeping the rules table accurate and cited.
8. **Code review agent for student repositories** that comments on a pull request with tests it ran. Hard part: sandboxing and a tight tool set.
9. **Local-language news summariser** for one district, from public feeds, with source links. Hard part: dedup across sources and honest attribution.
10. **Meeting-minutes agent** that joins a call recording, extracts decisions and owners, and files them. Hard part: precision on who owns what.

### Agriculture and rural

11. **Crop disease photo triage** with a confidence threshold and a "see an expert" path. Hard part: a model that admits uncertainty on out-of-distribution photos.
12. **Mandi price alerts by voice** for a crop and district. Hard part: reliable public price data ingestion.
13. **Irrigation scheduling from weather and soil inputs** with SMS output. Hard part: an honest, simple model rather than a fake precise one.
14. **Cold-storage or transport sharing** between small farmers. Hard part: the matching logic and trust; roles, as in Annapurna [2].
15. **Fertiliser dose calculator in a regional language**, offline-first. Hard part: getting the agronomy right and citing it.

### Education and campus

16. **Attendance by face recognition with liveness**, embeddings-only storage, per-class galleries. Hard part: threshold tuning and privacy design.
17. **Doubt-solving queue** for a class, with an LLM first pass and a teacher escalation. Hard part: knowing when the model should not answer.
18. **Placement tracker** that scrapes the college's notices and turns them into a calendar with deadlines. Hard part: parsing inconsistent notice formats.
19. **Lab equipment booking** with conflict detection and a waitlist. Hard part: none technical, which is why it ships.
20. **Peer tutoring marketplace** inside one campus, with verified student profiles. Hard part: trust and moderation.
21. **Exam paper generator from a syllabus** with difficulty tags and an answer key, reviewed by a teacher. Hard part: quality control and avoiding hallucinated facts.
22. **Accessibility reader** for scanned course PDFs: OCR to clean text to audio. Hard part: reading order on two-column pages.

### Health and public services

23. **Clinic queue and token system** with SMS updates for a primary health centre. Hard part: works on feature phones.
24. **Vaccination or check-up reminders** for a ward, by voice call in the local language. Hard part: opt-in, consent and unsubscribe from the first version.
25. **Blood donor coordination** with availability and distance, verified by a hospital contact. Hard part: verification without friction.
26. **Medical report explainer**: upload a lab report, get plain-language explanations of each line with the normal range cited, and a clear "ask your doctor" boundary. Hard part: restraint.
27. **Emergency contact card by QR** for two-wheeler riders. Hard part: none; the demo is the product.

### Fintech and small business

28. **GST invoice generator for a kirana shop** that works offline and syncs later. Hard part: offline-first data model.
29. **UPI QR with payment tracking for stalls and events**. Hard part: reconciliation.
30. **Expense splitting for hostels** with recurring bills and settlement suggestions. Hard part: none; polish wins.
31. **Loan document checklist assistant** that tells a first-time applicant what is missing from their file. Hard part: accurate, cited requirements.
32. **Small-business review responder** that drafts replies to Google reviews in the owner's voice, with approval before posting. Hard part: never auto-post.

### Civic, community and sustainability

33. **Surplus food coordination** between donors, NGOs and volunteers with verified impact. Hard part: roles and trust; this is Annapurna [2][7].
34. **Pothole and streetlight reporting** with photo, location and a public status board. Hard part: dedup of the same issue reported twice.
35. **Lost-and-found for a campus or a city event** with image matching. Hard part: matching without false positives.
36. **E-waste pickup scheduler** for a locality with a route for the collector. Hard part: route optimisation, kept simple.
37. **Water tanker demand aggregation** for a colony. Hard part: coordination logic and notifications.

### Developer tools and productivity

38. **One-click deploy of a student's Python project to a free host** with a generated README and Dockerfile. Hard part: handling the ten ways student projects are structured.
39. **Hackathon team finder** matching skills and availability inside one event. Hard part: cold start; seed it with the event's registrations.
40. **Prompt library with version stamps** per model and date, so a team knows which prompt worked where. Hard part: the discipline; I run one at tools.scult.in.

## Which ideas suit an AI hackathon specifically?

**The ones where the model does one narrow job with real inputs and a visible output: voice in and voice out, a photo to a structured record, a document set to cited answers, a repository to a review with evidence. Ideas 1 to 10 above are built for that. Avoid "a chatbot for X" unless X is a specific document set and the demo shows a citation; judges have seen a thousand generic chatbots.**



Open models make most of these feasible on a laptop: Whisper for speech [8], Ollama for a local LLM [9], and the Hugging Face hub for vision and embedding models [10].


## How do I adapt an idea to a Smart India Hackathon problem statement?

**Read the problem statement for its owner and its constraint. A ministry statement wants scale, compliance and integration with existing systems, so the idea should show a pilot that could grow and a data-handling story. A company statement wants one feature demonstrated on their kind of data. Map one idea from the list to the statement, then rewrite the user and the demo in the statement's own vocabulary. Never present a generic project with the statement's name pasted on.**


The official portal publishes each cycle's problem statements and rules, and they change every year, so read the current list before choosing [5]. The internal college round is where most teams are eliminated; treat that presentation as the final.

## What hackathon ideas work for beginners?

**Ideas 19, 27, 30 and 34: a booking system, an emergency QR card, an expense splitter, a reporting board. None needs a model, a dataset or an API key. Each can be finished, polished and demoed by a team learning as they go, and a finished beginner project beats an unfinished ambitious one on every rubric I have used. Add one small AI feature only if the core works by hour 20.**


## What ideas should I avoid?

**Anything that needs a dataset you do not have on day one. Anything whose demo depends on a third party approving an API key during the event. Anything with "blockchain" attached to a problem that a database solves. Anything that requires convincing a judge of a market instead of showing a user. Anything so broad that your three-minute demo would need ten. Novelty is not on the rubric; completeness is.**



## How do I present a hackathon idea?

**Lead with the user and the pain, in one sentence. Show the demo before you explain the architecture. Put one diagram of how it works. Say what you cut and why, which shows judgement. End with what you would build next and what you need. Three minutes, rehearsed three times. The idea gets thirty seconds; the demo gets ninety.**



## Can you help our team with an idea?

**If your college or hackathon wants a session on idea selection, scoping and demos before the event, or a judge or mentor during it, that is one of the things I do.** The longer list with 2026-specific angles is on the portfolio [4]. Email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How to convert handwriting to text, and turn text into handwriting
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/handwriting-to-text-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

Yes, you can convert handwriting to text. Handwritten text recognition, a form of OCR built for handwriting, is now built into phones, notes apps and AI assistants: point Google Lens or Apple's Live Text at a page, write with a stylus in a notes app, or upload a photo of your notes to an AI model. It also works in reverse: you can make typed text look like your handwriting with a custom font. This page explains how recognition works and walks through scanning, copying, converting, translating and creating handwriting. What is handwritten text recognition? Handwritten text recognition (HTR) is technology that reads handwriting from images or pen strokes and turns it into editable text. It is a specialised form of optical character recognition (OCR), which originally targeted printed text. Handwriting is harder than print because letters vary between people, join together and slant. Modern HTR uses deep learning models that read whole lines or pages, using context to guess unclear words, much as people do. Two modes exist: offline recognition from photos or scans, and online recognition from stylus strokes, which also uses the order and direction of each stroke and is more accurate. Results are good on neat writing and weaker on messy notes, unusual scripts and mixed languages, so proofreading is always needed. Can you convert handwriting to text? Yes. Phone tools such as Google Lens and Apple's Live Text, notes apps with stylus support, cloud OCR services, and AI models such as Gemini, ChatGPT and Claude can all turn handwriting into editable text. Also asked as: how to text handwriting Which to use: A few lines: Google Lens or Live Text on your phone. Stylus notes: convert inside Samsung Notes, Apple Notes or OneNote. Pages of notes: photograph them and ask an AI assistant to transcribe, keeping headings and lists. Forms and documents at scale: cloud services such as Google Cloud Vision or Azure AI Document Intelligence. In my OCR &amp; Speech Workspace, OCR runs page by page so each piece of text keeps its page number; that is worth copying for long notes, so you can always find the original. Can you scan handwriting to text? Yes. Photograph or scan the page in good light, then use a tool that recognises handwriting. On phones, the camera with Google Lens or Live Text does it directly; on computers, upload the scan to an OCR tool or AI assistant. For the best results: Use even light without shadows and hold the phone parallel to the page. Scan at a decent resolution; most phone cameras are enough. Crop to the text and avoid busy backgrounds. Write in dark ink on plain paper when you know you will scan. For multiple pages, use a scanner app to create a single PDF first. Then proofread, focusing on names, numbers and technical terms, where errors cluster. How do I copy handwritten text from an image? On Android, open the image in Google Photos or Lens, tap Lens, select the text and copy it. On iPhone, open the photo, press and hold the text with Live Text, and copy. On a computer, upload the image to Google Lens in the browser or to an AI assistant. Also asked as: how to copy handwriting text from image If selection fails, the writing may be too unclear or the image too small; try a sharper photo or zoom in on the section. AI assistants are often better than Lens for long passages because they use context: upload the image and ask "transcribe this handwriting exactly, keep line breaks, mark unclear words with [?]". Marking uncertain words is important, because AI may otherwise guess confidently. For sensitive documents, prefer on-device tools. Can notes apps convert handwriting to text? Yes. Apple Notes on iPad with Apple Pencil can convert handwriting to text and lets you write directly into text fields with Scribble; Samsung Notes converts handwriting with S Pen; Microsoft OneNote has ink-to-text conversion. Also asked as: can notes convert handwriting to text Notes apps work best with stylus input because they record strokes, which makes recognition more accurate than reading a photo. They also keep handwritten notes searchable even without converting them. Typical workflow: take notes by hand during class, then select a section and convert it when you need typed text for an assignment or to share. Check the app's language settings; recognition supports many languages, but mixed scripts and abbreviations may need manual fixes. Can you translate handwriting to text? Yes. Google Translate's camera mode and Google Lens can read handwriting and translate it into another language, and AI assistants can transcribe and translate a photo in one step. Point Google Translate's camera at the note or import a photo, choose the source and target languages, and it overlays or lists the translation. For longer handwritten letters or notes, upload the photo to an AI assistant and ask: "Transcribe this handwritten text in its original language, then translate it into English, and mark any words you are unsure of." Translation errors compound recognition errors, so for anything important, such as official documents, have a fluent person check the result. How do I turn handwriting into editable text on a computer? Photograph or scan your pages, then use OneNote's text extraction, Google Drive's OCR when opening an image or PDF with Google Docs, or an AI assistant for higher accuracy on messy notes. Paste the result into your document and proofread. A practical study workflow: scan a week's notes into one PDF, upload it to an AI assistant, and ask for a clean transcription with the original headings and bullet points, followed by a one-page summary. Keep the original scans, because transcription mistakes happen. If you write notes digitally with a stylus, convert inside the notes app instead, which is more accurate than photographs. For printed text, standard OCR is near perfect; it is handwriting that needs checking. How do I turn text into my handwriting? Create a font from a sample of your handwriting with a handwriting-font service: you fill in a template with each character, scan or photograph it, and the service generates a font file you install and type with. Also asked as: how to turn text into your handwriting Steps that work: Download the service's template and write each character neatly with a dark pen. Scan at good resolution and upload. Install the generated font file on your computer. Adjust spacing and size in your word processor. Uses include personalised cards, design projects and notes. Typed "handwriting" always looks more regular than real writing, which people can notice. Do not use it to fake work that must be handwritten, such as assignments or exam sheets where handwriting is required; that is academic misconduct. Is there an app that converts text to handwriting? Yes. Handwriting-font creators, text-to-handwriting websites that render typed text on a ruled-page image, and design tools with handwriting fonts all do this. Some robots and plotters even write with a real pen from typed text. Also asked as: is there any app which can convert text to handwriting Choose by purpose: for design and greeting cards, a handwriting font in Canva or your word processor is enough; for a personal touch, a font made from your own writing; for a realistic page image, a text-to-handwriting generator. Check privacy terms before uploading samples of your handwriting, which is personal data. And again, do not use these tools to submit handwritten work you did not write by hand. What text looks like handwriting? Handwriting-style fonts make typed text look handwritten. Free options on Google Fonts include Caveat, Indie Flower, Patrick Hand, Kalam and Shadows Into Light, and the Handwriting category lists many more. Pick by mood: Patrick Hand and Kalam are neat and readable, Caveat looks like quick notes, Indie Flower is playful. Kalam also supports Devanagari, useful for Hindi text. For readability, use handwriting fonts for headings, quotes or short notes, not long paragraphs, and keep body text in a clean font. On websites, load fonts efficiently and check that they render well on phones.

# How does face recognition work? Detection, embeddings, thresholds and liveness, from building FaceVision
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-does-face-recognition-work/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How does face recognition work?

**Face recognition works in four steps. A detector finds each face in the image and its landmarks. The face is aligned and cropped to a standard size. A recognition network turns the crop into an embedding, a vector of a few hundred numbers in which faces of the same person land close together. Finally the system compares that embedding with stored ones and declares a match when the distance falls under a threshold. Everything else, liveness, enrolment, privacy, is engineering around those four steps.**


The embedding idea comes from FaceNet, which trained a network so that the Euclidean distance between two face vectors directly measured how likely they were the same person [1]. ArcFace sharpened it with an angular margin loss that spreads identities further apart, and it is the recipe behind most open models today [2].

I built FaceVision in 2026 as a browser-only detection, recognition and liveness system: the camera frames never leave the device, only embeddings are sent to a FastAPI and PostgreSQL backend, and no image is ever stored [13]. This page is what that build taught me, with the papers underneath each step.

> The moment you decide never to store a face image, half your privacy problems disappear and the other half become simple. Store the vector, throw away the pixels.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour, from building FaceVision</cite>

## What is the difference between face detection and face recognition?

**Face detection finds faces: it returns bounding boxes and usually landmarks for eyes, nose and mouth, for every face in a frame, and it does not know or care who they are. Face recognition takes one detected face and identifies or verifies the person. Detection is the first stage of recognition, but a security camera that counts people, or a phone that focuses on a face, needs only detection.**



MTCNN was the standard detector for years [3]; RetinaFace improved accuracy on small and turned faces and remains a strong default [4]. Google's MediaPipe ships a fast detector that runs on phones and in browsers [11].

## What is a face embedding, and how are faces compared?

**A face embedding is a fixed-length vector, often 128 or 512 numbers, produced by a network trained so that the same person's faces cluster together and different people's faces sit apart. Comparison is a distance: cosine similarity or Euclidean distance between two vectors. If the distance is below a threshold, the system calls it a match. The threshold is not part of the model; it is a decision you make from your own error data.**



The embedding is why you never need to store the face image. A vector cannot be turned back into a photograph in any useful way, it is far smaller, and it can be compared in a database index like any other vector. FaceVision stores exactly this: the vector, the user id, the timestamp, nothing visual [13].

## How do I choose the match threshold?

**Collect pairs of embeddings from your real users and cameras, labelled same-person or different-person, then plot the two error rates as the threshold moves: false accepts, a stranger let in, and false rejects, the right person turned away. Choose the threshold that meets your risk. A door lock wants false accepts near zero and tolerates retries; a class attendance system tolerates a few false accepts and hates queues. Never ship a vendor's default threshold blind.**



NIST's ongoing Face Recognition Technology Evaluation publishes false match and false non-match rates for hundreds of algorithms under controlled conditions, and it is the reference for what state-of-the-art accuracy looks like [5]. It also shows how far the same algorithm's numbers move between a mugshot-quality image and a webcam frame, which is why your own data matters more than the leaderboard.

## Why does face recognition fail?

**For a short list of reasons that repeat everywhere: low light and backlight, motion blur, extreme pose, masks and sunglasses, low-resolution or heavily compressed cameras, faces too small in the frame, enrolment photos that look nothing like daily conditions, and a threshold tuned on a different population. Twins and close relatives are a real limit for some models. Most "the AI is broken" tickets are a camera or lighting problem.**



On twins: FaceVision, like every embedding system I have tested, sometimes cannot separate identical twins at a threshold that still rejects strangers. For high-stakes use, that is a reason to add a second factor, not a reason to loosen the threshold.

## Is face recognition biased, and how accurate is it across groups?

**Accuracy differs across demographic groups for most algorithms. NIST's 2019 demographic study measured higher false positive rates for some groups than others, with the size of the gap depending strongly on the algorithm [6]. The gap has narrowed in recent evaluations but has not vanished. The practical response is to test on your own user population, report the error rates per group, and choose a threshold and a fallback that protect the worst-served group, not the average.**


For a college attendance system in India, the relevant test set is your own students under your own classroom lights, not a benchmark shot in a studio elsewhere.

## What is liveness detection, and why do I need it?

**Liveness detection, also called presentation attack detection, checks that the face in front of the camera is a live person and not a printed photo, a phone screen showing a photo or video, or a mask. Without it, any recognition system that unlocks or pays can be defeated by a picture from social media. Active liveness asks the user to do something, blink, turn, follow a dot. Passive liveness analyses a single frame or short clip for texture, depth cues and screen artefacts.**



ISO/IEC 30107 defines the framework and terminology for presentation attack detection and the metrics vendors quote [7]. Texture analysis, the observation that a re-photographed face carries colour and frequency artefacts a live face does not, is one of the classic passive approaches [8]. FaceVision uses a passive check on the device before any embedding is computed, so a photo held to the camera is rejected before it can even be compared [13].


## Can I run face recognition in the browser, without a server seeing the face?

**Yes. ONNX Runtime Web runs detection, recognition and liveness models in the browser using WebAssembly or WebGPU [10]. The camera frame stays on the device, the models produce an embedding locally, and only the embedding travels to your API for comparison and storage. It is slower than a GPU server for large galleries, but for verification and small identification sets it is fast enough, and it removes the biggest privacy and compliance burden: you never possess a face image.**


The architecture of FaceVision, which is the concrete version of this answer:


Models are exported to ONNX from PyTorch or taken from open toolkits such as InsightFace, which publishes ArcFace-family recognition models and RetinaFace detectors [9]. Quantising them shrinks download size and speeds inference on phones, at a small accuracy cost you should measure.

## How do I build a face recognition attendance system?

**Enrol each person with three to five embeddings taken under the real classroom conditions, on the same kind of camera. At check-in, detect, run liveness, embed and compare against the enrolled set for that class only, which keeps the gallery small and the false-match rate low. Log the score, not the image. Add a fallback for rejections, such as a one-time code, so a bad lighting day does not stop a class. Publish the privacy notice before the first day.**


Attendance is the most common student project in this space and the one most often built wrong: images saved to a folder, a global gallery of thousands, no liveness, a threshold copied from a tutorial. Built right, with per-class galleries, on-device liveness and embeddings-only storage, it is also a strong portfolio piece, because you can explain each decision.

## Is face recognition legal in India, and how do I handle privacy?

**Facial data is biometric personal data, and India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, sets the framework for processing personal data with notice, consent, purpose limitation and security obligations [12]. Rules and enforcement continue to develop, so treat this as the direction, not legal advice. The engineering answer is independent of jurisdiction: collect consent, tell people what is stored and for how long, store embeddings rather than images, delete on request, and restrict who can run a search.**



I wrote a longer note on what changed in my own practice after FaceVision, and most of it is the list above [14].

## Which library or model should I use for face recognition?

**For a Python prototype: InsightFace for detection and ArcFace-family recognition, or the face_recognition library for simplicity at lower accuracy [9]. For phones and browsers: MediaPipe for detection [11] and an ONNX-exported ArcFace model in ONNX Runtime Web for recognition [10]. For anything that unlocks or pays: add a liveness model and test it against printed photos and phone screens yourself before you believe its numbers.**



## What are common face recognition interview questions?

**Explain detection versus recognition versus verification versus identification. Explain what an embedding is and why distance measures similarity. Explain how you would set a threshold and what false accept and false reject mean. Explain what liveness detection defends against. Explain how you would design the system so no face image is stored. If you can answer these from a project you built, you are ahead of most candidates.**



## Where should I start with a face recognition project?

**Build verification first, not identification: enrol yourself and two friends, run detection and embedding in the browser with ONNX Runtime Web, store only embeddings, and plot your own false accept and false reject curve from a hundred attempts. Then add passive liveness and try to fool it with a photo of yourself. That project teaches every concept on this page and is exactly the shape of FaceVision.**


If your college wants a hands-on session on computer vision that respects privacy from the first line of code, that is one of the talks I offer. Email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.
