# How to prepare a dataset for fine-tuning an LLM: formats, chat templates, how much data, synthetic data, validation and the checklist before you train
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-prepare-a-dataset-for-fine-tuning/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How do I prepare a dataset for fine-tuning an LLM?

**Start with a written spec of the behaviour you want, then collect or write examples that follow it exactly: for each, the input a user would give and the ideal output, in the chat format the base model expects. Deduplicate, validate every row against the spec, hold out a validation split, measure token lengths, and read a random sample by eye. The dataset is the fine-tune; the training run only copies what is in it, including its inconsistencies.**


FineTune Studio, the platform I built in 2026, validates the uploaded dataset before it lets a run start, because the most common reason a run produced a bad model had nothing to do with hyper-parameters: the data was inconsistent, mis-templated or leaked into the validation split [12]. This page is that validation, explained.

> Write twenty examples by hand before anything else. If twenty consistent examples are hard to write, the spec is not ready, and the fine-tune will faithfully learn the confusion.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour, from building FineTune Studio</cite>

## What should the spec contain?

**One paragraph: who the user is, what they send, what the model must produce, in what format, with what tone, and what it must do when the input is unclear or out of scope. Then three example pairs that follow it. Every later example is checked against this paragraph. A spec you cannot write in a paragraph is a task you are not ready to train.**


## Which dataset format should I use: Alpaca, ShareGPT or chat messages?

**Use the messages format, a list of role and content turns, system, user, assistant, because it maps directly onto the chat template every modern model uses and onto what TRL's trainer expects [7]. Alpaca's instruction, input and output fields [1] and ShareGPT's multi-turn conversations are older JSON shapes that convert to messages trivially. The format is a container; what the model actually sees is the template rendered from it.**



A row in the messages format, which is also the shape most APIs accept [9]:

```json
{"messages": [
  {"role": "system", "content": "You are a support agent for Acme. Answer only from the provided policy. If the policy does not cover the question, say so and offer to escalate."},
  {"role": "user", "content": "Policy: Refunds within 14 days with receipt.\n\nQuestion: I bought it 20 days ago, can I return it?"},
  {"role": "assistant", "content": "The policy allows refunds within 14 days of purchase with a receipt, so a return at 20 days is outside the window. I can escalate this to a supervisor if you would like."}
]}
```

## What is a chat template and why does it matter?

**A chat template is the exact string layout a model was trained on for conversations: the special tokens that mark the start and end of each turn and which role speaks. Every model family uses a different one. If you train with the wrong template, or hand-write the tokens with a small mistake, the model learns garbage or produces it at inference. Always render examples with the tokenizer's own template function [6], and use the same template when you serve the model.**


```python
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(BASE)
text = tok.apply_chat_template(row["messages"], tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=False)
# never build this string by hand; the template lives with the model
```

Template mismatch is the single most common cause of a fine-tuned chat model that "does not work", in my experience and in the support questions FineTune Studio users asked. My longer note on formats and templates is on the portfolio [11].

## How much data do I need to fine-tune an LLM?

**For tone, style and output format: a few hundred high-quality examples produce a visible, stable change. For a classification or extraction skill: a few thousand covering the classes and the edge cases. For adapting to a domain's language: tens of thousands. Below about a hundred, put the examples in the prompt instead. LIMA showed that a thousand carefully curated examples were enough to teach strong instruction-following, and that quality mattered more than quantity [2].**



These are orders of magnitude from experience, not laws; the only reliable number comes from training on half your data and checking whether the other half still improves the model.

## Can I use synthetic data for fine-tuning?

**Yes, and most fine-tuning datasets today are partly synthetic: a stronger model generates examples from your spec, from seed examples, or from documents. Self-Instruct and Alpaca showed the approach at scale [3][1]. It works when you filter hard: validate every generated row against the spec, remove duplicates and near-duplicates, spot-check by hand, and mix in real examples so the model does not learn the generator's tics and refusals. Unfiltered synthetic data teaches a copy of the generator, not your task.**



## How do I clean and deduplicate the dataset?

**Normalise whitespace and encoding. Remove exact duplicates, then near-duplicates by comparing normalised text or embeddings, because duplicated training data both wastes compute and makes models memorise [5]. Remove rows that violate the spec: wrong format, wrong language, refusals you did not intend, outputs that reference the prompt. Strip personal data you do not have consent to train on. Measure token lengths and trim or split outliers so no row exceeds your training sequence length.**



The Hugging Face Datasets library handles the mechanics, loading, mapping, filtering and splitting, for datasets of any size [8]. My own pre-training validation checklist, which FineTune Studio runs automatically, is written up separately [10].


## How do I split training and validation data?

**Hold out ten to twenty percent, chosen so that near-duplicates of a training row never land in validation, or the validation loss lies to you. For grouped data, all rows from one document, one user or one conversation go to the same split. Keep a third, small test set of examples you wrote by hand and never look at during tuning, for the final honest comparison of base versus fine-tuned.**


## What is label masking, and should I train on the user turns?

**Label masking means computing the loss only on the assistant's tokens, so the model learns to produce answers rather than to predict the user's questions. Most trainers do this for you when you use the messages format with a chat template and an assistant-only loss option [7]. Training on user turns wastes capacity and can teach the model to continue user text. Mask them unless you have a specific reason not to.**


## What are common dataset mistakes?

**Mixing two specs in one dataset, so the model learns to flip between them. Hand-writing chat tokens. Duplicated rows inflating confidence. A validation split that shares documents with training. Outputs that mention the instruction. Ten variations of the same easy example and none of the hard cases. Personal data nobody consented to. Not reading any rows. A model can only be as consistent as its data, and it will be exactly as inconsistent.**



## Dataset interview questions

**How much data do you need for a style fine-tune versus a skill? What is a chat template and what happens if you get it wrong? How do you generate synthetic data without teaching the generator's habits? How do you prevent leakage between splits? What is label masking? Each answer above is a paragraph; the best evidence is a dataset you built and a model whose behaviour you can trace to specific rows.**



## Where should I start?

**Pick one narrow behaviour, write the paragraph spec and twenty examples tonight, render them with the tokenizer's template, and read them back. Then generate two hundred more synthetically, filter them against the spec, and hold out twenty. That dataset will fine-tune a small model on a free GPU tomorrow.** For a hands-on fine-tuning workshop at your college, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How to prompt ChatGPT: system prompts, courses and prompts for resumes and images
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-prompt-chatgpt/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

To prompt ChatGPT well, tell it the goal, give the context it needs, set constraints such as length and audience, and say exactly what format you want, adding an example when format matters. Then refine with specific follow-ups. Behind every chat sits a system prompt that sets the assistant's role; you can add your own layer through custom instructions, Projects or a custom GPT. This page covers prompting basics, system prompts, courses, and ready-to-use prompts for roadmaps, resumes, images, photo edits and interior design. How do I write a good ChatGPT prompt? Include four things: the goal, the context, the constraints and the output format. "Explain recursion" becomes "I am a first-year BCA student. Explain recursion with one everyday analogy and one Python example, in under 200 words, then give me two practice problems." Habits that improve answers: Give background: your level, purpose and audience. Paste the material: the text, code or data you are asking about. Specify format: bullet points, table, JSON, word count. Show an example of the output you want. Ask for steps or reasoning on complex problems. Ask what it needs to know before answering, for open-ended tasks. When the answer misses, say precisely what to change instead of repeating the same prompt. What is the system prompt in ChatGPT? The system prompt is a hidden set of instructions that defines the assistant's role, rules and behaviour before your messages. In ChatGPT, OpenAI writes a system prompt, and your custom instructions, Project instructions or a GPT's instructions add to it. Also asked as: how to chatgpt prompt · what is system prompt in chatgpt System-level instructions shape every reply in a conversation: tone, what to refuse, what tools to use, how to format answers. That is why the same model can act as a tutor in one GPT and a code reviewer in another. In the OpenAI API, developers write these instructions themselves as system or developer messages. Good system prompts are specific about role and boundaries, short enough to follow, and tested on real examples. How do I add a system prompt in ChatGPT? Use custom instructions in ChatGPT's settings for rules that apply to all chats, Project instructions for one subject or project, or create a custom GPT with its own instructions for a reusable assistant. Also asked as: how to add system prompt in chatgpt Where each fits: Custom instructions: who you are and how you like answers, for every chat. Projects: instructions plus files for a course, a client or a long piece of work. Custom GPT: a shareable assistant with instructions, knowledge files and optional actions. Example instruction for a study Project: "You are my tutor for Operating Systems. Use the attached syllabus. Explain with examples, then ask me one question to check understanding. Do not write my assignments." Test with a few questions and refine. Can you change ChatGPT's system prompt? You cannot replace or remove OpenAI's own system prompt in the ChatGPT app, but you can add your own instructions on top through custom instructions, Projects and custom GPTs. Developers using the API control the whole system prompt themselves. Also asked as: can you change chatgpt system prompt Your added instructions shape tone, format and focus, but cannot override OpenAI's safety policies. Prompts found online claiming to "unlock" or "jailbreak" ChatGPT usually break the terms of use and produce unreliable output. If you need full control, for example for a product, use the API, where you write the system or developer message, choose the model and set parameters. In the app, clear custom instructions plus good prompts achieve almost everything most users need. Is there a ChatGPT prompt engineering course for developers? Yes. DeepLearning.AI's free short course "ChatGPT Prompt Engineering for Developers", taught with OpenAI, covers prompting principles and building with the API. OpenAI's and Anthropic's official prompt engineering guides are also free and kept up to date. Also asked as: course chatgpt prompt engineering for developers For developers, prompting is one part of a larger skill set: structured outputs with JSON schemas, tool calling, retrieval-augmented generation, evaluation with test sets, and managing cost and latency. After a short course, build a small app, such as an extractor that turns emails into structured data, and measure accuracy on fifty examples while you change prompts. That teaches more than any certificate, and gives you a project to show. What is a good ChatGPT prompt for a learning roadmap? Give your starting point, goal, time available and preferred style, and ask for a week-by-week plan with projects and checkpoints. For example: Also asked as: chatgpt roadmap prompt I am a second-year BCA student who knows basic Python. My goal is to get an internship as a GenAI engineer in six months. I can study 2 hours a day. Create a week-by-week roadmap with: topics, one free resource per topic, a small project every two weeks, and a checkpoint question to test myself. Prioritise building over watching videos. Then ask follow-ups: "make weeks 5 to 8 more practical" or "replace paid resources with free ones". Revisit the roadmap monthly and adjust to your progress. A roadmap you follow beats a perfect one you abandon. How do I prompt ChatGPT for a resume? Give it the job description and your real experience, and ask it to tailor and tighten, using only facts you provided. Never let it invent experience, numbers or skills. Also asked as: how to prompt chatgpt for resume A prompt that works: Here is a job description and my current resume. 1) List the skills the role needs that my resume does not show. 2) Rewrite my project bullets to match the role, using strong verbs and only facts from my resume. 3) Suggest a 2-line summary. Keep it to one page. Flag anything you are unsure about. Then edit the output in your own voice. Check every claim, because you must defend each line in an interview. Remove personal details such as ID numbers before pasting your resume into any chatbot. How do I prompt ChatGPT for images? Describe the subject, setting, style, lighting, composition and any text, and say what the image is for. For example: "A flat illustration for a college hackathon poster: four students around laptops, sticky notes on a wall, bright orange and white palette, top-down view, space at the top for a title." Also asked as: how to prompt chatgpt for images Tips: Name the style: photo, watercolour, flat vector, 3D render, pencil sketch. Specify aspect ratio for posters, slides or social posts. Put exact text in quotes and check spelling in the result. Refine with one change at a time: "same image, but evening light". Avoid real people's likeness, trademarks and copyrighted characters. Label AI-generated images where they could be mistaken for real photos. How do I write ChatGPT photo editing prompts? Upload the photo and say exactly what to change and what must stay the same. For example: "Replace the background with a plain light grey studio wall. Keep the person, clothing, face and lighting on the face unchanged. Do not add or remove objects." Also asked as: tutorial chatgpt photo editing prompt Prompts for common edits: "Remove the person in the background on the right; fill naturally." "Make it look like evening golden-hour light, keep everything else the same." "Extend the image to a 16:9 frame, continuing the scenery naturally." "Convert to a clean black-and-white portrait with soft contrast." AI edits regenerate the image, so faces and small details can shift; check carefully. Do not use AI-edited photos for official documents, and never edit images of others without consent. How do I prompt ChatGPT for interior design? Upload a photo of the room or give its dimensions, describe how you use it, your style and budget level, and ask for a layout, colour palette, furniture list and a visual concept. Specific constraints produce useful ideas. Also asked as: how to prompt chatgpt for interior design Example prompt: Here is a photo of my 10 x 12 ft hostel-style study room with one window on the left wall. I need a desk for two monitors, storage for books and space for a bed. Style: minimal, warm wood, plants. Suggest a layout, a colour palette with paint names to look for, and a shopping list by priority. Then generate an image of the redesigned room from the same angle. Treat the image as inspiration; measure everything before buying.

# How to start a tech community on campus: from five friends to 500 members, the sessions, the structure and the mistakes, from building TechVerse Enclave
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-start-a-tech-community-on-campus/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How do I start a tech community on campus?

**Pick one topic you can teach for an hour, book a room, tell five people, and run the session this week. Then run one next week. A community is a weekly session that happens whether five or fifty people attend; everything else, the name, the logo, the group chat, the sponsors, comes after the habit exists. TechVerse Enclave started in 2023 as a hackathon team and a handful of friends learning web development together. It has since grown past 500 members, and I have mentored more than 200 students through it. The first six months were the hardest and the most important.**


The full playbook, with the timeline and the numbers, is on the portfolio [1][3]. This page is the version for someone starting Monday.

> Nobody joins a community. They come to a session, and they come back to the next one because it happened. The community is the coming back.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour, founder of TechVerse Enclave</cite>

## What should the first session be?

**Something you built last month, shown live, then a hands-on hour where everyone leaves with a version running. A first session about "introduction to AI" attracts fifty curious people who never return. A first session where ten people deploy their first web page attracts ten people who return with friends. Teach what you know; the second session can be taught by whoever learned fastest.**



The session format I still use, with timings, is written up separately [4]: ten minutes of story, twenty of demonstration, forty of hands-on, and a public artefact from every attendee.

## How do I get people to show up and keep coming?

**Same time, same place, every week, announced the day before, with photos and a recap the same day. Make the first-timer's experience good: someone greets them, the setup instructions were sent in advance, they leave with something working. Ask every attendee to bring one person. Celebrate small ships publicly. Growth came for TechVerse Enclave when members started teaching, because each new teacher brought their own circle.**



## How should a student community be organised?

**Small roles with names: a lead, a sessions lead who owns the calendar, a content lead who posts, an outreach lead who invites speakers and talks to faculty, and a treasurer if money exists. A shared calendar planned a month ahead. A written handover document from day one, because the founders graduate. A faculty coordinator who signs forms and books rooms, kept informed monthly. Nothing more until the weekly session has run for a semester.**



The mistake that kills most college clubs is not low attendance; it is a founding batch that graduates without a handover. The lessons post covers what I got wrong here first [2].

## How do I get speakers, mentors and judges?

**Invite practitioners with a concrete ask: a topic from their own work, two dates, the audience, the format, what you offer. Start with alumni and engineers in your city, then people who already post about speaking at colleges. Many, including me, speak for free for student communities. Build a record first: a speaker says yes faster to a community with photos of ten past sessions than to one with a plan. Then ask each speaker for the next thing, judging your hackathon, monthly office hours.**


My detailed guide to writing the invitation is a separate page on this site; the short version is six things in one email and a follow-up after five days.


## How do I run a hackathon as a student community?

**Start with a 12-hour internal build day for your own members, then a one-day campus hackathon, then a bigger one with outside teams. Fix the rubric and the timeline before you fix the theme. Recruit judges who have built things and brief them for fifteen minutes. Protect the demo slot: three minutes each, a hard stop, a working projector. Sponsors come after the first successful event, not before. TechVerse Enclave's first hackathon was an afternoon in a classroom; the ones after had partners because the first one had photos.**


The organiser guide with the timeline, rubric and budget lines is on the portfolio [5].

## How do I get sponsors, funding and partner programmes?

**Programmes first, money second. Google Developer Groups on Campus, Microsoft Learn Student Ambassadors, the GitHub Campus Program and Major League Hacking give student communities structure, resources, swag, speakers and credibility, for free [6][7][8][9]. Apply once you have a semester of sessions to show. Local companies sponsor food and prizes for hackathons when you show them last year's photos and this year's plan. College funding follows visible activity, so make the activity visible first.**


## How does a community help your career?

**In every way that a certificate does not. My teammates for three winning hackathons came from it. My first clients came from it. The sessions I ran inside it became the sessions colleges invited me to give. The people I mentored became referrals. Recruiters read "founded a 500-member developer community and mentored 200 students" as leadership evidence no course provides. And teaching every week is the fastest way to actually understand what you are learning.**



## What mistakes do new communities make?

**Spending the first month on a name and a logo. Announcing a big event before running a small session. Founders doing everything and burning out. No handover, so the club dies with a batch. Chasing sponsors before there is anything to sponsor. Measuring the group chat's size instead of the room's. Every one of these I made or watched; the fix for all of them is the weekly session.**



## Can you help our community get started?

**Yes. I run sessions on building and running student communities, speak at inaugurations of new clubs, and connect organisers with the playbook and the templates.** Email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite. Free for student communities.

# How to structure an LLM project in Python: folder layout, config, prompts as files, evals, and the patterns that survive past the notebook
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-structure-an-llm-project-in-python/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How should I structure an LLM project in Python?

**As a proper package under `src/`, with separate modules for the model provider, prompts, retrieval, domain logic, API or CLI, and evaluation; typed settings loaded from environment variables; prompts stored as versioned files rather than string literals; Pydantic schemas at every model boundary; a `tests/` folder with a golden set and an `eval` command; and a task runner so `make eval` or `uv run eval` works on any machine. The structure exists so the model can change, the prompts can change and the retrieval can change without touching each other.**


Both production systems I maintain, the RAG platform and the document extraction service, share this shape, and the shape is why a provider swap in one took an afternoon rather than a week [11][12]. My shorter note on the layout is on the portfolio [13]. This page is the full version with the reasons.

> The first time you change models, the structure pays for itself. The second time you change prompts without a test set, you learn why the eval folder exists.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What does the folder layout look like?

**A `src/yourapp/` package with `providers/`, `prompts/`, `retrieval/`, `core/`, `api/` and `eval/` inside it; `tests/` beside `src/` with fixtures and a golden set; `data/` for local indexes and samples, gitignored where large; `scripts/` for one-off jobs; `pyproject.toml`, `Makefile` or task file, `.env.example`, `README.md`. The src layout prevents the common bug of importing the local folder instead of the installed package [1] and forces you to install the project properly.**



## How should I handle configuration and secrets?

**A single typed settings object loaded from environment variables, using Pydantic Settings or equivalent [2]: model names, endpoints, temperature, chunk sizes, feature flags, all with types and defaults. Secrets come from the environment and never from the repository; commit a `.env.example` with the keys and no values [10]. Every module receives the settings object or the specific values it needs; nothing reads `os.environ` directly. This is what lets the same code run on your laptop, in CI and in production.**



## Where should prompts live?

**In files, one per prompt, under `src/app/prompts/`, loaded by a small function that fills placeholders and records which version was used. A prompt is a piece of program logic that happens to be in English; treating it as a string literal buried in a function makes it impossible to diff, review or test. Name files by purpose and version, keep a changelog line at the top, and run the golden set whenever one changes. Templates with explicit placeholders beat f-strings, because the template can be reviewed without the surrounding code.**



## How do I handle model outputs safely?

**Define a Pydantic model for every structured output and parse at the boundary [3]. Use the provider's structured output or tool-calling mode to constrain generation where available [7][8], then still validate, because constraints reduce but do not eliminate malformed output. On failure, retry once with the validation error in the prompt, then fall back to a safe default or a human queue. The rest of the codebase receives typed objects and never raw model text.**


DocuLens is built on this rule: a strict schema per document type, validation at the boundary, deterministic rules afterwards, and a review queue for anything that fails [12]. It is the difference between a demo and a system a finance team trusts.


## How do I set up evaluation in the project?

**A `golden/` folder with labelled cases as JSON or JSONL: input, expected output or expected properties, tags. An `eval` module that runs every case through the real pipeline, computes metrics, retrieval recall, format validity, faithfulness judged by a model or rules, latency, cost, and writes a report. A command, `make eval` or `uv run eval`, that prints the score and exits non-zero if it drops below a threshold. Run it in CI on every prompt or retrieval change. Twenty cases is enough to start; grow it from production failures.**



## How should I log and trace?

**Structured logs, JSON in production, with a request ID that follows the call through retrieval, generation and validation [9]. Log the prompt version, model name, token counts, latency, retrieved document IDs and validation outcome for every call. Store prompts and outputs for a bounded time, with sensitive data redacted, so a failure report can be reproduced. When a user says the answer was wrong, you should be able to find exactly what the model saw.**


## Which tools should I use for the project itself?

**uv for environments and dependencies, because it is fast and produces a lockfile [4]. Ruff for linting and formatting in one tool [5]. pytest for tests [6]. Pydantic for schemas and settings [2][3]. FastAPI if the app serves HTTP. A Makefile or a task runner with `setup`, `test`, `eval`, `run` and `lint` targets so nobody memorises commands. Pre-commit hooks that run Ruff. Nothing exotic; boring tools mean a new contributor is productive in an hour.**



## How do I package and deploy it?

**A Dockerfile that installs from the lockfile, copies `src/`, and runs the API with a production server. Settings from environment variables, so the same image runs everywhere. Health and readiness endpoints. Indexes and data mounted or fetched at startup, not baked into the image if they change. A CI pipeline that runs lint, tests and evals before building the image. Deployment specifics depend on the host; the structure makes them small.**



## What mistakes make LLM projects unmaintainable?

**Prompts as f-strings scattered through functions. Provider calls made directly from business logic, so a model swap touches everything. Raw model text parsed with regex in five places. No golden set, so every change is a guess. API keys in the repository. A notebook as the only entry point. No request IDs, so failures cannot be traced. Everything in one file called `main.py` at two thousand lines. Each is fixed by one folder on this page.**



## Interview questions on LLM project structure

**Explain how you would structure a RAG application so the model can be swapped. Where do prompts live and how are they versioned? How do you validate outputs? What is in your eval set and when does it run? How do you handle secrets? How would you debug a wrong answer reported by a user? A repository that answers these by its layout is the strongest evidence you can bring.**



## Where should I start?

**Take your current notebook and create the six folders. Move the model call into providers, the prompt into a file, the output into a schema, and five examples into a golden set with an eval command. Two hours, and the project can now change safely.** For a workshop on shipping LLM applications from notebook to production, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How to win a hackathon: what judges score, how to pick an idea, and the demo that works live, from three first prizes
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-win-a-hackathon/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is a hackathon?

**A hackathon is a timed competition, usually 24 to 48 hours, sometimes a few weeks online, where small teams build a working prototype that solves a stated problem and then pitch it to judges. The output is a demo, not a plan. The prize is usually cash, credits or an incubation offer, but the lasting value is the project, the repository and the people you built it with.**


The word blends "hack", in the sense of building something quickly, with "marathon". In India the format ranges from a two-day event in a college seminar hall to Smart India Hackathon, the government-run national competition with a months-long process [1]. AI hackathons are the same format with problem statements that expect a model, an agent or a data pipeline in the solution.

I have been on both sides of the table: three first prizes as a builder, at IIT Roorkee, CSJMU and MeetKats, a loss I learned more from than any win, and time as a judge and mentor at college events. This page is the version of the talk I give students, with the parts that made the difference between winning and not.

> Every hackathon I won, we solved a smaller problem than the teams we beat. Every hackathon I lost, we tried to solve a bigger one.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## How does a hackathon work?

**Registration opens weeks ahead. Teams form, usually two to five people. On the day, organisers reveal or confirm the problem statements, the timer starts, and teams build. Mentors circulate. At the end, each team submits code and a short deck and gets a few minutes to demo and answer questions. Judges score against a rubric, and prizes follow.**



The single most important line in that timeline is "skeleton with the demo path stubbed end to end" in the first six hours. A team that can click through a fake version of the final demo at hour 6 will have a real one at hour 30. A team that builds features in isolation integrates at hour 33 and demos a crash.

## How do I find and join a hackathon in India?

**Devfolio and Unstop list most Indian college and company hackathons, Major League Hacking lists student events worldwide, Devpost covers global online ones, and Smart India Hackathon runs through colleges via its official portal. Follow the tech clubs of IITs, NITs and nearby colleges on Instagram and LinkedIn, because campus hackathons are announced there first. Register early; good events fill.**



Sources for these listings are the platforms themselves [2][3][4][5]. My recommendation for a first-year: one campus hackathon within a two-hour train ride, in person, before any online one. You learn more from watching thirty teams demo in one room than from a month of tutorials.

### Can a beginner participate in a hackathon?

**Yes, and you should, before you feel ready. Most college hackathons have a beginner track or no prerequisites at all. Join a team where one person can already build a basic web or Python app, take the role that matches what you can do, design, research, presentation, testing, and build the skill of finishing under a deadline. Nobody is judged on their first hackathon; they are judged on their demo.**


## How do I pick a hackathon idea that can win?

**Pick a problem a specific person has, that you can demonstrate end to end in three minutes, where the hardest part is something your team can actually build in the time you have. Start from the problem statement's audience, list five problems that person has, choose the one with the clearest before-and-after, and cut everything that is not on the path from the user's pain to your demo.**


Ideas that won for us, and why:

- **KrishGyan, Changethon 2025 at IIT Roorkee.** Farming advice in the farmer's own voice and language over WhatsApp: pest control, crop health and weather, spoken back, no reading or typing needed. It won because the demo was a voice note in and a voice note out, which any judge could follow, and because the audience was real and underserved [6].
- **BrandHive, Product Genesis at CSJMU.** A platform for small businesses and emerging influencers to grow organically without a marketing budget. It won because we showed the whole loop, not a slide of features [7].
- **Annapurna, BYTEBATTLE by MeetKats.** Coordinating surplus food between donors, NGOs and volunteers, with four roles and a verified-impact layer. It won on clarity of roles and a demo that walked one meal from a hotel kitchen to a shelter [8].

And the one that did not: STROT, where we built more and explained less, and a simpler team took the prize [9]. That loss is why every timeline I give now starts with cutting scope.


### What are good AI hackathon project ideas?

**The winning AI ideas apply a model to one narrow workflow with real inputs: voice-first advice for people who do not type, document extraction for a specific paper form, a RAG assistant over one institution's documents, a vision check for one quality problem, an agent that completes one repetitive task end to end. "ChatGPT for X" loses to "this one task, done, with this evidence".**


A frame that produces ideas fast: pick an audience, farmers, first-year students, small shops, clinics, college offices; pick a friction, a form, a queue, a language barrier, a lost document; ask what the AI removes. KrishGyan came out of exactly that frame: farmers, the reading barrier, voice.

## What do hackathon judges actually look for?

**Judges score four things, whatever the rubric calls them: feasibility, does it work and could it exist; innovation, is there a real insight, not just a new coat of paint; practicality, would the stated user actually use it; and problem solving, did you understand the problem before you built. Presentation and teamwork are usually smaller weights. A working demo of a modest idea beats a slide deck of a grand one every time.**



These four criteria, feasibility, innovation, practicality and problem solving, are the ones I put on the screen when I brief a room as a judge, and the ones I wrote about after sitting on panels [10]. The weights change; the questions do not.


### What questions do judges ask in Q&A?

**Who is this for and have you spoken to them? What happens when this fails? How is this different from the existing solution? What would you build next with a month? Which part did you write yourselves versus take from a library? Judges use Q&A to find out whether you understand your own project, so short honest answers beat confident vague ones.**


## How do I pitch a hackathon project?

**In three minutes: thirty seconds on who has the problem and what it costs them, ninety seconds of live demo on the happy path, thirty seconds on how it works with one architecture slide, and thirty seconds on what you would do next and what you are asking for. Say the user's name, not the technology's, in the first sentence. Rehearse it three times with a timer.**



For Smart India Hackathon the format is more formal and the template is prescribed, but the same order inside it wins: problem, demo, how, next. Teams that open with a slide of technologies lose the room in the first fifteen seconds.

### How do I give a demo that works live?

**Freeze your code at least two hours before demos. Rehearse the exact click path three times on the machine you will present from, on the venue Wi-Fi if you can. Seed the data so the demo never depends on a live network call you do not control. Record a backup video of the full path and have it open in a tab. Assign one person to drive and one to talk.**


The demo that failed for us at STROT failed on a live API call over venue Wi-Fi. Every demo since has run on seeded data with a recorded fallback, and none has failed.

## How should a hackathon team be formed?

**Three people with three roles: one who builds the core, one who owns the interface and the data, one who owns the problem, the deck and the pitch and also tests everything. Decide roles before the event, not at hour one. A friend who cannot code but can research users and present is worth more than a fourth developer.**


Every first prize we won was a team of three with those roles. Teams of five spend their first three hours negotiating and their last three merging conflicts.


## What is Smart India Hackathon and how do I crack it?

**Smart India Hackathon is a national competition run by the Ministry of Education's Innovation Cell in which student teams solve problem statements posted by government ministries and industry. Teams register through their college, are shortlisted internally, then compete at the national level. To do well: pick a problem statement whose owner you can reach, build a working prototype early, and make the presentation about the ministry's outcome, not your stack.**


The official portal carries the current year's problem statements, timeline and eligibility, and it changes each cycle, so read it rather than any summary, including this one [1]. What stays constant: the internal college round eliminates most teams, so treat the internal presentation as the real competition, and the national judges are domain experts from the problem's ministry, so the domain matters more than the demo polish.

## Do hackathons help your career or resume?

**Yes, when you turn them into evidence: a public repository with a readable README, a two-minute demo video, and a short write-up of the problem, the decision you made and the result. A line saying "participated in 6 hackathons" does nothing. A line saying "1st prize, Changethon 2025, IIT Roorkee, built a voice-first farming assistant over WhatsApp" with a link does the work of a semester of grades.**


On LinkedIn, add the hackathon under Honours & awards with the issuer and date, and post the demo video the same week; hackathon posts travel further than any other student content, in my experience running a 500-member community. On the resume, one line per win, with the problem and the result, and the repository link.

## What mistakes make teams lose?

**Building for 34 hours and presenting for 2. Choosing a problem to impress rather than to solve. No roles, so everyone builds the same screen. A live demo that depends on Wi-Fi. A deck that opens with the tech stack. Not talking to a single real user. Sleeping zero hours and demoing incoherently. Every one of these is cheaper to avoid than to recover from.**



## What should I do after the hackathon?

**Within a week: clean the repository, write the README, publish the demo video, and post the story. Within a month: decide whether the project deserves users, and if so, ship the smallest real version. Annapurna went from a hackathon prize to a tool people used because we kept the roles that worked and threw away the parts built for the judges.**



## Can I invite a judge or mentor to my college hackathon?

**Yes. Organisers can reach me for judging, mentoring or a session on hackathon strategy before your event, on-site across India or remote. What I need from you is the date, the format, the problem statements if fixed, and the rubric you plan to use, or I will bring the four-criteria one above.**


The details and the invite form are at pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite, and my email is pranjulrathour41@gmail.com. Free for student communities.

# How to write a tech resume as a fresher in India: the one-page format, what to put instead of a skills wall, and a free resume website that beats a PDF
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-to-write-a-tech-resume-for-freshers-in-india/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How should a fresher write a tech resume?

**One page. A header with your name, one line describing what you build, and links to email, GitHub and a portfolio, no photo, no objective paragraph. A projects section with three entries, each with the problem, the decision, and a measurable outcome, ahead of education. A short skills line, not a wall. Education below projects, since for a fresher the projects are the evidence and the degree is context. Nothing that needs a second page has earned its place yet.**


I have reviewed enough fresher resumes at hackathons and campus sessions to see the same mistakes repeat: a skills wall with forty items, an objective paragraph nobody reads, and projects buried under a "certifications" section three times its length. This page is the fix, plus the free resume-website option that often works better than the PDF itself [6].

> A resume is not a list of everything you know. It is three pieces of evidence that you can do the job, arranged so a tired recruiter finds them in ten seconds.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What should be at the top of the resume?

**Your name, a phone number, an email you actually check, and three links: GitHub, a portfolio or LinkedIn, and one more if relevant. Under that, one line: what you build and one proof, the same sentence your LinkedIn headline should carry [3]. Not "Computer Science student seeking opportunities". Not a paragraph. One sentence a recruiter can read while scrolling past forty other resumes.**



## What goes in the projects section, and how should it read?

**Three projects, each three lines: the problem in one sentence, the decision or hard part in one sentence, and the outcome in one sentence, ideally with a number. "Built a RAG system over 40 pages of college documents; added a confidence gate after early demos returned wrong answers confidently; recall at 5 improved from 61 percent to 89 percent, measured on a 30-question set." That is one project entry. It proves you can scope, iterate, and measure, in three lines.**



My guide to which projects to choose for this section, and the ones that actually get interviews, is written up separately [7].

## Should I have a skills section, and what should it look like?

**A short line or two, grouped by category, not a wall with progress bars: "Languages: Python, JavaScript. Tools: FastAPI, PostgreSQL, Git, Docker." No percentages, no five-star ratings for how well you know a language, which nobody trusts and which ATS systems ignore anyway. List what you can actually discuss for ten minutes in an interview, and nothing you would freeze on if asked a follow-up question.**




## How do I get past an ATS without gaming it?

**Use plain, standard section headings, Experience, Projects, Education, Skills, so parsing software reads them correctly. Avoid tables, columns, text boxes and graphics that confuse a parser, however good they look to a human eye. Mirror the language of the job posting honestly where it matches what you actually did, a posting that says "REST APIs" should be met with "REST APIs" in your resume if that is what you built, not a synonym. None of this is gaming a system; it is writing clearly enough that both a machine and a human parse the same document correctly.**


## What should education look like for a fresher?

**Degree, institution, graduation year, and a CGPA only if it genuinely helps, one line, below the projects section. Coursework only if a specific course is directly relevant and not implied by the degree itself. No list of every subject studied. A recruiter reading a fresher's resume already expects a degree; the projects section is what differentiates one BCA or B.Tech graduate from another.**


## Should I use a resume website instead of a PDF?

**Both, for different moments. Send a clean one-page PDF when a form or an email asks for a resume, since that is the expected format. Link a simple resume or portfolio website in the header for everyone who wants more, because it can hold live demo links, a longer project write-up, and updates without you re-sending a file [6]. A resume website is not a replacement for the PDF; it is the deeper layer the PDF's links point to.**



## What mistakes do freshers make on tech resumes?

**A two-page resume with a full page of certificates and half a project. An objective paragraph that says nothing a recruiter could not guess. A skills wall claiming expert-level everything. Projects described by technology stack instead of outcome, "Built using React, Node.js, MongoDB" with no sentence on what it did or what was hard. Broken links to private repositories. A resume never updated after the first draft, still listing a project from first year as the newest thing built.**



## Tech resume interview questions

**Not asked directly, but tested by every "walk me through a project" question: can you defend every line on the resume for ten minutes without notes. If a bullet point cannot survive a follow-up question, it should not be on the resume. The strongest resumes are the ones the candidate wrote entirely from memory of what they actually did.**



## Where should I start?

**Cut your current resume to one page tonight: header, three projects in three lines each, a short skills line, education last. Then link a portfolio site from the header.** For a resume and portfolio workshop that turns a semester of projects into an interview-ready one-pager, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# How does a vector database work? Examples, choosing one, and do you need it for RAG
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/how-vector-databases-work/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

A vector database stores embeddings, numeric vectors that represent meaning, together with the original data and metadata, and answers queries by finding the vectors closest to a query vector. Approximate nearest-neighbour indexes make this fast even over millions of items. That is the retrieval step behind semantic search and RAG. This page explains how it works and what vector search is, gives examples, helps you choose, answers whether RAG needs one and how to build one, covers Supabase, NoSQL and dimensions, and whether vector databases are dead. How does a vector database work? You insert items with an embedding vector, an ID and metadata. The database adds each vector to an index. At query time, you send a query vector, and the database uses the index to return the nearest stored vectors, optionally filtered by metadata. Also asked as: how does vector database work · examples vector database Exact search compares the query with every vector, which is slow at scale, so vector databases use approximate indexes. HNSW builds a layered graph where each vector links to near neighbours, and search walks the graph towards the query. Inverted-file indexes cluster vectors and search only the nearest clusters. Product quantisation compresses vectors to save memory. Databases add what libraries lack: persistence, updates and deletes, filtering, access control, replication and scaling. What is vector search in a database? Vector search finds items whose embeddings are most similar to a query embedding, measured by cosine similarity, dot product or Euclidean distance. It retrieves by meaning rather than exact words. Also asked as: what is vector search in database For example, searching "laptop overheating" can find a help article titled "fan noise and high temperature on notebooks" even with no shared keywords. Many databases now support vector search alongside their normal queries: PostgreSQL with pgvector, OpenSearch and Elasticsearch, MongoDB Atlas and others. Combining vector search with keyword search, called hybrid search, usually gives the best results, because keywords catch exact terms such as product codes that embeddings blur. What are some examples of vector databases? Examples include pgvector for PostgreSQL, Pinecone as a managed service, Qdrant, Weaviate and Milvus as open-source dedicated vector databases, Chroma for lightweight local use, and vector search features in OpenSearch, Elasticsearch and MongoDB Atlas. Related tools that are not full databases: FAISS, a library for fast similarity search in memory, and hnswlib, an index library. Cloud providers also offer vector capabilities in their managed databases and storage services. The landscape changes quickly, but the core ideas, embeddings, approximate indexes, filtering and hybrid search, stay the same across products. Which vector database should I choose? Choose the simplest option that meets your needs: pgvector if you already use PostgreSQL, Chroma or FAISS for prototypes, Qdrant, Weaviate or Milvus for a dedicated open-source service, and Pinecone if you want fully managed scaling. Also asked as: which vector database to choose Questions to decide: How many vectors now and in a year: thousands, millions or billions? Do you need metadata filters, multi-tenancy or access control? Do you need keyword plus vector search? Who will operate it: your team or a vendor? Where must data live for privacy or compliance? For most student and startup projects, pgvector on a hosted PostgreSQL is enough. Measure retrieval recall on your own questions before switching for performance reasons. Does RAG need a vector database? RAG needs retrieval, not necessarily a dedicated vector database. For small document sets, an in-memory index such as FAISS, or pgvector in your existing database, is enough; some systems even use keyword search alone. Also asked as: does rag need vector database What RAG really needs is good retrieval: clean chunks, a suitable embedding model, hybrid keyword plus vector search, reranking and evaluation. RAG.NextUpgrad runs hybrid dense and BM25 retrieval with reciprocal-rank fusion and re-ranking in about 220 MB on a free tier, which shows that heavy infrastructure is not required. Move to a dedicated vector database when scale, filtering, concurrency or operations demand it. How do I create a vector database for RAG? Chunk your documents, embed each chunk with one embedding model, store chunks with their vectors and metadata in a vector store, then retrieve with the same model at query time. With PostgreSQL and pgvector, it is a table with a vector column and an index. Also asked as: how to create vector database for rag create extension if not exists vector; create table chunks (id bigserial primary key, doc text, page int, content text, embedding vector(768)); create index on chunks using hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops); -- query: nearest 5 chunks to a query embedding select doc, page, content from chunks order by embedding &lt;=&gt; $1 limit 5; Match the vector dimension to your model, add a full-text index for keyword search, and store page numbers for citations. Does Supabase have a vector database? Yes. Supabase supports vector storage and search through pgvector, a PostgreSQL extension, so you can store embeddings next to your other data and query them with SQL or through Supabase's client libraries. Also asked as: does supabase have vector database Enable the extension, create a table with a vector column, add an index, and write a database function for similarity search that your app calls. Supabase's AI documentation includes guides for semantic search and RAG. Because it is PostgreSQL, you also get row-level security for access control, joins with user data and transactions, which dedicated vector databases may not offer. For student projects, Supabase's free tier is a convenient way to build a full RAG backend. Is a vector database NoSQL? Usually it is described as a NoSQL-style system, because dedicated vector databases do not use relational tables and SQL as their main model. But vector search also exists inside SQL databases, such as PostgreSQL with pgvector. Also asked as: is vector database nosql Dedicated vector databases expose APIs for collections of points or objects with vectors and metadata, closer to document stores. SQL databases with vector extensions let you mix vector similarity with joins, filters and transactions. The classification matters less than the features you need: query language, filtering, consistency, scale and operations. Many teams prefer keeping vectors in the same database as their application data to avoid syncing two systems. Is a vector database 3D? No. Vectors in a vector database usually have hundreds or thousands of dimensions, such as 384, 768 or 1536, not three. Each dimension is a learned feature of meaning, not a spatial direction. Also asked as: is vector database 3d Three-dimensional pictures of embeddings in tutorials are simplifications made with dimension-reduction methods such as PCA, t-SNE or UMAP, which squash high-dimensional vectors into two or three dimensions for visualisation. They help intuition, showing that similar items cluster, but distances in the picture are distorted. Search always happens in the full high-dimensional space. Is the vector database dead? No, but it is changing. Vector search is becoming a standard feature of general-purpose databases and storage services, long context windows reduce the need for retrieval in some cases, and agentic search with keywords works for some tasks. Dedicated vector databases still matter at large scale and for specialised needs. Also asked as: is vector database dead The durable part is retrieval itself: most AI applications still need to find the right information quickly, cite it and control access. Whether that runs in a dedicated vector database, PostgreSQL with pgvector, a search engine or a library depends on scale and team. Focus on retrieval quality and evaluation, and keep your design portable, so the storage choice can change as the market does.

# Hybrid search and reranking in RAG: BM25 plus embeddings, reciprocal rank fusion, cross-encoders, and why this pair fixes most bad answers
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/hybrid-search-and-reranking-in-rag/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is hybrid search in RAG?

**Hybrid search runs two retrievers on every query, a keyword retriever such as BM25 and a dense embedding retriever, and merges their ranked results into one list. Keyword search catches exact terms, product codes, names, error numbers and rare words that embeddings blur together. Embedding search catches paraphrases and meaning that share no words with the document. Fusing them gives higher recall than either alone, and the fusion itself can be a dozen lines of code with no tuning.**


Hybrid retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion and a cross-encoder reranker is the core of RAG.NextUpgrad's query path, and it is the part of the platform that moved retrieval recall most on the labelled question set [13]. My shorter notes on each half are on the portfolio [11][12]. This page is the pair together, with the papers and the code.

> Users ask for "error E-4021" as often as they ask "why did my upload fail". Only one of those is a semantic query. Ship both retrievers or you will fail half your users.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour, from building RAG.NextUpgrad</cite>

## Why does vector search alone miss results?

**Because embeddings compress meaning and lose exact strings. A product code, a person's name, an error number, an acronym or a version string carries little meaning to the model, so its vector lands near other codes and names rather than near the exact match. Numbers and negation blur too. Dense retrieval was shown to beat keywords for open-domain questions on average [3], and the average hides exactly the queries that matter most in support, legal and technical corpora.**


## What is BM25, and why is it still used?

**BM25 is a ranking function from classical information retrieval that scores a document for a query by how often the query's terms appear in it, weighted by how rare each term is across the collection and normalised for document length [1]. It needs no training, runs in microseconds over an inverted index, and finds exact terms perfectly. It cannot see that "reset my password" and "credential recovery" are the same request, which is exactly what embeddings are for. Together they cover each other's blind spots.**



Learned sparse models such as SPLADE bring some semantic expansion to the keyword side [6], and late-interaction models such as ColBERT keep per-token vectors to recover exact-term precision on the dense side [5]. Both are worth knowing; BM25 plus a dense model plus fusion remains the practical default.

## What is reciprocal rank fusion?

**Reciprocal rank fusion merges several ranked lists into one by giving each document a score equal to the sum, over every list it appears in, of one divided by a constant plus its rank in that list. Documents ranked high in either list rise; documents ranked high in both rise most. The constant, usually 60, dampens the influence of top ranks. It needs no score normalisation, because it uses ranks not scores, and Cormack, Clarke and Buettcher showed it beating more complex fusion methods [2].**


```python
def reciprocal_rank_fusion(*ranked_lists: list[str], k: int = 60) -> list[str]:
    scores: dict[str, float] = {}
    for ranked in ranked_lists:
        for rank, doc_id in enumerate(ranked, start=1):
            scores[doc_id] = scores.get(doc_id, 0.0) + 1.0 / (k + rank)
    return sorted(scores, key=scores.get, reverse=True)

fused = reciprocal_rank_fusion(dense_top_40, bm25_top_40)[:30]   # then rerank these
```

That function is in RAG.NextUpgrad almost exactly as written, because the paper's simplicity is the point: no learned weights, no score scales to reconcile, nothing to retune when you swap an embedding model [13].

## What is reranking, and why not just retrieve more?

**A reranker is a model that reads the question and a candidate passage together and outputs a relevance score. Retrievers compare a query vector with passage vectors that were computed separately, for speed; a cross-encoder looks at the pair jointly, which is far more accurate but too slow to run over the whole corpus. So you retrieve wide with the fast methods, thirty to fifty candidates, and rerank narrow, to the best three to eight. Retrieving more without reranking sends noise to the model, and models use long contexts unevenly [8].**


Passage reranking with BERT-style cross-encoders was introduced by Nogueira and Cho and remains the recipe [4]; Sentence Transformers publishes pretrained rerankers you can run on a CPU for small candidate sets [10].


## How do I choose k at each stage?

**Measure recall at each boundary on a labelled question set. Retrieve enough from each retriever that recall at the fusion output is above ninety percent; forty each is a common starting point. Fuse and keep enough that the reranker sees every plausible passage, twenty to fifty. Rerank down to what the model needs, three to eight, and check recall at that k is still above eighty-five. If recall drops sharply at the rerank step, the reranker is wrong for your domain; if it drops at fusion, one retriever is starving the other.**




## How much does hybrid search and reranking improve results?

**On the labelled sets I have worked with, fusion raised recall at thirty over either retriever alone, and the reranker raised recall at five without touching recall at thirty, which is exactly what each is supposed to do. Public benchmarks such as BEIR show dense models varying widely across domains and BM25 remaining a hard baseline on several [7], which is the research version of the same lesson. Your gain depends on your queries: corpora heavy in codes, names and numbers gain most from BM25; corpora of prose gain most from the reranker.**



## How do I implement hybrid search?

**Keep a keyword index alongside the vector index: Postgres full-text search or a BM25 library over the same chunks [9]; Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Qdrant, Weaviate and others also offer sparse or hybrid support. At query time, run both, fuse with the function above, rerank with a cross-encoder from Sentence Transformers or a hosted reranking API [10], and send the top few to the model. The whole path is a few hundred lines; the design decisions are the k values and the reranker choice.**



## When is hybrid search not worth it?

**Rarely, but there are cases. A tiny corpus where everything fits in the prompt does not need retrieval at all. A corpus of pure prose with no codes or names, where the reranker alone recovers what dense misses. A latency budget so tight that even microseconds matter, which is unusual. In every other case I have seen, the cost of a second retriever is small and the recall gain on exact-term queries is large. Default to hybrid and let your measurements argue you out of it.**



## Hybrid search and reranking interview questions

**Explain why embeddings miss exact terms and BM25 misses paraphrase. Explain reciprocal rank fusion and why it needs no normalisation. Explain the difference between a bi-encoder and a cross-encoder and why you cannot rerank the whole corpus. Describe how you would choose k at each stage and measure it. Say when you would use learned sparse or late interaction models. A retrieval system you built and ablated is the best evidence.**




## Where should I start?

**Add BM25 next to your vector search over the same chunks, fuse with the twelve-line function, and measure recall at thirty on twenty real questions before and after. Then add a cross-encoder and measure recall at five. Both changes take an afternoon and usually deliver the largest quality jump the system will ever see.** For a hands-on retrieval session at your college or team, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# Should I install Ollama? Install on Windows, Mac, Linux, WSL and Docker
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/install-ollama-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

Install Ollama if you want to run open-weight language models such as Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Mistral or DeepSeek on your own machine, for privacy, offline use, learning or building prototypes without per-token costs. It installs in a few minutes on Windows, macOS and Linux, and runs in Docker. This page helps you decide, then covers installing on Windows including a D drive, where models are stored, macOS, Ubuntu, WSL, Docker and pulling models inside a container, and running DeepSeek models. Should I install Ollama? Yes, if you want to learn how language models work hands-on, keep data private, work offline, or prototype apps without paying per token. No, if you only want the best answers for hard tasks, where hosted models such as Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini are much stronger. Your hardware decides the experience. With 8 GB of RAM you can run small models of a few billion parameters at usable speed. With 16 to 32 GB of RAM or a GPU with 8 GB or more of video memory, mid-size models become practical. Larger models need serious GPUs. Ollama itself is free and open source, and uninstalling it is simple, so trying it costs nothing but disk space: models range from a couple of gigabytes to tens of gigabytes each. How do I install Ollama on Windows? Download the Windows installer from ollama.com, run it, and Ollama starts in the background with an icon in the system tray. Then open a terminal and run a model. Also asked as: how to install ollama on windows ollama --version ollama run llama3.2 The first run downloads the model, then opens an interactive chat; type /bye to exit. Ollama also serves an API on http://localhost:11434, which tools such as LangChain and Open WebUI use. If you have an NVIDIA or AMD GPU, keep its drivers updated so Ollama can use it; check with ollama ps while a model runs to see whether it is on the GPU or CPU. Can I install Ollama on the D drive? Yes. The models are what take space, and you can store them on any drive by setting the OLLAMA_MODELS environment variable, for example to D:\ollama\models, then restarting Ollama. The installer also accepts a custom install directory. Also asked as: can i install ollama in d drive Steps for the models folder: Quit Ollama from the system tray. Open "Edit environment variables for your account" in Windows settings. Add a variable OLLAMA_MODELS with the value D:\ollama\models. Start Ollama again and pull a model; it downloads to the new folder. To install the program itself elsewhere, the Windows installer supports a directory option documented in Ollama's Windows guide. Moving existing models is as simple as moving the folder to the new path before restarting. Where does Ollama install models? By default, models are stored in a .ollama/models folder in your home directory: C:\Users\&lt;you&gt;\.ollama\models on Windows and ~/.ollama/models on macOS. On Linux, when installed as a service, they are under the ollama user's home, typically /usr/share/ollama/.ollama/models. Also asked as: where ollama install models Set OLLAMA_MODELS to change the location on any system. Models are stored as layered blobs with manifests, so the folder will not show friendly filenames; use ollama list to see installed models and ollama rm &lt;name&gt; to delete one and free space. Several models can share layers, so deleting one may free less space than its listed size. If disk space is tight, keep only the models you actually use. How do I install Ollama on a Mac? Download the macOS app from ollama.com, move it to Applications and open it. It adds the ollama command to your terminal, and you can run a model straight away with ollama run llama3.2. Also asked as: how to install ollama on mac Apple Silicon Macs, with M-series chips, run local models well because the GPU shares fast unified memory with the CPU, so a Mac with 16 GB or more can run mid-size models comfortably. Intel Macs work but are slower. You can also install through Homebrew if you prefer managing tools that way. Keep the app running in the menu bar so the local API at port 11434 stays available for other apps. How do I install Ollama on Ubuntu? Run the official install script, which installs Ollama and sets it up as a systemd service that starts automatically. curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh ollama run llama3.2 Check the service with systemctl status ollama and view logs with journalctl -u ollama. For NVIDIA GPUs, install the proprietary drivers first; the script detects them. To change settings such as the models folder or listening address, edit the service with sudo systemctl edit ollama and add environment variables like OLLAMA_MODELS or OLLAMA_HOST, then restart the service. As with any script piped to a shell, you can download and read it first. Can I install Ollama on WSL? Yes. Inside WSL 2 on Windows, install Ollama with the Linux install script, and with up-to-date NVIDIA drivers on Windows, Ollama in WSL can use the GPU. Alternatively, install the Windows version and call it from WSL over the local network. Choose based on your workflow. If your projects live in WSL, running Ollama there keeps everything in one environment. If you also use Windows tools, the Windows app is simpler and you can reach it from WSL at the Windows host's address. Avoid running both at once on the same port. WSL needs enough memory allocated; if models fail to load, raise the memory limit in your WSL configuration. Should I install Ollama in Docker? Docker is a good choice for servers, reproducible setups and running Ollama alongside other services such as a web UI or a database. On a personal laptop, the native installer is simpler and usually uses the GPU with less setup. Run the official image with a volume so models persist: docker run -d --name ollama -p 11434:11434 -v ollama:/root/.ollama ollama/ollama For NVIDIA GPUs, install the NVIDIA Container Toolkit and add --gpus=all. With Docker Compose, you can define Ollama, Open WebUI and your app together. Do not expose port 11434 to the internet without authentication in front of it; the Ollama API has no built-in login. How do I pull Ollama models in a Docker container? Run the ollama pull command inside the running container with docker exec, and the model is saved in the mounted volume, so it survives restarts. Also asked as: how to install / pull ollama models in docker container docker exec -it ollama ollama pull llama3.2 docker exec -it ollama ollama list docker exec -it ollama ollama run llama3.2 &quot;Explain BM25 in one line&quot; For automated setups, pull models in a start-up script or call the API's pull endpoint from your app on first run. Keep the volume, named ollama above, when updating the image, so you do not re-download models. If another container needs Ollama, connect them on the same Docker network and use http://ollama:11434 as the address. Can I install DeepSeek on Ollama? Yes. DeepSeek's open-weight models, including distilled versions of its reasoning model, are available in Ollama's library. Run one with ollama run deepseek-r1, adding a size tag to choose a smaller or larger variant. Pick a size that fits your memory: small distilled versions run on ordinary laptops, while the largest DeepSeek models need multiple high-end GPUs and are not practical locally. Reasoning models print their thinking before the final answer, so expect longer responses. Running locally means your prompts stay on your machine, which addresses privacy concerns some people have about using hosted services. Test on your own tasks; smaller distilled models are much weaker than the full model.
