# What does open source mean? Open LLMs, and is OpenAI, Claude or Ollama open
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/open-source-llms-explained/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

Open source means software whose source code is published under a licence that lets anyone use, study, modify and share it. In AI, many "open" language models are more precisely open-weight: you can download and run the trained model, but the training data and full training code are not published. This page explains the meaning, which LLMs are open and which are best, why and how to run them, and answers whether OpenAI, Claude, Ollama, Pinecone and LangChain are open source. What does open source mean? Open source means the source code is freely available under a licence that grants everyone the rights to use it for any purpose, study how it works, change it and share copies or improvements. The Open Source Initiative maintains the formal definition. Common open-source licences include permissive ones such as MIT and Apache 2.0, which allow almost any use including commercial, and copyleft ones such as GPL and AGPL, which require sharing changes under the same licence in certain cases. "Source-available" licences publish code but restrict some uses, such as offering the software as a competing service; those are not open source by the strict definition. Always read the licence before building a product on a project. What are open-source LLM models? Open-source or open-weight LLMs are language models whose trained weights are published for download, so you can run, inspect and fine-tune them yourself. Well-known families include Meta's Llama, Alibaba's Qwen, Mistral's open models, Google's Gemma, DeepSeek's models, Microsoft's Phi and OpenAI's open-weight releases. Also asked as: what are open source llm models Licences vary: some use permissive licences such as Apache 2.0, while others have custom terms that restrict certain uses or very large companies. Few release full training data, so most are open-weight rather than open source in the strict sense. They are available on Hugging Face and through tools like Ollama, and many come in several sizes and variants, such as instruct, coding and vision models. What are the best open-source models? The best open models change every few months. Strong general families include the latest Qwen, Llama, DeepSeek, Mistral and Gemma releases, plus OpenAI's open-weight models; specialised coding and embedding models lead in their niches. The best choice depends on your hardware and task. Also asked as: best open source models How to choose: Laptop with 8 to 16 GB RAM: 3B to 8B models at 4-bit quantisation. Single strong GPU: 14B to 32B models, or mixture-of-experts models with small active size. Coding: coder-tuned variants. RAG: a good open embedding model plus a mid-size instruct model. Languages: test Indian-language performance yourself if you need it. Check recent independent evaluations and test on your own prompts before settling. Why use an open-source LLM? Use open models for privacy, since data never leaves your infrastructure; for cost control at high volume; for customisation through fine-tuning; for offline or on-device use; and for independence from a single vendor's pricing and policy changes. Also asked as: why use open source llm Trade-offs to weigh: frontier hosted models are still stronger on the hardest reasoning and coding tasks; you are responsible for hosting, updates, security and evaluation; and GPUs cost money even when idle. A common pattern is to use an open model for routine, high-volume or sensitive tasks and a hosted model for hard ones. FineTune Studio exists because adapting open models with QLoRA is one of the main reasons teams choose them. How do I run an open-source LLM? The easiest way is Ollama: install it, then run ollama run llama3.2 or another model, and use the local API from your code. For more control, use llama.cpp or LM Studio; for serving many users on a GPU server, use vLLM. Also asked as: how to run open source llm ollama run qwen2.5:7b import requests r = requests.post(&quot;http://localhost:11434/api/chat&quot;, json={ &quot;model&quot;: &quot;qwen2.5:7b&quot;, &quot;stream&quot;: False, &quot;messages&quot;: [{&quot;role&quot;: &quot;user&quot;, &quot;content&quot;: &quot;Explain RAG in two sentences.&quot;}]}) print(r.json()[&quot;message&quot;][&quot;content&quot;]) Match model size to your memory, check ollama ps to confirm GPU use, and keep the local API private unless protected by authentication. Is OpenAI open source? OpenAI's flagship models, such as the GPT models behind ChatGPT, are proprietary and available only through its apps and API. OpenAI has released some open models and tools, including open-weight language models and the Whisper speech recognition model, and open-source libraries such as the Codex CLI. Despite the name, OpenAI moved away from releasing its main models openly years ago, citing safety and competition. Its open-weight releases are a separate line from its frontier models. So you can run some OpenAI models locally, but not the ones powering ChatGPT. For truly local alternatives to GPT-class assistants, use the strongest open models your hardware allows. Is Claude an open-source LLM? No. Claude, made by Anthropic, is a proprietary model family available through claude.ai, Claude Code, the Claude API and cloud platforms such as Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud Vertex AI. Its weights are not published. Also asked as: is claude open source llm Anthropic does publish research, safety work and open standards, such as the Model Context Protocol for connecting AI applications to tools and data, which is open source. If you need a model you can run entirely on your own hardware, choose an open-weight model; if you need Claude's capabilities, use it through its official channels and review the data terms for your use case. Is Ollama open source? Yes. Ollama is open source under the MIT licence, with its code on GitHub. It is free to use for running open models locally, and it offers optional cloud features with their own plans. Ollama builds on the open GGML ecosystem that also powers llama.cpp. The models you run through Ollama have their own licences, separate from Ollama's, so check each model's licence for commercial use. Because it is open source, you can inspect what it does, run it fully offline, and contribute fixes. It is one of the simplest ways to start with open LLMs on Windows, macOS and Linux. Is Pinecone open source? No. Pinecone is a proprietary, fully managed vector database service. You use it through its cloud API and client libraries; the database itself is not open source. If you need an open-source vector database, popular choices include Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus and Chroma, and pgvector, an open-source extension for PostgreSQL. Open options let you self-host for data control and avoid vendor lock-in, at the cost of running the infrastructure yourself. For many projects, especially student and early-stage ones, pgvector or Chroma is simpler and free, and you can move to a managed service later if scale requires it. Is LangChain open source? Yes. LangChain is open source under the MIT licence, with Python and JavaScript libraries on GitHub. LangGraph, its framework for stateful agents, is also open source. The company offers paid hosted products, such as observability and deployment tools, alongside the open libraries. LlamaIndex, another popular framework for RAG and agents, is also open source under the MIT licence. Open frameworks let you inspect how retrieval and agent loops work, which helps debugging. They change quickly, so pin versions, read migration notes when upgrading, and keep your own code's core logic simple enough that you could replace the framework if needed.

# Open source software and open source AI: what counts, and which models are open
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/open-source-software-and-ai/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

Open source software is software whose source code is published under a licence that lets anyone use, study, change and share it; Linux, Python, PostgreSQL, Git and VS Code's core are famous examples. In AI the term is contested: most models called open source are really open-weight, meaning you can download the trained weights, while the training data and full code stay private. This page lists essential open source software, explains open source AI, names the open models and agents, answers whether Google AI, n8n, Next.js and Supabase are open source, and shows how to contribute. What is the best open source software? The most valuable open source software for students and developers includes Linux, Git, Python, VS Code's open-source core, PostgreSQL, Docker's engine, Firefox, LibreOffice, VLC, GIMP and Blender, plus AI tools such as PyTorch, Hugging Face Transformers and Ollama. Also asked as: what are the best open source software By need: Development: Git, Python, Node.js, VS Code's core, PostgreSQL, Redis. AI and data: PyTorch, scikit-learn, Jupyter, Hugging Face libraries, Ollama, llama.cpp. Web: Next.js, React, Supabase, FastAPI. Everyday use: Firefox, LibreOffice, VLC, Thunderbird, Bitwarden. Creative: GIMP, Inkscape, Blender, OBS Studio, Audacity. Much of the modern internet and nearly every AI product runs on open source. Learning to read and contribute to these projects is one of the best ways to grow as an engineer. What is an open source AI model? An open source AI model is one whose weights, and ideally code and training details, are published under a licence that lets anyone use, study, modify and share it. In practice, most models called open source are open-weight models with varying licence terms. With an open-weight model you can download it, run it on your own hardware, fine-tune it with methods like QLoRA, and inspect its behaviour, which is not possible with closed models served only through APIs. Licences differ: some are fully permissive, such as Apache 2.0 or MIT, while others restrict commercial use above certain scales or certain uses. Always read the licence on the model card before building a product on a model. What does open source mean in AI? The Open Source Initiative's Open Source AI Definition says an AI system is open source when it grants the freedoms to use, study, modify and share it, which requires access to the model weights, the full code for training and running it, and enough information about the training data to reproduce a substantially equivalent system. By that standard, few popular models qualify fully, because companies rarely release complete training data details. That is why careful writers say open-weight for models whose weights are downloadable but whose data and training pipelines are not. Fully open models from research groups do exist and publish data, code and checkpoints. For most engineering decisions, the practical questions are: can I download the weights, does the licence allow my use, and can I fine-tune and deploy it? Which AI models are open source? Widely used open-weight model families include Meta's Llama, Alibaba's Qwen, Mistral's open models, Google's Gemma, DeepSeek's models, Microsoft's Phi and OpenAI's open-weight releases. Licences range from permissive to custom terms with restrictions. Popular choices by use: General chat and reasoning: Llama, Qwen, Mistral, DeepSeek models. Small and on-device: Gemma, Phi, small Llama and Qwen variants. Coding: coder variants of Qwen and others. Embeddings for RAG: open embedding models on Hugging Face. Speech: OpenAI's Whisper for transcription. You can run them with Ollama, llama.cpp or vLLM, or through hosted providers. GPT, Claude and Gemini models are proprietary and only available through their companies' apps and APIs. Is Google AI open source? Partly. Google's Gemini models are proprietary, available through Google's apps and APIs. Google also releases Gemma, a family of open-weight models, and open-sources major tools such as TensorFlow and JAX. Gemma models come in several sizes, including small ones that run on laptops and phones, and variants for specific uses. They are released under Google's Gemma terms, which allow broad use, including commercial use, with some conditions, so read the licence. Google researchers also published the original Transformer architecture, which underpins almost all modern language models. For students, Gemma is a good open model for experiments and fine-tuning practice, while Gemini is accessible through AI Studio's free tier. Which AI agents are open source? Open-source AI agents include coding agents such as OpenHands, Aider, Cline and the command-line agents Codex CLI and Gemini CLI, general agents such as Goose, and frameworks for building agents such as LangGraph, CrewAI and AutoGen. Open-source agents let you inspect exactly what the agent does, run it with local models, and adapt it to your workflow. Many work with several model providers, so you can switch between hosted models and local ones through Ollama. Quality depends heavily on the model behind them: an open agent with a weak local model performs far worse than the same agent with a frontier model. Read the permissions model of any agent before letting it run commands on your machine. Is n8n open source? Not by the strict definition. n8n's source code is public and you can self-host it, but it uses the Sustainable Use License, a fair-code licence that restricts some commercial uses, such as offering n8n itself as a paid service. The Open Source Initiative does not recognise that as open source. Also asked as: why is n8n open source n8n chose this model to keep the code visible and free for internal use while protecting its business from competitors reselling it. For most users, including students, individuals and companies automating their own workflows, self-hosting n8n is allowed. If you plan to build a product that embeds or resells n8n, read the licence carefully or contact n8n about commercial terms. Fully open-source alternatives exist for some automation needs. Is Next.js open source? Yes. Next.js, the React framework maintained by Vercel, is open source under the MIT licence, and its code is on GitHub. You can use it for any project, commercial or not, and deploy it anywhere, not only on Vercel. Vercel funds most of its development and offers hosting optimised for it, but self-hosting with Node.js or Docker is fully supported. The MIT licence only requires keeping the copyright notice. Next.js is a good project to learn from: its issues, discussions and examples show how a large open-source framework is run, and documentation fixes are a realistic first contribution. Is Supabase open source? Yes. Supabase, a backend platform built on PostgreSQL, is open source, with most of its code under the Apache 2.0 licence on GitHub. You can use the hosted service or self-host the stack with Docker. Supabase combines open-source components: PostgreSQL for the database, PostgREST for an automatic REST API, a Realtime server, authentication, storage and edge functions, plus pgvector support for AI applications such as RAG. Self-hosting gives you control over data location and costs, but you take on maintenance, backups and security. For student projects, the hosted free tier is usually the quickest start; check its current limits. How do I contribute to open source AI projects? Pick a project you already use, read its contributing guide, start with documentation fixes, tests or issues labelled "good first issue", and open small, well-explained pull requests. Consistency matters more than size. Also asked as: how to contribute to open source ai projects A practical path: Use the project in a real task and note where you got stuck. Improve the docs or examples that confused you. Reproduce a reported bug and add a failing test. Fix small bugs, following the project's style and running its tests. Join the community channels and help answer questions. Hugging Face libraries, LangChain, Ollama, vLLM and many model evaluation tools welcome contributions. Contributions on GitHub are public evidence of skill, and maintainers notice reliable contributors.

# What are OpenAI API keys? Getting one, data storage, models and expiry
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/openai-api-keys-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

An OpenAI API key is a secret token that lets your own code call OpenAI's models through its API, with every request billed to your OpenAI account. You create keys on the OpenAI platform, keep them in environment variables, and use them with OpenAI's SDKs or plain HTTP. This page covers what keys are and look like, where to get one, expiry, what happens to your data, how the API works, which models it offers, whether the API is itself an LLM, who owns it, and, for comparison, how Gemini API keys work. What are OpenAI API keys? OpenAI API keys are secret credentials that identify your project when your code sends requests to OpenAI's API. Anyone with your key can make requests charged to your account, so keys must be kept private like passwords. Keys belong to projects within an organisation, so you can separate keys for different apps, set spending limits and permissions per project, and revoke a key without affecting others. Never put a key in front-end JavaScript, a mobile app, a public GitHub repository or a screenshot. Call the API from your backend and keep the key in an environment variable or a secrets manager. If a key leaks, revoke it immediately in the dashboard and create a new one. What does an OpenAI API key look like? An OpenAI API key is a long random string beginning with sk-; newer project keys begin with sk-proj-. The full key is shown only once, when you create it, so copy it straight into a password manager or your .env file. Also asked as: what does openai api key look like The dashboard later shows only a masked version, so if you lose it, create a new key. In code, read it from the environment rather than pasting it in: from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI() # reads OPENAI_API_KEY from the environment Tools such as GitHub's secret scanning detect committed keys, and providers may disable keys found in public places, which is another reason to keep them out of code. Where do I get an OpenAI API key? Sign up on the OpenAI platform, add billing details or credits for your organisation, then open the API keys page and create a key for your project. A ChatGPT Plus or Pro subscription does not include API usage; the API is billed separately. Also asked as: where to get openai api Steps: Create or sign in to your account on the OpenAI platform. Set up billing and, ideally, a monthly spending limit. Create a project for your app. Generate an API key in that project and copy it once. Store it as OPENAI_API_KEY in your environment. Buy credits only from OpenAI's own platform. Websites selling "cheap OpenAI keys" are reselling stolen or shared keys, which breaks OpenAI's terms and can expose your data. Do OpenAI API keys expire? OpenAI API keys do not expire automatically; they work until you revoke them. However, a key can stop working if it is deleted, if the project or organisation is suspended, if billing fails, or if OpenAI disables a key detected as leaked. Good practice is to rotate keys periodically and whenever someone with access leaves a project. Use separate keys for development and production, and for each service, so revoking one does not break everything. If your app suddenly gets authentication errors, check the key in the dashboard, your billing status and whether the key belongs to the right project. Monitor usage so unexpected spikes, a sign of a leaked key, are noticed quickly. Does the OpenAI API store data? OpenAI states that data sent through the API is not used to train its models by default. API inputs and outputs are retained for a limited period, typically up to 30 days, for abuse and misuse monitoring, unless you qualify for zero data retention. Also asked as: does openai api store data Some features store data by design: files you upload, assistants, conversation state and stored responses persist until you delete them or as configured. Enterprise customers can get stronger commitments, including zero data retention for eligible endpoints and data residency options. Before sending personal or sensitive data, read OpenAI's current enterprise privacy page and your organisation's policies, minimise what you send, and avoid including identity numbers or passwords in prompts. How does the OpenAI API work? Your code sends an HTTPS request with your API key, a model name and input such as messages or a prompt; OpenAI runs the model and returns the output, along with token usage that determines cost. Also asked as: how does openai api work The main pieces: Text generation: send input and instructions, get a response; stream it for responsive UIs. Tools: let the model call your functions, search the web or run code. Structured outputs: require JSON that matches a schema. Embeddings: turn text into vectors for search and RAG. Images and audio: generate images, transcribe speech, synthesise voice. Requests are stateless unless you use features that store conversation state. Handle rate-limit and server errors with retries and backoff, which the official SDKs do automatically. What models does the OpenAI API offer? The OpenAI API offers families of models for different jobs: GPT models for text, reasoning and coding, smaller fast models for high-volume tasks, embedding models for search, image generation models, speech-to-text and text-to-speech models, and realtime models for voice. Also asked as: what are the openai api models Model names and versions change frequently, so check the models page for current options, context lengths and pricing. A practical approach: start with a mid-sized general model, measure quality on your task, then try a smaller model for cost or a reasoning model for hard cases. Pin a specific model version in production so behaviour does not change unexpectedly, and test before upgrading. Is the OpenAI API an LLM? No. The API is the interface, a web service, through which you access OpenAI's models, many of which are large language models. The LLM is the model running behind it; the API is how your software talks to it. Also asked as: is openai api an llm The distinction matters when designing systems. You can swap the model behind the same API call, use multiple providers through similar interfaces, or run an open-weight LLM locally behind an OpenAI-compatible API, as tools like Ollama and vLLM offer. Your application logic, such as retrieval, validation and tools, sits outside the model. In RAG.NextUpgrad, multi-provider fallback works precisely because the app talks to models through interchangeable interfaces. Who owns the OpenAI API? OpenAI owns and operates the OpenAI API. OpenAI is the company that develops the GPT models and ChatGPT. Microsoft is a major partner and investor and offers OpenAI models through its own Azure OpenAI Service, which is a separate product with Microsoft's terms. Also asked as: who owns openai api If your organisation uses Azure, the Azure version may be preferred for billing, compliance and regional hosting; the API shape is similar but authentication, endpoints and model availability differ. For individual developers and students, the OpenAI platform is the direct route. In both cases, the usage policies of the provider apply to your application. How many Gemini API keys can I have? You can create multiple Gemini API keys, typically within Google Cloud projects through Google AI Studio. Rate limits and quotas generally apply per project, not per key, so extra keys in one project do not give you more free usage. Use multiple keys to separate environments or apps and to rotate keys safely, not to get around limits; doing that through many accounts or projects can break the terms of service. Restrict keys where possible, such as limiting which APIs a key can call, store them in environment variables, and delete unused keys. If you need higher limits, enable billing on the project, which moves it to higher usage tiers.

# Personal branding for developers and CS students: building in public, LinkedIn and GitHub that get you hired, and speaking your way into a reputation
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/personal-branding-for-developers/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is personal branding for a developer, really?

**A public, searchable record of what you have built, explained clearly enough that a stranger can judge it, published on a schedule. That is the whole thing. It is not a logo, a colour palette or a tagline. Recruiters, founders and event organisers search for people who can do a specific thing; a brand is what makes you findable for that thing and credible when found. Mine is "GenAI engineer from India who ships production AI systems and speaks at colleges", and every post, repository and talk feeds that one sentence.**


I built a developer community to 500-plus members, won three hackathons, spoke at colleges and landed GenAI work without a placement cell, and the thread through all of it was posting what I built every week for years [4][5]. This page is that habit, made explicit, with the profile and channel decisions that mattered.

> Nobody discovers you. They search for something specific and find the person who has been publicly doing it for a year. Be that person for one thing.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What should a developer post about?

**What you built this week, what broke, what you learned, and what you would do differently. A build log with a screenshot beats an announcement. A failure explained beats a success declared. Specific beats general: "I cut RAG latency from 4 seconds to 1.2 by reranking to five passages" is a post; "AI is transforming everything" is noise. Post about the work, the decision and the result, in that order, and tag the tools and people involved when it is true.**



## Which platforms matter for a developer in India?

**LinkedIn, because recruiters, founders, faculty and event organisers in India live there and search there; it is where every speaking and hiring conversation I have had began [1][10]. GitHub, because it is where anyone serious verifies the claims [2]. A personal site, because it is the one place you control where everything resolves [3]. Then one writing home, Dev.to or a blog, for longer pieces [11]. X, Instagram and others are optional amplifiers. Two platforms done consistently beat six done occasionally.**



## How should a CS student set up LinkedIn?

**Headline: what you do and one proof, not your college and year. Banner: a photo from a session, a demo or a hackathon, not a stock image. About: five lines, first person, what you build, one result, what you are open to, how to reach you. Featured: three projects with demo links. Experience: projects and communities count; write them as outcomes. Post weekly. Comment substantively on ten posts a week in your field, because comments are how people without followers get seen.**


My longer guides to LinkedIn for students and to what recruiters actually search for are on the portfolio [6][10]. The single highest-leverage change most students can make in ten minutes: replace "Student at X College" in the headline with what you build.

## How should a developer set up GitHub?

**A profile README with your one sentence, your city, and three links. Five pinned repositories, each with a README that has the problem in one sentence, a screenshot or demo link, how to run it, and what you would do next. Steady commits over weeks rather than one upload per project. Archive tutorial clones. Recruiters spend under two minutes; those minutes should land on finished things with clear explanations.**


The GitHub note, with the README template I use, is written up separately [7].


## How do I write technical posts without a following?

**Start with what you just learned, because a beginner explaining a concept to last-month's self is the most useful writer for the many people at that stage. Structure: the problem, what you tried, what worked, what you would tell someone starting. Include one screenshot or code block. Publish on Dev.to or your blog and post a three-line summary with the link on LinkedIn. Nobody reads the first ten; the eleventh gets found by search, and search does not care about followers.**


My notes on writing a first technical post, and why this site exists as a search-first project rather than a follower-first one, are on the portfolio [8].

## How do I turn projects into talks and a speaker brand?

**Every shipped project is a talk waiting for a room. Offer your college club a session on what you built, with a live demo, then post the photos. Two or three sessions become a page listing the talks you offer, and that page is what organisers book from. Judging a hackathon after mentoring at one adds a second credential. Within a year, invitations arrive with the posts, because organisers search LinkedIn for people who have visibly done sessions before.**



The speaker-brand version of this, with what changed after my first campus sessions, is written up separately [9].

## How do I stay consistent without it eating my week?

**Reuse and schedule. One project produces a post, a demo video, a carousel, a talk and a blog piece; write once, cut five ways. Batch: one afternoon a month to draft four posts, scheduled weekly. Keep a running notes file of things that broke and lessons learned, so posts are extracts, not blank pages. Automate what can be automated, publishing and cross-posting, and keep the writing human. My own posting runs on a pipeline I built for exactly this, so the habit survives busy months.**



## What mistakes do students make with personal branding?

**Posting certificates instead of projects. Announcing instead of showing. Chasing virality with hot takes. Six platforms, none consistent. A LinkedIn headline that says only the college. Copying influencer formats that do not fit a student. Posting nothing for months and then a flood. Faking expertise, which experts spot instantly and never forget. The fix for all of them is the same weekly build log, in your own words.**




## Personal branding interview questions

**Not asked directly, but present in every interview: "tell me about a project" is easier when you have written about it ten times; "how do you learn" is answered by your posts; "why should we hire you" is answered by a profile the interviewer already read. The brand is the pre-read. Make it accurate.**



## Where should I start today?

**Change your LinkedIn headline to what you build, pin three repositories with real READMEs, and post one honest paragraph about what you shipped this week. Then do it again next week.** For a session at your college on building a developer reputation from a campus nobody has heard of, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# Pinecone vs Postgres and OpenSearch, and fixing common Pinecone problems
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/pinecone-vector-database-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

Pinecone is a managed vector database for storing embeddings and finding similar ones quickly, widely used for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension and OpenSearch are the most common alternatives. The right choice depends on your existing stack, scale and whether you need strong keyword search. This page compares them, explains vector databases versus vector stores and why RAG needs them, and fixes the Pinecone problems people hit most: setup errors, repeated results, weighting, listing vectors and parent-document retrieval. Postgres vs Pinecone: which should I use? Use PostgreSQL with pgvector if you already run Postgres and your collection is small to medium, so vectors, text and metadata live in one database with SQL filters and joins. Use Pinecone if you want a fully managed service that scales vector search without operating a database. Also asked as: postgres vs. pinecone Trade-offs: pgvector: one system, transactions, familiar SQL, free and open source; you tune indexes and scale it yourself. Pinecone: serverless scaling, fast setup, metadata filtering and namespaces; another service to pay for and keep in sync with your main database. For student projects and most startups, pgvector on a hosted Postgres such as Supabase is simpler. Move to a dedicated vector service when scale, latency or operational load justifies it, and measure first. Pinecone vs OpenSearch: which is better? OpenSearch is a search engine with strong keyword search, aggregations and vector search in one place; Pinecone is a specialised managed vector database. Choose OpenSearch if keyword relevance, log or document search and filtering are central; choose Pinecone for simple, managed vector retrieval. RAG quality often depends on keyword search as much as vectors, because exact terms such as product codes, names and error messages are missed by embeddings. OpenSearch gives you BM25 and vectors together, so hybrid search is natural, at the cost of running and tuning a cluster or paying for a managed one. Pinecone supports hybrid search with sparse and dense vectors too. Decide by your team's skills and existing infrastructure, then test retrieval recall on your own questions. What is the best open-source vector database for RAG? There is no single best. pgvector is the simplest if you use PostgreSQL; Qdrant, Weaviate and Milvus are popular dedicated open-source vector databases; Chroma is easy for prototypes; FAISS is a fast library rather than a database. Also asked as: best vector database for rag open source How to choose: Already on Postgres: pgvector. Prototype or notebook: Chroma or FAISS. Dedicated service with filtering and scale: Qdrant, Weaviate or Milvus. Need keyword plus vector search: OpenSearch or Weaviate's hybrid search. Retrieval quality depends more on chunking, embeddings, hybrid search and reranking than on the database. RAG.NextUpgrad runs hybrid dense and BM25 retrieval with reciprocal-rank fusion and re-ranking in about 220 MB on a free tier, so start simple and optimise what measurement shows matters. What is the difference between a vector database and a vector store? A vector database is a full database system for vectors: storage, indexing, filtering, updates, access control and scaling. A vector store is a looser term, often used in frameworks like LangChain, for any component that stores embeddings and returns similar ones, from an in-memory list to a full database. Also asked as: difference between vector database and vector store So every vector database can serve as a vector store, but not every vector store is a database. FAISS in memory, a Chroma collection on disk, pgvector and Pinecone can all be "vector stores" in LangChain. The distinction matters in production: persistence, concurrent updates, backups, filtering and monitoring are database features you will need once real users depend on the system. Why are vector databases critical for RAG systems? RAG needs to find the passages most relevant to a question among thousands or millions of chunks, quickly. Vector databases index embeddings so similarity search is fast at scale, and add metadata filters, updates and persistence that real systems need. Without an index, you would compare the question with every chunk on every query, which becomes slow as data grows. Vector databases use approximate nearest-neighbour indexes, such as HNSW, to return results in milliseconds. Filters, for example by department, date or user permissions, keep answers relevant and secure. Still, vectors are not enough on their own: combining them with keyword search and a reranker usually gives the biggest quality gains. How do I fix a Pinecone setup error? Most Pinecone setup errors come from using old client code, a missing or wrong API key, or an index dimension that does not match your embedding model. Update the client, use the current initialisation style and check dimensions. Also asked as: how do i solve this pinecone setup error i keep getting The current Python client looks like this: from pinecone import Pinecone pc = Pinecone(api_key=&quot;YOUR_KEY&quot;) # better: read from an environment variable index = pc.Index(&quot;my-index&quot;) index.upsert(vectors=[{&quot;id&quot;: &quot;doc1#0&quot;, &quot;values&quot;: vec, &quot;metadata&quot;: {&quot;source&quot;: &quot;doc1&quot;}}]) Old tutorials use pinecone.init(...) and an environment parameter, which newer clients reject. Make sure the index dimension equals your embedding size, for example 1536 or 768, and that the metric matches your embeddings. Read the full error message; it usually names the cause. Why does Pinecone keep returning the same result for different documents? Usually because of your data, not Pinecone: duplicate chunks, IDs reused so new upserts overwrite old vectors, boilerplate text such as headers dominating every chunk, or a bug where the same embedding is computed for every input. Also asked as: why does pinecone repeatedly return the same result from my series of documents Check in this order: Confirm IDs are unique per chunk; reusing an ID overwrites the earlier vector. Print a few stored vectors and confirm they differ. Strip repeated headers, footers and navigation text before embedding. Confirm you query the right namespace and index. Check that the query embedding uses the same model as the stored ones. Deduplicate near-identical chunks. After fixing, re-index and test with questions whose correct chunk you know. How do I add weights to rank results in Pinecone? Use hybrid search with both sparse and dense vectors and weight them: scale the dense vector by alpha and the sparse vector by one minus alpha before querying, so alpha controls how much semantic versus keyword matching counts. Also asked as: how do you add weights to rank results in pinecone Sparse vectors come from keyword methods such as BM25 or learned sparse models; dense vectors come from your embedding model. An alpha near 1 favours meaning, near 0 favours exact terms. Tune alpha on a test set of real questions. For other signals, such as recency or document authority, retrieve a larger candidate set and re-score it in your code or with a reranker. A cross-encoder reranker on the top results often improves ranking more than weighting alone. How do I fetch all vectors in a Pinecone namespace? List the vector IDs in the namespace, page by page, then fetch the vectors by ID in batches. Pinecone's client provides a list operation for serverless indexes that returns IDs, optionally filtered by an ID prefix. Also asked as: is there a method to fetch all the vectors of a namespace in pinecone for ids in index.list(namespace=&quot;docs&quot;): batch = index.fetch(ids=ids, namespace=&quot;docs&quot;) Designing IDs with prefixes, such as doc42#chunk3, makes it easy to list or delete all chunks of one document. If you need a full export regularly, keep your source of truth elsewhere, such as your documents and a database table of chunks, and treat the vector index as a rebuildable cache. That also makes switching vector databases much easier later. How do I implement a parent document retriever with Pinecone? Index small child chunks for precise matching, store each child's parent ID in metadata, and keep the larger parent sections in a separate store. At query time, retrieve the best children, then return their parents to the model. Also asked as: how can i implement auto-merging retriever (aka parent document retriever) directly with pinecone (or other vectordb Steps: Split each document into parents, such as sections, and children, such as paragraphs. Embed and upsert children to Pinecone with parent_id in metadata. Store parents in a key-value store or database table. Query Pinecone, collect unique parent IDs from the top children, and load those parents. Optionally merge adjacent children into a parent only when several of them match, the auto-merging idea. LangChain's ParentDocumentRetriever and LlamaIndex's auto-merging retriever implement this pattern with any vector store.

# What is privacy and security? The difference, and what it means for AI
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/privacy-and-security-explained/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

Privacy is about who is allowed to collect, see and use information about a person, and for what purpose. Security is the set of technical and organisational controls that keep information safe from people who are not allowed. They overlap but are not the same: a system can be very secure and still misuse your data. This page explains the difference, why both matter, what they mean for data, apps, social media and iPhones, how they apply to AI systems including inference attacks, and what the HIPAA privacy and security rules cover. What is privacy and security? Privacy is a person's right to control how information about them is collected, used and shared. Security is the protection of information and systems against unauthorised access, change or loss. Put simply, privacy answers "should this data be collected and used this way?", and security answers "is this data protected from those who should not have it?". A privacy decision is limiting a sign-up form to the fields you actually need. A security control is encrypting the database that stores those fields and requiring two-factor authentication for the admins. Good systems design both together: collect less, protect what you keep, and delete it when the purpose is over. Do privacy and security mean the same thing? No. Security is about protection; privacy is about appropriate use. You can have security without privacy, but you cannot have privacy without security. Two examples make the difference clear. A company that encrypts all its data perfectly but sells your browsing history to advertisers has strong security and poor privacy. A company with a strong privacy policy that leaves its database open on the internet has good intentions and no real privacy, because anyone can read the data. Security is necessary for privacy but not enough. Privacy adds questions security does not ask: do you have consent, is this the minimum data needed, how long will you keep it, and can the person see or delete it? Why is privacy and security important? They protect people from harm such as fraud, identity theft, stalking, discrimination and embarrassment, and they protect organisations from breaches, fines and lost trust. Laws in most countries now require both. For individuals, leaked phone numbers, ID details and passwords lead directly to scams and account takeovers. For organisations, a single breach can mean regulatory penalties, legal claims and customers who never return. For engineers, privacy and security are also design quality: systems that collect less data are simpler to secure and cheaper to run. In India, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 sets duties for anyone processing personal data, so these are now legal requirements, not just good practice. What is data privacy and security? Data privacy is the set of rules and practices for handling personal data properly: consent, purpose, minimisation, retention and individual rights. Data security is the protection of that data through encryption, access control, monitoring and backups. A practical checklist for any app that stores user data: Collect only the fields you need and record why you need each one. Encrypt data in transit with TLS and at rest in the database. Give each person and service the least access they need. Log access to sensitive data and review the logs. Set retention periods and actually delete old data. Let users see, correct and delete their data. Most data breaches come from ordinary failures: weak passwords, exposed storage buckets and unpatched software. What is digital privacy and security? Digital privacy and security is the same idea applied to your online life: controlling what your devices, apps and accounts reveal about you, and protecting them from being hacked or misused. The basics give most of the protection. Use a password manager and unique passwords, turn on two-factor authentication for email and banking, keep your phone and laptop updated, and install apps only from official stores. Review app permissions for location, contacts, camera and microphone, and remove the ones an app does not need. Be careful with public Wi-Fi for sensitive accounts, and treat unexpected links in messages as suspicious, because phishing is still the most common way accounts are lost. Your email account is the master key to the rest, so protect it most. What is privacy and security in AI? In AI, privacy means controlling what personal data goes into training, prompts, logs and outputs. Security means protecting models and AI apps from attacks such as prompt injection, data leakage and model theft. AI adds new risks to old ones. Models can memorise and repeat training data. Users paste personal or confidential information into prompts that may be logged. Prompt injection can trick an AI app into revealing data or taking actions it should not. Good practice is to minimise personal data, mask it before it reaches a model, restrict what tools an AI agent can call, and review the OWASP list of risks for LLM applications. In FaceVision I designed for this: recognition runs in the browser and the server stores face embeddings only, never images. What is a privacy inference attack in AI security? A privacy inference attack tries to learn private information from a trained model's outputs, for example whether a specific person's record was in the training data, or a sensitive attribute about them. Also asked as: what is privacy inference in ai security The main types: Membership inference: deciding whether a given record was used in training, often because models are more confident on data they have seen. Attribute inference: predicting a sensitive attribute, such as a health condition, from other known features. Model inversion and data extraction: reconstructing training examples, or getting a language model to repeat memorised text. Defences include differential privacy during training, which adds calibrated noise so no single record changes the model much, limiting how much detail outputs reveal, removing duplicates and personal data from training sets, and testing models with these attacks before release. What is privacy and security in online social media? On social media, privacy is about who can see your posts, profile and contacts, and what the platform does with your data. Security is about protecting your account from takeover and your information from scraping and scams. Steps worth taking on every platform: review who can see your posts and contact you, turn off location tagging, hide your phone number and email from your profile, and enable two-factor authentication. Be careful what you share: your college, daily routine and photos of documents give attackers more than you think. Check which third-party apps are connected to your account and remove old ones. Remember that "private" posts can still be screenshotted, and that the platform itself sees everything you post. What is privacy and security on iPhone? On iPhone, Privacy &amp; Security is the section of Settings where you control which apps can access your location, contacts, photos, camera, microphone and other data, and where security features such as Safety Check and Lockdown Mode live. Useful settings to review: Location Services: set apps to "While Using" or "Never", and turn off precise location where it is not needed. Tracking: refuse app tracking requests so apps cannot follow you across other apps. Photos and contacts: give limited access instead of full access. Safety Check: review and reset who has access to your information. Lockdown Mode: an extreme protection mode for people facing targeted attacks. Keep iOS updated, because many updates fix actively exploited security flaws. What are the HIPAA privacy and security rules? HIPAA is a United States law for health information. Its Privacy Rule sets when protected health information may be used or disclosed; its Security Rule sets the safeguards required to protect electronic health information. Also asked as: what is hipaa privacy and security rules The Privacy Rule covers patients' rights, such as access to their records, and limits on how hospitals, insurers and their partners share data. The Security Rule requires administrative, physical and technical safeguards: risk analysis, access controls, audit logs, encryption where appropriate and staff training. A third piece, the Breach Notification Rule, requires notice when protected data is exposed. If you build a health app for US clients you will meet HIPAA. In India, health data falls under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and sector rules, so check the requirements for each market you serve.

# What is RAG testing? How to test a RAG pipeline, and where RAG fails
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/rag-testing-and-failures/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

RAG testing is evaluating a retrieval-augmented generation system in two parts: whether retrieval finds the right passages for each question, and whether the generated answer is correct and faithful to those passages. Testing them separately tells you which half to fix. I built RAG.NextUpgrad with hybrid retrieval, re-ranking and a confidence gate, and testing is what made each change safe. This page covers how to test a pipeline and the answers, RAG architecture, how a RAG system differs from a model, why RAG is needed, where it fails and hurts, rerankers, and the unrelated "RAG status" in project management. What is RAG testing? RAG testing measures how well a retrieval-augmented system answers questions from its documents. It checks retrieval quality, such as recall of the right passages, and generation quality, such as faithfulness, correctness and citation accuracy. Also asked as: where rag fails · when rag hurts A RAG system can fail at either stage. If retrieval misses the passage with the answer, no model can answer correctly. If retrieval succeeds but the model ignores or misreads the passage, the answer is wrong anyway. Testing covers both with a fixed set of questions, known relevant passages and reference answers, scored automatically and spot-checked by people. Run the same tests after every change to chunking, embeddings, retrieval settings, prompts or models, so you know whether a change helped or hurt. How do I test a RAG pipeline? Build a test set of real questions with the source passage that answers each, then measure retrieval recall at k, the share of questions where the right passage appears in the top k results, before you look at answers at all. Also asked as: how to test rag pipeline A practical process: Collect 50 to 100 real user questions, including hard and unanswerable ones. Mark the document and passage that answers each. Run retrieval and compute recall at 5 and at 10, and mean reciprocal rank. Inspect failures: was the passage chunked badly, missing, or ranked too low? Change one thing at a time, chunk size, hybrid search or reranker, and re-run. Retrieval metrics are cheap and deterministic, so they are the fastest feedback loop you have. How do I test the RAG model's answers? Score generated answers for faithfulness, meaning every claim is supported by the retrieved passages, correctness against a reference answer, and citation accuracy. Use an LLM as a judge for scale, and check a sample by hand. Also asked as: how to test rag model Frameworks such as RAGAS compute faithfulness, answer relevance and context precision automatically. Include unanswerable questions in the test set and check that the system declines instead of inventing an answer, which is the behaviour a confidence gate enforces. Track latency and cost per query too. When an LLM judge and a human disagree, trust the human and adjust the judge's instructions. Keep the test set versioned alongside the code. What is RAG architecture? RAG architecture has an indexing pipeline and a query pipeline. Indexing loads documents, splits them into chunks, embeds them and stores them in an index. At query time, the system retrieves relevant chunks, often reranks them, and gives them to a language model to write a grounded answer. A production version usually adds: Hybrid retrieval: BM25 keyword search plus vector search, merged with reciprocal-rank fusion. Reranking: a cross-encoder reorders the top candidates by relevance. Prompting with citations: the model must cite chunk IDs or pages. Confidence gate: refuse when retrieval scores are weak. Fallbacks and monitoring: switch providers on failure, log every query. That is the shape of RAG.NextUpgrad, which runs in about 220 MB on a free tier. How is an AI model different from a RAG system? An AI model, such as a language model, answers from what it learned during training. A RAG system is an application that combines a model with a retrieval step, so answers come from documents you supply at question time. Also asked as: how is an ai model different from a rag model The practical differences: a model alone cannot know your private documents or events after its training cutoff, and cannot point to sources; a RAG system can, and you can update its knowledge by updating documents, without retraining. "RAG model" is a loose phrase; the original RAG paper trained a retriever and generator together, but most systems today combine an off-the-shelf model with a separate search index. Fine-tuning changes the model itself, and is better for style and format than for adding facts. Why is RAG needed? RAG is needed because language models do not know your private or recent information, cannot cite sources from memory, and sometimes invent facts. Retrieval supplies the right facts at question time, which makes answers current, specific and checkable. Typical uses are company knowledge assistants, customer support over product documentation, college and policy question answering, legal and research search, and chat over a user's own files. RAG is usually cheaper and easier to keep current than fine-tuning for knowledge, because updating a document is enough. It also improves trust: users can click a citation and read the source, which a plain chatbot cannot offer. Where does RAG fail? RAG fails most often at retrieval: documents are missing or outdated, chunking splits the answer across pieces, embeddings miss exact terms such as codes and names, or the right passage ranks below the cut-off. Generation fails when the model ignores context or answers beyond it. Common failure points: Missing content: the answer is not in the index at all. Bad chunks: tables, lists and headings separated from their meaning. Exact-match misses: product codes and error messages lost by vector search. Ranking: the right chunk retrieved but too low to be used. Context overload: too many chunks, with key facts lost in the middle. Unsupported answers: the model fills gaps from its own knowledge. Hybrid search, rerankers, better chunking and a refusal path address most of them. When does RAG hurt? RAG hurts when retrieval brings back irrelevant or misleading passages, because the model then answers confidently from the wrong context. It can also hurt on questions the model already handles well, such as general reasoning, by adding noise, latency and cost. Signs RAG is the wrong tool: questions need reasoning across a whole corpus, such as "what are the trends across all reports", which needs aggregation rather than top-k retrieval; the documents are low quality or contradictory; or the task is about style or format rather than facts, where fine-tuning or better prompts work better. Route queries: retrieve only when the question needs your documents, and let the model answer directly otherwise. What are the best reranking models for RAG? Cross-encoder rerankers give the biggest quality gain: open models such as the BGE rerankers and MS MARCO cross-encoders from the sentence-transformers library, and hosted options such as Cohere Rerank and Jina's rerankers. A reranker scores each query-passage pair together, which is more accurate than comparing separate embeddings, but slower, so you apply it only to the top 20 to 100 candidates from first-stage retrieval. Choose by language support, latency and licence, and measure recall before and after on your own test set. In RAG.NextUpgrad, re-ranking on top of hybrid dense and BM25 retrieval with reciprocal-rank fusion fixed many wrong answers cheaply, because the right passage was usually retrieved, just ranked too low. What is RAG status? In project management, RAG status means Red, Amber, Green: a traffic-light rating of a project's health. Green is on track, amber has risks or minor delays, and red has serious problems needing action. It is unrelated to retrieval-augmented generation. Teams report RAG status on dashboards and in status meetings for schedule, budget, scope and risks. Useful practice is to define clearly what each colour means for your project, report amber early rather than staying green until things turn red, and attach a short note on the cause and the next step. If you see "RAG" in an engineering context about AI, it almost always means retrieval-augmented generation instead.

# RAG vs fine-tuning: when to use each for LLMs, with examples
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/rag-vs-fine-tuning-2/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and fine-tuning solve different problems. RAG gives a model the right information at question time by retrieving passages from your documents; fine-tuning changes the model's weights so it behaves differently, such as following a format, a tone or a narrow task. Most products need RAG for knowledge and only sometimes fine-tuning for behaviour. I have built both: RAG.NextUpgrad for grounded answers and FineTune Studio for QLoRA fine-tuning, so this page answers the common questions with practical examples. Is it "fine tuning" or "fine-tuning"? Both spellings appear, and they mean the same thing. "Fine-tuning", with a hyphen, is the more standard form in technical writing as a noun and adjective, as in "fine-tuning a model" or "a fine-tuned model". Also asked as: fine tuning vs fine-tuning You will see "finetuning" as one word in some papers and code, such as library names, and "fine tuning" in casual writing and search queries. In documentation and reports, pick one form and use it consistently; "fine-tuning" is the safe choice. The concept is the same in every spelling: continuing to train a pretrained model on a smaller, task-specific dataset so it adapts to your use case. Fine-tuning LLMs vs RAG: what is the difference? RAG keeps the model as it is and supplies relevant documents with each question. Fine-tuning trains the model further on examples, changing its weights so it behaves differently without needing those examples in the prompt. Also asked as: fine tuning llms vs rag Compare them on what matters: Knowledge: RAG handles private and changing facts; fine-tuning bakes in knowledge poorly. Updates: RAG updates by editing documents; fine-tuning needs retraining. Citations: RAG can cite sources; fine-tuned models cannot. Behaviour and format: fine-tuning is strong; RAG does not change style. Cost: RAG costs more per query because of longer prompts; fine-tuning costs up front. They also combine well: a fine-tuned model that follows your format, with RAG for the facts. When should I use fine-tuning vs RAG? Use RAG when answers depend on documents, especially private, large or frequently changing ones. Use fine-tuning when you need consistent behaviour that prompts cannot achieve: a strict output format, a specific tone, a narrow classification task, or a smaller, cheaper model that matches a larger one on one job. Also asked as: when do we use llm fine tuning vs. llm rag Decision rules I use: Answer must cite a source or reflect today's documents: RAG. Output must always follow a complex structure: try structured outputs first, then fine-tune. High-volume narrow task where cost and latency matter: fine-tune a small model. Domain jargon the model misreads: RAG with good examples, then consider fine-tuning. Both knowledge and behaviour: RAG plus a fine-tuned model. Measure on a test set either way. Why does fine-tuning not work as well as RAG for knowledge? Fine-tuning teaches patterns more readily than facts. A model trained on your documents may pick up their style without reliably recalling specific details, may mix them with what it already knew, and cannot show where an answer came from. Also asked as: why fine tuning does not work as well as rag There are practical problems too. Every document change needs a new training run. Verifying which facts the model has learned is hard. Fine-tuning on new facts can increase hallucination, because the model learns to answer confidently about things it only partly absorbed. RAG avoids these: the exact passage is in the prompt, the answer can quote it, and updating knowledge means updating the index. That is why RAG.NextUpgrad grounds answers in retrieved passages with citations and refuses when evidence is weak, rather than relying on a model's memory. What is the difference between prompt engineering, RAG and fine-tuning? Prompt engineering changes the instructions and examples you send; RAG adds retrieved information to the prompt; fine-tuning changes the model itself. They form a ladder from cheapest and fastest to most involved. Also asked as: difference between prompt engineering rag and fine tuning Start at the bottom: Prompt engineering: clear instructions, examples, output format. Minutes to try, no infrastructure. RAG: an index of your documents and a retrieval step. Days to build well, easy to update. Fine-tuning: a dataset of examples and a training run. Days to weeks, needs evaluation and re-training for changes. Move up a rung only when the one below demonstrably fails on your test set. Many teams fine-tune when better prompts or retrieval would have solved the problem faster. What are some examples of fine-tuning? Good fine-tuning targets are behaviours: classifying support tickets into your categories, extracting fields into a strict schema, writing in a brand's voice, generating SQL for your database schema, or making a small model match a larger one on one task. Also asked as: examples of fine tuning Concrete examples: A sentiment or intent classifier trained on a few thousand labelled messages. A model that turns invoice text into a fixed JSON format every time. A customer-support model that answers in your company's tone and structure. A small open model distilled from a larger model's outputs for cheaper inference. A model adapted to Indian-English phrasing for a specific domain. FineTune Studio runs this loop from the browser: upload a dataset, train a QLoRA adapter, watch the loss curve live, and compare base and tuned outputs side by side. How long does fine-tuning take? With parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA or QLoRA, fine-tuning a small open model on a few thousand examples takes from minutes to a few hours on a single GPU. Full fine-tuning of large models takes far longer and needs many GPUs. Also asked as: how long does fine tuning take Time depends on model size, dataset size, sequence length, number of epochs and hardware. A 7B or 8B model with QLoRA on a few thousand short examples commonly trains within an hour or two on one modern GPU, including free or low-cost cloud options for small runs. Hosted fine-tuning services queue and run jobs for you, typically finishing within minutes to hours. Preparing a clean dataset and an evaluation set usually takes longer than training itself, and matters more for the result. What type of fine-tuning does the OpenAI API use? OpenAI's API offers supervised fine-tuning on example conversations, preference fine-tuning with Direct Preference Optimization using preferred and rejected answers, and reinforcement fine-tuning for reasoning models using graders. Vision fine-tuning with images is also supported on some models. Supervised fine-tuning is the common starting point: you upload JSONL examples of input messages and ideal assistant replies. Preference fine-tuning helps when you can say which of two answers is better more easily than writing the perfect one. Reinforcement fine-tuning suits tasks with checkable answers. OpenAI hosts the training and serves the resulting model through the same API; you do not get the weights. Which models can be fine-tuned changes, so check the fine-tuning guide. Why is a vector database required for fine-tuning or RAG? A vector database is required for RAG, not for fine-tuning. RAG stores document embeddings in a vector index so it can find relevant passages by meaning; fine-tuning trains on a dataset file and never needs a vector store. Also asked as: why is vector database required for fine tuning rag The confusion comes from both being ways to "teach a model about your documents". For RAG, the vector store, or PostgreSQL with pgvector, or a library such as FAISS, holds embeddings and returns the nearest chunks. Many production systems also add keyword search such as BM25, because embeddings miss exact terms. For fine-tuning, you need training examples in a format such as JSONL, a training framework or hosted service, and an evaluation set. If someone says you need a vector database to fine-tune, they are describing RAG. How does fine-tuning work for question answering on custom documents? You create question-and-answer pairs from your documents and train the model on them, so it learns to answer in that domain and format. It works for consistent style and common questions, but it is unreliable for exact facts, so it is usually combined with RAG. Also asked as: how does fine-tuning work in question answering for custom documents A better recipe for document Q&amp;A is RAG first: index the documents, retrieve passages for each question, and answer with citations. If answers are correct but the style or format is wrong, fine-tune on examples where the input includes retrieved passages and the output is the ideal grounded answer, which teaches the model to use context well. Evaluate on held-out questions, including ones the documents cannot answer, and check that the model declines rather than inventing.

# RAG vs fine-tuning vs prompt engineering: which one your problem actually needs, with a decision tree and real costs
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/rag-vs-fine-tuning/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## RAG vs fine-tuning: what is the difference?

**RAG, retrieval-augmented generation, changes what the model reads: at answer time it retrieves passages from your documents and answers from them, with citations. Fine-tuning changes what the model is: it trains the weights on your examples so the model's behaviour, style, format or skill shifts permanently. RAG is for knowledge the model lacks or that changes. Fine-tuning is for behaviour no prompt can produce. They solve different problems, and the most common mistake is using one for the other's job.**


I built both kinds of system in the same six months of 2026: RAG.NextUpgrad, a production retrieval platform with hybrid search, reranking and a confidence gate [9], and FineTune Studio, a QLoRA fine-tuning platform with live telemetry and base-versus-tuned evaluation [10]. Clients asked me the same question about both, and this page is the answer I now give before writing any code.

> Knowledge or behaviour? Answer that in one word and you have chosen your architecture. Everything after is engineering.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## When should I use RAG?

**When the answer depends on information the model does not have: your documents, your database, anything after its training cutoff, anything private. When answers must cite their source. When content changes often, because re-indexing a document takes seconds while retraining takes hours. When different users may see different documents, because retrieval can filter by permission and a model's weights cannot. When you need to ship this week, because a RAG prototype is an afternoon.**


Lewis et al. introduced the pattern for knowledge-intensive tasks precisely because a model's parameters are a poor place to store facts that must be exact and current [1]. Ovadia et al. compared knowledge injection by fine-tuning against retrieval directly and found retrieval consistently better at giving models new factual knowledge [3].

## When should I use fine-tuning?

**When the problem is how the model behaves, not what it knows: a consistent voice, a strict output format, a domain's phrasing, a classification or extraction skill the base model does poorly, or a narrow task you want a small, cheap, fast model to do well. When you have hundreds to thousands of clean examples of the right output. When the requirement is stable enough that retraining every month would not be needed. When prompting with examples has been tried and still falls short.**


LoRA made this affordable by training small adapters instead of all weights [2], and LIMA showed how few examples alignment needs when they are clean: a thousand, not a hundred thousand [4]. Both papers point the same way: fine-tuning is a scalpel for behaviour, not a container for facts.

## Where does prompt engineering fit?

**First. A prompt is free to change, takes effect instantly and often solves the problem: a clear task, an output format, a few examples, a rule for the not-enough-information case. Few-shot examples in the prompt were the original demonstration that models can learn a task without training [7]. Every RAG system still needs a well-engineered prompt that says "answer only from these passages and cite them", and every fine-tuning project should start by proving that prompting was insufficient.**



The official prompting guides are free and current; read one before spending on anything else [8].

## RAG vs fine-tuning: side by side

**The comparison, on the dimensions that decide real projects.**



## Can I combine RAG and fine-tuning?

**Yes, and mature systems usually do. RAG supplies the facts; a fine-tune supplies the behaviour: the house voice, a strict answer format, better use of retrieved passages, or a smaller model that follows citation rules reliably. You can also fine-tune the embedding model or the reranker on your own query-passage pairs to improve retrieval itself. Add the fine-tune after the RAG system works and is measured, never before, so you can see what the training actually changed.**



## Can fine-tuning add knowledge to a model?

**Weakly, unreliably and expensively. A model fine-tuned on facts may repeat some of them, but it cannot cite them, it does not know when they changed, and it blends them with prior beliefs. Ovadia et al. found retrieval outperformed fine-tuning for injecting new knowledge, and that repeated exposure to facts was needed for fine-tuning to teach them at all [3]. Luo et al. document the forgetting that aggressive fine-tuning causes [5]. If the fact must be right and traceable, retrieve it.**


This is the expensive mistake I see most: a team fine-tunes a model on their product manual, the manual changes, and the model confidently describes the old version with no way to show where it got it.


## What does each approach cost?

**RAG costs are in retrieval engineering up front, chunking, embeddings, indexing, evaluation, and then per query, because every answer sends retrieved passages as tokens. Fine-tuning costs are up front in the dataset, weeks of a person's time to write and clean examples, plus a few GPU hours that are cheap or free, and then again with every requirement change. Per-query, a fine-tuned small model is cheaper than a large model with a long RAG prompt. Total cost depends on volume and how often things change.**



## What are the failure modes of each?

**RAG fails when retrieval returns the wrong passage, when chunks lose context, when the prompt lets the model ignore the documents, or when passages conflict. Fine-tuning fails when the dataset is inconsistent, when the model overfits and memorises, when it forgets general ability, when the chat template is wrong, or when facts in the training data go stale. Prompting fails when phrasing breaks across model versions and when a task genuinely exceeds the model's ability. Each failure has a specific fix, and none of the fixes is "switch approaches" without measuring first.**



## Which is easier for a beginner or a student project?

**RAG. A retrieval system over documents you know is an afternoon to prototype, runs on a laptop with a free model API or a local model, and teaches chunking, embeddings, prompting, evaluation and hallucination in one project. Fine-tuning is a strong second project once you have a dataset you understand; QLoRA on a small model fits a free GPU. Doing both, and being able to say which problem each solved, is what interviewers want to hear.**



## RAG vs fine-tuning interview questions

**Define both and state the one-line rule. Give an example that needs RAG, one that needs fine-tuning and one that needs both. Explain why fine-tuning is a poor way to add facts, citing forgetting and the inability to cite. Explain how you would prove prompting was insufficient before training. Estimate the cost shape of each. Describe a system you built and which approach it used, and why.**



## Where to go from here

**Build the RAG version first, measure recall on twenty questions, and write down what it cannot do. That list is your fine-tuning specification, if you need one at all.** My longer decision write-up with client examples is on the portfolio [11]. For a session at your college on choosing and building these systems, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.
