# Redis and caching strategies for LLM apps: exact-match caching, semantic caching, and what to cache when every model call costs money and time
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/redis-and-caching-strategies-for-llm-apps/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## Why does caching matter so much for LLM applications?

**Because an LLM call is both slow, often one to several seconds, and billed by the token, unlike a typical database query that is usually fast and free at the margin. A cache hit for a repeated or near-duplicate question skips both costs entirely: no tokens billed, no round trip to the provider, an answer in milliseconds instead of seconds. For any application with real traffic, a meaningful fraction of questions repeat or nearly repeat, which makes caching one of the highest-leverage, lowest-risk optimisations available.**


Every production system I run treats caching as part of the architecture from day one, not a later optimisation, because the cost and latency gap between a cache hit and a fresh model call is too large to leave on the table.

> The fastest, cheapest LLM call is the one you don't make. Caching is how you make fewer of them without answering fewer questions.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What is exact-match caching, and how do I set it up with Redis?

**Exact-match caching stores the response for a specific input, and returns it instantly if the exact same input is seen again, typically keyed by a hash of the normalised prompt plus relevant parameters, model name, temperature, system prompt version [1]. Redis fits this well because it is a fast in-memory key-value store with built-in expiry, so a cache entry can be set to expire after a sensible time-to-live. This catches genuinely repeated questions, the same FAQ asked verbatim, but misses near-duplicates that are worded differently.**



## What is semantic caching, and when does it help?

**Semantic caching catches near-duplicate questions that are not worded identically: "what is RAG" and "can you explain retrieval augmented generation" mean the same thing but would miss an exact-match cache entirely. It works by embedding the incoming query, searching a small vector index of previously cached queries, and returning the cached response if a past query is similar enough, above a chosen similarity threshold [2][3]. This catches far more repeats than exact matching, at the cost of needing an embedding call per request and careful threshold tuning to avoid returning a cached answer to a subtly different question.**




## What should I never cache, and what needs careful scoping?

**Never cache anything containing per-user private data under a key shared across users; a cache is a way to leak one user's private answer to another user if scoped incorrectly. Never cache a response that depends on real-time information, current stock levels, today's date-sensitive content, without a very short TTL matched to how fast that information actually changes. Scope any cache key that includes personalised context, a user's name, their account data, their specific documents, to that user or session specifically, never globally.**



## How does caching interact with RAG, and how do I invalidate it correctly?

**A RAG answer's correctness depends on the documents it was generated from, so a cache entry must be invalidated the moment a source document changes, not just after a fixed TTL expires. The reliable pattern is to tie the cache key, or a cache-validity check, to a version identifier of the underlying document set, a hash or a last-updated timestamp, so a document update naturally invalidates every cache entry that depended on the old version, rather than serving a stale answer until an arbitrary timer runs out.**



## What is provider-side prompt caching, and how is it different?

**Some providers offer their own prompt caching, where a long, repeated prefix of a prompt, a large system prompt or a big block of retrieved context, is cached on the provider's side across calls, so you are billed less and served faster for the repeated portion even though the full request still goes to the model [4][5]. This is different from application-side caching like Redis: it does not skip the model call entirely, it makes the unavoidable model call cheaper and faster when large parts of the prompt repeat across requests, which stacks well alongside your own exact-match and semantic caching layers.**


## How do I know if my caching setup is actually worth it?

**Measure the real cache hit rate in production, not an assumption. A cache with a ten percent hit rate is complexity added for a small saving; a cache with a fifty percent hit rate on a high-traffic FAQ-style application is a major cost and latency win. Track hit rate, cost saved, and latency saved separately, and revisit the caching strategy, exact-match only, add semantic, adjust the similarity threshold, if the measured hit rate does not match what the traffic pattern suggested it should be.**



## Caching interview questions for AI applications

**Explain the difference between exact-match and semantic caching. Describe how you would scope cache keys to avoid leaking one user's data to another. Explain how you would invalidate a RAG cache when source documents change. Describe provider-side prompt caching and how it differs from an application cache. Explain how you would measure whether a caching layer is actually worth its complexity. The strongest answer includes a real hit-rate number you measured.**



## Where should I start?

**Add a simple exact-match Redis cache in front of your most repeated LLM call this week, measure the hit rate for a few days, and only add semantic caching if the traffic pattern shows enough near-duplicate questions to justify it.** For a hands-on session on cost and latency optimisation for LLM applications, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# Best resume format and templates for freshers, section by section
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/resume-format-for-freshers/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

The best resume format for freshers is a clean, one-page, single-column layout that puts your strongest evidence first: for tech roles, that means projects with links, then skills, education, internships and achievements. Simple templates beat designer ones because many companies screen resumes with applicant tracking systems that struggle with columns, tables and graphics. This page covers templates and format, CV versus resume, length, and what to write in the summary, profile, skills and hobbies sections, plus how to make a good resume in Canva. What are the best resume templates for freshers? The best templates are simple: one column, clear headings, standard fonts, and no photos, charts or skill bars. Google Docs and Word templates, LaTeX templates on Overleaf, and clean single-column Canva templates all work. What to look for: One column, so text reads in the right order for screening software. Section headings such as Projects, Skills, Education, Experience. Plenty of white space and consistent formatting. Room for project links and short bullet points. Avoid templates with two columns, icons for every skill, progress bars, photos or heavy colour. They look attractive but often parse badly and waste space. Recruiters spend seconds on a first read, so clarity wins. What is the right resume format for freshers? Use a reverse-chronological layout adapted for freshers: header, short summary, projects, skills, education, internships or experience, and achievements. Put the section that best proves your fit near the top. Also asked as: what is resume format for freshers For tech roles, a strong order is: Header: name, phone, email, LinkedIn, GitHub, portfolio. Summary: two lines tailored to the role. Projects: two or three with stack, what you built, a result and a link. Skills: grouped by languages, frameworks, tools, databases. Education: degree, college, years, CGPA if strong. Experience: internships, freelance work, leadership roles. Achievements: hackathons, competitive programming, certifications that matter. Use action verbs and real numbers where you have them. Where can I get a free resume template for freshers? Free sources include the resume templates in Google Docs and Microsoft Word, LaTeX templates on Overleaf, and free templates in Canva. Pick a single-column one and keep it plain. Also asked as: free resume for freshers template Google Docs is the quickest and exports clean PDFs. Overleaf templates produce neat, consistent resumes and are popular among engineering students; LaTeX takes an hour to learn. Canva is fine if you choose a minimal template and avoid graphic elements. Whatever you use, save the final version as a PDF, name it sensibly, such as "FirstName-LastName-Resume.pdf", and keep an editable copy so you can tailor it for each application. Should a fresher use a CV or a resume? In India, recruiters often use the words interchangeably and mean the same short document. Strictly, a resume is a one or two-page summary tailored to a job, while a CV is a longer, complete record of academic history, used for research, academia and some countries. For freshers applying to companies, send a one-page resume, even if the application form says "CV". Use a long academic CV only for research positions, PhD or master's applications abroad, or when an institution specifically asks for full academic details such as publications, conferences and teaching. When applying internationally, check local conventions: in the UK and Europe, "CV" often means a two-page resume. Can a fresher's resume be two pages? Keep it to one page. A fresher rarely has enough relevant experience to fill two pages with strong content, and recruiters reading quickly may never reach page two. Fit it on one page by cutting weak items: school-level achievements, generic skills like "MS Office" for a developer role, long objective statements, and course lists. Keep only projects and experience that support the role, with two or three bullet points each. If you have substantial research, publications or multiple internships, a second page can be justified, but then the first page must still carry your best evidence. Consistent, readable formatting matters more than squeezing in everything. What is the summary in a resume for freshers? The summary is a two to three-line introduction at the top that states your target role, your strongest skills and your best evidence. It replaces the old "objective" statement and should be tailored to each application. Also asked as: is cv or resume for freshers · can resume be 2 pages for freshers · what is summary in resume for freshers · what is skills in resume for freshers · what are hobbies in resume for freshers Example for a GenAI role: "Final-year BCA student building GenAI applications with Python, FastAPI and LLM APIs. Built a document question-answering app with retrieval and citations, deployed and used by classmates. Looking for a GenAI engineering internship." Keep it specific and factual. Avoid clichés such as "hard-working team player seeking a challenging role". If you cannot write something specific, skip the summary and let projects speak. What is the profile section in a resume for freshers? A profile section is another name for the summary: a short paragraph about who you are professionally and what you offer. Some templates also use "profile" for links such as LinkedIn, GitHub and portfolio. Also asked as: what is profile in resume for freshers Write the profile in the same way as a summary: role, key skills, best evidence, in two or three lines. If your template has a separate profile links section, include LinkedIn, GitHub and a portfolio site, and make sure each link works and shows your best work. A GitHub with clean, pinned projects and good READMEs supports every claim in your resume, so prepare it before you send applications. What should I write in the skills section of a fresher's resume? List skills you can prove, grouped by type and matched to the job description: programming languages, frameworks, databases, tools and platforms. Every skill should appear in at least one project or experience entry. An example for a developer: Languages: Python, JavaScript, SQL. Frameworks: FastAPI, React, Next.js. Data and AI: pandas, scikit-learn, LLM APIs, embeddings and vector search. Tools: Git, Docker, Linux, VS Code. Cloud: Vercel, Render, basic AWS or Azure. Avoid rating bars and percentages, which mean nothing to a reader. Skip skills you used once in a tutorial; interviewers will ask about anything listed. Should I add hobbies to a fresher's resume? Only if they add something: evidence of discipline, leadership, creativity or relevant skills, or a genuine conversation starter. If space is tight, drop hobbies before dropping projects. Hobbies that help are specific: "run a 500-member student tech community", "competitive chess, state level", "write a weekly blog on web development", or "build robots for a school robotics club". Generic lines such as "reading, music, travelling" add little. Never list hobbies you cannot talk about, because interviewers sometimes use them to break the ice. For tech roles, community and building activities can sit under "Achievements" or "Leadership" instead. How do I make a fresher's resume in Canva? Pick a single-column, minimal template, replace the content with your own, remove decorative graphics, photos and skill bars, use standard fonts, and download it as a PDF. Then check that the text can be selected and copied in order. Also asked as: how to make resume for freshers in canva Steps: Search Canva's resume templates and filter for simple, single-column designs. Set the page to A4 and keep margins reasonable. Use clear headings and bullet points, not text boxes scattered across the page. Add clickable links to GitHub, LinkedIn and your portfolio. Download as "PDF Standard" and test by copying all text into a plain text editor. If the copied text comes out jumbled, an applicant tracking system may read it the same way, so simplify the layout.

# Smart India Hackathon guide: how SIH works, how to register through your college, choose a problem statement, clear the internal round and present to ministry judges
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/smart-india-hackathon-guide/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is Smart India Hackathon?

**Smart India Hackathon is a nationwide competition organised by the Ministry of Education's Innovation Cell with AICTE and partners, in which student teams build solutions to problem statements posted by central and state government departments, public sector organisations and industry [1][2]. Teams register through their own college, go through an internal selection round, and shortlisted teams compete at the national level, where the problem statement's owners sit on the judging panels. It has software and hardware editions and runs on a months-long calendar.**


Everything specific to a year, the dates, the number of problem statements, the team size rules, the prize amounts, changes each cycle and is published on the official portal [1]. This page is about the parts that do not change: how the structure works and what wins inside it.

I have won three hackathons and lost one that taught me more, and I have judged and mentored at college events since. SIH is different from a weekend campus hackathon in two ways that decide everything: the judges own the problem, and the internal round is the real competition.

> At a campus hackathon you impress an engineer. At SIH you have to convince the person whose department will live with your solution. Build for the second person from day one.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## How does Smart India Hackathon work, step by step?

**Problem statements are published on the portal. Your college registers as a participating institute and appoints a coordinator. Students form teams within the rules and register under the college. The college runs an internal hackathon to shortlist teams, typically a handful per problem statement it nominates. Shortlisted teams submit ideas through the portal, are evaluated, and the selected ones are invited to the grand finale, a multi-day build at a nodal centre, judged by the problem statement owners and experts.**



The rules for team size, gender composition, mentor involvement and eligibility have varied between editions; the portal's current rules override anything you read elsewhere, including here [1].

## How do I register for Smart India Hackathon?

**Registration runs through your institute, not directly as an individual. Find your college's SIH coordinator, often in the training and placement cell or the innovation cell, confirm the college is registered for the current edition, form your team within the rules, and register your team under the college on the portal by the deadline. If your college is not registered, the coordinator registers the institute first. Start this a month before the internal round, because approvals move at college speed.**


If your college has never participated, a small group of students taking the portal's institute registration page to the principal with the previous year's results usually gets it done. That is how many first-time colleges join.

## How do I choose a problem statement?

**Read the full statement, not the title, and answer four questions: who owns it and what outcome do they need; what data or systems does the solution depend on and can you get or simulate them; what is the constraint that makes it hard for the owner today; and can your team build a working prototype of the core in the time available. Prefer statements where you can reach a real user of the department's service. Avoid ones that need data you will never see.**



KrishGyan, which won Changethon at IIT Roorkee, came from exactly this reading of a problem: farmers who do not read or type, a voice-first assistant in their language over WhatsApp [4]. The same reading applies to ministry statements: find the constraint everyone else will ignore, and design for it.

## How do I clear the internal college round?

**Treat the internal presentation as the final, because for most teams it is. Bring a working prototype, even a thin one, not a slide deck. Open with the department's problem in its own words, demo the core in two minutes, show one architecture slide, then say what a pilot would look like. Practise the pitch with a timer. Ask the coordinator what the internal judges weigh and match it. Most internal panels eliminate on clarity and feasibility, not on ambition.**



## What do SIH judges look for at the grand finale?

**The same four things every hackathon judge scores, weighted toward the owner's reality: feasibility, does it work and can it run in their environment; innovation, is there an insight about their problem; practicality, would their staff and citizens adopt it; and problem solving, did you understand the constraint. Ministry judges add a fifth: fit with existing systems and policy. Show that you know what the department already runs and how your solution attaches to it.**


Those four criteria are the ones I put on screen when I brief a judging room, and the ones I have written about after sitting on panels [5][6]. At SIH the panel includes the people who wrote the statement, so the fifth criterion carries more weight than at any campus event.


## What should the SIH presentation contain?

**The portal prescribes a template for the idea submission; use it exactly. Inside it, the order that wins: the problem as the department experiences it, the proposed solution in one diagram, a working demo or a video of one, the technical approach with honest limits, feasibility and the constraints you honoured, the impact for the department and the citizen, and a pilot plan. Keep every slide readable from the back of a room.**


The general pitch deck structure I recommend, adapted to whatever template the portal requires that year, is written up separately [7].

## How do I build the prototype for SIH?

**Build the core workflow end to end first, with seeded or simulated data that looks like the department's, and make it demonstrable in three minutes. Honour the constraints in the statement, low bandwidth, regional languages, feature phones, offline use, from the first version, because that is where ministry judges look. Keep an architecture that could plausibly run inside government infrastructure. Add features only after the demo path is solid.**



## What happens after Smart India Hackathon?

**Winners receive prizes, and in many cases the problem owner explores piloting or developing the solution further with the team; several past solutions have continued as products or government pilots. Whether you win or not, the project, the repository and the write-up are the durable result. Publish them, add the finale to LinkedIn under honours with the statement and department, and use the story in interviews. The line "grand finalist, Smart India Hackathon, problem statement from [department]" is understood by every Indian recruiter.**


Prize amounts and post-event arrangements are set per edition on the portal [1]; do not rely on figures from earlier years.


## Common mistakes SIH teams make

**Choosing a statement by its title. Building for three months without ever showing a department user. Presenting the tech stack before the problem. Ignoring the constraint in the statement, offline, language, device, and getting caught in Q&A. Six people with no roles. A demo that needs the venue's Wi-Fi. Reading the previous year's rules instead of this year's. Every one of these is avoidable with the checklists above.**



## Can you mentor or judge our SIH team or internal hackathon?

**Yes. I mentor teams on statement selection, scoping and the demo, and I judge and brief judging panels at college internal rounds, on-site across India or remote. Send the statement you are considering and your date.** Email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# System design for AI applications: how to answer 'design a RAG system' or 'design an AI agent' in an interview, and how to actually build one
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/system-design-for-ai-applications/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## How do I answer an AI system design question?

**With the same four-part shape as any system design answer, adapted to where AI systems actually break: clarify requirements first, latency budget, data volume, accuracy bar, and what happens when the model is wrong; sketch the full pipeline at a high level before going deep anywhere; go deep on the two or three components the interviewer is actually probing, usually retrieval quality, evaluation, or failure handling; and close with explicit failure modes and how the system degrades gracefully rather than breaking silently. The classic scaling concerns, load balancers, database sharding, still matter, but they are rarely where an AI system design question's real difficulty lives.**


I run a production RAG platform and have both sat on the interviewing side of this question and answered it as a candidate; this page is the framework I actually use, worked through twice.

> A classic system design answer worries about the database falling over. An AI system design answer has to worry about the model being confidently wrong, which a database never is.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What is the first thing I should do when given the question?

**Clarify requirements before drawing a single box. What is the data: how much, how messy, updated how often. What is the latency budget: is this a chat interface where two seconds feels slow, or a batch job where a minute is fine. What is the accuracy bar, and who is harmed by a wrong answer, a wrong answer in a college FAQ bot and a wrong answer in a medical triage tool need completely different amounts of caution. What happens when the system does not know: does it refuse, escalate to a human, or guess. Every one of these answers changes the design that follows.**



## How do I design a RAG system in an interview?

**Sketch the pipeline first, end to end, at a high level: ingestion and chunking, embedding and indexing, retrieval with hybrid search, reranking, generation with citations, and a confidence gate that refuses when evidence is weak. Then, based on what the interviewer probes, go deep on one or two pieces: how you would chunk a specific messy document type, how you would evaluate retrieval quality without labelled data, how you would handle a document that updates daily without re-embedding the whole corpus. Naming these trade-offs explicitly is what separates a strong answer from a recited diagram.**



My detailed breakdown of RAG evaluation specifically, which interviewers probe on more than any other RAG sub-topic, is written up separately [5].


## How do I design an AI agent in an interview?

**Start by asking whether the task actually needs an agent at all, a single well-built RAG pass often outperforms a multi-step agent on the same question, and saying so is a strong opening move [8]. If an agent is genuinely needed, describe the loop: a planner or router deciding the next action, a set of tools with strict schemas, a step limit, and a way to know when to stop. Cover reliability explicitly: what happens when a tool call fails, how you prevent an infinite loop, and how you validate the model's proposed actions before anything runs.**



## What failure modes should every AI system design answer cover?

**What happens when retrieval finds nothing relevant: refuse, do not guess. What happens when the model provider is down: a fallback provider, a cached response, or a clear error, never a silent failure. What happens when a tool call returns malformed data: validate and retry, do not pass it straight to the next step. What happens under load: rate limiting, queuing, and graceful degradation rather than the whole system falling over. Naming these unprompted, before the interviewer has to ask, is one of the clearest signals of real production experience.**



## How is this different from classic system design?

**Classic system design worries most about scale: sharding, caching, load balancing, consistency. AI system design carries all of that plus a layer classic systems do not have: the component that can be confidently, plausibly wrong, and the entire evaluation and guardrail layer that exists specifically to catch that. A classic database returns wrong data only when something has actually broken; a language model can return wrong data while functioning exactly as designed, which is why evaluation and confidence gating are first-class design concerns here, not an afterthought.**



## What mistakes do candidates make in AI system design interviews?

**Jumping straight to an architecture diagram without clarifying requirements first. Describing an agent for a task a single RAG pass would solve better and cheaper. Never mentioning evaluation, as if a system's accuracy is assumed rather than measured. Skipping failure modes entirely, describing only the happy path. Reciting a generic RAG diagram without adapting it to the specific data and constraints the interviewer just described. The fix for all of these is the same: treat the question as designing a real system for a real constraint, not reciting a diagram you memorised.**


## AI system design interview questions

**Design a RAG chatbot over a company's internal documentation. Design a document-extraction pipeline for invoices at scale. Design an agent that can answer questions using multiple internal tools. Design a system to detect when a model's confidence is too low to answer. For each, expect to be pushed on one specific component in depth after your high-level pass, so know which two or three parts of your own designs you can go deep on.**



## Where should I start?

**Take a system you have actually built, or RAG.NextUpgrad's public architecture as a worked example, and practise explaining it in the four-part shape: requirements, pipeline, depth, failure modes, out loud, in under five minutes.** For a mock interview and system design coaching session for GenAI roles, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What is text to speech and speech to text? AI voice tools compared
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/text-to-speech-and-speech-to-text/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

Text to speech (TTS) converts written text into spoken audio, and speech to text (STT), also called automatic speech recognition, converts spoken audio into written text. Both now use AI: neural networks trained on large amounts of recorded speech. This page explains how they work, how to convert speech to text on any device, the best converters, how OpenAI's Whisper compares with cloud services, what Gemini can do with audio, how to create an AI voice, and how to use the Microsoft tools, including dictation in Word. What is text to speech (TTS)? Text to speech is technology that reads text aloud in a synthetic voice. Modern TTS uses neural networks that generate natural-sounding speech with realistic rhythm and intonation, in many languages and voices. Also asked as: what is text to speech tts A TTS system first analyses the text, expanding numbers and abbreviations and working out pronunciation, then a neural model generates the audio. Uses include screen readers for visually impaired users, voice assistants, audiobook and video narration, navigation apps and language learning. Quality is now high enough that synthetic voices can be hard to tell from real ones, which is why responsible services restrict cloning a real person's voice without consent. When you use TTS in a project, label it as synthetic where listeners might be misled. Does speech to text use AI? Yes. Modern speech to text uses deep learning models, typically transformers, trained on very large amounts of transcribed audio. Older systems used statistical models with separate acoustic and language components. Today's models map audio directly to text and handle accents, background noise and natural speech far better than earlier systems. Some, like Whisper, were trained on hundreds of thousands of hours of multilingual audio from the web. Accuracy still depends on conditions: clear microphones, one speaker at a time and common vocabulary work best, while cross-talk, heavy noise, code-switching between languages and technical jargon cause errors. In the OCR &amp; Speech Workspace I built live speech-to-text into the same workspace as document chat, because once speech is text, search and summaries work on it too. Can you convert speech to text? Yes, on almost any device for free. Phones have voice typing in the keyboard, Windows has voice typing with Windows key plus H, macOS has Dictation, and Word, Google Docs and most messaging apps support dictation. For recordings rather than live speech, options include: Transcription in apps: Microsoft Word's Transcribe on the web, meeting tools such as Teams and Google Meet, and voice recorder apps. Open-source models: Whisper runs on your own computer, privately and free. Cloud APIs: Google Cloud Speech-to-Text, Azure AI Speech, Amazon Transcribe and others for apps and large volumes. AI assistants: Gemini and ChatGPT can transcribe uploaded audio within their limits. Always proofread names, numbers and technical terms, the most common error points. What is the best speech to text converter? There is no single best one; it depends on the job. For dictation, your device's built-in voice typing is best. For recordings and privacy, Whisper. For apps, live captions and scale, a cloud API such as Google, Azure or Amazon. How to choose: Accuracy on your audio: test three short clips in your accent, with your vocabulary and noise. Live or recorded: live captions need streaming support. Languages: check support for Indian languages and mixed Hindi-English speech if you need it. Speaker labels and timestamps: needed for meetings and interviews. Privacy: sensitive recordings are safer on a local model. For a student transcribing lectures, Whisper on your own laptop or Word's Transcribe is usually enough. Whisper vs other speech to text: which is better? Whisper is a free, open-source speech recognition model from OpenAI that is accurate across many languages and runs on your own hardware. Cloud speech services add real-time streaming, speaker separation, custom vocabularies and managed scale. Also asked as: whisper vs speech to text Choose Whisper when you want privacy, no per-minute cost and offline use, and you can provide a GPU or accept slower transcription on a CPU; faster community implementations make it practical on laptops. Choose a cloud service for live captions, call-centre volumes, guaranteed uptime or features like speaker diarisation built in. Accuracy differs by language and audio, so benchmark on your own samples: pip install -U openai-whisper whisper lecture.mp3 --model small --language en That writes text and subtitle files you can compare against a cloud service's output. Can Gemini do speech to text? Yes. Gemini models accept audio input, so they can transcribe recordings, and also summarise them, answer questions about them or translate them. You can do this in the Gemini app, in Google AI Studio or through the Gemini API. Also asked as: can gemini speech to text Upload an audio file and ask for a transcript with timestamps, or ask directly for meeting notes and action items. Because Gemini understands the content, it can also label speakers and clean up filler words if you ask. For long recordings, the API's file upload handles large files better than pasting. For precise, verbatim transcripts at scale with live streaming, Google Cloud Speech-to-Text is the more specialised option. Check the Gemini API audio documentation for supported formats and length limits. How do I create an AI voice with text to speech? Choose a TTS tool, paste your script, pick a voice, adjust speed and style, and export the audio. Most tools offer many ready-made voices; cloning a specific voice needs that person's consent and a service that supports it. Also asked as: how to text to speech ai voice Tips for natural results: Write for the ear: short sentences, contractions and clear punctuation for pauses. Spell out tricky names phonetically or use the tool's pronunciation settings. Use style controls or prompts, such as "calm and friendly", where available. Generate one paragraph at a time and listen before continuing. Export WAV or high-quality MP3 for video editing. Free options include the Gemini API's speech generation in Google AI Studio, Microsoft Edge's Read Aloud for listening, and video editors such as Clipchamp with built-in TTS. How do I use text to speech in Google AI Studio? Open Google AI Studio, choose the speech generation option, select a model that supports audio output, enter your text and a style instruction, pick a voice, and run it. You can play the audio and download it, or get the code to do the same through the Gemini API. Also asked as: how to text to speech in google ai studio Gemini's speech generation lets you steer delivery with natural-language instructions, such as "read this like an excited sports commentator", and supports multiple speakers for dialogue, with each speaker assigned a different voice. It is a quick way to prototype narration for a project demo or a podcast-style explainer. Usage is subject to AI Studio's free limits and the API's pricing, and models with audio output may be in preview, so check the speech generation documentation for current model names. Which Microsoft text to speech should I use? For listening to documents and web pages, use Read Aloud in Microsoft Edge or the Immersive Reader in Word. For video narration, use Clipchamp's built-in text to speech. For apps and developers, use Azure AI Speech, which offers many neural voices and languages. Windows also has Narrator, a full screen reader for accessibility. Azure AI Speech provides a text-to-speech API with standard neural voices, control over pronunciation and pauses through SSML, a markup language for speech, and options for custom voices with consent and approval. Many Indian English and Indian-language voices are available. For a student project, Edge's Read Aloud is enough to test how text sounds, and the Azure free tier is enough to build a small voice feature. How do I use speech to text in Microsoft Word? Open your document, select Home, then Dictate, and start speaking. Word types what you say and supports voice commands for punctuation such as "comma", "full stop" and "new line". Select Dictate again to stop. Also asked as: how to speech to text on microsoft word Dictate needs a Microsoft 365 account and an internet connection, and you can change the spoken language in its settings. To transcribe a recording instead, Word for the web has Transcribe, which uploads an audio file and produces a transcript with speakers and timestamps that you can insert into the document. On Windows you can also press Windows key plus H in any text box to use system voice typing. Proofread afterwards, especially names and numbers.

# Turning a student project into a startup: the real signal to look for, what changes, and what most student founders get wrong first
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/turning-a-student-project-into-a-startup/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## When does a student project actually deserve to become a startup?

**When strangers use it without being asked to, repeatedly, for a problem that costs them real time or money. Not when you are proud of the code, not when it won a hackathon, not when friends say it's a good idea. The signal that separates a project worth pursuing from one that should stay a project is unprompted, repeated use by people who owe you nothing, because that is the only signal that is hard to fake and hard to talk yourself into.**


Annapurna, a food-sharing platform I built for a hackathon, won first prize and then kept running as a real tool afterward, and the difference between it and other hackathon projects that stopped the day after judging was exactly this signal, not the idea's cleverness or the demo's polish [7].

> A hackathon prize measures whether judges liked your demo in three minutes. A startup measures whether a stranger comes back on their own, for weeks, with nobody grading them for it.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## Why do most student projects, including good ones, not deserve this?

**Because most student projects are built to demonstrate a skill or win a specific evaluation, a grade, a hackathon prize, an interview portfolio piece, and that goal is fully achieved the moment the evaluation ends. A project built to impress a judge for three minutes was never tested against the much harder question of whether a stranger would choose to keep using it a month later with no one watching. Most good projects are good demonstrations, not good businesses, and there is nothing wrong with that; the mistake is assuming every good demonstration is secretly a startup waiting to happen.**



## What actually changes when you move from project to startup attempt?

**You need users who did not choose you out of friendship, loyalty, or a grading relationship, which means finding and convincing strangers, the hardest part most student founders underestimate [2]. You need a reason to keep working without a deadline, grade or judging panel forcing progress, which most people discover they do not actually have once the artificial deadline disappears. You need to survive being told no, or being ignored, repeatedly, by people who have no obligation to engage with you at all. None of this is about the code getting harder; the code is often the easy part.**




## Is a hackathon win a signal that a project should become a startup?

**A hackathon win is a strong signal of judged execution: you built something that worked, demoed well, and impressed a panel in a short, high-pressure window. It is not a signal of market demand, which is measured over weeks by whether people choose to keep using the thing without a judge, a prize, or a room full of attention pushing them toward it. Some hackathon-winning projects do have real demand underneath, Annapurna did, but the win itself is not the evidence; what happens in the weeks after, with no one watching, is the evidence [7].**



## What is the honest test before committing real time?

**Would you keep working on this for a stranger who owes you nothing, with no deadline, no grade, and no one watching, for the next month? Not "is the idea good" or "do I believe in it", both of which are easy to answer yes to for almost anything you built. The honest test is behavioural: are you actually still doing the unglamorous work, talking to users, fixing the boring bug, following up on a lead, once the applause from the demo has faded. Most ideas fail this test quietly, and that is useful information, not failure.**


## What mistakes do student founders make first?

**Pursuing every reasonably good project as a potential startup, diluting effort across ideas instead of concentrating it on the one with a real signal. Confusing a hackathon prize or a good grade with market validation. Building for months in isolation before showing it to a single stranger outside their circle [3]. Assuming the hard part is the code, when for most consumer and small-business ideas the hard part is finding and keeping the first real users. Quitting a real signal too early because the early weeks of any real attempt are slow and unglamorous, indistinguishable from the early weeks of one that will fail.**



## Interview and pitch questions this topic prepares you for

**"Why did you stop working on that project" or "why did you keep going" comes up naturally once you have a project with real signal or a clear decision to move on from one without it. The strongest answer names the specific evidence, user behaviour, not vibes, that drove the decision either way, which reads as founder judgement whether or not you ultimately built a company.**



## Where should I start?

**Take your best finished project and show it to five strangers outside your immediate circle this week. Watch what they actually do, not what they politely say. That is the whole test.** For a session on evaluating student projects for real founder potential, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# Who is a web developer? Full stack skills, course length and portfolio ideas
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/web-developer-skills-portfolio/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

A web developer is someone who builds and maintains websites and web applications. Front-end developers build what users see and interact with in the browser, back-end developers build the servers, databases and APIs behind it, and full stack developers do both. This page explains the role, what to learn to become full stack, how long courses take, and how to build a portfolio and personal website that win jobs and freelance clients, with ideas and examples, plus whether course profiles belong on a resume. Who is a web developer? A web developer is a programmer who creates websites and web apps: they turn designs into working pages, connect them to data and services, and keep them fast, secure and reliable. They work in agencies, product companies, startups, as freelancers and in-house for businesses. Day to day, web developers write code in HTML, CSS and JavaScript or TypeScript, use frameworks such as React and Next.js, build APIs, work with databases, fix bugs, review code and deploy changes. Specialisations include front end, back end, full stack, performance and accessibility. AI tools now handle much routine code, so valuable developers are those who understand the whole system, make good design decisions, and ship reliable products. What would you learn to become a full stack web developer? You learn the front end, the back end, a database, and how to ship: HTML, CSS, JavaScript or TypeScript, a framework such as React or Next.js, a server language and framework, SQL, Git, authentication, testing and deployment. Also asked as: what would you learn to become a &quot;full stack web developer A practical stack and order: Foundations: HTML, CSS, responsive design, accessibility basics. JavaScript and TypeScript: the language, async code, the DOM. Front-end framework: React, then Next.js for full-stack routing and rendering. Back end: Node.js, or Python with FastAPI; REST APIs and authentication. Database: PostgreSQL and SQL; an ORM later. Tools: Git, GitHub, the command line, testing. Deployment: Vercel, Render or a cloud platform; environment variables and logs. Build a project at each stage instead of finishing all the theory first. How long does an online web developer course take? Most self-paced web development courses take three to nine months part-time to complete; intensive bootcamps run about three to six months full-time. Becoming job-ready usually takes six to twelve months of consistent practice and project work. Also asked as: online web developer course duration Course length matters less than output. Someone who spends six months building and deploying three real projects is better placed than someone who finishes a twelve-month course of exercises. Free, well-regarded options include The Odin Project, freeCodeCamp, MDN's learning area and web.dev. Paid courses can add structure and mentorship, but check their projects and reviews first. Plan a daily routine: an hour of learning and an hour of building beats weekend marathons. What are good web developer portfolio ideas? Build projects that solve real problems and show different skills: a full-stack app with authentication and a database, a fast, accessible business website, a dashboard that uses a public API, and one project with an AI feature. Also asked as: top 10 web developer portfolio Ideas that impress more than to-do apps: A booking or appointment system for a local clinic or salon. An events site for your college fest with registrations and a QR check-in. A dashboard visualising public data, such as air quality or cricket stats. A study tool that answers questions from your notes with an AI API. A redesigned website for a small business you know, with their permission. Each project should be live, have a clean README, and explain your decisions. What are some web developer portfolio examples? Strong portfolios share a pattern: a clear headline saying who you are and what you build, three to five featured projects with screenshots, live links and short case studies, a brief about section, and an easy way to contact you. What a good project card includes: The problem and who it is for, in one or two sentences. Your role and the stack. A screenshot or short video. Links to the live site and the code. One interesting challenge and how you solved it. A result: users, speed, or feedback. My own portfolio, at pranjulrathour.scult.in, follows this idea: shipped products first, each with what it does and how it was built. Keep design simple and fast; a slow, flashy portfolio works against a web developer. What do the top web developer portfolios have in common? The best ones are fast, clear and focused on evidence. They load quickly, work well on phones, make the developer's specialty obvious in seconds, and lead with a few excellent projects that have real write-ups. Common traits: A one-line positioning statement at the top. Few projects, each deep, with case studies. Good performance and accessibility scores, since the portfolio itself is a project. Personality in writing, not in heavy animations. Visible proof: client logos, testimonials, open-source contributions or hackathon results. Clear calls to action: email, GitHub, LinkedIn, resume. Look at portfolios of developers you admire, note what you remember after thirty seconds, and apply that. What is the best way to build a web developer portfolio website? Build it yourself with the stack you want to be hired for, such as Next.js, and deploy it on a free host with your own domain. A hand-built portfolio is itself a project that shows your skill. Also asked as: best web developer portfolio website Practical steps: Start from a simple layout: hero, projects, about, contact. Write project case studies in Markdown or MDX so they are easy to update. Optimise images, use good metadata and test on a phone. Add analytics to see which projects visitors open. Buy a domain with your name for credibility. Website builders such as Webflow or Framer are fine for designers, but for developers, a well-built custom site sends a stronger signal. Keep it updated; a portfolio last touched two years ago suggests you stopped building. How do I build the best personal website as a web developer? Make it fast, personal and useful: introduce yourself clearly, show your best work, and add writing, such as short articles about problems you solved. Writing gives visitors and search engines a reason to return. Also asked as: best web developer personal website A personal site can do more than a portfolio: host a blog, notes on what you are learning, talks or workshop slides, and project pages that rank in search for the problems they solve. Use structured data and good titles so your name and projects appear properly in search results. Link it from GitHub, LinkedIn and your resume. Over time, a personal site with consistent writing becomes one of the strongest assets in a developer's career. What are good freelance web developer website examples? A freelance web developer's site should sell outcomes to clients, not technologies to developers: who you help, what results you deliver, examples of past work, a clear process, and an easy way to start a conversation. Elements that convert visitors into clients: A headline aimed at clients, such as "Fast websites for clinics and local businesses". Case studies with before and after results: speed, enquiries, bookings. Services listed clearly: new websites, redesigns, maintenance. Testimonials with names and businesses, with permission. A simple process: call, proposal, build, launch, support. A contact form or WhatsApp link with a quick response promise. Keep pricing discussions for the call. Show local or industry examples relevant to the clients you want. Is a Khan Academy profile resume-worthy for a web or game developer? As a line in a learning section, it can show initiative, but it is not strong evidence for a developer role. Employers want to see what you built: deployed projects, code on GitHub and, for games, playable builds. Also asked as: is my khan academy profile resume-worthy for a web developer and game developer Use course platforms to learn, then convert that learning into projects. For web development, build and deploy two or three sites or apps. For game development, publish small playable games on a site such as itch.io, with source code. On your resume, list projects first with links, then skills, then education and courses. If you include course platforms, keep it brief and name the specific skills learned. A single good project outweighs many completed course badges.

# ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Copilot: what each one actually is, who makes it, what it's for, and how to tell them apart
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-are-chatgpt-claude-gemini-copilot/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is the difference between ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Copilot?

**ChatGPT is OpenAI's consumer and developer assistant, built on OpenAI's GPT models [1]. Claude is Anthropic's assistant, built on Anthropic's own Claude models [2]. Gemini is Google's assistant, built on Google's Gemini models [4]. Copilot is Microsoft's brand for AI assistance across its products, historically built on OpenAI models under a partnership, now increasingly mixing in Microsoft's own [5]. All four are chat interfaces to an underlying large language model; the differences that matter are which company controls the model, what each is tuned for, and where each shows up, in a browser tab, an IDE, or Office.**


I use several of these daily in production work and teach students to choose deliberately rather than defaulting to whichever name they heard first. My longer framework for choosing a model provider for an actual application, not a chat tab, is on the portfolio [11].

> These are four companies' front doors to their own models. The chat window is the least interesting part; the model behind it is what actually differs.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What is ChatGPT, and who makes it?

**ChatGPT is OpenAI's assistant product, the interface most people first meet a large language model through [1]. It runs on OpenAI's GPT-series models and has grown from a text chat window into a multimodal assistant that reads images, browses, runs code, and increasingly acts as an agent. "Is ChatGPT down" usually means an OpenAI-side outage or degraded service, checkable on OpenAI's own status page rather than guessed at [7], though a browser extension conflict or a regional network issue can look identical from the user's side.**


## What is Claude, and what is Claude Code?

**Claude is Anthropic's assistant, built on Anthropic's own Claude model family, generally positioned around careful reasoning, longer documents, and steerable behaviour [2][9]. Claude Code is a distinct product from the chat assistant: an agentic coding tool that runs in a terminal or editor, reads and edits a real codebase, runs commands, and works through multi-step engineering tasks rather than just answering questions in a chat window [3]. Anthropic's newer "Claude Cowork"-style collaborative features extend this agent pattern to broader work tasks beyond code.**



## What is Gemini, and what is Copilot?

**Gemini is Google's assistant, built on Google's own Gemini models, integrated across Google Search, Workspace and Android [4]. Copilot is Microsoft's umbrella brand for AI assistance woven through Windows, Office, and GitHub; GitHub Copilot specifically is the coding-completion and chat assistant inside an IDE, historically powered substantially by OpenAI's models under the Microsoft-OpenAI partnership, with Microsoft's own models increasingly part of the mix [5]. "Why is Copilot down" or "not working" is almost always a GitHub or Microsoft service issue, an extension needing a restart, or an expired sign-in, checkable the same way as any outage, on the provider's status page first.**



## What is Codex, and how does it compare to Claude Code?

**Codex is OpenAI's agentic coding product, in the same category as Claude Code: an AI system that works directly in a codebase, running commands and making multi-file changes rather than only chatting [6]. The comparison that matters for choosing between them is less "which is smarter" in the abstract and more which integrates with your existing workflow, editor, and CI, and which model family's coding behaviour you have personally found more reliable on your kind of codebase, since both improve on overlapping but not identical benchmarks release to release.**


## Is Ollama a competitor to these, and is it free?

**Not directly. Ollama is a tool for running open-weight models, Llama, Mistral, Gemma, Qwen and others, on your own machine, entirely free and offline [8]. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Copilot are hosted products built on closed or semi-closed models you access through an account and, for heavy use, a subscription or API bill. Ollama is the local, self-hosted alternative to all of them for tasks where privacy, cost, or offline access matter more than having the single most capable model available.**



## How do I choose which one to use for a task?

**For coding inside a real project, a coding agent, Claude Code or Codex, beats a general chat window because it can actually read and run your code. For long documents or careful step-by-step reasoning, compare Claude and the others on the specific document, since strengths shift by release. For anything tied into Google's ecosystem, Gemini's integration wins on convenience. For anything tied into Microsoft's ecosystem, Copilot wins the same way. For a quick one-off question, whichever is already open in a tab is the right answer; the differences matter for sustained work, not a single query.**



## What mistakes do people make comparing these assistants?

**Assuming "AI" is one thing and any assistant should behave like any other. Blaming your account for what is a provider-wide outage, or the reverse, assuming an outage when the problem is a browser extension. Using a general chat assistant for a coding agent's job, pasting code back and forth by hand when a coding agent would read the repository directly. Picking a favourite once and never re-checking as models change every few months. The fix for all of these is the same: know which product you are actually using and what it is built for.**



## Where should I start?

**Try the same real task, a piece of code, a document, a question you actually have, on two of these assistants this week and compare the answers yourself rather than trusting a ranking.** For a workshop that teaches students to evaluate AI tools rather than default to whichever is trending, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What are Copilot agents? Uses, memory, privacy, credits and SharePoint agents
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-are-copilot-agents/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

Copilot agents are focused AI assistants inside Microsoft 365 Copilot, each with its own instructions, knowledge sources and actions for a specific job, such as answering HR policy questions, helping new hires, or handling IT requests. Microsoft provides some built-in agents, and organisations build their own with Agent Builder or Copilot Studio. This page explains what agents are used for, when to use one, whether they learn or remember, how credits apply, privacy and where they run, how good they are in practice, and how agents work in SharePoint. What are Copilot agents? Copilot agents are specialised assistants built on Microsoft 365 Copilot. Each one combines instructions that define its role, knowledge it can search, and optionally actions it can take in other systems, so it handles one kind of task better than general Copilot. There are a few kinds. Retrieval agents answer from specific knowledge, such as a policy site. Task agents take actions, such as creating a ticket or updating a record. Autonomous agents run on triggers or schedules without a user starting a chat. Microsoft also ships prebuilt agents, such as research and analysis agents, and agents in Teams and SharePoint. You find agents in the Copilot app or Teams, and you can mention them in a chat to call them in. What are Copilot agents used for? Organisations use Copilot agents to answer recurring questions, guide people through processes and automate routine tasks: HR and policy questions, employee onboarding, IT helpdesk, sales preparation, project status and customer support. Examples that work well: An onboarding agent that answers new joiners' questions from the handbook and links the right forms. An IT agent that resolves common issues and opens a ticket when it cannot. A sales agent that summarises an account from CRM data before a call. A project agent that reports status from a SharePoint site and task lists. A college department agent that answers questions about syllabus, deadlines and lab rules. The common pattern is a clear audience, trusted sources and a defined hand-off to a person. When should I use a Copilot agent? Use an agent when the same kind of question or task keeps coming up, the answers live in known sources, and a focused assistant would be more accurate than general Copilot. Use general Copilot for one-off, varied requests. Signals an agent is worth building: a team answers the same twenty questions every week; a process has steps people often get wrong; information is scattered across sites and documents; or a task needs data from another system. Signals it is not: the questions are rare or completely different each time, the source documents are outdated or contradictory, or nobody will own and maintain the agent. Clean, current knowledge matters more than clever instructions. Do Copilot agents learn? Not in the sense of retraining themselves. Agents do not update the underlying model from your conversations. They improve when their owners update instructions, add or fix knowledge sources, and refine actions based on what users ask. That is by design: a model that changed itself from every conversation would be unpredictable and could absorb wrong or sensitive information. What looks like learning comes from fresh knowledge: when a policy document is updated in SharePoint, the agent's next answer reflects it. Owners should review conversation analytics regularly, note questions the agent answered poorly, and fix the source content or instructions. That loop is the real way agents get better over time. Do Copilot agents have memory? Within a conversation, yes: an agent remembers what has been said in that chat. Across conversations, memory is limited and depends on the agent and Microsoft's features; agents generally do not carry details from one user's chats into another's. Microsoft 365 Copilot has been adding personalisation and memory features for individual users, controlled by user and admin settings. Agents built in Copilot Studio can store and use variables during a conversation and can save information to systems such as Dataverse or a SharePoint list through actions, which acts as explicit, controlled memory. If an agent must remember something, such as a user's preferences or a case history, store it deliberately in a system of record rather than relying on chat history. Do Copilot agents use credits? It depends on the agent and licensing. Agents built in Copilot Studio consume Copilot Credits for their interactions and actions, especially when used by people without a Microsoft 365 Copilot licence, on external channels or when running autonomously. Also asked as: when to use copilot agents Users with a Microsoft 365 Copilot licence can use many agents within Microsoft 365 as part of that licence, while organisations without it pay for agent usage through Copilot Studio capacity or pay-as-you-go billing. Actions that call generative AI, search knowledge or run autonomously typically consume more. Microsoft updates these rules, so admins should check the current Copilot Studio licensing guide and monitor consumption in the Power Platform admin centre. Are Copilot agents private? Agents follow Microsoft 365's security model: they only access content that the user, or the configured identity for autonomous agents, is allowed to see, and data stays within your organisation's Microsoft 365 environment under enterprise data protection. Privacy risks come from configuration, not the platform. An agent with an uploaded file shares that file's content with everyone who can use the agent. An agent using a service account can expose data the end user should not see. SharePoint sites with overly broad permissions make agents surface documents widely. Before sharing an agent, check its knowledge and actions against its audience, and ask your admin about policies for agent creation and sharing. Where do Copilot agents run? Copilot agents run in Microsoft's cloud, within your organisation's Microsoft 365 tenant and Power Platform environments. You use them through Microsoft 365 Copilot, Teams, SharePoint, websites or other channels where they are published. Copilot Studio agents live in a Power Platform environment, which sets the region where their data is stored. Agent Builder agents are stored with Microsoft 365. The language models run in Microsoft's data centres under the same commitments as Microsoft 365 Copilot. Nothing runs on your laptop, except the app or browser you use to chat. For data residency questions, admins can check environment regions and Microsoft's data boundary commitments for their geography. Are Copilot agents any good? They are good when the scope is narrow, the knowledge is clean and current, and someone owns them. They disappoint when built as general "ask me anything" bots over messy, outdated document collections. What separates useful agents from poor ones: A specific audience and purpose written into the instructions. A small set of authoritative sources, with duplicates and old versions removed. Clear behaviour when the answer is not found: say so and hand over. Tested with real questions before launch. Reviewed regularly using analytics and feedback. The same lesson shaped RAG.NextUpgrad: retrieval quality and a refusal path when evidence is weak matter more than the model. An honest "I do not know" beats a confident wrong answer. How do Copilot agents work in SharePoint? SharePoint agents answer questions grounded in the content of a specific site, document library, folder or set of files. Every site can offer a ready-made agent, and site members can create custom agents scoped to chosen content. To create one, select the files or library, choose to create an agent, give it a name, instructions and starter prompts, and save it; it becomes an item in the library that you can share and use in Teams chats. The agent searches only its scoped content, within each user's permissions, and cites the documents it used. This works well for project sites, policy libraries and course material. Keep the scoped content tidy: archive old versions and use clear titles so the agent finds the right document.

# What are embeddings in AI? Text embeddings, vector similarity, choosing a model, and how embeddings power RAG and semantic search
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-are-embeddings-in-ai/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What are embeddings in AI?

**An embedding is a list of numbers, a vector, that a model produces to represent the meaning of an input: a sentence, a paragraph, an image, a sound clip. The model is trained so that inputs with similar meaning produce vectors that are close together and dissimilar inputs produce vectors far apart. Once text is a vector, meaning becomes geometry: you can measure similarity with a distance, search by nearest neighbour, cluster, and feed vectors to other models.**


Word2vec showed in 2013 that simple training objectives produce vectors where analogies work as arithmetic [1]. BERT produced contextual vectors for every token [2], and Sentence-BERT trained networks so that a whole sentence's vector could be compared with cosine similarity directly, which is the form every RAG system uses [3]. Dense passage retrieval then showed embeddings beating keyword search for question answering [4].

In every retrieval system I have built, the embedding model is chosen once, early, and it decides what "similar" means for the life of the index. This page is how I make that choice, and what I tell students who confuse embeddings with tokens.

> An embedding model is a definition of similarity, frozen into numbers. Pick the one whose idea of similar matches your users' idea of relevant.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## How do embedding models work?

**A transformer reads the input and produces a vector for every token; a pooling step, usually the mean or a special token's vector, collapses them to one vector for the whole input; a final normalisation makes it unit length. Training uses pairs: a query and a passage that answers it, or two sentences that mean the same, pushed together, with unrelated pairs pushed apart, a contrastive objective. Millions of such pairs teach the model which differences matter and which do not.**



Two terms collide here. An "embedding layer" inside any neural network maps token ids to vectors as the first step of processing; an "embedding model" is a whole network whose output is a vector for the input. The second is what RAG and search use.

## What is the difference between embeddings and tokens?

**Tokens are the pieces of text a model reads, word fragments mapped to integer ids; there are as many tokens as pieces. An embedding is one vector representing an entire input's meaning. A 500-word passage might be 650 tokens and exactly one embedding. Tokens are how language models consume text; embeddings are how retrieval systems compare it. People search for this distinction often because both are "numbers that represent text", and they are not the same numbers.**



## What do dimensions mean, and how many do I need?

**Dimensions are the length of the vector, commonly 384, 768, 1,024 or 1,536, sometimes 3,072 or more. More dimensions can capture more nuance and cost more storage and search time. The right number is whatever your chosen model produces; it is not a knob to maximise. Matryoshka-trained models let you truncate a long vector to a shorter prefix with graceful quality loss, which is useful when storage matters [7]. Test truncation on your own retrieval set before relying on it.**


A 1,536-dimension vector for a million chunks is about six gigabytes in 32-bit floats before any index overhead. A 384-dimension model is a quarter of that. Whether it retrieves worse for your documents is an empirical question, and it is often closer than the size suggests.

## How is similarity between embeddings measured?

**By a distance or similarity function between two vectors. Cosine similarity, the cosine of the angle between them, is the standard for text; on unit-length vectors it equals the dot product and ranges from minus one to one. Euclidean distance is common in image search. Use the metric the model's documentation specifies, normalise vectors at index time, and never mix metrics or models within one index.**


There is no universal "good" cosine score. The same model can put unrelated texts at 0.6 and paraphrases at 0.85; another model spreads them differently. Thresholds come from your own labelled pairs, not from a blog post.

## Which embedding model should I use?

**Shortlist by the retrieval task on the MTEB leaderboard, filtered for your language and a size you can run [5][6]. Prefer models trained on query-to-passage pairs for RAG. Then evaluate two or three on twenty of your own questions against your own documents, measuring recall at k. Choose the smallest model that meets your target. For Hindi and mixed-language content, check multilingual models specifically; English-only leaders can collapse.**



The MTEB paper explains the benchmark's tasks and why a single average hides large differences between tasks [5]. Sentence Transformers is the library most open models ship with [10]; commercial APIs document their models and dimensions [11]. My own decision notes on switching models in a production RAG system are on the portfolio [13].


## How are embeddings used in RAG and semantic search?

**At index time, each document chunk is embedded and stored in a vector index. At query time the question is embedded with the same model and the nearest chunks are retrieved, then reranked and passed to the language model as context. Semantic search is the same retrieval without the generation step: the results are the chunks or documents themselves. Embeddings make "how do I reset my password" match a passage titled "Credential recovery" even though they share no words.**



That table is why every retrieval system I ship is hybrid: dense retrieval for meaning, BM25 for exact terms, fused with reciprocal rank fusion [12].

## What else can I do with embeddings?

**Deduplicate near-identical documents by finding pairs above a similarity threshold. Cluster support tickets or feedback into themes. Classify text by nearest labelled examples, which needs no training run. Recommend items whose descriptions are close to what a user liked. Detect topic drift in a conversation. Match resumes to job descriptions by section. Anything that reduces to "which of these is most like that" is an embedding problem.**


## What are multimodal, image and code embeddings?

**Multimodal models place images and text in the same vector space, so a text query can retrieve images and an image can retrieve captions; CLIP established the approach [8]. Image embeddings power visual search and duplicate detection. Code embeddings, trained on code and natural language pairs, let you search a codebase by describing what a function does. Each is a separate model with its own space; a text embedding and an image embedding from unrelated models cannot be compared.**


## What are the limitations of embeddings?

**They compress meaning, so they lose detail, especially exact strings, numbers and negation: "no refund" and "refund" can land close. They inherit their training data's biases and domain, so a general model can misjudge medical or legal text. They are model-specific, so switching models means re-embedding everything. They cannot be reversed into the original text, which is a privacy advantage and an interpretability limit. Late-interaction methods such as ColBERT keep per-token vectors to recover some lost precision, at higher storage cost [9].**



## What are common embedding interview questions?

**Explain what an embedding is to a non-engineer. Explain why cosine similarity is used and why vectors are normalised. Compare tokens and embeddings. Describe how you would choose an embedding model for a RAG system and how you would evaluate it. Explain why keyword search is still needed. Say what happens when you switch models. If you have built one retrieval system, these are all stories rather than definitions.**



## Where should I start with embeddings?

**Install Sentence Transformers, embed a hundred sentences you wrote, and print the nearest neighbours of a few. Then embed a real document set, ask twenty questions, and measure how often the right chunk is in the top five. Swap the model and measure again. That afternoon teaches everything above.** If your college wants a hands-on session on retrieval, embeddings and RAG, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.
