# What are large language models? How LLMs work, training, and small vs large
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-are-large-language-models/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

Large language models (LLMs) are neural networks, usually transformers with billions of parameters, trained on huge amounts of text and code to predict the next token. From that one objective they learn grammar, facts, reasoning patterns and coding, which is why one model can answer questions, write, translate and program. This page explains how they work, what they are trained on, how many exist, how small and large models differ, what instruction tuning changes, why pretrained models already handle many tasks, what vLLM does for serving, and where to read more. What are large language models? Large language models are AI models trained on very large text datasets to understand and generate language. "Large" refers to their size, from a few billion to hundreds of billions of parameters, and to the scale of their training data. Also asked as: large vs small language models · what is vllm? efficient ai inference for large language models GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, Mistral, Qwen and DeepSeek are all LLM families. They power chat assistants, coding tools, search features, translation and document analysis. An LLM on its own only generates text; products add tools, retrieval, memory and safety layers around it. In my own work, RAG.NextUpgrad wraps LLMs with hybrid retrieval and a confidence gate, and FineTune Studio adapts open models with QLoRA, which shows the two main ways engineers shape an LLM: give it the right context, or change its weights. How do large language models work? An LLM splits text into tokens, turns each into a vector, and passes the sequence through many transformer layers whose attention mechanism lets each token draw on every earlier token. The final layer outputs a probability for every possible next token. Also asked as: how large language models work pdf Generation repeats that step: pick a next token from the probabilities, append it, and predict again. Settings such as temperature control how adventurous the choice is. The model's knowledge lives in its parameters, learned during training; it does not look things up unless a tool or retrieval system gives it documents. That is why LLMs can be fluent and wrong at the same time: they produce the most plausible continuation, which usually, but not always, matches the truth. What are large language models trained on? LLMs are pretrained on very large collections of text and code: filtered web pages, books, encyclopedias, academic papers, code repositories and other licensed or public data. Later stages use smaller curated datasets of instructions, conversations and human preference ratings. Training data is cleaned heavily: duplicates, low-quality pages and some personal or harmful content are filtered out, and mixtures are balanced across languages and domains. Model makers rarely publish full data details, and the use of copyrighted material is the subject of ongoing legal debate. Training data has a cutoff date, so models lack knowledge of later events unless connected to search or retrieval. The quality of data matters more than raw quantity, which is why curated datasets and synthetic data now play a large role. How many large language models are there? Thousands. Major labs release a few flagship families, while open-weight models and their fine-tuned variants number in the many thousands on Hugging Face, which hosts over a million models of all kinds. The landscape has three layers. Frontier proprietary models, such as those from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, available through apps and APIs. Open-weight base models from Meta, Mistral, Alibaba's Qwen team, Google's Gemma, DeepSeek and others, which anyone can download. And the long tail of community fine-tunes and quantised versions built on those bases. For practical choices, you rarely need more than a shortlist: one strong hosted model, one fast cheap model, and one open model you can run or fine-tune yourself. What is the difference between small and large language models? Small language models, typically from under one billion to a few billion parameters, are cheaper, faster and can run on laptops and phones. Large models, from tens to hundreds of billions of parameters, handle complex reasoning, long documents and broad knowledge much better. Also asked as: difference between instruction tuning vs non instruction tuning large language models Small models are good at focused tasks: classification, extraction, simple summaries and autocomplete, especially after fine-tuning on a specific job. They also keep data on the device. Large models are better at open-ended questions, multi-step reasoning, coding across files and following complex instructions. Size is not everything: training quality, data and fine-tuning let today's small models beat much larger models from a few years ago. When should I use a small vs a large language model? Use a small model when the task is narrow, volume is high, latency matters or data must stay on the device. Use a large model when the task is open-ended, mistakes are costly, or it needs reasoning across long context. A practical approach is routing: send easy requests to a small, cheap model and hard ones to a large model, based on rules or a quick classifier. Another is distillation: use a large model to label data or generate examples, then fine-tune a small model on them for production. With QLoRA, fine-tuning a small open model fits on a single consumer GPU, which is what FineTune Studio makes possible from the browser. Always measure on your own test set before choosing. What is the difference between instruction-tuned and non-instruction-tuned LLMs? A base, non-instruction-tuned model only continues text; give it a question and it may continue with more questions. An instruction-tuned model has been further trained on examples of instructions and good responses, so it follows requests and answers helpfully. Instruction tuning, shown at scale in Google's FLAN work and OpenAI's InstructGPT, trains the model on many tasks phrased as instructions, often followed by preference tuning with human or AI feedback. Chat assistants are instruction-tuned. Base models are still useful: for further fine-tuning on your own format, for text completion and for research. When downloading open models, choose the "instruct" or "chat" variant for assistants and the base variant only if you plan to fine-tune it into something specific. Do large pretrained language models already "know" NLP tasks? Largely, yes. Pretraining on huge text teaches models to perform many tasks, such as translation, summarisation, question answering and classification, from a prompt alone, without task-specific training. GPT-2 and GPT-3 demonstrated this zero-shot and few-shot ability. Also asked as: do large pretrained language models already &quot;know&quot; about nlp tasks The knowledge is latent: the model has seen enough examples of summaries, translations and answers in its data that a well-phrased prompt or a few examples activate the behaviour. Instruction tuning makes this much more reliable. It is not perfect, though: performance varies by task and language, and specialised tasks, such as medical coding or a company's document format, still benefit from retrieval of examples or fine-tuning. Always evaluate on your own data instead of assuming the model already knows. What is vLLM? vLLM is an open-source library for serving large language models efficiently. Its PagedAttention technique manages the memory for attention keys and values in blocks, like virtual memory pages, so many requests share the GPU with little waste. Combined with continuous batching, which adds new requests to a running batch instead of waiting for it to finish, vLLM achieves much higher throughput than naive serving on the same hardware. It exposes an OpenAI-compatible API, supports many open models, quantisation and multiple GPUs. Use vLLM when you host open models for many users on a GPU server. For a single user on a laptop, simpler tools such as Ollama or llama.cpp are easier. Is there a good PDF that explains how large language models work? Yes. Jurafsky and Martin's Speech and Language Processing, whose third-edition draft chapters on transformers and large language models are free online as PDFs, is a clear academic introduction. The original Transformer paper and the GPT-3 paper are free on arXiv. A reading path: The transformer and LLM chapters of Speech and Language Processing for foundations. "Attention Is All You Need" for the architecture. "Language Models are Few-Shot Learners" for why scale and prompting matter. The FLAN and InstructGPT papers for instruction tuning. The PagedAttention paper for serving. Read with a notebook open and implement a tiny transformer; building one, even small, makes the papers much easier to follow.

# What are LLM models? Meaning, examples, weights, parameters and model cards
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-are-llm-models/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

LLM stands for large language model: a neural network, usually a transformer, trained on very large amounts of text to predict the next token, which lets it understand and generate language, write code and reason through problems. ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini are apps built on LLMs. This page explains what LLMs are and how they produce answers, gives examples and types, discusses how to pick the best one, what they are used for, and what weights, parameters and model cards mean, which matters once you start using open models. What does LLM mean in AI? In AI, LLM means large language model: a model with billions of parameters trained on a huge text corpus to predict and generate text. "Large" refers to the model's size and its training data. LLMs are a type of generative AI and a subset of deep learning. They power chat assistants, coding tools, search features, translation and document analysis. Many newer LLMs are multimodal, also accepting images, audio or video, but the name has stuck. When people say "the LLM" in a product discussion, they mean the model doing the generation, as opposed to the surrounding application with its tools, retrieval and interface. What are LLM models? LLM models are the specific trained models, such as a particular version of GPT, Claude, Gemini or Llama, that you call through an API or run locally. Each is a file of learned weights plus the code to run it, released in sizes and variants. Also asked as: how do llm models work A single model family usually comes in several sizes, from small fast models to large capable ones, and in variants: a base model that only continues text, an instruction-tuned model that follows requests, and sometimes reasoning, coding or vision versions. Closed models, such as GPT, Claude and Gemini, are available through their companies' apps and APIs. Open-weight models, such as Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma and DeepSeek, can be downloaded and run on your own hardware. How do LLM models generate an answer? At inference time, an LLM converts your prompt into tokens, processes them through its transformer layers, outputs a probability for every possible next token, picks one, appends it, and repeats until it finishes the answer. Each step uses attention to relate the new token to everything before it, and a cache of earlier computations makes generation faster. Sampling settings such as temperature and top-p control how predictable the choices are. Reasoning models spend extra tokens thinking before the final answer. The model has no live connection to the internet or your files unless an application supplies them through tools or retrieval, which is why grounding with documents, as in retrieval-augmented generation, is essential for accurate, current answers. What are some examples of LLM models? Well-known LLM families include OpenAI's GPT models, Anthropic's Claude, Google's Gemini and open Gemma models, Meta's Llama, Mistral's models, Alibaba's Qwen, DeepSeek's models and Microsoft's Phi. Also asked as: what are llm models examples By access: Closed, via apps and APIs: GPT, Claude, Gemini. Open weights, downloadable: Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma, DeepSeek, Phi and OpenAI's open-weight releases. Specialised: coding models, embedding models for search, and vision-language models. New versions arrive every few months, so model names change quickly; families are more stable than version numbers. Hugging Face hosts thousands of open models and fine-tuned variants. What are the different types of LLM models? LLMs differ by training stage, purpose, access and architecture: base versus instruction-tuned, general versus specialised, closed versus open-weight, dense versus mixture-of-experts, and text-only versus multimodal. Also asked as: what are different llm models The distinctions that matter in practice: Base vs instruct: base models continue text; instruct models follow requests and are what assistants use. Reasoning models: trained to think step by step for harder problems, slower and more costly. Coding models: tuned on code and tool use. Embedding models: produce vectors for search rather than text. Multimodal models: accept images, audio or video. Small vs large: small models run on devices; large ones handle harder tasks. Choose the type to match your task before choosing a brand. What is the best LLM model? There is no single best LLM. Frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google lead on hard reasoning and coding, open-weight models lead on privacy and control, and smaller models win on speed and cost. The best one is the one that performs best on your task within your constraints. How to choose: Define the task and a test set of twenty to fifty real examples. Try two or three candidate models, including one smaller, cheaper one. Measure accuracy, latency and cost per request. Consider privacy, data residency and licence. Public leaderboards, such as community rankings, give a broad signal but not an answer for your use case. Design your code so switching models is a configuration change, as with the multi-provider fallback in RAG.NextUpgrad. What are LLM models primarily used for? LLMs are mainly used for writing and editing, answering questions, summarising, translating, coding assistance, extracting structured data from documents, classification, conversational assistants, and as the reasoning engine in AI agents. In products, the most valuable uses combine an LLM with your data and systems: customer support grounded in documentation, document processing with validation, coding agents that run tests, and research assistants that cite sources. LLMs are weaker at exact arithmetic, guaranteed factual accuracy without sources, and anything requiring up-to-date knowledge without retrieval. Good engineering puts the model where language understanding helps and uses deterministic code for the rest, which is how DocuLens AI pairs extraction by an LLM with deterministic compliance scoring. What are LLM model weights? Model weights are the learned numbers inside a neural network, set during training, that determine how inputs are transformed into outputs. An LLM's knowledge and abilities are encoded in its weights. When a company "releases the weights", you can download the files, typically gigabytes in size, and run or fine-tune the model yourself. Formats include safetensors for frameworks such as PyTorch and Hugging Face Transformers, and GGUF for tools like llama.cpp and Ollama. Quantisation stores weights with fewer bits, such as 4-bit instead of 16-bit, to cut memory use. Fine-tuning with methods like LoRA trains small extra weight matrices instead of changing all weights, which is far cheaper. What are LLM model parameters? Parameters are the individual learned values in a model, mostly its weights, and the parameter count, such as 7 billion or 70 billion, measures model size. More parameters generally mean more capacity, but also more memory and slower inference. Memory is roughly parameters multiplied by bytes per parameter: a 7B model needs about 14 GB at 16-bit precision and about 4 GB at 4-bit. Parameter count is not everything: training data quality, training method and architecture matter a lot, and well-trained small models can beat older large ones. Mixture-of-experts models have many total parameters but use only some for each token, so their active parameters determine speed. "Parameters" can also mean generation settings such as temperature, so check the context. What are LLM model cards? A model card is documentation published with a model that explains its intended uses, training data at a high level, evaluation results, known limitations, risks and licence. The idea comes from the 2018 paper "Model Cards for Model Reporting". On Hugging Face, every model page shows its model card, usually a README with metadata. Read it before using a model: check the licence, especially for commercial use, the languages and tasks it supports, its context length, evaluation benchmarks, recommended prompt format and any safety notes. When you fine-tune and share a model, write a model card too: what you trained it for, on what data, how you evaluated it, and where it should not be used.

# What are vision-language models and multimodal AI? How VLMs see images, what they can and cannot do, and building student projects with them
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-are-vision-language-models/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What are vision-language models?

**Vision-language models, VLMs, are models that take an image, or several, alongside text and produce text: a caption, an answer to a question about the picture, the fields on a form, the trend in a chart, the code in a screenshot. An image encoder turns the picture into a sequence of visual tokens; a language model attends to those tokens along with the prompt and generates. Multimodal AI is the broader term for models that handle several input types, images, audio, video, text; VLMs are the image-and-text case that most products use today.**


DocuLens AI, the document extraction system I built in 2026, sits on exactly this capability: a model reads an invoice or contract image and returns typed fields, which deterministic rules then validate and score [13]. My notes on choosing between CLIP, ViT and multimodal LLMs, and on student projects that use them, are on the portfolio [11][12].

> A vision-language model is a very good reader of pictures that occasionally makes things up with total confidence. Build the validation before you build the demo.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour, from building DocuLens AI</cite>

## How do vision-language models work?

**An image encoder, usually a vision transformer that splits the picture into patches and processes them like words [5], produces a grid of embeddings. A projection maps those embeddings into the language model's token space. The language model then attends over the visual tokens and the text prompt together and generates an answer, exactly as it would for text alone. Training aligns the two sides on image-text pairs and then on instruction data: questions about images with good answers [3][4].**



CLIP established that images and text could share one embedding space by contrastive training on web pairs [1]; Flamingo showed a frozen language model could be taught to read visual tokens [2]; BLIP-2 made the bridge efficient with a small query transformer [3]; LLaVA showed instruction tuning on generated visual conversations produced a capable open assistant cheaply [4]. Today's models descend from that line.

## What can vision-language models do?

**Describe images and scenes. Answer questions about a picture. Read text in images, including handwriting and messy scans, often better than classic OCR on hard inputs. Extract structured fields from documents and forms. Interpret charts, tables and diagrams. Explain screenshots and UI. Compare two images. Reason over a sequence of frames. In practice the highest-value uses are document understanding and "look at this and tell me what to do", where the alternative was a human reading.**



## What can vision-language models not do well?

**Count reliably beyond a handful. Localise precisely, so their bounding boxes are approximate. Read very small text or dense tables without errors. Run in real time on video. Run on a phone without heavy quantization. And, above all, resist inventing: a VLM asked for a value that is not in the image will often produce a plausible one. Treat every extracted number as unverified until a rule or a human confirms it, exactly as you would for text LLM output.**



DocuLens exists as a product because of that last line: extraction through a model with a strict schema, then deterministic validation and scoring so the same document produces the same result every time [13].

## VLM vs classic vision models: which should I use?

**Use a classic detector or classifier when you need speed, precise localisation, counting, on-device inference or thousands of frames a second: production lines, cameras, phones. Use a VLM when the task is open-ended understanding, reading, extraction or reasoning about an image and you can afford a model call per image. Use CLIP-style embeddings for search and similarity. Many systems combine them: a detector finds the region, a VLM reads it.**



My decision notes on CLIP versus ViT versus multimodal LLMs, with the projects each suited, are written up separately [12].


## Which vision-language models can I use?

**Commercial APIs from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google accept images alongside text and are the fastest way to start [8][9][10]. Open-weight VLMs on Hugging Face, in the image-text-to-text category, run on your own GPU and include small variants that fit a laptop [7]. For documents specifically, OCR-free models such as Donut showed the pixels-to-structured-output path [6], and current open VLMs do it well. Choose by where the images may travel: private documents argue for open models on your hardware.**


## How much do vision-language models cost?

**Images are billed as tokens, and an image typically costs the equivalent of several hundred to a couple of thousand text tokens depending on resolution and provider, plus the output tokens. So a document extraction call is more expensive than a text call of the same output length, and a video processed frame by frame gets expensive quickly. Downscale images to the resolution the task needs, crop to the region of interest, batch offline work, and route only hard images to the large model. Check current pricing on the provider pages [8][9][10].**


## What projects should students build with vision-language models?

**One narrow workflow with real inputs each. A prescription or lab-report reader with a strict schema and a doctor-check boundary. A whiteboard-to-notes tool that turns a photo of a lecture board into structured notes. A receipt-to-expense app for a hostel with totals validated by rules. A chart explainer for research papers that outputs the numbers as a table. A shelf-stock checker for a small shop that flags empty slots. Each is demonstrable in three minutes and teaches the validation habits that make VLM products trustworthy.**



My five student project ideas beyond chat with a PDF, with the hard part of each, are on the portfolio [11].


## Vision-language model interview questions

**Explain how an image becomes tokens a language model can read. Compare CLIP-style contrastive models with instruction-tuned VLMs. Name three things VLMs do badly and how you would design around each. Explain when you would still use a detector. Describe how you would validate extracted fields. Estimate the cost of processing a thousand documents. A document extraction project with validation is the strongest evidence.**



## Where should I start?

**Photograph ten receipts or forms, send each to a VLM with a strict JSON schema, and write three rules that check the output. Count how many the rules catch. That afternoon teaches the capability, the failure mode and the fix.** For a hands-on session on multimodal AI and document intelligence at your college, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What does fine-tuning do? How to fine-tune LLMs, LoRA, datasets and GPT models
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-does-fine-tuning-do/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

Fine-tuning takes a pretrained model and continues training it on your own examples, so it learns to behave the way you need: follow a format, use a tone, classify into your categories, or handle a narrow task more cheaply. It changes the model's weights, unlike prompting or retrieval. I built FineTune Studio, which runs QLoRA fine-tuning from the browser with live loss curves and base-versus-tuned comparison, so this page answers practical questions: why fine-tune, how, LoRA, datasets, ChatGPT and GPT models, gpt-oss-20b, and the classic four-step recipe. What does fine-tuning do? Fine-tuning adjusts a pretrained model's weights using examples of inputs and desired outputs, so the model produces those kinds of outputs more reliably without needing long instructions or examples in every prompt. It is best at teaching behaviour: a strict output schema, a consistent writing style, domain-specific phrasing, or a classification scheme. It is weaker at teaching facts, because models absorb patterns more readily than specific details, and fine-tuned knowledge is hard to update or cite. That is why the common recommendation is RAG for knowledge and fine-tuning for behaviour, sometimes together: a fine-tuned model that is good at using retrieved context. Why fine-tune LLMs? Fine-tune when prompting cannot get consistent results, when you need a smaller, faster or cheaper model to match a bigger one on a specific task, or when outputs must follow a precise format or style every time. Also asked as: what does fine tune do · why fine tune llms · how to fine tune dataset Good reasons: Consistency: the same format and tone across thousands of requests. Cost and latency: a small fine-tuned model replaces a large general one. Shorter prompts: behaviour is built in, so prompts and costs shrink. Domain language: jargon, abbreviations or local language mixes. Privacy: fine-tune an open model and run it on your own hardware. Before fine-tuning, try better prompts and structured outputs, and measure on a test set; fine-tune only if the gap remains. How do you fine-tune an LLM? Collect examples of inputs and ideal outputs, split them into training and test sets, choose a base model, train with a method such as LoRA or QLoRA, then compare the tuned model with the base model on the test set before using it. Also asked as: how do you fine tune llm The steps in practice: Define the task and a success metric, such as exact-match accuracy or a rubric score. Build the dataset in chat format, with consistent instructions. Pick a base model that is already decent at the task. Train: start with a few epochs and a modest learning rate; watch training and validation loss. Evaluate on held-out examples against the base model. Deploy the adapter or merged model, and monitor outputs. FineTune Studio streams the loss curve live so you can stop a run that is diverging or overfitting. How do I fine-tune with LoRA? LoRA freezes the original model and trains small low-rank matrices added to some layers, usually the attention projections. With Hugging Face PEFT and TRL, you load a base model, attach a LoRA configuration, and train on your dataset. Also asked as: how to lora fine tune from peft import LoraConfig from trl import SFTTrainer, SFTConfig from datasets import load_dataset data = load_dataset(&quot;json&quot;, data_files=&quot;train.jsonl&quot;)[&quot;train&quot;] # {&quot;messages&quot;: [...]} per line lora = LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.05, target_modules=&quot;all-linear&quot;, task_type=&quot;CAUSAL_LM&quot;) trainer = SFTTrainer(model=&quot;Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct&quot;, train_dataset=data, peft_config=lora, args=SFTConfig(output_dir=&quot;out&quot;, num_train_epochs=2)) trainer.train() For larger models on one GPU, add 4-bit loading, which is QLoRA. Save the adapter, which is small, and load it on top of the base model for inference. How do I build a dataset for fine-tuning? Write examples that look exactly like real use: the same kind of inputs your app will receive and the ideal outputs, in a consistent format. Quality and consistency matter far more than size. Guidelines: Start with a few hundred high-quality examples; scale to thousands for harder tasks. Cover the variety of real inputs, including edge cases and tricky ones. Keep the system instruction and output format identical across examples. Remove duplicates, contradictions and errors. Hold out 10 to 20 per cent as a test set never used in training. Include examples where the right answer is to decline or ask for clarification. You can use a strong model to draft examples, but review them; errors in training data become errors in the model. How do I fine-tune ChatGPT? You cannot fine-tune the ChatGPT app itself. You can fine-tune supported OpenAI models through the OpenAI API, then use the resulting custom model in your own application. In ChatGPT, custom GPTs and Projects give customisation through instructions and files, without changing weights. Also asked as: how to fine tune chatgpt So the choice depends on the goal. For a personal assistant that follows your instructions and uses your documents, a custom GPT or Project is enough. For an application that needs a model to follow a format reliably at scale, fine-tune through the API with your dataset, evaluate it, and call the fine-tuned model by its ID. Consider whether a strong base model with good prompts and retrieval already meets your quality bar. Can you fine-tune GPT models? Yes, some. OpenAI's API supports fine-tuning for selected models, with supervised fine-tuning, preference fine-tuning and, for some reasoning models, reinforcement fine-tuning. The list of supported models changes, so check the fine-tuning guide. Also asked as: can you fine tune gpt models The workflow is the same for any supported model: prepare JSONL training data in chat format, upload it, create a fine-tuning job with the base model name, monitor it, and evaluate the resulting model against the base. OpenAI hosts and serves the fine-tuned model, and you do not receive its weights. If you need to own and run the weights yourself, fine-tune an open-weight model instead, such as OpenAI's open-weight releases or Llama, Qwen and Mistral models. Can you fine-tune GPT-5 mini? Whether a specific model such as GPT-5 mini can be fine-tuned depends on OpenAI's current list of fine-tunable models, which changes as new models launch. Check the fine-tuning guide and models page for what is supported today. Also asked as: can you fine tune gpt 5 mini OpenAI has often made fine-tuning available for smaller, cheaper model variants, because they benefit most and are cheapest to serve. If your target model is not fine-tunable, alternatives include fine-tuning the most similar supported model, using structured outputs and few-shot prompting with the target model, distilling from a strong model's outputs into a supported smaller one, or fine-tuning an open-weight model you host. How do I fine-tune gpt-oss-20b? gpt-oss-20b is one of OpenAI's open-weight models, so you can download it and fine-tune it yourself with LoRA using Hugging Face Transformers, PEFT and TRL, or optimised tools, on a GPU with enough memory. Also asked as: how to fine tune gpt oss 20b Practical points: Use the model's chat format, its harmony response format, for training examples, matching how it will be prompted. Train LoRA adapters rather than all weights; the model uses a mixture-of-experts design, so follow recipes published for it. Start with a small dataset and short run to confirm loss decreases and outputs improve. Evaluate against the base model on held-out examples, including reasoning-heavy cases. Respect the model's licence, which is permissive, and test safety behaviour after tuning. The larger gpt-oss-120b needs data-centre GPUs for fine-tuning. How do you fine-tune GPT-3.5 Turbo in four steps? The classic four steps are: prepare training data in chat-format JSONL, upload the file, create a fine-tuning job, then use and evaluate the fine-tuned model. GPT-3.5 Turbo is a legacy model, but the same steps apply to current fine-tunable models. Also asked as: how to fine-tune gpt-3.5-turbo in four steps from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI() f = client.files.create(file=open(&quot;train.jsonl&quot;, &quot;rb&quot;), purpose=&quot;fine-tune&quot;) # steps 1-2 job = client.fine_tuning.jobs.create(training_file=f.id, model=&quot;BASE_MODEL_NAME&quot;) # step 3 # step 4: when the job succeeds, call the model with job.fine_tuned_model Replace the base model name with a currently supported one from the documentation. Validate your JSONL before uploading, keep a test set aside, and compare the tuned model with the base on it before switching production traffic.

# What three hackathon wins and one loss taught me: KrishGyan at IIT Roorkee, BrandHive at CSJMU, Annapurna at MeetKats, and STROT
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-hackathon-wins-and-losses-taught-me/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What did winning three hackathons actually teach?

**That the prize goes to the team that solves a small problem completely and shows it working, not to the team with the biggest idea. Changethon 2025 at IIT Roorkee, Product Genesis at Vividhotsava 2025 at CSJMU, and BYTEBATTLE by MeetKats were three different rooms, three different problems and three first prizes with the same shape: a named user, one flow demonstrated end to end, a rehearsed pitch, a team of three. The fourth room, STROT, taught the same lesson from the other side.**


These stories exist in longer form on the portfolio, one per event [1][2][3][4]. This page is the version I tell when a college club asks what actually mattered, with the highlight reel removed.

> I have won with less code than the teams I beat, and lost with more. The code was never the variable.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## Changethon 2025, IIT Roorkee: KrishGyan

**The problem statement was social impact; the audience we chose was farmers who do not read or type. KrishGyan let a farmer send a voice note on WhatsApp in their own language and get spoken advice back on pests, crop health and weather, drawing on AI-powered agricultural data. It won first prize at the National Social Summit's hackathon because the demo was a voice note in and a voice note out, which any judge could follow, and because nobody else in the room had designed for a user who cannot read [1].**



The lesson: find the constraint the other teams will ignore, and design for it. The constraint was literacy and it decided the architecture, voice on WhatsApp, before we wrote a line.

## Product Genesis, Vividhotsava 2025, CSJMU: BrandHive

**A product-building competition rather than a pure code sprint. BrandHive was a platform for small businesses and emerging influencers to grow their organic presence without a marketing budget, bringing three components together in one loop. It won because we showed the whole loop live rather than a slide listing features, and because we pitched to the shopkeeper in the room, not to the judges [2].**


The lesson: judges cannot score a feature list. They can score a loop they watched close. Every pitch since has been built around one complete loop.

## BYTEBATTLE, MeetKats: Annapurna

**Surplus food coordination: hotels and events with leftover meals, NGOs that distribute, volunteers who carry, and a verification layer so impact is real. Four roles, one flow. Annapurna won first prize because a judge could watch one meal move from a kitchen to a shelter through four clear hands, and because roles made the demo legible. It later became a tool people actually used, and its code is public [3][6][7].**


The lesson: clear roles win twice, once in the demo, where each role is a step a judge can follow, and once afterwards, when the same roles become the product's structure. The story of turning it into a real tool is separate [6].

## STROT: the one we did not win

**We built more than any team in the room and explained less. The demo depended on a live API call over venue Wi-Fi, and it failed in front of the judges. The team that won had a simpler product, a seeded demo that ran without a network, and a pitch rehearsed to the second. They deserved it. I have quoted that loss in more talks than any of the wins, because it is where the rules on this page come from [4][8].**



I also placed top three at a hackathon at IIT Kanpur, and there are other rooms where we did not win first that taught smaller versions of the same lessons [5].

## What do the wins have in common?

**A named user with a real friction. One flow demonstrated end to end, in under three minutes. A constraint honoured that others ignored: literacy, budget, timing. A team of three with three roles: builder, interface and data, pitch and problem. Scope cut early, so the last hours went to rehearsal. None of these is about talent, and all of them are decisions a first-year can make at hour one.**




## What did the loss teach that the wins could not?

**How to lose usefully. Congratulate the winners specifically, ask the judges one question about what would have changed the score, write the answer down, and use it at the next event. Post about the loss the same week; students remember honest posts longer than trophy posts. The loss also taught the operational rules I now hand every team I mentor: seed the data, freeze early, rehearse on the presenting machine, keep a backup video. None of the wins would have taught those, because nothing had gone wrong.**


## How did hackathons change what I build and how I judge?

**Every production system I have shipped since carries the hackathon habits: name the user first, build the demo path end to end before features, cut scope, rehearse the release. As a judge, I score the demo I saw and the answers I heard, I brief panels on the four criteria that decided these rooms, and I give each team one specific sentence, because that is what I wished a judge had told us at STROT. As a mentor, the first thing I ask any team is what they will cut.**




## What would I tell a team before their first hackathon?

**Pick the user before the idea. Cut until the demo fits in three minutes. Decide roles tonight. Build the demo path first and the features never, if the path is not done. Freeze two hours before. Rehearse three times where you will present. Then, win or lose, write the story down the same week, because the story is what you keep. The four rooms above are mine; yours start with the next registration.**



## Want these lessons for your team?

**I run pre-hackathon sessions on scoping, demos and pitching, and I judge and mentor at college events and internal Smart India Hackathon rounds, free for student communities.** Email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What is agentic RAG and Graph RAG? Query rewriting, multi-step retrieval, knowledge graphs, and when a plain RAG pipeline is not enough
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-agentic-rag-and-graph-rag/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is agentic RAG?

**Agentic RAG wraps the retrieval pipeline in a decision loop run by the model: decide whether retrieval is needed at all, rewrite or decompose the query, choose which index or tool to search, inspect what came back, and retrieve again or differently if the evidence is weak, before generating. A plain RAG pipeline does one fixed retrieve-then-generate pass [1]; an agentic one lets the model steer, using patterns from ReAct and its descendants [9]. It answers harder, multi-step questions at the cost of more model calls, more latency and more ways to fail.**


RAG.NextUpgrad, the production platform I built, is deliberately not agentic in the full sense: it has one pass with hybrid retrieval, reranking and a confidence gate, and that pass scores above ninety percent recall on the labelled set [15]. This page is about what the agentic and graph layers add, what they cost, and the test I use to decide whether a system needs them. My notes on multi-hop questions and query rewriting are on the portfolio [13][14].

> Every agentic RAG system I have audited that was struggling had a chunking or ranking problem underneath. Fix the pipeline first. Add planning when the pipeline is good and the questions still fail.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## How does agentic RAG differ from a plain RAG pipeline?

**A plain pipeline is a fixed sequence: embed, retrieve, rerank, generate, once. An agentic system inserts model decisions between the stages: a router that picks the retriever, a rewriter that improves the query, a grader that checks whether retrieved passages actually answer the question, and a loop that retries with a different query or source. The decisions are prompts or small classifiers; the loop is a graph with a step limit. Every decision is a place for the model to be right or wrong, and a place to measure.**



## What is query rewriting, and what is HyDE?

**Query rewriting has the model turn the user's question into a better retrieval query: expanding abbreviations, adding likely terms, splitting a compound question into sub-questions, or removing conversational noise. HyDE, hypothetical document embeddings, goes further: the model writes a short hypothetical answer, and that text is embedded and used to search, because an answer-shaped passage is closer in vector space to real answer passages than a short question is [5]. Both are one extra model call and often the biggest agentic-style gain available.**



Query rewriting is the one agentic element I add to almost every system, because conversational follow-ups such as "and for the other plan?" are unretrievable as written [14].

## What are Self-RAG and corrective RAG?

**Self-RAG trains a model to emit reflection tokens that decide whether to retrieve, whether a passage is relevant, whether the generation is supported, and whether it is useful, so retrieval and self-critique happen inside generation [3]. Corrective RAG adds a lightweight evaluator that grades retrieved documents as correct, incorrect or ambiguous and triggers web search or query refinement when retrieval looks wrong [4]. Both formalise the same idea a confidence gate implements more simply: check the evidence before you trust it.**


The confidence gate in RAG.NextUpgrad is the minimal version of this family: it inspects reranker scores and passage agreement and refuses when support is weak, with no extra model call [15]. Start there; graduate to graded loops when the refusal rate on answerable questions is measurably too high.

## What is Graph RAG?

**Graph RAG builds a knowledge graph from the corpus, extracting entities and the relationships between them with a model, clusters the graph into communities, writes a summary for each community, and then retrieves through the graph: by entity for specific questions, by community summary for global ones. Microsoft's Graph RAG paper showed gains on query-focused summarisation, questions such as "what are the main themes across these documents", where chunk retrieval has nothing to retrieve because the answer is not in any single chunk [6][7].**



RAPTOR reaches a similar goal, multi-level retrieval, by recursively clustering and summarising chunks into a tree, without extracting an explicit graph [8]. Both trade index-time cost for the ability to answer questions about the whole.

## When do I actually need agentic RAG or Graph RAG?

**When the plain pipeline is measurably good and specific question types still fail. Multi-hop questions that need two retrievals, "who leads the team that built the tool mentioned in the June report", need interleaved retrieval and reasoning, which IRCoT and agentic loops provide [10]. Global questions about a corpus need Graph RAG or RAPTOR. Questions spanning several systems need a router. Everything else, which is most questions in most products, needs chunking, hybrid search and reranking done well.**




## How do I build an agentic RAG system?

**Model it as a graph with explicit state: nodes for rewrite, retrieve, grade, generate and refuse, edges chosen by the grader's output, a step limit and a token budget. LangGraph is the common framework for this shape [11]; the same loop is a couple of hundred lines without one. Log every decision. Evaluate the agentic system against the plain pipeline on the same labelled set and keep it only where it measurably wins. Anthropic's guidance applies: the simplest architecture that works, and the model's judgement only where it is actually needed [12].**



## What does agentic RAG cost?

**Several model calls per question instead of one, plus latency that users notice, plus a larger failure surface: a rewriter that drifts, a grader that is too strict, a loop that runs to its limit. A rewriter and a grader roughly double cost; a full multi-agent design can multiply it several times. Graph RAG shifts cost to index time, with many model calls to extract entities and write summaries, which repeats when documents change. Budget both before building, and measure whether the gain in recall or answer quality pays for it.**



## What are common mistakes with agentic and Graph RAG?

**Adding an agent loop to a pipeline with bad chunking. No step limit, so a hard question loops until the budget dies. A grader that rejects good passages and triggers endless retries. Graph RAG for a corpus of precise procedures where chunk citations were the requirement. Not logging decisions, so failures cannot be traced. Evaluating the agentic system alone instead of against the plain baseline. Every one of these is avoided by measuring first and adding layers only where the measurement demands them.**



## Agentic RAG interview questions

**Define agentic RAG and Graph RAG and say what each fixes. Explain query rewriting and HyDE. Describe Self-RAG or corrective RAG in a sentence. Give a question a plain pipeline cannot answer and say which layer fixes it. Explain how you would decide whether to add an agentic layer, and how you would measure the result. Describe the cost trade-offs. The strongest answer includes a pipeline you measured and a layer you chose not to add.**




## Where should I start?

**Measure your plain pipeline's recall on twenty labelled questions. Read the misses. If they are conversational follow-ups, add query rewriting. If they are multi-hop, add a retrieval check and one retry. If they are global questions about the corpus, prototype RAPTOR or Graph RAG on a subset and compare. Add nothing you cannot measure.** For a hands-on session on retrieval systems from the notebook to the operator level, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What is an AI agent? Definition, examples, tools, and how to build one free
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-an-ai-agent-2/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

An AI agent is a system in which a language model works towards a goal in a loop: it decides the next step, calls a tool such as search, a database query or code execution, reads the result, and continues until the task is done or it needs a person. That loop is what separates an agent from a chatbot that only replies. This page defines agents with examples, separates agents from agentic AI, explains tools, skills and harnesses, and shows how to build one for free and which frameworks and builders to consider. What is an AI agent? An AI agent is software that uses an AI model to choose and take actions towards a goal, observing the results of each action before deciding the next. It typically has a model, instructions, a set of tools, memory of what it has done, and a loop that runs until the goal is reached. Also asked as: what is ai agent definition · what is ai agent vs agentic ai The key word is decide. In a fixed workflow, the developer writes every step. In an agent, the model chooses which tool to call and with what inputs, based on the situation. That flexibility handles messy, varied tasks, such as researching a question or fixing a failing test, but it also makes agents less predictable. Good agents limit that freedom with clear instructions, a small set of well-described tools, step limits and approval for risky actions. What is an AI agent, explained with an example? Take a support agent for a college's admissions office. A student asks "has my application fee been received, and when is the counselling date?". The agent looks up the application in the database, checks the payment status, searches the admissions notice for dates, and replies with both answers and links. Also asked as: what is ai agent explain with example Step by step: The model reads the question and decides it needs two lookups. It calls get_application(student_id) and reads the payment status. It calls search_notices("counselling date") and reads the passage. It writes the answer, citing the notice. If the record is missing, it hands over to a staff member instead of guessing. A chatbot would answer from general knowledge; the agent acts on real systems. What is the difference between an AI agent and agentic AI? Agentic AI is the broad approach of giving AI systems autonomy to plan and act towards goals. An AI agent is a specific system built that way. Agentic describes the quality; an agent is the thing. In practice, "agentic" also describes a spectrum. A chatbot with search that decides when to search is slightly agentic. A coding agent that plans a change, edits ten files, runs tests and fixes failures is highly agentic. Many production systems sit in between: mostly fixed workflows with a few agentic steps where judgement helps. That middle ground is often the best design, because each added degree of autonomy adds failure modes. Choose the least autonomy that solves the problem. What are AI agent tools? Tools are functions an agent can call: search the web, query a database, read a file, run code, send an email, call an API. Each tool has a name, a description and an input schema, and the model chooses tools based on those descriptions. A tool definition looks like a function signature with documentation: search_orders(customer_email: string), "Find a customer's recent orders; use when the user asks about an order". The quality of descriptions decides how well the agent picks tools, so write them as you would for a new teammate. Tools should validate inputs, return compact results and fail with clear error messages the model can act on. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for packaging tools so many agents and apps can use them. What are AI agent skills? Skills are packaged know-how an agent loads when a task needs it: instructions, examples, templates and sometimes scripts for a specific job, such as creating a report in your company format or following your testing procedure. The agent first sees only a short description of each skill and loads the full contents when relevant, which keeps its context small even with many skills available. That differs from tools, which are actions it can take, and from the system prompt, which is always loaded. Skills are supported in Claude's apps and API, Claude Code and other agent environments. Write a skill like a good checklist for a colleague: when to use it, the exact steps, and an example of the expected output. What is an AI agent harness? The harness is the code around the model that turns it into an agent: it runs the loop, sends the model its instructions and context, executes the tools it asks for, enforces limits and permissions, manages memory and logs everything. Also asked as: what is ai agent harness The model only produces text, including tool requests; the harness does the actual work. A good harness handles errors and retries, caps the number of steps and cost, asks a person before risky actions, trims or summarises context as it grows, and records every step for debugging. Claude Code and other coding agents are harnesses around models; frameworks such as LangGraph and agent SDKs help you build your own. Much of an agent's reliability comes from its harness, not the model. Can I build an AI agent? Yes. If you can write basic Python and call an API, you can build a simple agent in an afternoon: a model API, two or three tools as Python functions, and a loop that runs the model's tool calls until it gives a final answer. Also asked as: can i build ai agent A sensible first project is an agent that answers questions about your own documents and can look up one live data source, such as a timetable or an API. Log every step so you can see how it decides. Then add evaluation: twenty test questions with expected answers, run after every change. Agents look impressive in demos and fail in subtle ways in real use; the evaluation set is how you find and fix those failures. How do I make an AI agent for free? Use a free-tier model API, such as Google's Gemini API through AI Studio, or a local model with Ollama, and write a small agent loop in Python with an open-source framework or none at all. Also asked as: how to make ai agent for free A minimal agent with free tools: Model: Gemini's free tier, or a local model such as a Llama or Qwen model in Ollama. Tools: plain Python functions, such as a calculator, a search over your notes, a weather API with a free key. Loop: send the conversation and tool definitions, run any tool calls, append results, repeat with a step limit. Interface: a terminal, or Streamlit for a quick web page. Hosting: run locally, or a free tier on Hugging Face Spaces. Keep API keys in environment variables and never let a free agent take irreversible actions without confirmation. What is the best AI agent framework? There is no single best one. LangGraph suits complex, stateful workflows with explicit control; the OpenAI Agents SDK and the Claude Agent SDK are lightweight and close to their providers' models; CrewAI and AutoGen focus on multi-agent setups; LlamaIndex suits document-heavy agents. Choose by your needs: control and observability for production, provider flexibility if you may switch models, and a community large enough to find answers. Many experienced builders start with no framework at all, a plain loop over the model's tool-calling API, because it is easier to debug and understand. Add a framework when you need what it offers, such as persistence, branching or human-in-the-loop steps, not before. What is the best AI agent builder? For no-code and low-code agents, Microsoft Copilot Studio suits Microsoft 365 organisations, OpenAI's agent tools and custom GPTs suit ChatGPT users, and workflow tools such as n8n and Zapier offer agent steps for automations. For developers, code frameworks give more control. Pick by where the agent will live and what it must reach: Teams and SharePoint point to Copilot Studio; Google Workspace points to Google's agent tools; many SaaS integrations point to n8n or Zapier; custom products point to code. Whatever you choose, judge it on how well you can test, monitor and limit the agent, not on how quickly the demo appears. The builder that makes failures visible is the better one.

# What is an AI agent? Agentic AI explained: tools, function calling, MCP, frameworks, and why most agents fail
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-an-ai-agent/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is an AI agent?

**An AI agent is a language model running in a loop with tools. Given a goal, the model decides on an action, your code executes it, a search, a database query, an API call, a file edit, the result is fed back, and the model decides the next action, until it judges the goal met or a stopping rule fires. The model supplies judgement; the tools supply reach; the loop supplies persistence. Without the loop it is a chatbot; without tools it is a planner that cannot act.**


The pattern was named ReAct by Yao et al., reasoning and acting interleaved, with the model writing a thought, an action and reading an observation on each turn [1]. Toolformer showed models could learn when to call tools [2], Reflexion added self-critique between attempts [3], and the survey by Wang et al. maps the many variants that followed [4]. Anthropic's practitioner guide distinguishes fixed workflows, where code decides the steps, from true agents, where the model does, and argues for the simplest design that works [5].

I ship both kinds. My publishing pipeline is a workflow: code decides the order, models write the text. The coding assistant that helped build it is an agent: it reads, edits and runs tests until the tests pass. The distinction is the first thing to get right, because a workflow is cheaper, more predictable and easier to test, and most "agent" products are workflows that would be better admitted as such.

> Every agent I have built started as a workflow that needed one decision I could not write as an if-statement. That decision is where the model belongs. Everywhere else, write code.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What is agentic AI, and how is it different from generative AI?

**Generative AI produces content on request: text, images, code, audio. Agentic AI uses a generative model to pursue a goal through actions over multiple steps, using tools and reacting to results. The same model can do both; the difference is the harness around it. A chat window is generative. A system that reads your inbox, drafts replies, checks your calendar and books the meeting is agentic.**



## How do AI agents work?

**Each turn, the agent's context holds the goal, the tool definitions, the history of previous actions and their results. The model reads it and outputs either a final answer or a tool call: the tool's name and arguments as structured data. Your code validates the call, runs the tool, appends the result to the context, and calls the model again. Guardrails sit around the loop: a maximum number of steps, a budget, permissions per tool, and confirmation for irreversible actions.**



The whole loop is under a hundred lines in any language. The frameworks add memory management, retries, streaming, tracing and multi-agent orchestration on top; none of that changes the loop.

## What is tool calling or function calling?

**Tool calling, also called function calling, is the API feature that lets a model request an action in a machine-readable form instead of free text. You describe each tool with a name, a description and a JSON schema for its arguments. When the model decides a tool is needed it returns a call object with the tool name and arguments; your code runs the function and returns the result as a tool message. It is what makes agents reliable enough to build on, because you never parse prose to find the action.**


The shape, in the form both major providers use [7][8]:

```json
{
  "name": "search_docs",
  "description": "Search the company knowledge base. Use for any question about policies or products.",
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "query": {"type": "string", "description": "What to search for, in the user's words"},
      "top_k": {"type": "integer", "default": 5}
    },
    "required": ["query"]
  }
}
```

Two rules that decide whether the model picks the right tool: the description says when to use it, not just what it does, and the tools do not overlap. Ten tools with fuzzy boundaries produce worse agents than three tools with sharp ones.

## What is MCP, the Model Context Protocol?

**The Model Context Protocol is an open standard for exposing tools, data sources and prompt templates to AI applications through a common interface, so that a tool server written once can be used by any client that speaks the protocol, a coding assistant, a chat app, an agent framework, without a custom integration each time [6]. An MCP server declares its tools with schemas; the client lists them, the model calls them, the server executes. It turns "integrate this API with this agent" into "run this server".**


I run a public MCP server at tools.scult.in that exposes the same free tools and prompt library the website offers, so an agent can call the schema generator or pull a stamped prompt with one line of configuration and no signup [12]. Building it taught me the practical value of the protocol: the client side is finished by other people, so a server is the whole product.


## How do I build an AI agent from scratch?

**Pick one task with a verifiable outcome, define one to three tools with tight descriptions and schemas, write the loop with a step limit and a budget, log every call, and run it on twenty real cases before adding anything. Only then decide whether it needs memory, more tools, a planner or a second agent. Most successful agents in production have fewer than five tools and a very clear stopping condition.**


The loop, in plain Python against a tool-calling API:

```python
def run_agent(goal: str, tools: dict, max_steps: int = 12) -> str:
    history = [{"role": "user", "content": goal}]
    for step in range(max_steps):
        reply = llm(history, tools=[t.schema for t in tools.values()])
        if reply.tool_calls is None:
            return reply.text                      # final answer
        for call in reply.tool_calls:
            tool = tools[call.name]
            if tool.needs_confirmation and not confirm(call):
                return "Stopped: action needs approval"
            result = tool.run(**call.arguments)    # validated by the schema
            history.append(tool_result(call.id, result))
            log(step, call, result)
    return "Stopped: step limit reached"
```

Everything a framework gives you is a refinement of those lines. Write them once yourself; you will debug every framework faster afterwards.


### Which AI agent framework should I use?

**For a first agent, none: the loop above and your provider's SDK. When you need branching, retries, persistence and human-in-the-loop steps, LangGraph models the agent as a graph with explicit state and is the most widely used [9]. Provider SDKs from Anthropic and OpenAI now include agent loops and tool handling. For non-developers, n8n and similar automation tools wire models and APIs visually [11]. Choose by how much control you need over state and failure, not by popularity.**


## What are multi-agent systems?

**A multi-agent system splits a task across several agents with different tools or roles, a researcher, a writer, a reviewer, coordinated by a planner or a fixed handoff. It helps when the task decomposes cleanly and each part needs a different context, and it hurts when the coordination overhead, cost and failure surface outgrow the benefit. Start with one agent; move to several only when one agent's context or tool set becomes unmanageable.**


Anthropic's guide makes the same recommendation from a larger sample of deployments than I have: composable patterns first, prompt chaining, routing, parallelisation, orchestrator-workers, and autonomous agents only for open-ended problems where the model's judgement is needed at every step [5].

## Why do AI agents fail?

**Agents fail for predictable reasons: the goal was vague, so the model optimised the wrong thing; too many overlapping tools, so it picked badly; no stopping rule, so it looped; a tool returned an error the model could not interpret; the context filled with history and it forgot the goal; it took an irreversible action nobody confirmed; or a document it read contained instructions and it followed them. Almost all of these are design failures, fixed in the harness rather than the model.**



OWASP lists excessive agency and prompt injection among the top risks for LLM applications, and agents are where both bite hardest, because an injected instruction can now cause an action, not just a bad sentence [10].

## What is agent memory?

**Agent memory is whatever the agent can consult beyond the current context: the conversation so far, a scratchpad of notes it writes to itself, a vector store of past interactions or documents it can retrieve from, and structured facts in a database. Short-term memory is the context window; long-term memory is retrieval. Most agents need less memory than their builders assume and more discipline about what to forget.**


## Are AI agents worth learning, and what jobs use them?

**Yes. Agents are how language models get connected to real systems, and every AI engineering role I see in 2026 expects familiarity with tool calling, at least one orchestration pattern and the safety basics. Learn them by building one that does a job you actually have, connect it to a real API, and measure how often it finishes the task. That measured number, on a public repository, is worth more than any course certificate.**


I will not quote an "agentic AI engineer salary" because I have no measured source for one; job posts in India in 2026 mostly list it under AI engineer or GenAI engineer roles, and pay tracks those roles in the same city and company tier.



## What are common AI agent interview questions?

**Explain the agent loop and where the model's judgement is actually needed. Compare a workflow with an agent and say when you would choose each. Describe how tool calling works and how you write a tool description. Explain how you would stop an agent from taking a harmful action, and how you would measure whether it works. Describe a failure you debugged. If you have built even one agent with a real tool, you can answer all five.**



## Where can I try an agent for free?

**Point any MCP-capable client at the server at tools.scult.in and you have an agent with a working tool set in a minute, no signup [12].** Then build your own with one tool. If your college or hackathon wants a hands-on session on agents, tool calling and MCP, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What is an AI hackathon? Rules, project ideas and tools, from a winner
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-an-ai-hackathon/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

An AI hackathon is a time-boxed competition, usually 24 to 48 hours, where teams build a working prototype that uses artificial intelligence to solve a problem, then present it to judges. The theme might be generative AI, machine learning or agents, and the best projects pair a real user problem with a demo that works. I have won three hackathon first prizes and judged and mentored others, so this page draws on both sides of the table: what each kind of AI hackathon is, whether AI tools are allowed, the projects and tools that win, and the big hackathons to aim for. What is an AI hackathon? An AI hackathon is an event where teams of two to five people build, in a fixed time, a prototype that uses AI to solve a problem, and pitch it with a live demo. Judges score the problem, the solution, technical depth and the presentation. Also asked as: what is ai hackathon · what is gen ai hackathon Hackathons run in colleges, at companies and online, often with themes such as healthcare, agriculture, education or sustainability. You usually get a problem statement or an open theme, mentors to unblock you, and food and sleep in short supply. The output is not a finished product; it is a convincing proof that an idea works. KrishGyan, which won Changethon 2025 at IIT Roorkee, was exactly that: farming advice delivered in the farmer's own voice and language over WhatsApp, demonstrated live. What is a GenAI hackathon? A GenAI hackathon focuses on generative AI: projects built with large language models, image, audio or video generation. Typical builds are chat assistants over documents, content tools, voice interfaces and copilots for a specific job. Organisers often provide API credits from model providers and judge how well teams go beyond a plain chatbot. Strong GenAI projects ground the model in real data with retrieval, use structured outputs so results can drive actions, and handle failure honestly, for example by refusing to answer when evidence is weak. Judges have seen many "chat with your PDF" demos, so a clear user, a specific workflow and a measurable result stand out more than the model you used. What is an AI/ML hackathon? An AI/ML hackathon covers both generative AI and classic machine learning: prediction, classification, recommendation, computer vision and analytics. Some are data challenges where you train models on a provided dataset and are scored on accuracy. Also asked as: what is ai ml hackathon There are two formats. In build hackathons, you create an application and the model is one part of it. In data challenges, closer to Kaggle competitions, a leaderboard ranks your predictions on hidden test data. For build formats, use pre-trained models and focus on the product. For data challenges, invest in clean features, solid validation and a few well-tuned models rather than exotic architectures. Read which format you are entering before the event, because the winning strategies are completely different. What is an agentic AI hackathon? An agentic AI hackathon asks teams to build AI agents: systems that plan and take multi-step actions with tools, such as searching, calling APIs, filling forms or writing code, rather than only answering questions. Also asked as: what is agentic ai hackathon Judges look for agents that complete a real task end to end, show their steps, and stay safe: asking for confirmation before irreversible actions, staying within permissions, and recovering from errors. Good agent projects keep scope narrow, for example "an agent that books a lab slot and emails the confirmation", and give the agent a few well-described tools. Standards such as the Model Context Protocol make it quicker to connect tools. Log every step the agent takes; a visible trace makes the demo more convincing and helps you debug at 3 a.m. Is AI allowed in hackathons? Usually yes. Most hackathons now allow AI coding assistants and AI APIs, but some restrict pre-written code, require code written during the event, or ban specific tools. Always read the rules and ask organisers when unsure. Even where AI is allowed, judges test understanding. Expect questions such as "why did you choose this approach?" or "what happens if the model returns an empty answer?". As a judge, I trust teams that can explain their architecture and trade-offs, and I am wary of polished demos the team cannot explain. Use AI tools to move faster, keep a Git history that shows your work during the event, and disclose generated assets where the rules ask for it. What are the best AI hackathon projects? The best AI hackathon projects solve a specific problem for a specific person, use AI where it adds something people cannot easily do, and work live in front of judges. Social impact and a clear user story score well. Patterns that win: Voice and local language access: like KrishGyan, AI that serves people who cannot use English apps. Coordination problems: like Annapurna, which won BYTEBATTLE by matching surplus food with people who need it. Document automation: extracting fields from forms, invoices or certificates with validation. Grounded assistants: answers from a trusted source, with citations, for a college, clinic or government scheme. Accessibility: tools for people with visual, hearing or learning difficulties. Pick one user, one painful task and one wow moment in the demo. What are the best AI tools for a hackathon? Use hosted model APIs, a quick front end, a simple backend and free deployment. Training models during a hackathon rarely pays off; integrating good ones well does. Also asked as: best ai tools for hackathon A practical stack: Models: an API from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google or Groq for fast inference; open models through Hugging Face when needed. Speech: speech-to-text and text-to-speech APIs for voice features. Retrieval: a small vector index or pgvector for document Q&amp;A. Backend: FastAPI or Node.js. Front end: Next.js, React or Streamlit for the fastest UI. Deployment: free tiers on Vercel, Render or Hugging Face Spaces. Coding help: an AI coding assistant, used with care. Set up keys, a repository and a deployed "hello world" before the clock starts if the rules allow it. What do you see at an AI hackathon? You see teams split between ambitious ideas and working demos, last-minute integration problems, and a final hour where most of the outcome is decided by who has a stable demo and a clear story. Also asked as: what i saw at an ai hackathon From the judge's table, the patterns repeat. Many teams build similar chatbots; the ones that stand out have spoken to a real user, narrowed the problem and show one feature working end to end. Live demos fail more often from network and API key problems than from bad ideas, so the winners rehearse and keep a recorded backup. Mentors are underused: ten minutes with one early can save hours. And the best teams stop adding features a few hours before the end to polish the demo and the pitch. What is India's biggest AI hackathon? There is no single official title, but Smart India Hackathon, run with the Ministry of Education's Innovation Cell, is among the largest hackathons in India, and many of its problem statements involve AI and machine learning. Beyond it, large AI-themed hackathons in India are run by technology companies, cloud providers and startups, and listed on platforms such as Devfolio and Unstop, along with college tech festivals at IITs, NITs and other institutes. Sizes and themes change every year, so check the current season's listings. For a student, the "biggest" hackathon matters less than a well-run one in your area with good mentors, where you can finish a project and meet people. What is a global AI hackathon? A global AI hackathon is an online or multi-city event open to participants from many countries, often run by AI companies, cloud providers or communities, with remote judging and prizes such as cash, credits or incubation support. Also asked as: what is global ai hackathon They are a good option if there are few events near you: you can join from anywhere, team up with people from other countries and get feedback from international judges. The trade-offs are time zones, less mentoring and a very large number of submissions, so a short, sharp demo video and a clear README matter more than at in-person events. Find them on Devfolio, Devpost, Major League Hacking and the developer pages of AI companies. Treat each one as a deadline to ship a portfolio project.
