# What is ChatGPT Codex? How it works, limits, and when to use it
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-chatgpt-codex/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

ChatGPT Codex is OpenAI's software engineering agent. Unlike chatting about code, Codex works on your actual repository: it reads the code, edits files, runs commands and tests in a sandbox, and gives you a diff or pull request to review. You can use it from ChatGPT in the browser, from the Codex CLI in your terminal, or from an IDE extension. This page explains how it works, which models power it, when to use it instead of ChatGPT, how memory and limits differ, which plans include it, and how to start. What is ChatGPT Codex? Codex is OpenAI's coding agent. You give it a task such as "fix the failing date parser test", and it works in a copy of your repository, makes the change, runs the tests and presents the result for review. It is available in several places that share one account: the Codex section of ChatGPT, which runs tasks in OpenAI's cloud on a connected GitHub repository; the open-source Codex CLI, which runs on your own machine; and extensions for editors such as VS Code. Cloud tasks can run in parallel, so you can hand off several small tasks and review them later. The name Codex was first used in 2021 for an earlier code model; today it refers to the agent and its coding-tuned models. How does ChatGPT Codex work? Codex runs a loop: it reads your request and the relevant code, plans the change, edits files, runs commands such as tests and linters, reads the results and repeats until the task is done or it needs your input. For cloud tasks, Codex starts a sandboxed container with your repository, installs dependencies using setup steps you can configure, and works inside it, so it cannot touch your machine. When finished, it shows the diff, a summary and the commands it ran, and you can open a pull request. With the CLI it works in your local folder, and you choose how much freedom it has, from asking before every command to working automatically inside the project. Instructions in an AGENTS.md file at the repository root tell it how to build, test and style the code. What are the GPT Codex models? Codex models are versions of OpenAI's GPT models tuned for software engineering: writing code, following repository conventions, running tests and working through long agentic tasks. The Codex agent uses them by default. Also asked as: what are gpt codex models The first Codex model, released in 2021 and described in OpenAI's paper on evaluating code models, powered the original GitHub Copilot and was later retired. The current generation is built on OpenAI's GPT-5 family, with coding-specialised variants such as GPT-5-Codex, and newer versions arrive regularly. You can usually choose the model and reasoning level in the Codex settings or CLI: higher reasoning is slower but better for hard changes. Developers can also call coding models through the OpenAI API. Check OpenAI's model list for the current names. When should I use ChatGPT vs Codex? Use ChatGPT to learn, explain, brainstorm and design. Use Codex when you want a change made in a real codebase, tested and delivered as a diff or pull request. Also asked as: when to use chatgpt vs codex A simple rule: ChatGPT: "Explain how JWT authentication works", "compare FastAPI and Flask for my project", "review this function I pasted". Codex: "Add JWT authentication to this FastAPI app with tests", "upgrade the project to the new library version and fix the breaking changes". ChatGPT sees only what you paste, so its code suggestions do not know your project structure. Codex sees the whole repository and can run it, which makes its changes far more likely to work. Many developers use both: design in ChatGPT, implement with Codex. Should I use Codex or ChatGPT for work? For engineering work in a team repository, Codex is the better fit because it works on the code, follows the repository's rules and produces reviewable pull requests. ChatGPT is better for documents, analysis, emails and thinking through problems. Also asked as: when to use codex vcs chatgpt work On business and enterprise plans, admins control which repositories Codex can access and how its environments are configured, which matters for company code. Keep the usual review process: Codex output goes through code review and continuous integration like any teammate's work. Never paste secrets into ChatGPT or Codex prompts, and keep API keys in your environment configuration. If your employer restricts AI tools on its code, follow that policy; using a personal account on company code is a common way to break it. Do ChatGPT and Codex share memory? No. Codex does not use ChatGPT's memory of your past conversations. It learns about your project from the repository itself and from instructions you write, usually in an AGENTS.md file. This is deliberate. A coding agent should behave the same for everyone working on a repository, so project knowledge belongs in files that are versioned with the code, not in one person's chat history. A good AGENTS.md covers how to install dependencies, run tests and lint, the project's structure, coding conventions, and things to avoid. You can add more specific files in subfolders for parts of a large project. Your account settings, such as connected repositories, are shared across ChatGPT and Codex, but conversation memory is not. Are ChatGPT and Codex limits different? Yes. Codex has its own usage limits, separate from ChatGPT message limits, and they vary by plan. Local CLI use and cloud tasks are counted, and limits reset over rolling time windows. Heavier tasks and higher reasoning levels use more of the allowance than small ones, so a long refactor counts for more than a one-line fix. OpenAI publishes the current limits for each plan in its help centre, and they have changed several times since launch. If you hit limits often, split work into smaller tasks, choose a lower reasoning level for routine changes, and avoid asking Codex to explore a huge repository without pointing it at the right folder. Developers can also run the CLI with an API key and pay per use instead. Does ChatGPT Plus give unlimited use of Codex? No. ChatGPT Plus includes Codex with usage limits, and higher plans such as Pro raise them substantially. No plan gives truly unlimited Codex use. For a student or solo developer, Plus limits are usually enough for regular coding sessions if tasks are well scoped. If you hit the limit, you wait for the window to reset, upgrade, or switch to API-key usage in the CLI. Treat any claim of "unlimited" access through a third-party site as a red flag: shared or resold accounts break OpenAI's terms and can expose your code. Check the plan comparison page for the current inclusion and limits before you decide. Does ChatGPT Go have Codex? ChatGPT Go is OpenAI's lower-cost plan, offered first in India and then in other countries. Its features differ from Plus, and whether Codex is included, and with what limits, depends on OpenAI's current plan details. Codex has been included in Plus and higher individual plans and in business plans. Plan features change, so check OpenAI's pricing page or help centre for what Go includes in your country today rather than relying on a forum post. If Go does not include enough Codex use for you, the alternatives are the Codex CLI with an API key, paying per use, or other coding agents with free tiers. For learning to code, the chat itself on any plan is already a strong tutor. Is there a ChatGPT Codex tutorial? Yes. OpenAI's Codex documentation and the Codex CLI repository have setup guides. The fastest way to learn is one small task in a repository with tests, done end to end. Also asked as: tutorial chatgpt codex A first session with the CLI: npm install -g @openai/codex cd my-project codex Sign in with your ChatGPT account, then: Ask "explain the structure of this project and how to run the tests". Add an AGENTS.md with the test command and coding rules. Give a narrow task: "add input validation to the signup route and a test for it". Approve commands one by one, read the diff, run the tests yourself. Commit, then try a cloud task from ChatGPT on the same repository.

# What is Chroma DB? How it works, install, run locally, and is it open source
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-chroma-db/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

Chroma DB is an open-source vector database built for AI applications. It stores text chunks, their embeddings and metadata, and finds the most similar items to a query, which makes it a popular retrieval layer for RAG chatbots and semantic search. It runs inside a Python process, as a standalone server, or as a hosted service. This page covers why to use it, how it works and what it is built on, whether it is local and open source, who makes it, and how to install, run and delete it. What is Chroma DB? Chroma DB is a vector database, sometimes called an embedding database, that lets applications store embeddings and search them by similarity. It is designed to be simple for developers: a few lines of Python give you a working semantic search. Also asked as: how to run chroma db · how to delete chroma db Data lives in collections, each holding documents, their embeddings, metadata and IDs. Chroma can compute embeddings with a built-in or configured embedding function, or accept embeddings you compute yourself. Queries return the nearest items with their distances, optionally filtered by metadata, such as subject or date. Chroma integrates with LangChain, LlamaIndex and other frameworks, which is why it appears in many RAG tutorials. Why use Chroma DB? Use Chroma when you want a fast, free, easy way to add semantic search or RAG to a project, especially in Python. It needs no separate infrastructure to start, and the same code can later point to a Chroma server or hosted service. It suits prototypes, student projects, internal tools and small to medium production apps. Reasons to choose something else: you already run PostgreSQL and prefer one database, so pgvector is simpler; you need a managed service at very large scale; or you need strong keyword search alongside vectors, where engines with built-in BM25 help. Whichever store you choose, retrieval quality depends more on chunking, hybrid search and reranking than on the database. How does Chroma DB work? When you add documents, Chroma stores each document's text, metadata and embedding, and adds the embedding to an approximate nearest-neighbour index. When you query, it embeds the query with the same function and returns the closest items. The search index uses HNSW, a graph-based method that finds near neighbours quickly without comparing every vector. Metadata filters narrow results before or during search. Distances are computed with a configurable metric such as cosine or L2; use the one recommended for your embedding model. Because results are approximate, very large collections may need tuning of index parameters, and measuring recall on real queries tells you whether results are good enough. What is Chroma DB built on? Chroma's core has been rewritten in Rust in recent versions, with Python and JavaScript clients. In local mode it stores data on disk, using SQLite for metadata and records, and an HNSW index for vector search. The architecture supports three ways of running: embedded in your process for simplicity, a client-server mode where a Chroma server holds the data and many clients connect, and a distributed cloud service run by the company. For most users, the details matter only for performance tuning and deployment; the API stays the same. Check the documentation for the current architecture, as the project has evolved quickly. Is Chroma DB local? It can be. Chroma can run entirely on your machine, either in memory or persisted to a local folder, with no data leaving your computer. It can also run as a server on your own infrastructure, or be used as a hosted cloud service. Local mode is ideal for development, privacy-sensitive data and offline work: use chromadb.PersistentClient(path="./store") to save data between runs. Note that embedding functions may still call external APIs if you configure a hosted embedding model; for a fully local setup, use a local embedding model, for example through sentence-transformers or Ollama. For apps with several processes or servers, run Chroma as a server so all instances share one database. Is Chroma DB open source? Yes. Chroma is open source under the Apache 2.0 licence, with its code on GitHub. You can use it in personal and commercial projects, self-host it and modify it. The company behind it also offers a hosted cloud product with its own terms and pricing, while the open-source database remains free to self-host. Because it is open, you can inspect how indexing and querying work, which helps when debugging retrieval quality or performance. Check the repository's releases and changelog before upgrading, since fast-moving projects sometimes change storage formats or APIs between versions. Who owns Chroma DB? Chroma DB is developed by Chroma, a company founded in 2022 that builds the open-source database and a hosted cloud service. The open-source code is licensed under Apache 2.0, so the community can use and contribute to it. For users, ownership matters mainly for support and longevity: the open-source licence means your ability to use the database does not depend on buying anything, while the company funds ongoing development. If you use the hosted service, its terms, data location and pricing apply. For critical systems, keep your source documents and a way to rebuild the index, so you are never locked into one vector store. How do I install Chroma DB? Install the Python package with pip, then import it. For a JavaScript project, install the JavaScript client and run a Chroma server. Also asked as: how to install chroma db pip install chromadb import chromadb client = chromadb.PersistentClient(path=&quot;./chroma_store&quot;) col = client.get_or_create_collection(&quot;docs&quot;) col.upsert(ids=[&quot;a1&quot;], documents=[&quot;Chroma stores embeddings for semantic search.&quot;]) print(col.query(query_texts=[&quot;what does chroma store?&quot;], n_results=1)[&quot;documents&quot;]) Use a virtual environment, and pin the version in requirements.txt. If installation fails on an older system or unusual CPU, check the troubleshooting section of the documentation for build requirements. How do I run Chroma DB as a server? Use the Chroma command-line tool to start a server with a data folder, or run the official Docker image, then connect from your app with an HTTP client. chroma run --path ./chroma_data # starts a local server import chromadb client = chromadb.HttpClient(host=&quot;localhost&quot;, port=8000) Server mode lets several app instances, or apps in different languages, share one database. In Docker, mount a volume for the data directory so it persists across restarts. Do not expose the server to the internet without authentication; put it on a private network or behind an authenticated proxy, and back up the data directory. How do I delete a Chroma DB collection or database? Delete a collection with client.delete_collection("name"), delete specific items with collection.delete(ids=[...]) or a metadata filter, and remove the whole local database by deleting its persistence folder while no process is using it. client.delete_collection(&quot;docs&quot;) # whole collection col.delete(where={&quot;source&quot;: &quot;old_policy.pdf&quot;}) # items by metadata Before deleting, make sure you can rebuild from source documents. In tests, use a temporary folder or an in-memory client so each test starts clean. If you change the embedding model, deleting and rebuilding the collection is required, since old and new vectors are not comparable.

# What is chunking in RAG? Chunk size, overlap, structure-aware splitting and the experiments that actually decide retrieval quality
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-chunking-in-rag/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is chunking in RAG?

**Chunking is splitting documents into passages, chunks, that are embedded and indexed individually so retrieval can return the piece of a document relevant to a question rather than the whole document. Every later stage of a RAG system, embedding, retrieval, reranking, generation, can only choose among the chunks you created, so chunking sets the ceiling on answer quality. A chunk that lost its context cannot be recovered by a better model.**


Most RAG quality problems I have debugged were chunking problems in disguise. The model looked like it was hallucinating; the retriever was handing it half a table, or a paragraph whose subject lived in the previous chunk. Barnett et al. list missing content and wrongly ranked passages among the seven failure points of RAG systems, and both usually trace back to how documents were split [3].

> Before you tune prompts or switch models, print the chunks your retriever returned. Nine times out of ten, the bug is sitting right there in plain text.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour, from building RAG.NextUpgrad</cite>

## Why does chunking matter so much?

**Three reasons. Embeddings represent one meaning per vector, so a chunk mixing several topics produces a blurred vector that matches nothing well. Retrieval returns whole chunks, so a chunk with the answer buried in unrelated text wastes the model's context and attention, and models attend poorly to the middle of long contexts [4]. And chunks are the unit of citation, so a chunk without its heading or page cannot be pointed at. Good chunks are precise, self-contained and traceable.**


## What are the chunking strategies?

**Fixed-size chunking splits every N tokens with an overlap and ignores structure; it is a baseline, not a strategy. Recursive splitting tries paragraph, then sentence, then word boundaries to hit a size. Structure-aware chunking splits on the document's own units, headings, paragraphs, list items, table rows, code blocks, and keeps them whole. Semantic chunking groups sentences by embedding similarity. Parent-child chunking indexes small chunks for precise retrieval but returns their larger parent for context. Most production systems use structure-aware splitting with a size cap and parent-child retrieval.**



LangChain and LlamaIndex ship implementations of each [7][8]; Unstructured partitions PDFs, Word files and HTML into typed elements you can chunk structurally [9]. The survey by Gao et al. covers these and the research variants [2].

## What is the best chunk size for RAG?

**Whatever size lets a chunk answer a realistic user question on its own, and that differs by corpus. Policy documents and manuals often work at a few hundred tokens; API references at one function signature plus its description; legal clauses at the clause; support tickets at the ticket. Anyone quoting one number without asking about your documents is guessing. Pick three candidate sizes, index each, run twenty real questions, measure recall at k, and keep the winner.**



My own experiments on this, with the numbers for the corpora I tested, are written up separately [12]. The pattern that repeated: smaller chunks retrieve more precisely but need a parent or a heading to be understood; larger chunks are understood alone but retrieve less precisely. Parent-child gets both.

## How much overlap should chunks have?

**Small: enough to catch a sentence that straddles a boundary, roughly ten to fifteen percent of the chunk, and none at all when you split on structure that already respects sentence and paragraph ends. Large overlaps duplicate text, inflate the index, and make the reranker see the same passage twice. If you find yourself increasing overlap to fix retrieval, the real problem is where the boundaries fall, and the fix is structure-aware splitting.**


## Should I add context to each chunk?

**Yes. Prepend the document title and the section heading path to every chunk, so a passage that says "the limit is 5 requests per second" is indexed and retrieved as "API Reference, Section 4.2 Rate limits: the limit is 5 requests per second". This single change did more for retrieval accuracy in RAG.NextUpgrad than any embedding model swap [13]. Contextual retrieval goes further by having a model write a short situating sentence for each chunk before embedding, at index-time cost [6].**



## How do I chunk PDFs, tables and code?

**PDFs: extract with layout awareness so columns, headers and footers are handled, then split on headings and paragraphs, keeping page numbers on every chunk; PyMuPDF and Unstructured both expose structure [9][10]. Tables: keep each table whole, or split by row groups while repeating the header row in every chunk, and consider a text summary of the table as an extra chunk. Code: split on functions, classes and files, never mid-function, and include the file path and imports as context. Slide decks: one slide per chunk with the title.**




## What is parent-child or hierarchical chunking?

**Index small chunks for precise matching, but store a pointer from each to a larger parent, the section or the page, and return the parent to the model at generation time. Retrieval is precise because small chunks have sharp embeddings; generation has context because the model reads the whole section. RAPTOR takes the idea further by building a tree of summaries over the corpus and retrieving at multiple levels [5]. For most systems, two levels, child and section, capture most of the benefit.**


## How do I evaluate chunking?

**Directly, at the retrieval stage, before any generation: build a set of real questions each labelled with the passage that answers it, and measure recall at k for your chunking configuration. Then read the misses. Was the answer split across two chunks? Was it retrieved but ranked low because the chunk was diluted? Was the heading lost? Each miss points at a specific chunking change. Generation metrics come later; you cannot generate a correct answer from a chunk that was never retrieved.**



## What are common chunking mistakes?

**Copying a chunk size from a tutorial. Splitting mid-sentence, mid-table or mid-function. Dropping the heading. Chunking a PDF's text in extraction order on a two-column page. Overlap so large that the reranker sees duplicates. No page or source metadata, so citations are impossible. Re-chunking without re-embedding. Never reading the retrieved chunks by eye. Every one of these produces a system that looks like it hallucinates and is actually retrieving garbage.**



## Chunking interview questions

**Explain why chunking matters more than the model. Compare fixed, recursive and structure-aware splitting. Say how you would choose a chunk size and defend the method, not the number. Explain parent-child retrieval. Describe how you would chunk a PDF with tables. Explain what metadata a chunk needs and why. These are stories if you have built a RAG system, definitions if you have not.**



## Where should I start?

**Take one real document set, write twenty questions and mark their answers, and index the corpus three ways: fixed 512 tokens, structure-aware, and structure-aware with headings prepended. Measure recall at 10 for each. The third will win, and you will understand why in a way no article can teach.** My longer guide and the experiment write-up are on the portfolio [11][12]. For a hands-on retrieval session at your college, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What is a context window, and what is context engineering? Token limits, why bigger isn't always better, and deciding what a model actually sees
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-context-window-and-context-engineering/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is a context window?

**A context window is the maximum number of tokens a model can process in a single call, shared across everything that goes in: the system prompt, retrieved documents, the conversation history, and the model's own output. If a request's total token count exceeds the window, either the call fails outright or the oldest content is silently truncated, depending on how the application handles it, which is why token counting is something a serious application tracks explicitly rather than discovers by accident [2][7].**


RAG.NextUpgrad, the platform I run, budgets this explicitly: a fixed slice for the system prompt, a capped slice for retrieved passages, and whatever remains for conversation history, because letting any one of those grow unchecked starves the others.

> A context window is not a bigger brain. It is a bigger desk. What matters is still what you put on it and where.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## Does a bigger context window mean the model understands more?

**Not proportionally. Models with very large context windows can accept far more tokens, but studies on how models actually use long contexts found a real "lost in the middle" effect: performance on information placed in the middle of a long context is measurably worse than the same information placed near the beginning or end [1]. A larger window changes what fits into a call; it does not guarantee the model weighs every part of that content equally well, which is why "needle in a haystack" tests exist specifically to measure this per model and context length [5].**



## Does a huge context window remove the need for RAG?

**No. Even with a context window large enough to hold an entire document collection, sending all of it on every call is slower and more expensive than retrieving the few passages actually relevant to a question, and the lost-in-the-middle effect means precision still matters: a well-retrieved, well-ordered handful of passages regularly outperforms a huge unfiltered dump of text on the same question [1][8]. Long context changes the trade-off, sometimes it is cheaper to skip retrieval for a single small document, but it does not eliminate the case for retrieval at real scale.**



My longer notes on why RAG still matters, and on chunking specifically, are on the RAG explainer and the chunking page [8][9].


## What is context engineering?

**Context engineering is the discipline of deciding exactly what enters a model's context window, in what order, and in what form, as a distinct skill from prompt engineering, which is about how you phrase instructions [6]. It covers what system instructions to include, which retrieved passages to keep and how to order them, how much conversation history to carry forward and how to summarise the rest, and what tool definitions or examples earn a place in an already-constrained budget. Anthropic's framing treats it as engineering a shared, finite resource rather than writing a clever paragraph [6].**



## How do I manage a context budget in a real application?

**Fix an explicit token budget per section before you write a line of code: so many tokens for the system prompt, a capped number for retrieved passages, so many for recent conversation turns, with the rest reserved for the model's own output. Summarise or drop older conversation history rather than letting it grow unbounded. Order retrieved passages by relevance with the most important ones near the start or end, not buried in the middle, given the lost-in-the-middle effect [1]. Count tokens with the provider's actual tokenizer, not a rough word-count estimate, since the two diverge enough to matter near a limit [7].**



## What happens when I exceed the context window?

**Depending on the provider and how your application calls it, the request either fails with an explicit error, or, in poorly built applications, silently truncates the oldest content, which can quietly drop the system prompt or the earliest turns of a conversation without any visible error. Neither is acceptable in production without you choosing it deliberately. Handle this explicitly: check token counts before sending, and truncate or summarise on your own terms rather than letting the provider or a library do it silently.**



## How much does context length affect cost and latency?

**Directly and significantly: nearly every provider bills by total tokens processed, input and output, so a request that sends more context costs more regardless of how much of it the model actually needed, and larger inputs generally take longer to process even before generation begins [3][10]. This is the practical argument for retrieval and careful context budgets even when a model's window could technically hold everything: cost and latency scale with what you send, not with what would have been sufficient.**



## Context window and context engineering interview questions

**Explain what a context window is and what shares its budget. Describe the lost-in-the-middle effect and its practical implication for ordering retrieved content. Explain why a long-context model still benefits from retrieval. Define context engineering and contrast it with prompt engineering. Describe how you would budget tokens across a RAG conversation. The strongest answer names a specific ordering or truncation decision you made and why.**



## Where should I start?

**Count the tokens in your current system prompt, your typical retrieved passages, and a typical conversation history, and see how much of the window each actually uses. Most budgets are more lopsided than people assume.** For a hands-on session on context and prompt engineering for real applications, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What is Copilot AI? Microsoft's assistant explained, and how it compares
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-copilot-ai/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

Copilot AI is Microsoft's generative AI assistant: a chatbot that answers questions, writes, summarises, creates images and helps with tasks across Windows, Edge, Bing, Microsoft 365 and, as GitHub Copilot, code editors. It runs mainly on OpenAI's GPT models with Microsoft's own systems around them. This page covers what it is, who makes it, what it is good for, how agentic it really is, how it compares with ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude, and how GitHub Copilot compares with Cursor for coding. What is Copilot AI? Copilot AI is Microsoft's AI assistant. You type or speak a request, and it answers in natural language, drawing on a large language model and, where useful, live web results from Bing. Microsoft launched it as Bing Chat in 2023 and renamed it Copilot later that year. Today the name covers a family: the consumer Copilot app and website, Copilot in Windows and Edge, Microsoft 365 Copilot inside Word, Excel, Outlook and Teams, GitHub Copilot for programmers, and Copilot Studio for building agents. They share a brand, not a single product, so the answer to "can Copilot do X" depends on which one you mean. For most students, "Copilot" means the free consumer assistant at copilot.microsoft.com or in Windows. Is Copilot an AI tool? Yes. Copilot is an AI tool in the plain sense: software whose core feature is a machine learning model that generates answers, text, images and code in response to your prompts. Also asked as: is copilot ai tool What separates it from a plain chatbot is integration. In Edge it can summarise the page you are reading, in Windows it can work with what is on your screen when you allow it, and in Microsoft 365 it can read the document you have open. That integration is the reason to choose it. If you spend your day in Word, Outlook and Teams, an assistant that already sees those files saves more time than a smarter model in a separate tab. Is Copilot generative AI? Yes. Copilot is generative AI: it produces new text, code and images rather than only classifying or retrieving existing content. Its answers are generated token by token by a large language model. That has consequences you should design around. Generated answers are plausible by construction, not guaranteed correct, so a confident wrong date or invented reference is possible. Copilot reduces this by grounding answers in Bing search results or your files and showing citations, which you should open before relying on a claim. For images it uses image generation models through features such as the image creator. For code, GitHub Copilot generates suggestions that compile more often than not but still need review and tests. Who owns Copilot AI? Microsoft owns and makes Copilot. GitHub Copilot is made by GitHub, which Microsoft owns. The underlying GPT models come mainly from OpenAI, a separate company in which Microsoft is a major investor and partner. So the split is: OpenAI trains the core models, Microsoft builds the product, the grounding in Bing and Microsoft Graph, the safety systems, the apps and the enterprise controls. Microsoft has also built its own models for some features and has added models from other providers in parts of Microsoft 365 Copilot and Copilot Studio. For a user the practical point is that Microsoft's privacy terms and admin controls govern your data in Copilot, not OpenAI's consumer terms. What does Copilot use for AI? Copilot uses large language models, mainly OpenAI's GPT family, combined with Bing search for web grounding, Microsoft Graph for work data in Microsoft 365, and Microsoft's own safety and orchestration layers. A request typically flows like this: the orchestrator decides whether to search the web or your files, retrieves relevant content, builds a prompt with it, sends that to the model, then filters and cites the result. That retrieval step is what lets it answer about yesterday's news or last week's meeting, which a model cannot know from training alone. It is the same design behind any production RAG system, including the one I shipped in RAG.NextUpgrad. Which exact model serves a request changes as Microsoft updates the service, and Microsoft does not always show it. What is Copilot AI used for? People use Copilot to search and summarise the web, draft and rewrite text, summarise documents and meetings, analyse spreadsheets, generate images, and write or explain code with GitHub Copilot. Uses that work well for students and early-career engineers: Summarising a long PDF or web page before reading it properly. Turning rough notes into a structured report, email or slide outline. Explaining an error message or a piece of code line by line. Drafting a cover letter, then rewriting it in your own voice. Comparing two tools or concepts, with citations you can check. Uses to avoid: anything where a wrong fact is costly and you cannot verify it, and pasting confidential college or company data into a personal account. Is Copilot agentic AI? Partly. Copilot is mainly an assistant that answers when asked, but Microsoft has added agentic features that plan and carry out multi-step tasks, such as research agents, actions in the browser and GitHub Copilot's agent mode. Agentic means the system chooses steps and tools on its own towards a goal: it might search, open pages, edit files and check its work before reporting back. GitHub Copilot's agent mode does this in a code editor, and its coding agent can work on a GitHub issue and open a pull request. Copilot Studio lets organisations build their own agents with actions. These features usually ask for permission before acting and log what they did. Treat them like a junior colleague: give narrow tasks and review the result. How does Copilot compare to other AI? Copilot, ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude are all capable general assistants. The real difference is where each one is integrated, not raw intelligence: Copilot in Windows and Microsoft 365, Gemini in Google Workspace and Android, ChatGPT and Claude as standalone apps. A sensible way to choose: Copilot: you live in Outlook, Word, Excel and Teams, or your college or employer provides it. Gemini: you live in Gmail, Docs and Android. ChatGPT: you want one broad assistant with voice, image generation and many integrations. Claude: you work with long documents and code and want careful writing. Models leapfrog each other every few months, so test the same real task in two of them rather than trusting a ranking. Copilot vs Cursor AI: which is better for coding? They are different shapes of tool. GitHub Copilot is an assistant that plugs into the editor you already use; Cursor is a full code editor, built from VS Code, designed around AI. Both now offer chat, multi-file edits and agent modes. Choose GitHub Copilot if your team already uses VS Code, Visual Studio or JetBrains IDEs, needs GitHub's enterprise controls, or wants the coding agent that works on issues. Choose Cursor if you want AI woven into every part of the editor, with whole-codebase context and quick multi-file changes. Both let you pick from several frontier models. The fair test is one real task in your own repository, such as adding an endpoint with tests, done in each tool. Whichever you use, read every diff and run the tests. What are Copilot AI credits? AI credits are a monthly allowance that some consumer Microsoft plans use to meter Copilot features inside the Microsoft 365 apps and Designer. Each AI action draws from the allowance until it resets. Also asked as: what is copilot ai credits The idea is simple: everyday chat in the free Copilot app is broadly available, while heavier features inside Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and Designer on consumer plans are counted. Work and school accounts with a Microsoft 365 Copilot licence are licensed per user instead of by credits. How many credits a plan includes, and which actions use them, has changed more than once, so check Microsoft's current plan and support pages instead of a number quoted in an older article. If you hit the limit often, that is a sign to move heavy work, such as long document drafting, to a tool where you are not metered.

# What is edge AI and on-device AI? Running models in the browser and on phones with ONNX Runtime, WebGPU and quantization, from building a browser-only face recognition system
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-edge-ai-and-on-device-ai/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is edge AI?

**Edge AI is running machine learning inference on the device that has the data, a phone, a laptop, a browser tab, a camera, a sensor board, instead of sending the data to a server. The model is downloaded once and runs locally, so predictions arrive in milliseconds, work offline, cost nothing per call, and the raw input, a face, a voice, a document, never leaves the device. On-device AI, browser AI and TinyML are the same idea at different scales.**


I built FaceVision in 2026 as a browser-only face detection, recognition and liveness system: the camera frames are processed in the user's browser with ONNX Runtime Web, only a numeric embedding is sent to the server, and no image is ever stored [11]. That architecture is the concrete version of every argument on this page.

> The most effective privacy feature I have ever shipped was not encryption or a policy. It was never having the data in the first place.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour, from building FaceVision</cite>

## Why run AI on the device instead of the cloud?

**Four reasons, and each alone can justify it. Privacy: raw data stays with the user, which simplifies compliance and trust. Latency: no network round trip, so camera and audio features feel instant. Cost: no per-inference server bill, which matters when usage grows. Availability: it works offline and on bad connections, which in India is not an edge case. The trade-offs are model size, device variability and the work of exporting and testing.**



## What is ONNX, and what is ONNX Runtime?

**ONNX is an open file format for trained models that most frameworks can export to, so a model trained in PyTorch can run in a different runtime [1]. ONNX Runtime is Microsoft's inference engine for that format, with builds for servers, mobile and the web; ONNX Runtime Web runs models in the browser using WebAssembly on the CPU or WebGPU on the graphics card [2]. Together they are the most portable path from a training notebook to a device.**



My step-by-step guide to ONNX Runtime Web, with the preprocessing pitfalls, is on the portfolio [13].

## What is WebGPU, and does browser AI need it?

**WebGPU is the web standard that gives browser code access to the graphics card for general computation, not just rendering [3]. For AI in the browser it means models run several times faster than on WebAssembly alone, which turns real-time camera and audio models from a demo into a product. It does not replace WebAssembly: you ship both and fall back to the CPU path on browsers or devices without WebGPU support. Small models run acceptably on WebAssembly; larger ones need WebGPU.**


## What models can run on a device or in a browser?

**Comfortably: face detection and recognition, object detection with MobileNet-class or small YOLO models, image classification, OCR for clean text, speech recognition with small Whisper variants, text embeddings, and classifiers. Possibly: small language models of one to three billion parameters, quantized, on a laptop or a recent phone, with llama.cpp or a browser runtime. Not yet: large language models, high-resolution generative image models, or anything that needs tens of gigabytes.**



MobileNets set the pattern for models designed for devices [8]; Transformers.js brings Hugging Face models to the browser [4]; MediaPipe ships ready-made vision and audio pipelines for web and mobile [7].

## How do I make a model small enough for a device?

**Quantize to 8-bit or 4-bit integers, which cuts size and speeds inference on most hardware with a small accuracy loss [9]. Prune or distil into a smaller architecture when quantization is not enough. Fix input sizes and remove training-only operations at export. Then measure accuracy and latency on the actual target devices, because a model that passes in a notebook can fail on a low-end phone's memory or a browser's WebAssembly limits.**




## How does FaceVision keep faces on the device?

**The browser captures camera frames and runs three ONNX models locally: a face detector, a liveness check, and a recognition network that produces a 512-number embedding. Only that embedding is posted to a FastAPI backend, which stores it in PostgreSQL per user and compares it on verification. No image is transmitted or stored anywhere. If the server is breached, the attacker has vectors that cannot be turned back into faces. The design is on GitHub [11], and the reasoning about privacy is written up separately [12].**



## What are the platform options beyond the browser?

**On Android, LiteRT, formerly TensorFlow Lite, and ONNX Runtime Mobile [5][2]. On iOS, Core ML, with converters from PyTorch and ONNX [6]. On laptops and small servers, ONNX Runtime and llama.cpp for language models [10]. For ready-made vision and audio, MediaPipe on all of them [7]. The browser is the widest reach with the least installation; native platforms give more performance and background execution.**


## What are common edge AI use cases?

**Face and document capture for onboarding, attendance and KYC with privacy by design. Real-time translation and captions. Offline speech recognition for field workers and farmers. Quality inspection on factory cameras. Health and fitness sensing on wearables. Smart-camera detection without a cloud subscription. Browser tools that process a user's data without ever seeing it, which is how 13 of the 15 free tools at tools.scult.in work.**



## Edge AI interview questions

**Explain the trade-offs between on-device and cloud inference. Explain what ONNX and ONNX Runtime are for. Describe how you would take a PyTorch model to a browser and what could go wrong in preprocessing. Explain quantization's effect on size and accuracy. Design a privacy-preserving face verification system. Each answer is above, and a browser demo you built is the strongest evidence.**




## Where should I start?

**Export a small image classifier to ONNX, load it with ONNX Runtime Web in a plain HTML page, and classify a webcam frame without a server. Then quantize it and measure the speed difference. That afternoon is the whole field in miniature.** For a hands-on session on privacy-first vision systems at your college, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What is function calling (tool use) in LLMs? How models call your code, structured outputs, and building a reliable tool-using agent
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-function-calling-and-tool-use-in-llms/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is function calling in an LLM?

**Function calling, also called tool use, is a mechanism where you describe a set of functions to a model, name, description, and a JSON schema of its arguments, and the model, instead of only returning prose, can return a structured request to call one of those functions with specific argument values. Your application code receives that request, validates it, actually runs the function, and optionally feeds the result back to the model to continue. The model never executes code itself; it only ever proposes what to call and with what [1][2].**


Every agentic system I have built, and every document-extraction pipeline, depends on this mechanism in one of its two disguises: as a way to let a model act, or as a way to force a model's output into a shape your code can trust.

> A model that calls a function has not done anything yet. It has asked you to do something, in a format your code can check before it runs.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## Is tool calling the same thing as function calling?

**Yes, in current usage they are the same mechanism under two names: OpenAI and Google call it function calling [1][3], Anthropic calls the equivalent capability tool use [2], and both describe the same shape, a schema-described capability the model can request to invoke. Some documentation reserves "tool" for a slightly broader idea that includes non-function capabilities such as web search or code execution provided by the platform itself, with "function calling" specifically meaning your own custom functions, but in practice the terms are used interchangeably almost everywhere.**


## How does function calling actually work, step by step?

**You send the model a prompt plus a list of function definitions, each with a name, a description, and a JSON Schema for its parameters. The model, based on the conversation, decides whether calling one of those functions would help, and if so, returns a structured object naming the function and its argument values instead of, or alongside, ordinary text. Your code parses that object, validates the arguments against your own rules, executes the real function, and sends the result back to the model as a new message so it can continue the conversation or produce a final answer.**



## What is structured output, and how does it relate to function calling?

**Structured output is function calling used for a single purpose: forcing the model's response into a schema you define, rather than letting it call an arbitrary tool. You define one "function" that represents the shape of the answer you want, a set of extracted fields, a classification, a form, and the model is constrained to fill it in rather than write free text [8]. This is the same JSON-Schema-and-validation mechanism as tool use; it is simply used to make model output reliably parseable rather than to trigger an action.**




## How does multi-step tool use turn a chatbot into an agent?

**A single function call answers one question. An agent repeats the loop: call a tool, read the result, decide whether the goal is met or another tool call is needed, and continue until it is, or until a step limit is hit. This pattern, reason then act then observe, was formalised as ReAct [5] and is what separates a simple assistant from something that can, say, search documentation, run a calculation, and check its own answer before replying. The Model Context Protocol standardises how tools are described and connected across different agent implementations [6].**


My longer explanation of agent architectures generally is on the AI agent page [9], and how tool descriptions get standardised across systems is on the MCP page [10].

## How do I make function calling reliable in production?

**Validate every proposed function call against a strict schema and your own business rules before running anything; never assume the model's arguments are safe just because they parsed. Set timeouts and retries around the actual function execution, not just the model call. Give the model a clear error message back when a call fails or arguments are invalid, so it can retry sensibly rather than looping blindly. Log every call, its arguments, and its result, so a bad outcome can be traced to exactly what was requested and what ran. Never let a model-proposed call touch anything destructive, a delete, a payment, a send, without an explicit confirmation boundary outside the model's control.**



My notes on project structure put the provider, the tool definitions, and the execution layer in separate modules for exactly this reason: validation and logging belong at the boundary, not scattered through the code [11].

## What goes wrong with function calling in practice?

**The model hallucinates a plausible-looking call with arguments that do not correspond to anything real, an order ID that does not exist, a date outside range; this is caught only by validation, never by the model itself. A tool description is ambiguous, and the model picks the wrong function among several similar ones. A multi-step loop runs without a step limit and burns cost on an unproductive path. Errors from a failed call are not surfaced back to the model in a useful form, so it repeats the same failing call. Every one of these is a process failure, not a fundamental limitation, and every one has a known fix.**



## Function calling interview questions

**Explain what happens, step by step, when a model calls a function. Explain the difference between the model proposing a call and your code executing it. Describe how you would validate a proposed function call before running it. Explain how structured outputs reuse the same mechanism as tool use. Describe how a multi-step agent loop terminates. The strongest answer names a specific validation rule you added after something went wrong.**



## Where should I start?

**Define one simple function, a calculator or a lookup against a small local list, give it to a model with a strict schema, and make it call the function for a question that needs it. Log the full call and result. That one afternoon teaches the whole mechanism.** For a hands-on session on building reliable tool-using agents, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What is generative AI, and where can you actually learn it for free? A clear definition and a vetted list of free courses and certificates
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-generative-ai-and-where-to-learn-it-free/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is generative AI?

**Generative AI is the category of AI systems trained to create new content, text, images, audio, video, code, rather than only classify, predict a number, or recommend from a fixed set of options. A generative model learns the statistical shape of its training data well enough to produce plausible new examples of it: a language model generates the next word, a diffusion model generates pixels, a codec model generates audio. Classic machine learning mostly answers "which category" or "what number"; generative AI answers "produce a new thing like this."**


Every system I have built professionally sits inside this category somewhere: a RAG platform that generates answers, a fine-tuning studio that trains generative language models, a document extractor that generates structured fields from images. This page is the plain definition, and underneath it, the free courses that are actually worth the hours, filtered from the ones that are mostly a certificate PDF.

> Generative AI is not a separate technology from machine learning. It is machine learning pointed at "produce a new artefact" instead of "predict a label."
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## How is generative AI different from classic machine learning?

**Classic machine learning, and classic AI more broadly, is mostly discriminative: given an input, predict a category, a score, or a ranking, spam or not spam, this customer will churn, this image contains a cat. Generative AI is trained to model the full distribution of the data well enough to sample new examples from it. The training objective and the mathematics overlap heavily, the same neural network architectures show up on both sides, but the task the model is optimised for is different, and that difference is what makes an LLM able to write an essay while a classic classifier can only ever pick from options you gave it.**



## Is an LLM the same as generative AI?

**An LLM, a large language model, is one specific kind of generative model: one trained to generate text (and, in multimodal versions, respond to images too) [10]. Generative AI is the broader category that also includes image generators such as diffusion models, audio and speech generators, video generators, and code generators. Every LLM is a generative AI system; not every generative AI system is an LLM. When people say "generative AI" and mean ChatGPT specifically, they usually mean the LLM case, but the term covers much more.**


## Where is generative AI actually used?

**Writing and editing assistance, code generation and completion, customer support and internal knowledge assistants built with RAG, image and video generation for marketing and design, voice cloning and text-to-speech, data augmentation for training other models, drug and material discovery through generated molecular structures, and increasingly agentic systems that use generation as one step inside a larger workflow. The common thread is a task where "produce a plausible new thing" is more valuable than "pick from a fixed menu."**




## Which free courses on generative AI are actually worth it?

**Very few. The market is full of half-hour "courses" that end in a shareable certificate and teach almost nothing, and a handful of providers that genuinely teach the material for free. Google's Introduction to Generative AI is a solid, short, accurate primer [2]. Microsoft's Generative AI for Beginners is a free multi-lesson curriculum with real code [3]. DeepLearning.AI's short courses are consistently well made and free, though the certificates from some of their paid specializations are not [4][5]. Hugging Face's NLP and Agents courses are free, technical, and hands-on [6][7]. Anthropic Academy teaches building with Claude specifically [8]. fast.ai remains one of the best free deep learning courses that exist, code-first [9].**



## What should I actually do with these courses?

**Pick one short course for vocabulary, one hands-on course that has you write code, and stop collecting courses after that. The certificate is not the goal. Within a week of finishing, build something small using what you learned, a script, a tiny app, a notebook, and measure whether it works. Post it. That sequence, one primer, one hands-on course, one shipped thing, teaches more than ten certificates with nothing behind them, and it is what a resume or an interviewer can actually verify.**



## What mistakes do people make chasing generative AI courses?

**Collecting certificates from courses that are mostly marketing for a paid upsell. Treating a certificate as equivalent to a shipped project on a resume, when interviewers weight them very differently. Starting with the most advanced course available instead of the one that matches where you actually are. Never building anything between courses, so the vocabulary never turns into a skill. Ignoring that the field moves fast enough that a two-year-old course on a specific tool may already be stale, even if the fundamentals it teaches are not.**



## Generative AI interview questions

**Define generative AI and contrast it with discriminative machine learning. Explain where an LLM sits inside the broader category. Give three applications beyond chatbots. Explain, honestly, what you built after your last course and what it measured. The question behind the question is always the same: did the course change what you can do, or only what your certificate says.**



## Where should I start?

**Take Google's short primer this week, then Microsoft's Generative AI for Beginners for the code, then build one small thing with what you learned and share it.** For a hands-on session that takes students from definition to a shipped generative AI project in one workshop, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What is GPT in ChatGPT? What it stands for, actions, and embeddings
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-gpt-in-chatgpt/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

GPT in ChatGPT is the large language model underneath the chat app. GPT stands for Generative Pre-trained Transformer: a neural network that generates text, was first pre-trained on a huge amount of text, and uses the transformer architecture. ChatGPT is the product built around those models, adding a chat interface, memory, tools such as search and code execution, and safety systems. This page explains each word in GPT, which GPT powers Copilot, what GPT actions are, whether GPT-2 embeddings work for classification, how GPT uses water, and what GPT can do with video. What is GPT in ChatGPT? GPT is the family of large language models made by OpenAI, and ChatGPT is the chat application that runs on them. When you type a message, ChatGPT sends it, with your conversation and instructions, to a GPT model, which generates the reply. The distinction matters when you build things. ChatGPT has features the bare model does not: conversation history, memory across chats, web search, file uploads, image generation and a code tool. Developers who use the OpenAI API get the model and must add those pieces themselves. ChatGPT also chooses which model handles a request in some modes, routing simple questions to fast models and hard ones to reasoning models. So "ChatGPT said X" really means a GPT model, plus ChatGPT's tools and settings, produced X. What does GPT stand for? GPT stands for Generative Pre-trained Transformer. OpenAI introduced the name with its first GPT model in 2018, and every later generation, from GPT-2 and GPT-3 to the current models, keeps it. The 2018 paper showed that a transformer pre-trained on a large body of unlabelled text, then fine-tuned for specific tasks, beat models designed for each task separately. GPT-2 in 2019 showed that a larger model could do many tasks without task-specific fine-tuning. GPT-3 in 2020 scaled this further and made prompting, simply describing the task in text, a practical way to use a model. ChatGPT, launched in late 2022, added instruction tuning and human feedback so the model follows requests conversationally. What does GPT stand for in the context of AI? Each word describes a design choice. Generative: the model produces new text one token at a time. Pre-trained: it first learns general language patterns from a massive dataset before any specific use. Transformer: the neural network architecture it is built on. In more detail: Generative: it predicts the next token given everything before it, and repeating that prediction produces sentences, code and answers. Pre-trained: the expensive learning happens once, on a large corpus; later steps such as instruction tuning and fine-tuning adapt it cheaply. Transformer: an architecture from 2017 built on attention, which lets every token weigh every earlier token, so the model can use context across long passages. GPT models are decoder-only transformers: each token attends only to earlier tokens, which suits generation. Which GPT does Copilot use? Microsoft Copilot runs mainly on OpenAI's GPT models, and Microsoft has moved it to newer GPT generations as they launch, including the GPT-5 family. It chooses the model for each request automatically and also uses Microsoft's own models for some features. Microsoft 365 Copilot similarly uses GPT models hosted in Microsoft's cloud, and Microsoft has added models from other providers in some features. GitHub Copilot is different: it has a model picker with options from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, and new models are announced on GitHub's changelog. Microsoft rarely promises a fixed model for a feature, because it updates the service continuously. For most users the model name matters less than the grounding: whether Copilot is answering from the web, your files or your code. What are GPT actions? GPT actions let a custom GPT in ChatGPT call an external API. You describe the API with an OpenAPI schema, and the GPT decides when to call it, fills in the parameters from the conversation, and uses the response in its answer. For example, a college events GPT could have an action get_events(date) that calls your events API, so a student can ask "what is happening on campus on Friday?" and get live data instead of a guess. Actions support authentication with an API key or OAuth, so a GPT can act for a signed-in user. They are the no-code end of tool use. For richer apps with their own interface inside ChatGPT, OpenAI's newer Apps SDK, built on the Model Context Protocol, is the more capable route. How do GPT actions work? When you build a custom GPT, you paste an OpenAPI schema describing your endpoints, set authentication, and write instructions about when to use them. During a chat, the model decides to call an endpoint, ChatGPT makes the HTTP request, and the model reads the JSON response. Also asked as: how do gpt actions work youtube Steps to build one: Create a GPT in the GPT editor and write clear instructions. Under Actions, add your OpenAPI schema with clear operationIds and descriptions for each endpoint. Configure authentication: none, API key or OAuth. Add a privacy policy URL if you plan to share it. Test in the preview pane and inspect each call and response. Most failures come from vague endpoint descriptions; the model chooses tools from the text you write, so describe each one as you would to a new teammate. Can we use GPT-2 sentence embeddings for classification tasks? Yes. You can take GPT-2's hidden states, pool them into one vector per sentence, and train a simple classifier such as logistic regression on top. It works, but sentence-embedding models trained for this purpose usually give better results. Also asked as: can we use gpt-2 sentence embedding for classification tasks GPT-2 is a decoder-only model, so each token only sees the tokens before it. Mean pooling over all tokens or using the last token's state are the usual choices: from transformers import GPT2Tokenizer, GPT2Model import torch tok = GPT2Tokenizer.from_pretrained(&quot;gpt2&quot;); tok.pad_token = tok.eos_token model = GPT2Model.from_pretrained(&quot;gpt2&quot;) batch = tok([&quot;great product&quot;, &quot;terrible support&quot;], return_tensors=&quot;pt&quot;, padding=True) with torch.no_grad(): h = model(**batch).last_hidden_state mask = batch[&quot;attention_mask&quot;].unsqueeze(-1) emb = (h * mask).sum(1) / mask.sum(1) # one 768-d vector per sentence Compare against a Sentence-BERT style model on the same data before choosing. How does GPT use water? GPT models do not use water directly; the data centres that train and run them do, mainly for cooling servers and indirectly through the water used to generate their electricity. The amount depends heavily on location, season and cooling technology. A 2023 study from researchers at the University of California estimated that training GPT-3 in Microsoft's US data centres directly evaporated hundreds of thousands of litres of fresh water, and that running models adds more over time. Such figures are estimates with wide ranges, because companies do not publish per-model water use. Data centres in hot, dry regions use more water for evaporative cooling; others use air cooling or recycled water and use more electricity instead. Major cloud providers publish annual sustainability reports with their overall water use. Can GPT watch videos? Not in the way people do. GPT models in ChatGPT can analyse images, so they can examine frames taken from a video, and transcripts from its audio, but they do not reliably watch a full-length video from start to finish. The practical approach is to extract a transcript with a speech-to-text tool and a set of key frames, for example one every few seconds or at scene changes, and give those to the model with a precise question. In ChatGPT's mobile app, voice mode can use the live camera, which helps for quick questions about what is in front of you. Some other models, such as Google's Gemini, accept video files directly through their API and are a better fit when you need to analyse long footage. Can GPT make videos? GPT models themselves generate text and, in ChatGPT, images. Video generation comes from a separate OpenAI model, Sora, available through its own app and website for eligible users. You can still use GPT for most of video production: scripts, storyboards, shot lists, captions, titles and thumbnail ideas. With its code tool, ChatGPT can sometimes assemble a simple slideshow video from images by writing Python, but that is a workaround. For generated footage, write a detailed prompt in Sora describing the subject, setting, camera movement and style, generate several takes, and edit the best clips in a normal video editor. Label AI-generated footage when you publish it.

# What is MCP, the Model Context Protocol? How MCP servers work, MCP vs function calling vs APIs, and how to build one, from running a public server
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-mcp-model-context-protocol/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is MCP, the Model Context Protocol?

**MCP is an open protocol, introduced by Anthropic in late 2024 and now maintained as an open standard, that defines how an AI application connects to external tools, data sources and prompt templates through a common interface [1][3]. A server exposes capabilities; a client inside the AI application discovers and uses them; the model decides when to call them. The point is reuse: a server for your database, your docs or your tool set is written once and works with every client that speaks MCP, instead of a custom integration per assistant.**


I run a public MCP server at tools.scult.in that exposes the same free tools and the prompt library the website offers, so an agent can call, say, the schema generator or fetch a stamped prompt with one line of client configuration and no signup [9]. Building it taught me what the protocol is for in practice: the client side is finished by other people, so a server is the whole product. This page is what I wish I had read first, and the longer build note is on the portfolio [10].

> Before MCP, every tool was an integration project per assistant. After MCP, a tool is a server, and the assistants come to it.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour, from running the tools.scult.in MCP server</cite>

## How does MCP work?

**Three parts. The host is the AI application, a coding assistant, a chat app, an agent runtime. Inside it, an MCP client connects to one or more MCP servers, over standard input and output for local servers or HTTP for remote ones, using JSON-RPC messages [6]. The server declares what it offers: tools with JSON schemas, resources with URIs, prompt templates. The client lists them and hands the tool definitions to the model. When the model emits a tool call, the client forwards it to the server, the server executes and returns a result, and the result goes back into the model's context.**



## What are tools, resources and prompts in MCP?

**Tools are functions the model can call, each with a name, a description and a JSON schema for arguments; they are for actions and computations. Resources are data the client can read by URI, files, database rows, documents, for context rather than action. Prompts are reusable templates the server offers, with arguments, so a client can present them as slash commands or presets. Most servers are tools-first; resources and prompts are where the protocol gets interesting for knowledge and workflow servers.**



## What is the difference between MCP and function calling?

**Function calling is a feature of a model provider's API: you send tool definitions, the model returns structured tool calls, you execute them [4][5]. MCP is a protocol between the application and tool servers. They compose rather than compete: the MCP client fetches tool definitions from servers and passes them to the model through function calling; when the model calls one, the client routes the call to the right server. Without MCP you write and host every tool inside your app. With MCP, tools live in servers anyone can plug in.**



## MCP vs API: do I still need a REST API?

**Yes, usually underneath. An MCP server typically wraps an existing API or database and exposes a handful of model-friendly tools with descriptions that say when to use them. The REST API stays for your own front end and for programmatic clients; the MCP server is the model-facing surface. The design skill is in the wrapping: three well-described tools that map to user intents beat thirty tools that mirror your endpoints one to one.**


## How do I build an MCP server?

**Pick the official SDK in your language, define two or three tools with tight descriptions and JSON schemas, implement each as a function that returns text or structured content, and run the server over standard input and output for local use or HTTP for remote use [2]. Test it with a client you already use, a coding assistant that supports MCP, before writing more tools. Add resources and prompts only if a client would use them. Publish with a README that shows the one-line client configuration.**



The pattern for a tool definition, in the shape the SDKs use:

```json
{
  "name": "get_prompt",
  "description": "Fetch a version-stamped prompt from the tools.scult.in library by slug. Use when the user asks for a tested prompt for a task such as a RAG system prompt or a code review checklist.",
  "inputSchema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "slug": {"type": "string", "description": "Prompt identifier, e.g. rag-system-prompt-v3"}
    },
    "required": ["slug"]
  }
}
```

The description is the interface. Models pick tools by reading it, and a vague description is the most common reason a good tool never gets called.


## How do I use MCP servers in a coding assistant or chat app?

**Add the server to the client's configuration, usually a JSON file or a settings page, with the command to start it or the URL to reach it. The client connects, lists the tools, and they appear to the model in every conversation. Start with one server; too many tools dilute the model's choices. Prefer servers with a few sharp tools and clear descriptions. Remove servers you stop using.**


## What are the security risks of MCP?

**The same as for any agent with tools, concentrated. A tool with write access can be triggered by a prompt injection hidden in a document the model read. A malicious or compromised server can return content that steers the model. Servers run with whatever permissions you give the process. Defences: least-privilege tools, read-only by default; explicit confirmation for anything destructive or outward-facing; treating every tool result as untrusted data; pinning and reviewing the servers you install; logging every call. OWASP's LLM risk list applies directly [7].**



## When should I use MCP, and when not?

**Use MCP when more than one AI client will use the same tools, when you want users to plug your product into their assistant, or when you want to reuse servers others have built. Skip it when a single application calls its own functions and nothing else ever will; plain function calling inside the app is simpler. Anthropic's guidance on agents applies here too: the simplest architecture that works, and tools only where the model's judgement is actually needed [8].**



## What does running a public MCP server teach?

**That descriptions matter more than code, that clients differ in how they present tools, that logs are the only way to learn what models actually call, and that a server with no signup and no keys gets used in ways you did not plan. The tools.scult.in server exposes the free tools and the 1,211-prompt library; the most-called tool is not the one I expected, and the description edits I made from the logs improved call accuracy more than any code change [9][10].**



## MCP interview questions

**Explain the host, client and server roles. Compare MCP with function calling and say how they compose. Name the three primitives and an example of each. Describe the security model and the two biggest risks. Explain what makes a tool description good. Say when you would not use MCP. Having built even a two-tool server turns all of these into stories.**



## Where should I start?

**Point an MCP-capable client at the server at tools.scult.in and use a tool in a real conversation [9]. Then build a two-tool server over something you own, a folder of notes, a small database, test it from the same client, and read the logs.** For a hands-on session on agents, tool calling and MCP at your college or team, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.
