# What is Copilot 365? How Microsoft 365 Copilot works in Excel, Outlook and more
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-microsoft-365-copilot/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

Microsoft 365 Copilot, often called Copilot 365, is an AI assistant built into Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and Teams that answers from your work emails, files, chats and meetings as well as the web. It matters because it is the first AI tool many students meet in an internship or first job. This page explains how it works under the hood, which plans include it, how it behaves in Excel, Outlook and Visual Studio, and how Copilot Studio lets you build your own agents. What is Copilot 365? Copilot 365 is Microsoft 365 Copilot: a large language model assistant inside the Microsoft 365 apps that can draft, summarise and analyse using your organisation's content, within the permissions you already have. Also asked as: how copilot works You reach it from a Copilot button in each app, or from Copilot Chat in Teams and the Microsoft 365 app. In Word it drafts and rewrites documents; in PowerPoint it builds a deck from a Word file; in Teams it summarises a meeting you missed and lists the action items. What makes it different from a public chatbot is grounding: a question like "what did the client ask for last week?" is answered from your actual emails and meeting transcripts, with references back to the source items, rather than from the model's general knowledge. How does Copilot work? Copilot takes your prompt, searches the content you have access to through Microsoft Graph, adds the relevant pieces to the prompt, sends it to a large language model, then checks the answer before showing it. That is retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) at company scale. The flow: Grounding: Microsoft Graph and the semantic index find relevant emails, files, chats and meetings that your account is permitted to open. Generation: the enriched prompt goes to a large language model hosted within the Microsoft 365 service boundary. Post-processing: responsible-AI and compliance checks run, and the answer returns with citations to the source items. It is the same pattern I built in RAG.NextUpgrad: retrieve permitted content first, answer only from it, and cite where each claim came from. Answer quality depends on retrieval, so messy, duplicated or over-shared files produce messy answers. Does Copilot come with Microsoft 365? Partly. Work accounts get Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat, which is web-grounded, while the full work-grounded Microsoft 365 Copilot is an add-on licence. Consumer plans include some Copilot features in the apps with usage limits. The practical test is what you see. If Copilot in Word or Outlook can answer questions about your organisation's files and meetings, you have the full licence. If you only get a chat that answers from the web and the files you upload, you have Copilot Chat. Students should check with their college IT team, because institutional plans differ a lot. Plans and included features change regularly, so the current comparison is always on Microsoft's own plan pages rather than in an older article. What is the difference between Copilot and Microsoft 365 Copilot? Microsoft Copilot is the free consumer assistant for personal Microsoft accounts, grounded in the web. Microsoft 365 Copilot is the work product, grounded in your organisation's data with enterprise data protection and admin controls. The brand covers several products, which confuses people: Microsoft Copilot: the consumer app and website, for personal use. Microsoft 365 Copilot: the work assistant across Word, Excel, Outlook and Teams. GitHub Copilot: the coding assistant in VS Code, Visual Studio and JetBrains IDEs. Copilot Studio: a low-code tool for building your own agents. For work data the difference that matters is protection. Under enterprise data protection, Microsoft states that prompts and responses are not used to train its foundation models and that existing permissions and compliance policies apply. How does Copilot work in Excel? Copilot in Excel reads the table you are working in and helps you analyse it: it suggests formulas, adds calculated columns, highlights and sorts data, builds charts and PivotTables, and explains what it found. Also asked as: how copilot works in excel Two habits avoid most failures. First, format the data as a table with Ctrl+T and give every column a clear header, because Copilot works on structured ranges. Second, save the workbook to OneDrive or SharePoint, since Copilot relies on the cloud version of the file. Then ask specific questions: "add a column with profit margin as a percentage" works better than "analyse this". Always check the formula it inserts before you trust the numbers; it is a fast first draft, not an auditor. For heavier analysis Copilot can also use Python in Excel to run statistics or forecasts on the table. How does Copilot work in Outlook? In Outlook, Copilot summarises long email threads, drafts replies from a short instruction, and coaches you on the tone and clarity of a message before you send it. Also asked as: how copilot works in outlook Open a thread and choose the summary option to get the key points and open questions at the top. To reply, type an instruction such as "accept the meeting, ask for the agenda, keep it short" and adjust the length and tone of the draft. Coaching reviews a draft you wrote and suggests changes, which is useful for formal emails to professors or recruiters. With the full licence it can also pull context from related files and meetings. Read every draft before sending: it can confidently state a date or commitment that was never agreed. How does Copilot work in Visual Studio? In Visual Studio the assistant is GitHub Copilot, not Microsoft 365 Copilot. It suggests code as you type, answers questions about your solution in a chat window, and in recent versions can make multi-file edits in agent mode. Also asked as: how copilot works in visual studio Sign in with a GitHub account that has Copilot access; GitHub offers a free tier with monthly limits and paid plans with more. Inline completions appear as grey text that you accept with Tab. In the chat window, slash commands such as /explain, /fix, /tests and /doc act on the selected code, and # references pull in specific files. Agent mode plans a change, edits several files and runs the build to check itself. The habits that matter are the same as with any assistant: small requests, review every diff, and run the tests. How does Copilot Studio work? Copilot Studio is Microsoft's low-code tool for building agents. You give an agent instructions, knowledge sources and actions, and it uses a language model to decide how to answer each message and which action to call. Also asked as: how copilot studio works Knowledge can be public websites, SharePoint sites, uploaded files or business data in Dataverse. Actions connect the agent to systems through Power Platform connectors, Power Automate flows or custom APIs, so it can create a ticket or look up an order instead of only chatting. Topics still exist for fixed conversations such as a refund policy. You test the agent in the built-in chat pane, then publish it to Teams, a website or Microsoft 365 Copilot. The design rules are those of any agent: narrow scope, clear instructions and logs you can review. Is there a tutorial for Copilot in Microsoft 365? Yes. Microsoft Learn has free training paths for Microsoft 365 Copilot, and the quickest way to learn is one real task a day in the app you already use. Also asked as: tutorial copilot microsoft 365 A practical first week: Day 1, Teams: ask Copilot to summarise a recorded meeting and list action items with owners. Day 2, Outlook: summarise your longest thread and draft a reply from a one-line instruction. Day 3, Word: turn rough notes into a structured report, then ask for a shorter version. Day 4, Excel: format a dataset as a table and ask three specific analysis questions. Day 5, PowerPoint: create a deck from the Word report and fix it by hand. Write prompts with a goal, context, the source to use and the format you expect. That structure improves results more than any trick. Where can I see the Copilot 365 roadmap? The Microsoft 365 roadmap website lists planned and rolling-out features. Filter it by the Microsoft 365 Copilot product to see what is in development, rolling out or launched, with target months. Also asked as: roadmap copilot 365 Each roadmap item has an ID, a status and the apps and platforms it affects, so admins use it to prepare training before a feature arrives. Dates move, and some items roll out in stages by region and release channel, so treat a target month as an estimate. For what has already changed, the release notes for Microsoft 365 Copilot on Microsoft Learn are more reliable than news coverage. If you build on top of Copilot with Copilot Studio or plugins, check the roadmap before each project, because a built-in feature may arrive that replaces your custom work.

# What is object detection? YOLO explained, detection vs classification vs segmentation, training on your own data, and running it in real time on a budget GPU
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-object-detection-yolo/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is object detection?

**Object detection is the computer vision task of finding every object of interest in an image and returning, for each, a bounding box, a class label and a confidence score. Where image classification answers "what is in this picture", detection answers "what is here and exactly where", and it does so for many objects at once. It powers counting, tracking, quality inspection, safety monitoring, retail analytics and the perception stacks of robots and vehicles.**


I have built vision systems that run in browsers and on modest servers, including FaceVision, a face detection and recognition pipeline that runs entirely in the browser, and the lessons about cameras, lighting and evaluation carry directly to general object detection. My notes on budget hardware, camera problems and evaluation are on the portfolio [11][12][13].

> The model that scored highest on the dataset was not the one that worked on the factory camera. The camera is part of the model. Test on it.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## Classification vs detection vs segmentation: what is the difference?

**Classification assigns one label to the whole image. Detection assigns a box and a label to each object. Semantic segmentation assigns a class to every pixel. Instance segmentation combines detection and segmentation: a pixel mask per object. Each step up gives more information and costs more compute and, above all, more labelling effort, because a box takes seconds to draw and a mask takes minutes. Choose the least detailed output that answers your question.**



## How does YOLO work?

**YOLO, "you only look once", treats detection as a single regression problem: one network pass over the whole image predicts boxes, class probabilities and confidences for a grid of locations at once, instead of proposing regions first and classifying each, as two-stage detectors such as Faster R-CNN do [1][2]. Non-maximum suppression then removes duplicate boxes for the same object. The single pass is why YOLO-family models run in real time on a laptop GPU or even a phone, at some cost in accuracy on very small or crowded objects.**



DETR later showed a transformer could detect end to end without anchors or suppression [3]. For most student and production projects in 2026, a current YOLO-family model from the Ultralytics library is the practical default: documented, exportable and fast [6].

## How is object detection accuracy measured?

**With intersection over union and mean average precision. IoU is the overlap between a predicted box and the ground-truth box divided by their union; a prediction counts as correct if IoU exceeds a threshold, commonly 0.5. Average precision summarises the precision-recall curve for one class across confidence thresholds; mAP averages it across classes. COCO reports mAP averaged over IoU thresholds from 0.5 to 0.95, which is stricter than the older PASCAL VOC 0.5 [4][5]. Compare models on the same metric and the same dataset, or the comparison is meaningless.**



## How do I train an object detector on my own data?

**Collect images from the camera and conditions you will deploy on. Label boxes with a tool such as Label Studio or Roboflow, consistently, with a written labelling guide [7][8]. Split by scene, not by frame, so near-identical frames do not leak into validation. Start from a pretrained YOLO-family model and fine-tune on your set; a few hundred well-labelled images per class is often enough for a first version [6]. Evaluate mAP on the held-out set, then look at the false positives and false negatives by eye, which tells you what to label next.**



Labelling quality dominates. Two hundred images with tight, consistent boxes beat two thousand with sloppy ones, and every hour spent on a labelling guide saves three hours of debugging the model.


## Why does my detector fail on real cameras?

**Because the deployment camera differs from the training images: lower resolution, motion blur, different mounting angle, backlight, dust on the lens, compression from a video stream, objects smaller in the frame than in the dataset. Fix the input before touching the model: more light, a better angle, higher resolution, a cleaner stream. Then add training images from that camera. Then lower the confidence threshold for recall or raise it for precision, depending on which error costs more.**


My write-up of the camera problems that broke vision models I shipped, and the fixes, is on the portfolio [12]. The one-line summary: the camera is part of the model.

## How do I run object detection in real time on a budget?

**Pick a small model variant, export it to ONNX or TensorRT, quantize to 8-bit, and run at a reduced input resolution and frame rate that still catches what you need. A laptop GPU or a recent CPU handles small YOLO variants at video frame rates; a phone or browser handles them at lower rates through ONNX Runtime Web or a mobile runtime [9]. Skip frames when nothing moves, and track objects between detections instead of detecting on every frame. Measure latency on the target device, not the training machine.**



My notes on real-time detection on a budget GPU, with the measured frame rates, are written up separately [11].

## What are common object detection use cases?

**Counting people or vehicles. Quality inspection on production lines. Safety compliance, helmets and vests on sites. Shelf and stock monitoring in retail. Crop and pest detection in agriculture. Document layout detection, finding tables and signatures on pages. Wildlife and traffic monitoring. Robotics perception. In every case the demo is easy and the deployment is the work: cameras, lighting, edge hardware and a definition of what counts as correct.**


## Which tools and libraries should I use?

**For training and inference: the Ultralytics YOLO library, with export to ONNX and other formats built in [6]. For labelling: Label Studio if you want open source and control, Roboflow if you want a hosted workflow with augmentation and export [7][8]. For image handling and camera capture: OpenCV [10]. For running in the browser: ONNX Runtime Web [9]. Learn the concepts once and the tools become interchangeable.**



## Object detection interview questions

**Explain detection versus classification versus segmentation. Explain how a one-stage detector like YOLO differs from a two-stage detector. Define IoU and mAP and the difference between mAP at 0.5 and at 0.5 to 0.95. Describe how you would build a dataset and avoid leakage. Explain how you would get a detector running on a phone. Describe a failure on a real camera and the fix. Each is answered above; a detector you trained and deployed is the strongest evidence.**




## Where should I start?

**Take fifty photos of one object type with your phone in the room where you would deploy, label them, fine-tune a small YOLO variant, measure mAP on ten held-out photos, and run the model on your webcam. Then export it to ONNX and run it in a browser tab. That weekend covers the entire page.** For a hands-on computer vision session at your college, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What is OCR? How OCR software works, the best OCR tools, and OCR vs scanning
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-ocr-software/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

OCR, optical character recognition, is technology that turns images of text, such as scans, photos and image-only PDFs, into editable, searchable text. An OCR scanner is a scanner, or scanner app, that runs OCR after capturing the page. Modern OCR is built on machine learning, and vision-language models now read complex pages, tables and handwriting far better than older engines. I built page-batched PDF OCR into the OCR &amp; Speech Workspace, so this page covers how OCR works, OCR versus scanning, and the best tools, plus a practical Tesseract guide. What is an OCR scanner? An OCR scanner is a scanner, scanner app or multifunction printer that captures an image of a document and then runs optical character recognition on it, producing a searchable PDF or editable text instead of just a picture. Also asked as: what is ocr scanner Many office scanners and phone scanner apps do this automatically: scan a page and you can select, copy and search its text. The quality depends on the scan, with clean, flat, well-lit pages at a reasonable resolution working best, and on the OCR engine. For printed text, results are near perfect; tables, multi-column layouts, stamps, poor photocopies and handwriting are harder. If text selection works on your scanned PDF, OCR has already been applied. What does OCR mean on a scanner? On a scanner, OCR is the option that makes the scanned document's text readable by the computer. With OCR on, the output is usually a searchable PDF, with the image plus an invisible text layer, or an editable document. Also asked as: what does ocr mean on scanner When to turn it on: for anything you will search, copy from, translate or feed to software, such as notes, contracts, invoices and textbooks. When it does not matter: photos or documents you only need to view. OCR settings often include the language, which improves accuracy, and output format, such as searchable PDF or Word. Choose the correct language, including Hindi or other Indian scripts where supported, for best results. What is the difference between OCR and a scanner? A scanner is hardware or a camera app that captures an image of a page. OCR is software that reads the text in that image. A scan without OCR is just a picture; OCR turns it into text you can edit and search. Also asked as: difference between ocr and scanner You can run OCR without a scanner, on a photo or an existing PDF, and you can scan without OCR. Many scanners bundle OCR software, and phone apps combine both steps. For workflows such as digitising notes, processing invoices or building a searchable archive, you want both: good capture for a clean image, then OCR for text. Capture quality often matters more than the OCR engine, so scan straight, flat and well lit. How does OCR software work? OCR software cleans up the image, finds where text is on the page, recognises the characters or words in each text region, and assembles the results into lines, paragraphs and layout, often with a confidence score per word. Also asked as: how ocr software works The stages: Pre-processing: straighten, remove noise, adjust contrast, binarise. Layout analysis: detect columns, paragraphs, tables and reading order. Text recognition: a neural network reads each line into characters. Post-processing: dictionaries and language models fix likely errors. Output: plain text, searchable PDF, or structured data with coordinates. Document AI services add field extraction, such as invoice totals and dates, on top of OCR. DocuLens AI does this with schema validation, so extracted fields are checked before use. Is OCR machine learning? Modern OCR is machine learning. Today's engines use neural networks, such as convolutional and recurrent networks or transformers, trained on large collections of text images. Early OCR systems used hand-built rules and template matching. Tesseract, the popular open-source engine, has used an LSTM neural network for text recognition since version 4. Cloud services use deep learning for layout and recognition. Newest of all, vision-language models read a page image directly and output text, tables or structured data, using context much as a person would. Machine learning is why OCR now handles varied fonts, photos and some handwriting, but it also means errors can look plausible, so validation still matters. What is the best OCR software? It depends on your documents. For everyday use, the OCR built into Google Lens, Apple's Live Text, Microsoft OneNote and Adobe Acrobat is excellent. For developers, Tesseract is the standard free engine, and cloud services such as Google Cloud Vision, Azure AI Document Intelligence and Mistral's OCR handle complex documents at scale. Choose by need: Quick text from photos: Google Lens or Live Text. Searchable PDFs from scans: Adobe Acrobat or the free OCRmyPDF. Free and offline: Tesseract. Invoices, forms, tables: Azure AI Document Intelligence or Google Document AI. Complex pages and handwriting: vision-language models and AI OCR services. Test two tools on ten of your own documents before committing. What is the best OCR software for PC? On Windows, Microsoft OneNote and the Snipping Tool's text actions handle quick OCR for free, Adobe Acrobat converts scans into searchable PDFs, and Tesseract or OCRmyPDF give free, offline batch OCR. For complex documents, cloud document AI services do best. For students and small offices, a practical free setup is: OneNote or the Snipping Tool for copying text from screenshots, and OCRmyPDF to make scanned PDFs searchable in bulk: ocrmypdf --language eng input.pdf output.pdf For Hindi or other languages, install the matching Tesseract language data and pass it, for example --language hin+eng. Keep originals, and spot-check output, especially tables. What is the best OCR scanner app? On phones, Google Lens and Apple's built-in camera with Live Text are the quickest for copying text, while scanner apps such as Adobe Scan and the scan feature in Google Drive or Apple Notes create multi-page, searchable PDFs. Look for automatic edge detection, perspective correction, multi-page scanning, OCR language options and export to PDF. For privacy-sensitive documents, prefer apps that process on the device or that you trust with your data. Scanning tips: place pages on a contrasting surface, use even light without shadows, hold the phone parallel to the page, and scan each page separately rather than spreads. What is the best vision-language model for OCR? Leading multimodal models from Google, OpenAI, Anthropic and Mistral all read documents well, and specialised OCR models from AI providers are tuned for page-level extraction. The best choice depends on your languages, layouts and cost. Also asked as: best vision language model for ocr Vision-language models shine on complex layouts, tables, forms, mixed content and handwriting, and can output structured formats such as Markdown or JSON directly. Their weakness is occasional invented text on unclear regions, which traditional OCR rarely does in the same way. Good practice is to process documents page by page, keep page numbers with every chunk, request structured output, and validate key fields against rules. That is the approach in my OCR &amp; Speech Workspace, where OCR runs in page batches and answers cite pages. How do I use Tesseract for OCR? Install Tesseract and its language packs, then run it on an image from the command line or through Python with pytesseract. Clean, high-resolution images give the best results. Also asked as: a practical guide to ocr with tesseract tesseract notes.png output -l eng # writes output.txt import pytesseract from PIL import Image text = pytesseract.image_to_string(Image.open(&quot;notes.png&quot;), lang=&quot;eng&quot;) print(text) Improve accuracy by converting to greyscale, increasing resolution, straightening skewed images and choosing the right page segmentation mode with --psm. Use OCRmyPDF to add a text layer to scanned PDFs. Tesseract handles printed text well and struggles with handwriting and complex tables, where AI document models are a better fit.

# What does open source mean for AI models? Open-weight vs open-source, licenses that actually matter, and how to contribute
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-open-source-and-open-weight-ai-models/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What does "open source" mean for an AI model?

**In most cases, less than the term implies. A model marketed as open source is usually open-weight: the trained numerical parameters are downloadable and runnable, but the training data, and often the full training code and exact recipe, are not published, which means you cannot fully reproduce the model from scratch the way open source software lets you rebuild a program from its source. The Open Source Initiative has proposed a stricter definition requiring the training data and code be available too, which very few released models actually meet [1].**


I run production systems on both open-weight and closed-API models, and choosing correctly means reading past the marketing word "open" to what is actually published and what the license actually permits.

> "Open" on an AI model's homepage usually means you can download the weights. It rarely means you can see how they were made.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What is the difference between open-weight and open-source?

**Open-weight means the trained parameters are released for anyone to download and run; open-source, in the traditional software sense, means the source, here the training data, training code, and methodology, is also available so the artefact can be independently reproduced and audited. Most widely used "open" models, Llama, Mistral, Gemma, are open-weight: genuinely useful for running locally, fine-tuning, and building on, but not fully reproducible or auditable the way a codebase under an OSI-approved license is.**



## Which licenses actually matter, and what do they restrict?

**Apache 2.0 and MIT are permissive software licenses, widely used for genuinely unrestricted open-weight releases, allowing commercial use, modification and redistribution with minimal conditions [4]. Meta's Llama community license permits broad use but includes real restrictions, including a clause requiring a separate licence from Meta once a deployment exceeds a stated number of monthly active users, and requirements around naming derivative models [3]. Reading the actual license text, not the announcement blog post, is the only way to know what you can legally do with a specific model.**




## Why does open-weight matter practically, beyond the philosophy?

**Because it lets you run inference and fine-tuning entirely on your own hardware, with no per-token API bill, no data leaving your infrastructure, and no dependency on a provider's uptime or policy changes. This matters most for privacy-sensitive applications, cost at high volume, offline or air-gapped deployments, and situations where you need to fine-tune a model's behaviour deeply rather than only prompt it. Hugging Face is the main hub where these models, and the tools around them, live [5].**


## Should a student project use an open-weight model or an API?

**For most student projects, an API is simpler and cheaper at small scale, no hardware, no hosting. Reach for an open-weight model when the project specifically needs offline operation, strict data privacy, a fine-tuning experiment, or when you are trying to demonstrate hands-on model skills rather than API integration skills for a portfolio. A project explicitly about running or fine-tuning a model is a stronger signal of depth than the same project built entirely on a hosted API.**



## How do I actually contribute to open-source AI projects?

**You do not need to train a model to contribute meaningfully. Improve documentation that confused you as a newcomer. Write or improve an evaluation script. Fix a small, well-scoped bug in a popular library, LangChain, Hugging Face's transformers, a serving framework. Add a missing example or tutorial. Report a reproducible bug with clear steps, which is itself a real contribution [6]. Start with issues labelled "good first issue" on a project you already use, since familiarity with the codebase from actually using it is worth more starting capital than picking a random popular repository.**



My longer notes on open-source contributions specifically for students are on the portfolio [9].

## What mistakes do people make around open source AI?

**Assuming "open source" means fully reproducible and auditable, when it usually means open-weight only. Building a commercial product on a model without reading the license's restrictions on scale or use case. Assuming a fine-tuned derivative automatically inherits full rights to redistribute, when the base model's license terms usually still apply. Contributing a large, unsolicited feature pull request as a first contribution instead of a small, reviewable one.**



## Open source AI interview questions

**Explain the difference between open-weight and fully open-source. Name a license with a real commercial restriction and what it requires. Explain why a student might choose an open-weight model over an API for a specific project. Describe a way to contribute to open-source AI without training a model. The strongest answer references a license you actually read, not a claim from a blog post.**



## Where should I start?

**Pick one open-weight model you might use, and actually read its license file end to end before you build anything on it. Then find one small documentation or bug-fix contribution to make to a library you already use.** For a session on open-source AI, licensing, and contribution for students, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What is OpenAI Whisper? How it works, running it locally, API and translation
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-openai-whisper/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

Whisper is an open-source speech recognition model from OpenAI that turns spoken audio into text in dozens of languages, and can translate speech into English. It was released in 2022 under the MIT licence, so you can run it on your own computer for free, or use OpenAI's hosted speech-to-text API. This page explains what the model is and how it works, who owns it, running it locally, whether the API is free, translation, security, and how it differs from Wispr Flow, a similarly named dictation app. What is OpenAI Whisper? Whisper is an automatic speech recognition (ASR) system made by OpenAI. It transcribes audio into text, detects the spoken language, adds timestamps and can translate other languages into English. OpenAI released the code and model weights openly in September 2022. Because it is open source and strong out of the box, Whisper became the default choice for transcription in many apps: meeting notes, podcast transcripts, subtitles, voice notes and accessibility tools. It handles accents, background noise and technical vocabulary better than many earlier systems, though not perfectly. Developers use it locally through Python or faster community implementations, or through OpenAI's API, which also offers newer transcription models. What is the Whisper AI model? Whisper is a family of transformer models in several sizes, from tiny to large, trading speed for accuracy. Smaller models run quickly on a laptop CPU; the large models are most accurate and benefit from a GPU. Also asked as: what is whisper open ai · what is whisper ai model · what is whisper flow ai The sizes are tiny, base, small, medium and large, with English-only variants of the smaller sizes and later large versions, including a faster "turbo" version, that improved accuracy and speed. Choosing a size: tiny or base: quick drafts, low-power devices. small: a good default on laptops. medium or large: best accuracy, especially for non-English audio and noisy recordings. Test two sizes on your own audio; the right choice depends on your accent mix, noise and speed needs. How does Whisper AI work? Whisper converts audio into a log-Mel spectrogram, a picture of sound frequencies over time, in 30-second windows. A transformer encoder processes that spectrogram, and a decoder generates the text token by token, along with special tokens for language, task and timestamps. Its strength comes from training data: 680,000 hours of multilingual audio paired with transcripts collected from the web, described as weak supervision because the labels are imperfect. Training on such varied data made it robust to accents, recording quality and domains without fine-tuning. The same model handles several tasks, chosen by special tokens: transcribe, translate to English, detect language. Long recordings are processed window by window. Its known weaknesses include occasional hallucinated text during silence or music, and errors with rare names. Who owns Whisper AI? OpenAI created Whisper and maintains the official repository. Because it is released under the MIT licence, anyone can use, modify and include it in commercial products, provided they keep the licence notice. That openness is why many companies and open-source projects build on it, including faster reimplementations such as whisper.cpp and faster-whisper, and products that wrap it with interfaces, diarisation and editing tools. OpenAI also offers hosted transcription through its API, including newer proprietary transcription models. Apps that say they use "Whisper" may be running the open model themselves or calling OpenAI's API, which affects where your audio goes. Is Whisper AI local? It can be. The open-source Whisper model runs entirely on your own computer, offline, with no audio sent anywhere. OpenAI's API version runs on OpenAI's servers instead. Running locally is useful for privacy, such as interviews, medical or legal recordings and personal voice notes, and for cost, since there is no per-minute charge. The trade-off is speed and setup: large models are slow on a CPU, so use a GPU or an optimised implementation such as whisper.cpp or faster-whisper. Apple Silicon Macs and modern NVIDIA GPUs run Whisper well. For live captions with low latency, streaming setups need more engineering than batch transcription. How do I use Whisper AI locally? Install Python and ffmpeg, install the Whisper package, and run it on an audio file from the command line or from Python. Also asked as: how to use whisper ai locally pip install -U openai-whisper whisper meeting.mp3 --model small --language en --output_format srt import whisper model = whisper.load_model(&quot;small&quot;) result = model.transcribe(&quot;meeting.mp3&quot;) print(result[&quot;text&quot;]) Output formats include plain text, subtitles (SRT, VTT) and JSON with timestamps. For speed on a laptop, try faster-whisper or whisper.cpp, which run the same models more efficiently. Set the language explicitly when you know it; automatic detection can misfire on short clips. Is the Whisper AI API free? No. OpenAI's hosted speech-to-text API is paid per minute of audio. The open-source model is free to run on your own hardware, which is the free route. Also asked as: is whisper ai api free The API is convenient: no setup, fast processing and access to newer transcription models in addition to Whisper. It suits apps that need reliable transcription at scale without managing GPUs. For students and personal projects, running the open model locally or in Google Colab is free and often enough. Check OpenAI's pricing page for current rates and file limits, which apply to uploads, so split very long recordings into parts. Can Whisper AI translate? Yes, but only into English. Whisper can take speech in many languages and output an English translation directly, using its translate task. It does not translate English speech into other languages. Use it with --task translate on the command line or task="translate" in Python. Quality depends on the source language and audio; widely spoken languages translate best. For translation into Hindi or other languages, transcribe first in the original language, then translate the text with a language model or a translation service. For Indian languages, test carefully, because accuracy varies by language and accent, and mixed Hindi-English speech is challenging for most systems. Is Whisper AI secure? Run locally, Whisper is as secure as your own computer: the audio and text never leave it. Through an API or a third-party app, security depends on that provider's handling of your recordings. Points to check before using a hosted service for sensitive audio: whether recordings and transcripts are stored and for how long, whether they are used for training, where processing happens, and whether a data processing agreement is available. Get consent before recording anyone. Also watch for hallucinated text: Whisper sometimes produces words that were never spoken, especially during silence or music, which matters for legal, medical or accessibility uses, so review transcripts against the audio. What is Wispr Flow? Wispr Flow is a voice dictation app from a company called Wispr that lets you speak anywhere you type, on desktop and mobile, and turns speech into cleaned-up text. Despite the similar name, it is a separate product, not OpenAI's Whisper model. Dictation apps like Wispr Flow focus on the writing experience: removing filler words, fixing punctuation, adapting tone to the app you are typing in, and working across your applications. Which speech models such apps use behind the scenes is up to the company. If you want free, private transcription of recordings, open-source Whisper on your machine is the closer match; if you want fast dictation across every app, a dedicated dictation tool is more convenient. Check any app's privacy policy, because dictated text often includes sensitive messages.

# What is overfitting in machine learning, and how do you actually prevent it? Train/validation/test splits, regularization, and catching it early
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-overfitting-and-how-to-prevent-it/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is overfitting?

**Overfitting is when a model learns the specifics of its training data, including its noise and quirks, instead of the general pattern underneath it, so it performs very well on the data it was trained on and measurably worse on new data it has not seen. The model has effectively memorised answers rather than learned to reason from inputs to outputs, and the gap between training performance and validation or real-world performance is the tell.**


Every training run I evaluate, classic model or LLM fine-tune, gets checked against this exact failure before I trust a good-looking training metric.

> A model that aces its training data and stumbles on anything new hasn't learned. It has memorised the answer key.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## How is overfitting different from underfitting?

**Overfitting is too much capacity relative to the signal in the data, or too little regularization, so the model fits noise as if it were signal. Underfitting is the opposite: the model is too simple, or trained too little, to capture even the real pattern, and performs poorly on both training and new data. Overfitting shows a large gap between training and validation performance; underfitting shows both scores mediocre and close together. The fixes are opposite too: overfitting needs less capacity or more regularization, underfitting needs more capacity or more training.**



## How does a train/validation/test split actually catch overfitting?

**Training data is what the model learns from. Validation data is held out and checked periodically during training, specifically to notice when validation performance stops improving or starts getting worse while training performance keeps improving, which is overfitting happening in real time. Test data is held out entirely until the very end, used exactly once, to report a final, honest number that was never used to make any decision during development. Without this separation, you have no way to distinguish a model that generalises from one that has simply memorised what you are checking it against.**




## What actually prevents overfitting?

**Regularization techniques such as L1 and L2 penalties discourage the model from relying too heavily on any single feature or weight [1]. Dropout randomly disables a fraction of neurons during training, forcing the network to not depend on any one path through it [2]. Early stopping halts training the moment validation performance stops improving, rather than training until training performance maxes out. More data, and more varied data, reduces the model's ability to memorise specifics because there are simply more specifics than it has capacity to memorise. Simplifying the model, fewer parameters or a shallower architecture, directly reduces its capacity to overfit in the first place.**



## What does overfitting look like when fine-tuning an LLM specifically?

**The model starts repeating training examples' exact phrasing verbatim, even in contexts where it does not quite fit, a strong sign it has memorised specific training completions rather than learned the underlying behaviour. Validation loss on held-out examples rises while training loss keeps falling, the same signature as classic overfitting, but often appearing faster than in classic ML because fine-tuning datasets are typically much smaller than pretraining corpora. The standard fixes shift accordingly: fewer training epochs, a lower learning rate, more varied examples per behaviour rather than many near-duplicates, and parameter-efficient methods like LoRA, which constrain how much the model's weights can shift in the first place [5].**



My longer walkthrough of reading a fine-tuning loss curve specifically, including what a healthy one looks like against an overfitting one, is on the portfolio [9].

## How do I catch overfitting early rather than after the fact?

**Watch the training and validation loss curves together from the first epoch, not just the final metric. The moment validation loss stops improving while training loss keeps dropping, that gap is overfitting starting, and it is far cheaper to stop or adjust there than to discover it only after evaluating a finished model. Set up automatic checkpointing at the point of best validation performance, not the last epoch, so the model you actually keep is the one before the overfitting started, not after.**



## What mistakes do people make with overfitting?

**Reporting training accuracy as if it were the model's real performance. Peeking at the test set during development and unconsciously tuning toward it, which quietly turns the test set into a second validation set and inflates the final number's honesty. Training for a fixed number of epochs regardless of what the validation curve says. Assuming more data always fixes overfitting, when sometimes the actual fix is a simpler model or a smaller learning rate. Ignoring that a small, over-repeated fine-tuning dataset can cause the exact same failure a huge classic-ML model shows with too little data.**



## Overfitting interview questions

**Define overfitting and contrast it with underfitting. Explain why a validation set is necessary and what leaking the test set into development actually breaks. Name three concrete techniques to prevent overfitting and what each one limits. Explain how overfitting shows up differently when fine-tuning an LLM compared with training a classic model. Describe how you would catch it early in a real training run. The strongest answer includes a loss curve you actually read and a decision it drove.**



## Where should I start?

**Look at the training and validation loss curves from your last training run, classic model or fine-tune, side by side. If you cannot find that plot, that is the first thing to fix before the next run.** For a hands-on session on training and evaluating models honestly, from loss curves to held-out test sets, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What is prompt engineering? How it works, examples, courses and jobs
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-prompt-engineering-2/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

Prompt engineering is the practice of designing the instructions, context and examples you give an AI model so that it produces accurate, useful and consistent output. For everyday users it means writing clearer requests; for developers it means system prompts, structured outputs and evaluation inside applications. This page defines it, explains how and why it works, gives examples, points to the best courses and official guides, estimates how long it takes to learn, where to practise, what the jobs look like, and whether it still matters as models improve. What is prompt engineering? Prompt engineering is the process of crafting and refining inputs to a generative AI model, including instructions, context, examples and output format, to get reliable results for a specific task. Also asked as: what is prompt engineering definition · where to practice prompt engineering It covers simple techniques, such as stating the goal and audience, and engineering practices, such as writing system prompts, giving few-shot examples, requiring JSON that matches a schema, splitting tasks into steps, and testing prompts against a set of cases. In applications, prompts are part of the code: versioned, reviewed and evaluated. Good prompt engineering is less about magic phrases and more about clear communication plus measurement. How does AI prompt engineering work? A language model generates text based on everything in its input. Prompt engineering shapes that input: clear instructions, relevant context and examples make the desired answer the most likely continuation, and format rules constrain the output. Common techniques: Role and goal: who the model should act as and what success looks like. Context: the documents, data or code the answer must use. Few-shot examples: two or three input-output pairs showing the format. Decomposition: break complex tasks into steps or separate calls. Reasoning: ask the model to think through the problem before answering. Output contracts: a JSON schema or exact template. Then test on varied examples and adjust based on failures. Why does prompt engineering work? It works because models condition every word they generate on the input. Specific instructions and examples narrow the range of likely outputs towards what you want, while vague prompts leave the model to guess. Research showed early on that large models can learn tasks from a few examples in the prompt, called few-shot learning, and that asking for step-by-step reasoning improves results on maths and logic, known as chain-of-thought prompting. Instruction tuning makes modern models follow directions well, so clear directions matter more than tricks. Context is the biggest lever: giving the model the right document turns a guess into a grounded answer, which is the principle behind retrieval-augmented generation. What are some prompt engineering examples? Examples range from everyday requests to production patterns. A weak prompt is "summarise this"; a strong one is "Summarise this lecture transcript for a first-year student in five bullet points, each under 20 words, then list three terms to revise." Also asked as: what are prompt engineering examples More patterns: Extraction: "Extract name, date and amount from this invoice as JSON matching this schema. Use null if missing." Classification: "Label this support email as billing, technical or other. Reply with the label only." Grounded Q&amp;A: "Answer only from the passages below and cite passage IDs. If the answer is not there, say so." Code review: "Review this function for bugs and security issues. List each with a line number and a fix." Tutoring: "Ask me one question at a time on recursion and explain my mistakes." What are the best prompt engineering courses? Start with free resources: DeepLearning.AI's short course on ChatGPT prompt engineering for developers, and the official prompting guides from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. Then learn by building and evaluating a small application. Also asked as: what are prompt engineering courses Choose courses that teach transferable skills: structured outputs, evaluation with test sets, retrieval-augmented generation, tool use and safety, not lists of "magic prompts". Paid courses can help with structure, but the material changes quickly as models improve, so prefer recently updated content. A practical self-course: pick one task, such as extracting fields from receipts, build a test set of fifty examples, and improve the prompt until accuracy stops rising, logging every change. Where is OpenAI's prompt engineering guide? OpenAI publishes a prompt engineering guide in its platform documentation, covering clear instructions, providing reference text, splitting complex tasks, giving the model time to think, using tools and testing changes systematically. Also asked as: guide prompt engineering openai Read it alongside Anthropic's and Google's guides, since the core advice overlaps and each adds model-specific tips, such as how to use system messages, XML-style tags or structured outputs. Guides are updated as models change, so check the date and prefer official documentation over older blog posts. The most valuable advice in all of them is the same: be specific, give context and examples, and evaluate. How long does it take to learn prompt engineering? The basics take a few days of practice: clear instructions, context, examples and format. Using prompts well inside real applications takes weeks to months, because it involves evaluation, structured outputs, retrieval, tool use and handling edge cases. Also asked as: how long to learn prompt engineering A realistic path for a developer: one week to learn techniques and build a few prompts; two to four weeks to build a small app with a test set and measure improvements; ongoing practice as models change. For non-technical users, a few hours of deliberate practice with real tasks, such as emails, summaries and study notes, already makes a big difference. Speed comes from writing many prompts and examining failures, not from reading lists of templates. Where can I practise prompt engineering? Practise in the free tiers of ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini for everyday tasks, and in developer playgrounds such as Google AI Studio, the OpenAI Playground and Anthropic's Console for system prompts, parameters and structured outputs. Good practice tasks: Turn messy notes into a structured study guide. Extract fields from ten real receipts into JSON, then measure accuracy. Build a classifier for messages into three categories with a test set. Write a grounded Q&amp;A prompt over a document and test unanswerable questions. Compare two models on the same prompts. Keep a prompt log: the prompt, the model, the result and what you changed. That log is how you improve. What are prompt engineering jobs? Dedicated "prompt engineer" roles exist but are uncommon; prompt engineering is now mostly a skill within roles such as AI engineer, GenAI developer, ML engineer, AI product manager, conversation designer, technical writer and domain experts who build AI workflows. Employers hiring for GenAI work expect prompt skills plus software engineering: APIs, retrieval, evaluation, deployment and cost control. Domain experts, such as lawyers, doctors and teachers, with strong prompting skills are also valuable for building and testing AI tools in their fields. To show the skill, build a project with a measurable result, such as "improved extraction accuracy from 78 to 95 per cent on 200 documents by restructuring the prompt and adding validation", documented in a README. Does prompt engineering still matter? Yes, but its form has changed. Models now follow plain instructions well, so tricks matter less, while clear specifications, good context, structured outputs and evaluation matter more than ever, especially in products and agents. What has faded: elaborate magic phrases and fragile hacks. What remains: clearly defining the task, supplying the right information, setting output contracts, and testing systematically. In agentic systems, writing tool descriptions and system instructions is prompt engineering under another name. As models improve, the bottleneck shifts from wording to knowing exactly what you want and giving the model what it needs to do it.

# What is quantization in LLMs? 4-bit and 8-bit models, GGUF vs AWQ vs GPTQ, quality loss, and running big models on small hardware
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-quantization-in-llms/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is quantization in LLMs?

**Quantization is storing a model's weights, and sometimes its activations, in fewer bits than they were trained in: 8-bit or 4-bit integers instead of 16-bit floats. Each weight is mapped to a small grid of values with a scale factor per block, so the model takes a half or a quarter of the memory and often runs faster, at the cost of a small approximation error. It is why a 7-billion-parameter model that needs about 14 GB in 16-bit runs on a laptop with 8 GB in 4-bit.**


Quantization is the reason open models became usable outside data centres. LLM.int8() showed 8-bit inference at scale with almost no loss [1]; the k-bit scaling-law paper argued that for a fixed memory budget, 4-bit weights on a bigger model usually beat 16-bit weights on a smaller one [5]. QLoRA then made 4-bit the basis for training, not just inference [2].

I quantize every model that leaves FineTune Studio, because a fine-tuned adapter is only useful once it is running somewhere, and "somewhere" is usually a machine smaller than the one that trained it [12].

> Quantization is the difference between a model that impressed you in a notebook and a model your users can actually run.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## How does quantization work?

**Weights are grouped into blocks, typically 32 to 128 values. For each block, the largest magnitude sets a scale, and every weight is rounded to the nearest point on a small integer grid, 256 points for 8-bit, 16 for 4-bit. At inference, the integers are multiplied back by the scale, exactly or approximately, before the matrix multiplication. Smarter methods choose the grid or the rounding to minimise error on real activations rather than on the weights alone.**



### What is NF4?

**NF4, NormalFloat4, is the 4-bit data type QLoRA introduced: instead of an evenly spaced grid, its 16 levels are placed where normally distributed weights actually cluster, so the same 4 bits capture more of the distribution [2]. It is a training-time quantization for the frozen base model, held in memory while adapters train; it is not a serving format. When people fine-tune "in 4-bit", this is usually what they mean.**


## What are GGUF, AWQ and GPTQ?

**GGUF is a file format used by llama.cpp that packages a quantized model with its metadata for fast loading on CPUs, Apple Silicon and consumer GPUs; its quantization schemes are named like Q4_K_M and Q8_0 [6]. GPTQ is a post-training method that quantizes weights layer by layer using calibration data to minimise output error, aimed at GPU inference [3]. AWQ observes that a small fraction of weights matter far more, protects them by scaling, and quantizes the rest, also for GPUs [4]. Same goal, different trade-offs and runtimes.**



The rule of thumb I give: GGUF if it runs on a laptop or a phone, AWQ or GPTQ if it runs on a GPU server behind vLLM [10], NF4 through bitsandbytes if you are training [7]. The Transformers quantization guide covers loading each [8].

## How much quality do you lose with quantization?

**Little at 8-bit, usually within noise on most benchmarks. Modest at 4-bit for chat, summarisation and extraction, and more noticeable on arithmetic, code generation and long multi-step reasoning, where small errors compound. Below 4 bits the drop steepens quickly. Larger models tolerate quantization better than small ones, so a 4-bit 13B usually beats a 16-bit 7B in the same memory [5]. Measure on your own task before trusting any of these generalisations.**




## How is quantization related to QLoRA and fine-tuning?

**QLoRA quantizes the frozen base model to NF4 so it fits in memory while small adapters train in higher precision [2]. That is quantization for training. After training you merge the adapter into the 16-bit base weights and then quantize the merged model for serving with GGUF, AWQ or GPTQ. Do not quantize before merging, and do not merge into a 4-bit base for serving; reload the base in 16-bit, merge, then quantize.**



My own notes on this pipeline, with the commands, are on the portfolio [11].


## How much memory does a quantized model need?

**Roughly parameters in billions times bytes per weight, plus a few gigabytes for activations and the KV cache that grows with context length and concurrent users. Two bytes per weight at 16-bit, one at 8-bit, about half a byte at 4-bit. So 7B is about 14, 7 and 4 to 5 GB; 13B about 26, 13 and 8 GB; 70B about 140, 70 and 40 GB. Long contexts add memory fast, which is why a model that "fits" can still run out at 32,000 tokens.**



## How do I quantize a model myself?

**For local use: convert the merged model to GGUF with llama.cpp's conversion script and quantize to a variant such as Q4_K_M or Q8_0, then run it with llama.cpp or Ollama [6][9]. For GPU serving: quantize with AWQ or GPTQ using a few hundred calibration samples that resemble your real inputs, then serve with vLLM [10]. For loading in Transformers without a conversion step: bitsandbytes 8-bit or 4-bit at load time [7]. Always keep the 16-bit merged model as the source of truth.**


## Which quantization should I choose?

**Decide by where the model runs and what it does. Laptop or phone: GGUF Q4_K_M as the default, Q8_0 if memory allows. GPU server: AWQ or GPTQ 4-bit behind vLLM, 8-bit if quality on hard tasks matters. Training: NF4 via bitsandbytes. Maths, code or long reasoning as the main task: prefer 8-bit or a bigger 4-bit model. Then confirm on your eval set. The wrong answer is to skip the measurement.**



## Quantization interview questions

**Explain what quantization does and why it saves memory. Compare 8-bit and 4-bit loss. Explain the difference between GGUF, AWQ and GPTQ and where each runs. Explain NF4 and its role in QLoRA. Describe the adapter-to-serving pipeline. Estimate the memory of a 13B model at 4-bit. Each is answered above; the strongest evidence is a model you quantized and measured.**



## Where should I start?

**Pull a 7B model in GGUF through Ollama at Q4_K_M and at Q8_0, ask each the same twenty questions including some arithmetic and code, and note where they differ. Then quantize a model you fine-tuned yourself and run the same comparison against the 16-bit merged version.** For a hands-on session on fine-tuning and deploying models on modest hardware, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.
