# What is RAG in AI? Retrieval-augmented generation, explained from a production system
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-rag-in-ai/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is RAG in AI?

**RAG, retrieval-augmented generation, is a way of building AI answers in two moves: first search a store of your own documents for the passages most relevant to the question, then hand those passages to a large language model and have it write the answer from them, with citations.** The model no longer answers from memory alone. It answers from evidence you chose, which is why RAG is the default architecture for chatbots over company documents, support desks, legal and medical search, and any product where "I'm not sure" beats a confident guess.


The term comes from a 2020 paper by Patrick Lewis and colleagues at Facebook AI Research, which combined a dense retriever with a sequence-to-sequence generator and showed the pair beat purely parametric models on knowledge-intensive tasks while producing more specific, factual language [1]. The idea has since grown into an entire engineering discipline, catalogued in surveys such as Gao et al. [2].

The one-sentence version I give students: a plain LLM is a very well-read person answering with the library door locked. RAG unlocks the door, walks them to the right shelf, and asks them to quote the page.

> A RAG demo works on the one document you tested it with. A RAG product works on the document a stranger uploads at 2 a.m. Everything in this guide is about closing that gap.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour, from building RAG.NextUpgrad</cite>

## How does RAG work?

**RAG runs in two phases. Offline, you split documents into chunks, turn each chunk into an embedding vector and store it in an index. Online, you embed the user's question, pull the closest chunks, optionally rerank them, and prompt the model with the question plus those chunks so it answers from them.**



The offline phase is where most quality is won or lost, because everything downstream can only choose among the chunks you created. The online phase is where latency and cost live, since each question costs an embedding call, a search, possibly a reranker pass and a generation.

In RAG.NextUpgrad, the platform I built at NextUpgrad in 2026, the online path looks like this: the query is embedded and also tokenised for BM25, both retrievers return candidates, reciprocal rank fusion merges them, a cross-encoder reranks the top set, a confidence gate checks whether the evidence actually supports an answer, and only then does the model stream a response with inline citations [17].

### What is a RAG pipeline?

**A RAG pipeline is the chain of components that turns a raw document collection and a user question into a cited answer: loaders, a chunker, an embedding model, a vector index, usually a keyword index, a retriever, a reranker, a prompt template, the LLM and an evaluation harness.** Frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex give you each piece; the engineering is in choosing and tuning them for your documents.


### What is a RAG model?

**There is no separate "RAG model". RAG is a system pattern that wraps an ordinary language model, open or closed, with a retriever.** The original paper trained the retriever and generator jointly [1], but almost every production system today uses an off-the-shelf embedding model for retrieval and an off-the-shelf LLM for generation, connected by code.


## Why do we need RAG? Why is it important?

**RAG solves three problems a plain LLM cannot: it knows nothing after its training cutoff, it knows nothing about your private data, and when it lacks facts it invents plausible text. Retrieval supplies current, private, checkable facts at answer time, so the model can quote instead of guess.**


The practical benefits, in the order clients care about them:

- **Grounding and citations.** Every sentence can point at the passage it came from, which makes answers auditable. This matters more than raw accuracy in regulated work.
- **Freshness without retraining.** Add a document to the index and it is answerable a minute later. Retraining or fine-tuning a model for new facts takes hours and still does not cite.
- **Access control.** Retrieval can filter by user, tenant or clearance before the model ever sees the text. A fine-tuned model has no such boundary.
- **Cost.** Retrieval is cheap compared with training, and with a small model plus good retrieval you often match a much larger model answering from memory.

The limit is just as important: RAG helps with what the model knows, not how it reasons or writes. If your problem is tone, format or a specialised skill, retrieval will not fix it. That is where fine-tuning belongs.

## What is the difference between RAG and fine-tuning?

**RAG changes what the model can see at answer time; fine-tuning changes the model's weights, so it changes how the model behaves. Use RAG when the answer depends on facts, documents or anything that changes. Use fine-tuning when you need a consistent style, a strict output format, a niche skill, or lower latency and cost on a narrow task. Many production systems do both.**




I have built both kinds of platform in the same year, RAG.NextUpgrad and FineTune Studio, and the question I ask clients is one word: is the problem *knowledge* or *behaviour*? Knowledge is retrieval. Behaviour is training. A support bot that must know your refund policy is a knowledge problem. A model that must write incident reports in your house format is a behaviour problem. A bot that must do both is RAG for the policy and a small fine-tune for the voice.

### What is the difference between RAG and prompt engineering?

**Prompt engineering writes better instructions for the model; RAG adds a retrieval system that supplies evidence to those instructions. Prompt engineering alone cannot give the model facts it never saw, but every RAG system still needs a well-engineered prompt that tells the model to answer only from the passages and to say so when they are insufficient.**


## What is chunking in RAG, and what is the best chunking strategy?

**Chunking is splitting documents into passages that can be embedded and retrieved on their own. The best strategy respects the document's structure, headings, paragraphs, table rows and code blocks, keeps chunks small enough to be precise and large enough to be understood alone, and prepends the section heading to each chunk so a passage carries its context.**


There is no universal chunk size, and anyone quoting one without asking about your documents is guessing. What holds across the projects I have shipped:

1. **Chunk for the question, not the document.** A chunk should be able to answer a realistic user question by itself. For policy documents that is often a few hundred tokens; for API references it can be one function signature plus its description.
2. **Overlap is insurance, not a strategy.** A small overlap catches sentences that straddle a boundary. Large overlaps duplicate what the reranker sees and inflate the index.
3. **Never split inside a structure.** Tables, code blocks, numbered procedures, and a heading with its first paragraph belong together. Splitting them yields chunks that are individually meaningless.
4. **Carry the heading.** Prepending "Section 4.2, Rate limits" to a chunk that says "the limit is 5 requests per second" did more for answer accuracy in RAG.NextUpgrad than any embedding model change.


Barnett et al. list missing content and wrongly ranked chunks among the seven failure points of RAG systems, and both usually trace back to chunking decisions [10].

## What are embeddings, and which embedding model is best for RAG?

**An embedding is a list of numbers, a vector, that represents the meaning of a piece of text so that texts about the same thing end up close together. RAG uses embeddings to find chunks that are semantically similar to the question even when they share no keywords. The best model is the one that scores well on retrieval for your language and domain on the MTEB benchmark and fits your latency and cost budget; test two or three on your own questions before committing.**


Dense retrieval with learned embeddings was shown to beat traditional keyword retrieval for open-domain question answering by Karpukhin et al. in 2020 [3], and that result is why almost every RAG system starts with a vector index. Three practical notes:

- **Dimensions are a trade-off, not a score.** A 1,536-dimension vector costs more storage and search time than a 384-dimension one. Whether it retrieves better for you is an empirical question.
- **Embeddings are not tokens.** Tokens are the pieces a model reads; an embedding is a single vector summarising a whole chunk. People search for the difference often enough that it deserves saying plainly.
- **Switching models means re-embedding everything.** Vectors from two models are not comparable. Budget for a full re-index when you upgrade.

The MTEB leaderboard on Hugging Face ranks open and commercial embedding models on retrieval and other tasks [14]. Use it to shortlist, then evaluate on your own documents, because leaderboard corpora are not your corpus.

## What is a vector database, and do I need one?

**A vector database stores embeddings and answers "which stored vectors are closest to this one" quickly, usually with an approximate nearest-neighbour index. You need one when your index outgrows memory, needs filtering by metadata, or must serve many concurrent users. For a prototype or a few hundred thousand chunks, a library such as FAISS or the pgvector extension inside the Postgres you already run is enough.**



FAISS is described in Johnson, Douze and Jégou's 2017 paper and remains the reference implementation for in-process search [7]. pgvector adds vector columns and indexes to PostgreSQL [15]. Qdrant is documented at qdrant.tech [16]. My default for a new client project is pgvector, because the vectors then live next to the metadata, the permissions and the audit log, and "one more database to operate" is a real cost for a small team.

## What is hybrid search in RAG?

**Hybrid search runs two retrievers on every question, a keyword retriever such as BM25 and a dense embedding retriever, then merges their ranked lists. Keywords catch exact terms, product codes, names and rare words that embeddings blur; embeddings catch paraphrases and meaning that keywords miss. Fusing them, most simply with reciprocal rank fusion, gives better recall than either alone.**


BM25 is the classic probabilistic ranking function, described in full by Robertson and Zaragoza [4]. Reciprocal rank fusion, from Cormack, Clarke and Buettcher, scores each document by the sum of 1 divided by (a constant plus its rank) in every list, which needs no score normalisation and was shown to outperform more complex fusion methods [5]. It is a dozen lines of code and it is in RAG.NextUpgrad exactly because of that paper.

The pattern I see in support corpora: users ask with the product's own words ("error E-4021", "Form 16"), and dense retrieval alone often returns something semantically nearby but wrong. BM25 nails the exact token. The reverse happens for how-do-I questions phrased in plain language, where BM25 misses and embeddings win. Hybrid is not a luxury; it is the fix for both.

## What is reranking in RAG?

**Reranking is a second scoring pass over the top retrieved candidates using a model that reads the question and the passage together, a cross-encoder, and outputs a relevance score. Retrievers compare vectors computed separately for speed; a reranker looks at the pair, which is far more accurate, so you retrieve, say, 30 candidates and rerank to the best 5 before generation.**


Passage reranking with BERT-style cross-encoders was introduced by Nogueira and Cho in 2019 and remains the standard recipe [6]. It also addresses a known weakness of long prompts: Liu et al. showed that models use information at the start and end of a long context far better than information in the middle [8], so sending five well-ordered passages beats sending thirty in a heap.

## How do I build a RAG chatbot?

**Start with one document type and ten real questions. Load and chunk the documents with structure-aware splitting, embed with a model you shortlisted from MTEB, index in pgvector or FAISS, add BM25, retrieve with both and fuse with reciprocal rank fusion, rerank with a cross-encoder, and prompt the model to answer only from the passages and to cite them. Measure retrieval recall on your ten questions before touching the prompt. Then add streaming, a confidence gate and logging.**


The skeleton of the query side, without any framework, is short enough to read:

```python
def answer(question: str) -> dict:
    q_vec = embed(question)                       # same model used at index time
    dense = vector_index.search(q_vec, k=30)      # pgvector / FAISS / Qdrant
    sparse = bm25_index.search(question, k=30)    # keyword retriever
    fused = reciprocal_rank_fusion([dense, sparse], k=60)
    top = rerank(question, fused[:30])[:5]        # cross-encoder scores the pairs
    if confidence(question, top) < THRESHOLD:     # evidence too weak
        return {"answer": None, "reason": "no supporting passages", "sources": []}
    prompt = build_prompt(question, top)          # "answer only from these passages, cite [n]"
    return {"answer": llm(prompt), "sources": [c.source for c in top]}
```

Everything else, ingestion jobs, a UI, authentication, tenant filters, is ordinary software engineering. In RAG.NextUpgrad that engineering includes Docker, CI/CD, structured logging, and a test suite of 196 tests, and the whole service runs in about 220 MB of RAM on a free tier, which is a useful reminder that RAG is not inherently heavy [17].


### Which framework should I use, LangChain or LlamaIndex, or none?

**Use a framework to prototype and to borrow loaders, then own the retrieval code yourself once you know what your system needs.** Both LangChain and LlamaIndex are excellent for getting to a first answer in an afternoon. The trouble comes later, when a bug sits under three layers of abstraction. The query path above is a few hundred lines; you can read all of it.


## How do I evaluate a RAG pipeline?

**Evaluate retrieval and generation separately. For retrieval, build a set of real questions with the passages that should be returned and measure recall at k, the share of questions where a correct passage is in the top k. For generation, measure faithfulness, whether every claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved passages, and answer relevance. Frameworks such as RAGAS automate the generation metrics with an LLM judge, but the retrieval set you must build by hand.**


RAGAS, from Es et al., defines faithfulness, answer relevance and context relevance as reference-free metrics scored by a model [9]. They are useful, and they are not a substitute for a human-labelled retrieval set, because a system can be perfectly faithful to the wrong passage.


The metric that changed my own systems most was the simplest: for each question, was the right chunk anywhere in the top 30? When it was not, no prompt or model could help, and the fix was always upstream, in chunking or in adding keyword retrieval.

## Why does RAG fail, and how do I fix it?

**RAG fails for a small number of repeatable reasons: the answer was never in the index, it was in the index but chunked so it lost its meaning, retrieval ranked the right chunk too low, the model ignored the passages and answered from memory, or the passages contradicted each other and the model picked wrong. Each has a specific fix, and the fix is almost never "a bigger model".**



Barnett et al. catalogue seven failure points from three case studies, from missing content to incomplete answers, and their central observation matches my experience: you only discover most failures in operation, so logging every retrieval and every answer is part of the architecture, not an add-on [10].

## What is a confidence gate, and why did I build one?

**A confidence gate is a check between retrieval and generation that measures how strongly the retrieved passages support an answer, and refuses to generate when support is weak. Instead of a fluent hallucination the user sees "I could not find this in the documents", with the option to rephrase or upload more. It turns the most dangerous RAG failure, a confident wrong answer, into an honest non-answer.**


In RAG.NextUpgrad the gate looks at reranker scores and the agreement between passages before any tokens are generated. The threshold is tuned on the evaluation set so that it rarely blocks answerable questions. This is the single feature clients noticed most, and I wrote up the reasoning in a separate article [18]. Research is moving the same way: Self-RAG trains a model to decide when to retrieve and to critique its own output with reflection tokens [12].

> The model is never allowed to guess. If the evidence is not there, the honest answer is that the evidence is not there, and the product says so out loud.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour, RAG.NextUpgrad design note</cite>

## What is agentic RAG, and what is Graph RAG?

**Agentic RAG puts a planning loop around retrieval: the model decides whether to retrieve, rewrites the query, calls several retrievers or tools, checks the results, and retrieves again if needed, instead of doing one fixed search. Graph RAG builds a knowledge graph of entities and relationships from the documents and retrieves over that graph, which helps with questions that need connections across many documents, such as "what are the main themes in this corpus".**



Microsoft's Graph RAG paper describes building an entity graph with community summaries and shows gains on global, sense-making questions over a corpus [13]. HyDE, another retrieval upgrade, has the model write a hypothetical answer first and embeds that to search, which helps when questions are short and vague [11]. My advice to students is to climb the levels above in order. Agentic loops and graphs are level-eight problems; most systems I audit are stuck at level two.

## Is RAG still relevant with long context windows?

**Yes. Long context windows let you paste more into a prompt, but they do not tell you which of a million documents to paste, they cost per token on every question, and models still attend unevenly across long inputs. Retrieval is how you choose what deserves the context window. Longer windows make RAG easier, because you can send more and better passages, not unnecessary.**


Liu et al.'s finding that accuracy drops when relevant information sits in the middle of a long context is the empirical reason retrieval and reranking still matter [8]. The economics are the practical reason: a 200-page manual is hundreds of thousands of tokens; five reranked passages are a few thousand.

## What are common RAG interview questions?

**Expect to explain the two phases, to compare RAG with fine-tuning, to describe chunking trade-offs, to justify hybrid search and reranking, to define recall and faithfulness, and to walk through a failure you debugged. Interviewers are testing whether you have operated a RAG system, not whether you can recite the paper.**


The questions that separate candidates, from the interviewing I have done for SCULT INDIA and from the sessions I run for students:

1. How do you know your retrieval is working before you look at the answers?
2. A user says the bot gave a wrong answer. Walk me through your debugging, in order.
3. Why would you add BM25 to a system that already has embeddings?
4. What happens when two retrieved passages disagree?
5. How do you stop the model answering when the documents do not contain the answer?

If you can answer those five from experience, you can build the system. The rest of this guide is the experience, compressed.


## Where can I learn RAG properly?

**Read the original paper and the 2023 survey for the map, build one pipeline by hand without a framework so you understand every stage, then evaluate it on your own questions. That order, paper, build, measure, teaches more than any course, and it is exactly what I ask of students who want to work on retrieval systems with me.**


A good first project is a RAG system over your own college's notes, syllabus and previous-year papers, because you can judge the answers yourself and the documents are messy in exactly the ways real client documents are. I mentor students through TechVerse Enclave on projects like this, and the ones who finish have something no certificate gives them: a system they can explain failure by failure. If you want to talk RAG at your college or hackathon, my email is pranjulrathour41@gmail.com and the invite page is at pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What is RAG in LLMs? How RAG works, building it, and fixing bad results
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-rag-in-llm/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

RAG, retrieval-augmented generation, is a way of using a large language model where the system first retrieves relevant passages from your own documents and then has the LLM answer from them. It gives LLMs knowledge they were not trained on, keeps answers current without retraining, and lets every answer cite its source. I built RAG.NextUpgrad, a production RAG platform with hybrid retrieval, re-ranking and a confidence gate, so this page explains RAG in LLMs from practice: how it works, how to build and update it, how to evaluate it on a budget, and why results go wrong. What is RAG in LLMs? RAG in LLMs means retrieval-augmented generation: before the model answers, a retriever searches a document collection for passages relevant to the question, and those passages are added to the prompt so the LLM answers from them. The term comes from a 2020 research paper that combined a neural retriever with a generator. Today it describes a broad pattern used in company knowledge bots, customer support, document Q&amp;A and research assistants. The LLM provides language understanding and fluent answers; retrieval provides the facts. Done well, users get specific answers with citations they can check, instead of the model's general and possibly outdated memory. What is a RAG system? A RAG system is the full application that implements retrieval-augmented generation: document ingestion and chunking, an index such as a vector store with keyword search, a retrieval and reranking step, a prompt that grounds the LLM, and evaluation and monitoring. Also asked as: what is rag system Components in a production system: Ingestion: load PDFs, web pages and databases; clean text; keep metadata. Chunking: split into passages that keep meaning together. Indexing: embeddings in a vector index plus a keyword index. Retrieval: hybrid search, merged with reciprocal-rank fusion. Reranking: a cross-encoder reorders the top candidates. Generation: grounded prompt, citations, refusal on weak evidence. Operations: updates, logging, evaluation, cost control. How does RAG work with an LLM? The user's question is turned into a search, the most relevant chunks are retrieved and ranked, and the top few are placed into the LLM's prompt with instructions to answer only from them and cite them. The LLM writes the answer. Also asked as: how does rag work in llm Step by step: embed the question; search the vector index and the keyword index; merge and rerank results; select the top passages within the context budget; build a prompt with the passages labelled by ID; generate the answer with citations; check that citations point to real passages; and decline if the evidence was weak. Streaming the answer keeps the experience fast. Logging the retrieved passages for every query is what lets you debug wrong answers later. How does RAG enhance an LLM? RAG gives an LLM access to private, recent and specific information, reduces hallucinations by grounding answers in sources, enables citations, and lets you update knowledge by updating documents instead of retraining the model. Also asked as: how does rag enhance llm It also lowers cost and risk compared with fine-tuning for knowledge: smaller models can answer well when given the right passages, and access control can be applied at retrieval time so users only get answers from documents they are allowed to see. The limits are equally important: RAG cannot fix bad source documents, and if retrieval misses the right passage, the model has nothing correct to work with. That is why retrieval quality is the main lever. What is the difference between RAG and an LLM? An LLM is a trained model that generates text from its input. RAG is a system design that adds a retrieval step before the LLM, so the model's input includes relevant documents. RAG uses an LLM; it is not an alternative to one. Also asked as: difference between rag and llm Without RAG, the LLM answers from what it learned in training, with no access to your files and no sources. With RAG, it answers from passages your system chose. That changes accuracy, freshness and trust. RAG is also different from fine-tuning, which changes the model's weights; RAG changes only what the model reads at question time, which makes it far easier to update and audit. How do I build a RAG-based LLM application? Start with a small, real document set and a list of real questions, build a simple pipeline end to end, measure retrieval and answer quality, then improve the weakest part. Resist adding complexity before you can measure it. Also asked as: a comprehensive guide for building rag-based llm applications A build order that works: Collect 50 real questions with known answers in your documents. Ingest and chunk documents by structure, such as headings, with page numbers in metadata. Index with embeddings and BM25; merge results with reciprocal-rank fusion. Add a cross-encoder reranker on the top candidates. Prompt the LLM to answer only from passages, with citations. Add a confidence gate that declines on weak evidence. Evaluate after every change. RAG.NextUpgrad follows this design and runs in about 220 MB on a free tier. How do I keep information updated in a RAG system? Re-index incrementally: detect new, changed and deleted documents, re-chunk and re-embed only what changed, and delete outdated chunks so old versions never reach the model. Store document versions and timestamps in metadata. Also asked as: how to keep updated information in a rag system Practical habits: Give every chunk an ID derived from its document and position, so updates replace rather than duplicate. Track a hash of each document to detect changes cheaply. Schedule syncs from source systems, or trigger them on changes. Filter or boost by date for time-sensitive questions. Show the source date in citations so users see how current an answer is. If you change the embedding model, re-embed everything; vectors from different models are not comparable. How do I evaluate a RAG system with a local or free-tier model? Build a test set, measure retrieval with simple metrics that need no model, and use a local model through Ollama or a free API tier as a judge for answer faithfulness, checking a sample by hand to confirm the judge agrees with you. Also asked as: how to evaluate my rag system using local / free tier api model Steps: Write 50 questions with the passage that answers each. Compute recall at 5 and 10 for retrieval: free, fast and deterministic. Generate answers and ask a judge model: is every claim supported by the passages? Include unanswerable questions and measure how often the system declines. Hand-check 20 judged answers to calibrate. Small local judges are less reliable than large ones, so keep the rubric simple, binary where possible, and trust retrieval metrics most. Why do RAG hallucinations often start at ingestion? Because bad ingestion corrupts what the model reads: broken PDF extraction, tables flattened into nonsense, headers repeated in every chunk, lost page structure, or chunks that split a fact from its context. The LLM then faithfully answers from garbled or misleading text. Also asked as: why your rag system hallucinations start at ingestion, not the llm Fixes at ingestion: Use layout-aware extraction or OCR for scanned and complex PDFs. Keep tables as tables, or convert them to clear text rows. Strip repeated headers, footers and navigation. Chunk by headings and paragraphs, with overlap where meaning spans boundaries. Carry titles and section names into each chunk. Inspect random chunks by eye before indexing; many "model" problems disappear once the text is clean. Why does a large FAISS RAG system return irrelevant results? With many chunks, pure semantic search tends to surface passages that are topically similar but not relevant, especially when chunks are noisy, embeddings are mismatched, or the index uses approximate settings that trade recall for speed. Also asked as: why does my 150k chunks faiss-based rag system return irrelevant results for semantic search queries Common causes and fixes: Mixed or mismatched embeddings: use one model for indexing and queries, and normalise vectors for cosine similarity. Noisy chunks: remove boilerplate and duplicates. Approximate index settings: raise nprobe for IVF or efSearch for HNSW and measure recall. No keyword search: add BM25 and fuse results. No reranking: rerank the top 50 with a cross-encoder. Wrong scope: filter by metadata such as document type or date. Measure recall at 10 before and after each change.

# What is RLHF, instruction tuning and DPO? How base models become assistants, what alignment training actually does, and when a small team should use it
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-rlhf-instruction-tuning-and-dpo/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is RLHF?

**Reinforcement learning from human feedback is the training stage that turns an instruction-following model into one whose answers people prefer. Humans compare pairs of model answers to the same prompt and pick the better one; a reward model is trained to predict those preferences; the language model is then optimised with reinforcement learning, classically PPO, to produce answers the reward model scores highly, with a penalty for drifting too far from the starting model [1][2]. It is how InstructGPT and the first ChatGPT were trained, and it is why assistants sound the way they do [1][3].**


Fine-tune Studio, the training platform I built, stops at supervised fine-tuning for a reason that this page explains: for most teams, the preference stage costs more in data than it returns in quality, and knowing where it does pay off is the useful part [14].

> Every alignment method is a way to spend human judgement efficiently. The algorithm is a detail; the comparisons are the product.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## What is a base model, and what is instruction tuning?

**A base model is trained only to predict the next token over a huge corpus, so given "What is the capital of France?" it may continue with another question rather than an answer, because that is what documents look like. Instruction tuning, also called supervised fine-tuning or SFT, trains the base model on demonstrations: prompts paired with good responses, in a chat format, so it learns to answer rather than continue [1][9]. FLAN showed instruction-tuned models generalise to unseen tasks [9]; LIMA showed a thousand very good demonstrations can be enough for the format [10].**



## How does RLHF work step by step?

**Start from an instruction-tuned model. Sample several answers per prompt. Have humans rank or compare them. Train a reward model, usually a copy of the language model with a scalar head, to predict which answer wins. Then run reinforcement learning: the policy generates an answer, the reward model scores it, and the policy is updated to increase the score while a KL penalty keeps it close to the SFT model so it does not collapse into reward-gaming gibberish [1]. Iterate with fresh comparisons as the policy changes.**



## What is DPO, and why did it replace much of RLHF?

**Direct preference optimisation skips the reward model and the reinforcement learning. It takes the same comparison data, preferred and rejected answer per prompt, and trains the language model directly with a loss that raises the likelihood of the preferred answer relative to the rejected one, measured against a frozen reference model [4]. The paper shows this is mathematically equivalent to optimising the RLHF objective under the usual reward model assumptions, with none of the instability or infrastructure of PPO. It became the default for open models because a fine-tuning script can run it.**



## What are ORPO, KTO and GRPO?

**Variants that change what data or memory the preference stage needs. ORPO folds preference learning into the SFT stage with an odds-ratio term, so no reference model is needed and one training run does both [6]. KTO works from single answers labelled good or bad instead of pairs, which is much cheaper to collect from real users, who give thumbs up or down rather than comparing two answers [7]. GRPO is a reinforcement learning method that estimates the baseline from a group of sampled answers rather than a value model, used to train reasoning models on verifiable rewards such as maths answers [8].**



## What is RLAIF and Constitutional AI?

**Reinforcement learning from AI feedback replaces some or all of the human comparisons with judgements from a model, guided by written principles. Constitutional AI is the best-known form: the model critiques and revises its own answers against a set of principles, the revisions become SFT data, and a model-generated preference set trains the reward model [5]. It makes preference data cheap and scalable, at the cost of inheriting the judging model's biases. Most current open preference datasets are at least partly model-judged.**



## What does preference data look like, and how much do I need?

**A prompt, a chosen answer and a rejected answer, in the model's chat format, with the difference between them being the behaviour you want to teach: more accurate, better formatted, more concise, safer, more on-brand. Quality dominates quantity; a few thousand clean pairs where the preference is unambiguous beat fifty thousand noisy ones. The cheapest real source is your own product: two generations, a user choice, or thumbs up and down for KTO. The most common mistake is pairs where the rejected answer is obviously broken, which teaches the model nothing about the hard cases.**



## What goes wrong in RLHF and DPO?

**Reward hacking: the policy finds outputs the reward model over-scores, such as longer answers, confident tone or particular phrases, without being better. Sycophancy: models learn that agreeing with the user is preferred, and start agreeing when the user is wrong [11]. Over-refusal: safety preferences push the model to decline reasonable requests. Mode collapse: the model's answers become samey. Length bias is the most common of all, because raters prefer longer answers slightly and the optimiser amplifies it. Each is a data or reward problem and shows up in evals before users notice, if you have evals.**



## Should a student or small team do RLHF or DPO?

**Usually not yet. Supervised fine-tuning with LoRA on a few thousand good examples captures most of what a small team needs: format, tone, domain vocabulary, task behaviour. Preference tuning pays off when you have real comparisons from users, a measured quality gap that SFT could not close, and an eval set to prove the gap closed. If you have those, DPO or KTO with the TRL library on a LoRA adapter is a weekend of work on a rented GPU [12][13]. If you do not, the time is better spent on data and evals.**



## How do I run DPO in practice?

**Start from your SFT model. Build the preference set in the chosen and rejected format. Use the TRL DPO trainer with a LoRA adapter, a small learning rate, one to three epochs, and the SFT model as the frozen reference [13]. Evaluate against the SFT model on a held-out set with a model judge and with your task metrics. Check for length inflation explicitly. Keep the adapter that wins the eval, and log everything so the run can be reproduced.**



## RLHF and DPO interview questions

**Explain the three training stages. Describe how a reward model is trained and why the KL penalty exists. Derive or sketch why DPO needs no reward model. Compare DPO, KTO and ORPO by the data each needs. Name three failure modes and their causes. Explain what GRPO changes and where verifiable rewards apply. Say when you would not do preference tuning. The strongest answer includes an SFT run you evaluated and a reason you did or did not go further.**



## Where should I start?

**Read the DPO paper's first four pages, then run the TRL DPO example on a small model with a public preference set for one epoch and compare outputs against the starting model. An evening, and the abstractions become concrete.** For a workshop on fine-tuning and alignment for students, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What is system design? Interviews, examples, AI system design, and preparation
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-system-design/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

System design is the process of deciding how a software system is built to meet its requirements: which components it has, how data flows between them, where data is stored, how it scales, and what happens when parts fail. It is also a standard interview round for software engineers. This page explains system design and how it differs from architecture, what interviews test and how to prepare, works through an example, covers AI and agentic system design, asks whether it is AI-proof, and clears up two other meanings: VLSI system design and UI design systems. What is system design? System design is planning the structure of a software system: its components, such as services, databases, caches and queues, the interfaces between them, and the trade-offs that let it meet functional needs and goals such as scale, latency, reliability and cost. Also asked as: system design vs architecture A system design starts from requirements: what users must be able to do, and how many users, how fast, how reliable. Then you choose components and data models, estimate load, plan for failure, and decide on trade-offs, such as consistency versus availability, or cost versus speed. Good designs are as simple as the requirements allow and evolve as the product grows. The skill combines knowledge of building blocks with judgement about which ones fit. What is a system design interview? A system design interview asks you to design a system, such as a URL shortener, a chat app or a news feed, in about 45 to 60 minutes, explaining your reasoning aloud. Interviewers assess how you clarify requirements, structure the problem and reason about trade-offs. Also asked as: what is system design interview A typical flow: clarify functional and non-functional requirements, estimate scale, sketch a high-level design, define APIs and data models, then go deep on one or two parts, such as storage or caching, and discuss bottlenecks, failures and improvements. There is no single correct answer. Interviewers look for structured thinking, sensible choices with reasons, awareness of trade-offs and good communication. For junior roles, expect simpler problems and more focus on fundamentals; for senior roles, more depth on scale and reliability. How do I prepare for system design? Learn the building blocks, practise a set of classic designs out loud with a fixed structure, and connect it all to your own projects. Six to eight weeks of steady practice is enough for most junior and mid-level interviews. Also asked as: how to prepare system design A preparation plan: Concepts: load balancers, caching, databases and indexing, replication and sharding, queues, CDNs, consistency, rate limiting. Estimation: requests per second, storage per year, bandwidth. Classic problems: URL shortener, chat, news feed, file storage, rate limiter, notification system. Structure: requirements, estimates, high-level design, deep dive, trade-offs. Mock interviews: practise with a friend or record yourself. Read The System Design Primer and Designing Data-Intensive Applications for depth. What is an example of system design? A URL shortener is the classic example: users submit a long URL and get a short code; visiting the short link redirects to the original. It is simple to describe but raises real design questions about IDs, storage, caching and scale. Also asked as: what is system design example A sketch: API: POST /shorten returns a code; GET /{code} redirects. ID generation: base62-encode a unique counter or a random ID, checking for collisions. Storage: a key-value store or database table mapping code to URL. Caching: popular codes in an in-memory cache, since reads vastly outnumber writes. Scale: stateless app servers behind a load balancer; replicate the database for reads. Extras: analytics through an asynchronous queue, expiry, abuse checks. Practise explaining each choice and its alternatives. What is the difference between system design and software architecture? They overlap heavily. Software architecture usually refers to the high-level structure and principles of a system and the decisions that are expensive to change; system design is the broader activity of designing a specific system, from architecture down to data models, APIs and capacity planning. In practice, architecture answers questions like "monolith or services, synchronous or event-driven, which data stores", and system design also covers "this table, this index, this cache policy, this API contract, this number of servers". Architects focus on long-term structure across many systems and teams; system design interviews test whether you can design one system end to end. Both depend on understanding requirements and trade-offs. What is system design in AI? AI system design adds machine learning concerns to classic design: data pipelines, feature or document processing, model training or selection, serving and scaling inference, retrieval for LLM apps, evaluation, monitoring for quality drift, and cost per request. For an LLM application, a design might include document ingestion and chunking, an embedding model and vector index, hybrid retrieval and reranking, an LLM call with a grounded prompt, guardrails, caching, fallbacks across providers, and evaluation and logging. RAG.NextUpgrad is a compact example: hybrid dense and BM25 retrieval with reciprocal-rank fusion, re-ranking, cited streaming answers, a confidence gate that refuses weak evidence, multi-provider fallback, and a small enough footprint, about 220 MB, to run on a free tier. Interviews for AI roles increasingly include designs like this. What is agentic AI system design? Agentic AI system design is designing systems where a model plans and takes actions with tools. Beyond normal design, it covers the agent loop, tool definitions and permissions, state and memory, limits on steps and cost, human approval for risky actions, evaluation and observability. Key decisions include how much autonomy to grant, since workflows with a few agentic steps are often more reliable than fully autonomous agents; how tools authenticate and what they may change; how to persist state so long tasks can resume; how to defend against prompt injection from content the agent reads; and how to trace every step for debugging. Designs should define failure behaviour clearly: when unsure, the agent asks or stops rather than guessing. Is system design AI-proof? No skill is entirely AI-proof, but system design is among the most durable. AI tools can suggest components and draw diagrams, but deciding trade-offs for a specific business, team, budget and risk tolerance requires judgement and accountability that remain human responsibilities. Also asked as: is system design ai proof AI actually raises the value of design skills. As coding becomes faster with AI assistance, the bottleneck shifts to deciding what to build and how pieces fit together, and to reviewing AI-generated code against that design. Engineers who can design systems, including AI systems, evaluate trade-offs and explain decisions clearly are well placed. Use AI tools to explore alternatives faster, but own the decisions. What is system design in VLSI? In VLSI, very large-scale integration, system design means designing electronic chips: defining the architecture of a chip or system-on-chip, then implementing it in hardware description languages, verifying it, and taking it through synthesis, layout and fabrication. The flow typically goes from specification and architecture, to register-transfer level design in Verilog or VHDL, functional verification, logic synthesis, physical design including placement and routing, timing analysis and sign-off checks. It is a different field from software system design, though both involve architecture, trade-offs and verification. Electronics students interested in it should learn digital design, HDLs and verification, and get familiar with EDA tools from vendors such as Cadence, Synopsys and Siemens. How do I use a design system? A design system, in UI and product design, is a shared library of components, styles and guidelines, such as buttons, colours, typography and spacing, used to build consistent interfaces. Use it by building screens from its components instead of styling from scratch. Also asked as: how to use a design system To use one well: learn its tokens for colours, spacing and type; use existing components before creating new ones; follow its accessibility and usage guidelines; and contribute improvements back rather than making one-off variations. Popular examples include Google's Material Design and many open-source React component libraries. Despite the similar name, it is unrelated to system design interviews, which are about software architecture and scale.

# What is a vector embedding? Embedding models, search, and long texts
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-vector-embedding/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

A vector embedding is a list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of data, such as a word, sentence, image or document, so that similar things have vectors close together. Embedding models produce these vectors, and vector search uses them to find the most similar items to a query, which is the retrieval step in RAG systems like RAG.NextUpgrad. This page explains embeddings and embedding models, how search works, terminology, building an embedding layer from scratch, long texts, embeddings versus TF-IDF, rerankers, and choosing a model. What is a vector embedding? A vector embedding is a fixed-length list of numbers, often hundreds or thousands long, that encodes the meaning or features of an input. Inputs with similar meaning map to vectors that are close in that space, measured by cosine similarity or distance. Also asked as: what is vector embedding · how do people usually handle creating an embedding vector of longer texts (32000 characters For example, "How do I reset my password?" and "I forgot my login" have different words but similar embeddings, so a search using embeddings matches them. Embeddings exist for text, images, audio and code, and multimodal models can place images and text in the same space. They power semantic search, recommendations, clustering, duplicate detection and classification, and they are the backbone of retrieval-augmented generation. What is an embedding model? An embedding model is a neural network that converts input, such as text, into an embedding vector. Text embedding models are trained so that related sentences or passages produce nearby vectors and unrelated ones produce distant vectors. Also asked as: what is embedding model · embedding model vs reranking model You can use hosted embedding models through APIs from providers such as OpenAI, Google and others, or open models from Hugging Face, such as sentence-transformers and newer open embedding families, run locally or through Ollama. Important properties are the vector dimension, maximum input length, supported languages and quality on retrieval benchmarks. The rule that matters most in practice: use the same embedding model for indexing documents and for embedding queries, or the vectors will not be comparable. How does an embedding model work? Modern text embedding models are transformer encoders. They tokenise the text, process tokens with attention so each token's representation reflects its context, and pool the token vectors, for example by averaging, into one vector for the whole text. Also asked as: how does embedding model work They learn useful vectors through contrastive training: pairs of related texts, such as a question and its answer passage, are pulled together, while unrelated texts are pushed apart. Training on millions of such pairs teaches the model which meanings are similar. Sentence-BERT popularised this approach for sentence embeddings. Some models also accept instructions, such as "represent this query for retrieval", which improves search quality, so follow each model's usage notes on its model card. How does vector embedding search work? You embed every document chunk once and store the vectors in an index. At query time, you embed the query with the same model and find the stored vectors nearest to it, returning their chunks as results. Comparing a query with every vector works for small collections but becomes slow at scale, so vector databases use approximate nearest-neighbour indexes, such as HNSW graphs or inverted-file indexes, that return nearly the best matches in milliseconds. Normalise vectors and use cosine similarity or inner product as the model recommends. In production, combine vector search with keyword search, merge the lists with reciprocal-rank fusion, and add metadata filters, because embeddings alone often miss exact terms such as IDs and error codes. Are "vector embedding" and "embedding vector" interchangeable? Yes, in practice they mean the same thing: the vector produced by an embedding model. "Embedding" alone is also common. Strictly, "embedding" can mean the mapping itself, while "embedding vector" is one output of it. Also asked as: are the terms &quot;vector embedding&quot; and &quot;embedding vector&quot; interchangeable You will also see "dense vector" or "dense representation", in contrast to sparse vectors from keyword methods such as BM25 or TF-IDF, where most values are zero. In vector database documentation, "vectors" usually refers to embeddings. When writing documentation or reports, pick one term and use it consistently, and say which model produced the vectors, because embeddings from different models are not interchangeable. How can I create an embedding layer from scratch? An embedding layer is a lookup table: a matrix with one row per word in your vocabulary, initialised randomly and learned during training. In PyTorch, nn.Embedding provides it; training the network on a task updates the rows so useful word relationships emerge. Also asked as: how can i create an embedding layer to convert words to a vector space from scratch import torch, torch.nn as nn vocab = {&quot;&lt;pad&gt;&quot;: 0, &quot;ai&quot;: 1, &quot;model&quot;: 2, &quot;data&quot;: 3} emb = nn.Embedding(num_embeddings=len(vocab), embedding_dim=8, padding_idx=0) ids = torch.tensor([[1, 2, 3]]) vectors = emb(ids) # shape (1, 3, 8) To learn word vectors without a downstream task, train word2vec-style: predict surrounding words from a word, or the reverse, which makes words in similar contexts get similar vectors. For real projects, pre-trained sentence embedding models are far better than training from scratch. How do you create embeddings for long texts? Split long texts into chunks, embed each chunk, and store them separately with a reference to the source document. A single vector for a 32,000-character document averages away detail, and many embedding models cannot accept that much text anyway. Chunking guidelines: Split by structure, such as headings and paragraphs, to keep ideas together. Use chunks of a few hundred tokens, with small overlap where meaning spans boundaries. Include the document title and section heading in each chunk's text. Keep page numbers and IDs in metadata for citations. If you need one vector per document, for example for clustering, average the chunk embeddings or use a long-context embedding model, but retrieve at chunk level for question answering. Vector embeddings vs TF-IDF: which is better for document similarity? Embeddings usually perform better when meaning matters and wording differs, such as paraphrases and questions versus answers. TF-IDF and BM25 perform better for exact terms, rare names, codes and specialised jargon. Combining both usually beats either alone. Also asked as: document similarity: vector embedding versus tf-idf performance TF-IDF and bag-of-words count words, so "car" and "automobile" do not match, but "error 0x80070005" matches exactly. Embeddings capture semantics but can blur specific identifiers. TF-IDF is also cheap, transparent and needs no model. A sound approach is to evaluate both on your own data with labelled similar pairs or search queries, then use hybrid retrieval: run both, and merge results with reciprocal-rank fusion, as RAG.NextUpgrad does with dense retrieval and BM25. What is the difference between an embedding model and a reranking model? An embedding model encodes the query and each document separately into vectors, which makes search over millions of documents fast. A reranking model, usually a cross-encoder, reads the query and one document together and outputs a relevance score, which is more accurate but too slow to run over everything. So they work in two stages: embeddings, often with keyword search, retrieve the top 50 to 100 candidates quickly, and the reranker reorders those candidates by true relevance. Adding a reranker is one of the most effective ways to improve RAG answers, because the right passage is often retrieved but ranked too low to reach the prompt. Measure retrieval recall at 5 before and after adding one. What is the best embedding model for semantic search? There is no universal best. Check the MTEB leaderboard for retrieval scores, then test two or three candidates on your own queries, considering language support, maximum input length, vector size, speed and cost. Also asked as: best semantic search embedding model Practical guidance: Hosted and easy: embedding APIs from major providers. Open and local: strong sentence-transformers and newer open embedding models, runnable with Ollama or Hugging Face. Indian languages or mixed Hindi-English: choose a multilingual model and test on your own data. Large scale: smaller dimensions reduce storage and speed up search. Build a test set of 50 real queries with known relevant passages, and pick the model with the best recall at 5 for your data, not the best leaderboard score.

# What is vibe coding? Origin, best platforms, Claude and GitHub, and jobs
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-vibe-coding-2/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

Vibe coding is building software by describing what you want to an AI tool in plain language, running what it produces, and steering by results rather than writing or reading every line yourself. Andrej Karpathy coined the term in February 2025, and it spread quickly with app builders and coding agents. It is a fast way to prototype and a risky way to ship. This page covers its origin, the main apps and platforms, how to do it with Claude and GitHub Copilot, Power Apps, when to use it, whether it helps you get a job, and its future. What is vibe coding in AI? Vibe coding is a style of AI-assisted programming where you describe the app or feature you want, let an AI generate the code, test it by using it, and keep asking for changes until it works, focusing on the result rather than the code itself. Also asked as: how to vibe coding with claude · how to vibe coding github It differs from traditional AI-assisted coding, where a developer reads and owns every line the assistant suggests. In vibe coding the human acts more like a product owner: "add a login page", "make the button blue", "fix this error". It lowers the barrier to building, letting non-programmers create working tools. The trade-off is hidden problems: security holes, duplicated logic, fragile code and dependencies nobody understands, which surface later. When was vibe coding coined? Andrej Karpathy, an AI researcher who co-founded OpenAI and led AI at Tesla, coined "vibe coding" in a post in February 2025, describing coding where you "give in to the vibes" and let the AI handle the code. The term caught on quickly because it named something many people were already doing with tools such as Cursor, Claude, ChatGPT and app builders. Within months, it was used in product marketing, job posts and debates about software quality. It describes a practice made possible by much stronger coding models and agentic tools in 2024 and 2025, which could write and fix whole features rather than single lines. What are vibe coding apps? Vibe coding apps let you build software from natural language. Browser-based app builders such as Lovable, Bolt, v0 by Vercel and Replit generate and host full apps from prompts; coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot's agent mode and Codex work inside real codebases. The two groups suit different people. App builders give the fastest path from idea to a running web app with hosting included, ideal for non-developers and prototypes. Coding agents work with your own repository, tools and tests, ideal for developers who want speed with control. Many builders start a prototype in an app builder, export the code, and continue in a coding agent when the project becomes serious. Which vibe coding platform is best? For non-developers building a web app prototype, Lovable, Bolt, v0 and Replit are the easiest. For developers working on real projects, Claude Code, Cursor and GitHub Copilot's agent mode give more control and better results on existing codebases. How to choose: Speed to a hosted demo: an app builder. Your own stack and repository: a coding agent. Team on GitHub with enterprise controls: GitHub Copilot. Long, multi-file changes: Claude Code or Cursor's agent. Free start: free tiers of several tools, which change often. Try two on the same small project, such as a hackathon registration app, and compare how much you had to fix. How do I vibe code with Claude? Use Claude Code in your terminal or IDE for real projects, or artifacts on claude.ai for quick prototypes. Describe the feature, let Claude build it, run it, and ask for fixes with exact error messages. A workflow with Claude Code: Start a project folder with Git, and add a CLAUDE.md describing the stack and rules. Ask for a plan first: "Plan a Next.js app for hackathon registrations with a form and admin list." Build feature by feature, running the app after each step. Ask for tests alongside features. Commit after every working step so you can roll back. Ask Claude to review the code for security issues before sharing. Keep API keys in .env files and never paste secrets into prompts. How do I vibe code with GitHub? Use GitHub Copilot's agent mode in VS Code to build features from natural language, and the Copilot coding agent on GitHub to hand off issues and review the pull requests it opens. GitHub then gives you version history, reviews and continuous integration. Steps: Create a repository and open it in VS Code with Copilot. Add .github/copilot-instructions.md with your stack and conventions. In agent mode, describe a feature and review each change before accepting. Set up GitHub Actions to run tests on every push. For small tasks, write an issue with clear acceptance criteria and assign it to Copilot. Version control is what makes vibe coding safe: every change is reviewable and reversible. What is vibe coding in Power Apps? In Power Apps, Microsoft's low-code platform, vibe coding refers to building business apps by describing them in natural language with Copilot, which generates the app's screens, data tables and logic for you to refine. You describe something like "an app for tracking lab equipment loans with a form, a list and an approval step", and Copilot proposes the data structure and screens, which you then adjust conversationally or in the editor. Because it runs on the Power Platform, the result inherits Microsoft 365 sign-in, Dataverse data storage and admin governance, which suits organisations. Microsoft's natural-language app-building features have been changing quickly, so check current Power Apps documentation for what is available. When should I use vibe coding? Use vibe coding for prototypes, hackathon builds, internal tools, personal scripts and exploring ideas, where speed matters more than long-term maintainability. Avoid pure vibe coding for production systems that handle money, personal data or security-sensitive operations. Also asked as: when to use vibe coding Signs it fits: a short-lived project, a demo, a tool only you use, or a first version to test with users. Signs it does not: payments, authentication, health or legal data, or code that a team must maintain for years. For those, use AI as a pair programmer instead: generate code, but read it, test it and understand it. Security basics, such as input validation and access control, are where vibe-coded apps fail most often. Can vibe coding get you a job? Not on its own. Employers hire people who can build reliable software and explain how it works. Vibe coding can help you ship more projects faster, which helps, but only if you understand and can defend what you built. How to make it count: use AI tools to build real projects, then study the code, refactor it, add tests and write a README explaining design decisions. In interviews, you will be asked why you chose an approach, how you handled errors and what you would change. Hackathon judges ask the same, and I have seen teams lose points for polished demos they could not explain. Skill with AI coding tools is now expected; understanding is what sets you apart. Why is vibe coding the future? Because building software through natural language makes creation accessible to far more people and makes developers much faster. The future is likely a mix: vibe coding for exploration and simple apps, and engineering discipline for systems people depend on. Also asked as: why vibe coding is the future As models improve, more of the code will be written by AI, and the human role shifts to defining requirements, designing systems, reviewing changes, testing and taking responsibility for quality and security. That favours people who combine product sense with engineering judgement. Students should learn to use AI coding tools fluently while building strong fundamentals, because when the vibes fail, someone has to debug the system.

# What is vLLM? vLLM vs Ollama vs llama.cpp vs SGLang, and how to actually serve an LLM in production
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-vllm-ollama-and-llm-inference-serving/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-09-24

## What is vLLM?

**vLLM is an open-source inference server for large language models built around PagedAttention, a memory-management technique that lets many concurrent requests share a GPU's memory efficiently by managing the attention key-value cache the way an operating system manages virtual memory, in pages, rather than reserving one large contiguous block per request [1][2]. The practical result is much higher throughput on the same hardware compared with naively calling a model's `generate()` method for each request, which is why vLLM is the default choice for serving open-weight models at real request volume.**


Every production system I run that serves an open model sits on some form of batched serving; the difference between "it works in a notebook" and "it serves five hundred requests a minute without falling over" is almost entirely this layer.

> A model that answers one request beautifully and a service that answers a thousand requests a minute are different engineering problems. vLLM, SGLang and friends are the answer to the second one.
> <cite>Pranjul Rathour</cite>

## Why can't I just call `model.generate()` for production traffic?

**Because it processes one request, or a small fixed batch, at a time, and each request occupies GPU memory for its full duration even while it is producing tokens slowly one at a time. Real traffic arrives as many concurrent requests of different lengths, and naive batching either wastes memory reserving worst-case space for every request or wastes GPU time waiting for a batch to fill before starting. Continuous batching solves the second problem, starting and finishing requests within a batch as they arrive and complete rather than waiting for a fixed batch to fill [8]. PagedAttention solves the first, sharing memory pages between requests instead of reserving a contiguous block per request [1].**



## What is Ollama, and how is it different from vLLM?

**Ollama is a tool for running open-weight models easily on a laptop or a single machine, wrapping llama.cpp with a simple CLI, a model library, and an API that feels like calling a hosted service [3]. It optimises for ease of local use, quantized models that fit on consumer hardware, and a good single-user experience, not maximum concurrent throughput. Running Ollama to serve many simultaneous users at scale is possible but is not what it is built or tuned for; vLLM is built specifically for that case.**


## What is llama.cpp, and where does it fit?

**llama.cpp is a C++ inference engine for running LLMs efficiently on CPUs and consumer GPUs, using quantized model formats such as GGUF to shrink memory use [4]. It underlies Ollama and many other local-inference tools. Its strength is portability and running well on hardware without a data-centre GPU, phones, laptops, Raspberry Pi-class devices; it is not designed around maximising throughput for many concurrent server requests the way vLLM is.**



## What is SGLang, and how does it compare to vLLM?

**SGLang is an inference framework that combines fast serving, similar in spirit to vLLM's continuous batching and paged memory, with a structured-generation front end that lets you express constrained outputs, branching, and reused prompt prefixes efficiently [5][6]. Its RadixAttention technique caches shared prompt prefixes across requests, which is particularly effective for workloads with repeated system prompts or few-shot examples, agents calling the same tools repeatedly. Benchmarks between vLLM and SGLang shift with every release of both; the honest answer is to benchmark your own workload rather than trust either project's numbers alone.**



## How do I decide what I actually need?

**Count your expected concurrent requests per second and your latency budget, then pick backward from that. A weekend project or an internal tool with a handful of users rarely needs more than Ollama on a single GPU or even a good CPU. A product with real concurrent traffic needs vLLM or SGLang on dedicated GPU serving from day one, because retrofitting proper batching after launch under load is a much worse day than provisioning for it up front.**



## What does this cost, and how does quantization fit in?

**Serving throughput and quantization are separate levers that stack: a quantized model uses less memory and can run on smaller GPUs, while a serving engine like vLLM uses that freed memory to run more concurrent requests rather than only fitting a bigger model [9]. The cheapest production setup is usually a quantized model served through vLLM or SGLang on the smallest GPU that hits your latency target, re-benchmarked whenever a new quantization method or a smaller strong model appears, since the frontier moves every few months.**



## LLM serving interview questions

**Explain what problem continuous batching solves. Describe PagedAttention in your own words. Compare vLLM, SGLang, Ollama and llama.cpp and say when you would choose each. Explain how quantization and serving throughput interact. Describe how you would capacity-plan a serving setup for a given requests-per-second target. The strongest answer includes a real throughput number you measured, not a number you read.**


## Where should I start?

**Stand up vLLM on a rented GPU with a small open model and hit it with a simple load-testing script, then repeat with Ollama on the same hardware and compare throughput yourself. The gap will be obvious within the first ten minutes.** For a hands-on session on serving LLMs in production, from a notebook to real concurrent traffic, email pranjulrathour41@gmail.com or use pranjulrathour.scult.in/invite.

# What is workflow automation? How it works, with AI, and versus RPA
URL: https://pranjulrathour.github.io/what-is-workflow-automation/
Author: Pranjul Rathour (pranjulrathour41@gmail.com)
Updated: 2026-10-23

Workflow automation is using software to run a repeatable sequence of business steps, such as approving a leave request, onboarding a customer or processing an invoice, automatically instead of by hand. A trigger starts the workflow, and the software moves data between apps, applies rules and takes actions. With AI, workflows can also read documents, classify messages and draft replies. This page explains how it works, which tools to use, examples, how it differs from RPA, how to add AI safely, and how to learn it. What is workflow automation? Workflow automation is the use of software to carry out a series of tasks, decisions and hand-offs that people used to do manually, following defined rules, so that work moves from start to finish with little human effort. Also asked as: workflow automation vs rpa Typical candidates are tasks that are frequent, rule-based and boring: copying form responses into a spreadsheet, sending welcome emails, routing support tickets, creating invoices from orders, or posting alerts to a team chat. Automating them saves time, removes copy-paste errors and makes the process consistent and auditable. People stay in the loop for exceptions and decisions that need judgement. The aim is not to remove people but to stop them doing work a machine does better. How does workflow automation work? A workflow starts with a trigger, then runs a series of steps: fetch or transform data, check conditions, and take actions in other systems through their APIs. Each run is logged so failures can be seen and retried. A simple example: a trigger fires when a new row is added to a Google Sheet; a step formats the data; a condition checks whether the amount is above a threshold; an action creates a record in the CRM and another sends a message to the sales channel. Under the hood, the tool calls each app's API with stored credentials. Good workflows also handle errors: retries with back-off, alerts when a step fails, and idempotency so that a retry does not create duplicates. That last point is where most homemade automations break. What is a workflow automation tool? A workflow automation tool is software that lets you build, run and monitor automated workflows, usually with a visual editor of triggers and steps and ready-made connectors to common apps. Zapier, Make, n8n and Microsoft Power Automate are popular examples. They suit different people. Zapier is the easiest for non-developers connecting popular SaaS apps. Make offers more complex visual logic. n8n is popular with developers because it can be self-hosted, runs custom JavaScript or Python steps and has strong AI nodes. Power Automate fits organisations on Microsoft 365. For data and engineering pipelines, developers use code-first orchestrators such as Apache Airflow or Temporal instead, because they need versioning, testing and scale. What are some workflow automation examples? Common examples include lead capture into a CRM, employee onboarding, invoice processing, support ticket routing, social media scheduling, report generation and alerts when a metric crosses a threshold. Examples a student or small team can build this week: A contact form that saves to a sheet, emails a confirmation and notifies you on Telegram or Slack. A daily job that pulls yesterday's sales or website visits and emails a summary. An inbox rule that labels invoices, extracts amounts and adds them to a spreadsheet. A GitHub workflow that runs tests and deploys on every push. A hackathon registration flow that checks team sizes and sends welcome kits. Pick one you do by hand every week; that is the best first automation. What is the difference between workflow automation and RPA? Workflow automation connects systems through their APIs and data. Robotic process automation (RPA) uses software robots that operate an application's user interface like a person, clicking buttons and typing into fields. Use RPA when a system has no API, such as an old desktop application or a government portal, because it is the only way in. Its weakness is fragility: a moved button or a changed page layout can break the robot. API-based workflow automation is faster, more reliable and easier to maintain. In practice, mature teams combine them: workflow tools orchestrate the process and call an RPA bot only for the one legacy step that needs it. UiPath and Power Automate Desktop are common RPA tools. What is workflow automation using AI? AI workflow automation adds steps that need judgement, such as reading an email, extracting fields from a document, classifying a request or drafting a reply, to workflows that used to handle only fixed rules. A classic workflow can route an email if the subject contains "invoice". An AI workflow can read any email, decide whether it is an invoice, a complaint or a meeting request, extract the amount and due date, and draft a response. AI agents go further, choosing which tools to call to reach a goal. This is powerful but less predictable than rules, so the AI step must be constrained: structured output, validation, confidence thresholds, and a human review queue for uncertain cases. Deterministic rules should still make the final decision on anything with money or legal effect. How do I use AI for workflow automation? Put the model where judgement is needed and keep everything else deterministic. Give it a narrow job, require structured JSON output, validate it against a schema, and route low-confidence results to a person. Also asked as: how to use ai for workflow automation That is the design I used in DocuLens AI: a Groq-hosted Llama model extracts fields from invoices and contracts, the output is validated against a schema, and compliance scoring is deterministic code, not the model's opinion. A practical starting pattern in n8n or Make: trigger on a new email, send the text to an LLM with a prompt that returns {"type", "amount", "due_date", "confidence"}, check the JSON, then branch: high confidence goes to the spreadsheet, low confidence goes to a review list. Log every input and output so you can measure accuracy. What is the best AI workflow automation platform? There is no single best one. n8n is a strong choice for developers who want AI agents, custom code and self-hosting; Zapier for the fastest setup with popular apps; Make for complex visual flows; Power Automate for Microsoft 365 organisations. Choose by four questions. Where does your data live: Google Workspace, Microsoft 365 or your own database? Who will maintain it: a developer or a non-technical team? Do you need self-hosting for data control? How many runs a month will you need, since pricing usually scales with runs or tasks? For custom AI products, a code-first approach with Python, a queue and an orchestrator gives the most control. Prototype the same flow on two platforms before committing. Is there an AI workflow automation tutorial? Yes. The official documentation of n8n, Zapier, Make and Power Automate includes step-by-step tutorials, including AI steps. The fastest way to learn is to build one real automation end to end. A one-evening tutorial with n8n: Run n8n locally or use its cloud trial, and create a workflow with a Gmail or IMAP trigger. Add an AI step that classifies each email and returns JSON. Add an IF node that checks the class and confidence. Send high-confidence results to a Google Sheet and the rest to a Slack or Telegram message for review. Add an error workflow that alerts you when a step fails. Then run it for a week and read the logs. What is the best AI workflow automation course? The best course is the official learning material of the tool you choose, plus a project you build yourself. n8n, Zapier and Microsoft Learn for Power Automate all have free tutorials and learning paths. Look for courses that cover more than the visual editor: APIs and webhooks, JSON, authentication with OAuth and API keys, error handling, and how to evaluate AI steps. Those skills transfer between tools, while button-by-button lessons date quickly. If you know some Python, learning to call an LLM API and validate its output teaches more than a no-code course alone. A finished automation on your GitHub or in a short demo video is worth more to an employer or client than a certificate.
